3. On a related note: The paper notes that Open-SAT is more efficient because it "retrieves fewer but more relevant" tiles than one of the baselines. Explicitly showing a higher Precision score would have been the most direct and powerful way to quantify this claim. Without it, we have to infer this efficiency from the F1 score and the charts in Figure 8 which is not immediately clear. Besides only a small increase in F1 together with a big increase in Recall certainly means Precision is compromised.  

There are some questions that would be beneficial in the discussion into the methodology:

1. Regarding the choice of the LLM, is there a specific reason why GPT-4o was chosen? It is difficult to imagine an LLM would know about co-occuring objects in satellite images  unless these were incliuded in the training. Did the authors research other LLMs and choose this one for performance or was it arbitrary?
2. If you assume alpha and B are both 1 then why define them at all?
3. It is not clear how the encoding step of the image embeddings work? How do they do this?

title: Open-SAT: LLM-Guided Training-Free Query Embedding Refinement for Open-Vocabulary Satellite Image Retrieval
review:
This paper addresses the interesting and important challenge of open-vocabulary satellite image retrieval by proposing Open-SAT, a new training-free algorithm. The core idea of refining query embeddings at inference time is interesting; it leverages an LLM to generate contextual surrounding objects and applies a simple yet clever vector arithmetic to enhance the query's discriminative power. This approach, combined with a threshold-free retrieval mechanism, is well-communicated and demonstrates strong empirical performance on several benchmarks, improving retrieval accuracy over baseline methods. The impact of achieving this without any additional model training or fine-tuning makes the contribution noteworthy and presents a promising direction for efficient, adaptable retrieval systems.

However, while the proposed method is intriguing, its validation and analysis lack the depth required to establish its generalizability and robustness. The primary concern is the significant mismatch between the "open-vocabulary" claim and the evaluation on closed-set benchmarks with a limited number of classes, which fails to convince the reader of the method's applicability in more complex, real-world industrial scenarios. Furthermore, the paper lacks crucial ablation studies on key hyperparameters that heavily influence performance, such as the number of generated surrounding objects, the impact of using different or less powerful LLMs than GPT-4o, and the sensitivity to the vector operation's coefficients/preprocessing (e.g., normalization). The paper would benefit from a more detailed description of the methodology. Currently, key ablations are missing from the main text, and there is no appendix to supplement this information. Without a deeper justification for why this specific form of vector arithmetic works beyond a high-level analogy, the method feels more like a complex heuristic than a principled, generalizable solution. Consequently, a reader is left with promising results but insufficient insight into the method's limitations or how to reliably adapt it to their own domain, thus limiting the paper's overall impact and take-home message.

title: MADS: Multi-Agent Dialogue Simulation for Diverse Persuasion Data Generation
review:
This paper proposes a multi-agent framework, including user agents, dialogue agent and optimization agent, aims to generate high-quality and diverse persuasive multi-turn dialogue data through multi-agent self-play.

User agents is responsible for simulating diverse personal behaviors; dialogue agent performs the task in a persuasive manner; optimization agent evaluates the dialogue.

This paper presents a chain-of-attituate (CoA) model and evaluates the performance of diversity of CoA in a persuasive strategy, finally demonstrated that  incorporating Zodiac Sign and MBTI attributes leads to a notable increase.

Smaller models fine-tuned with augmented data show better results compared with baselines without augmented data, indicating the broad applicability of simulation-based training data.

This paper also evaluates the performance of proposed MADS in simulated scenarios and real-word applications, both show clear improvements.

However, this paper does not show the statistic of augmented data, which could be added in the final version.

title: MADS: Multi-Agent Dialogue Simulation for Diverse Persuasion Data Generation
review:
This work proposed MADS (Multi-Agent Dialogue Simulation), a scalable framework for generating persuasive multi-turn dialogues via agent self-play. The contributions including:

The MADS framework, based on Chain-of-Attitude (CoA) modeling, shows that incorporating symbolic traits (e.g., zodiac signs, MBTI types) significantly improves the diversity of simulated dialogue data, leading to richer persuasion strategies even with unchanged prompts.
MADS employs an automated prompt customization system that tailors prompts to specific user segments, boosting persuasion success rates. It combines large-scale multi-turn dialogues with automatic strategy annotation to fine-tune smaller LLMs effectively.
Deployed in practical settings, MADS achieves over 28% improvement in user intent rate compared to traditional agent-based solutions, demonstrating its effectiveness in domain-specific model customization.
The shortcoming of this work has been well described in the almost one-page long "Limitations" section.

Following are some suggestions:

The formulas in the paper need to be numbered.
What's the meaning of M in Line 231?
Concerning the 'business attributes' in Section 4.1, how many distinct attributes are identified and how to describe them?
In section 4.1, it is mentioned that "the distribution of strategy types becomes more balanced compared to the baseline". It would be better to give more data to support this point.

title: MADS: Multi-Agent Dialogue Simulation for Diverse Persuasion Data Generation
review: Simulating (using Agent self -play) persuasion and negotiation dialog in different business context is very useful as we have lack of data sets. In this respect, the work is useful. title: Domain-specific Language Models for real time Medical Prescription Verification
review:
This manuscript presents a lightweight domain-specific language model (LM), for the real-time verification of medical prescriptions from medication prescription document images (converted to text via OCR and layout analysis). Extensive pharmacy-specific model training was applied. The domain-specific LM is claimed to perform comparably to LLMs such as Sonnet 3.5, but with significantly faster inference time and at lower operating cost.

This shows the potential of tailored LM solutions for specific tasks, as opposed to the current LLM and foundation model paradigm. However, some issues might be considered:

5. For Table 2, it might be clarified as to whether the inference time and cost statistics are for the zero-shot or 3-shot implementations.

6. In Section 5.3, for the experiment results, it might be clarified as to what input was provided for the comparison models. For example, were the other models provided the original scanned image, the raw extracted OCR text, or the text after layout analysis?

title: Domain-specific Language Models for real time Medical Prescription Verification
review:
**Summary**  

The paper titled *"Domain-specific Language Models for Real-Time Medical Prescription Verification"* proposes a variant of an encoder-only transformer model that integrates both textual and layout information for entity extraction. While the title and abstract suggest a focus on prescription verification, the actual scope of the work centers primarily on entity extraction from prescription documents.

**Strengths**  

- The proposed transformer model for entity extraction is well-motivated and clearly defined.  
- The paper provides detailed implementation information, which supports reproducibility.  
- Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, showing advantages in inference time and cost compared to LLM-based baselines.

**Weaknesses**  

- **Misleading Title and Abstract**: The title and abstract emphasize prescription verification, but the paper primarily addresses entity extraction. A more accurate framing would improve clarity and alignment.  
- **Limited Evaluation Scope**: The paper does not directly evaluate the model’s impact on the broader prescription verification task. Including such evaluation would strengthen the relevance of the work.  
- **Insufficient Explanation of Position Representation**: Lines 271–273 introduce the position representation (e.g., *Ptl(x0, y0)*), but the explanation is brief and lacks illustrative examples.  
- **Lack of Analytical Depth**: The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of experimental results. For instance, the rationale behind requiring 400 epochs for fine-tuning is unclear, and no information is provided about the training dynamics (e.g., loss curves).  
- **Minor Formatting Issues**: Citation formatting in the introduction section is inconsistent with the rest of the paper.

title: Query Generation with Direct Preference Optimization for Document Expansion in E-commerce Search
review:
This paper presents QGDPO, an innovative technique designed to enhance e-commerce search results. It refines the existing Doc2Query process by using DPO to guide the system toward generating more relevant search queries, effectively preventing it from producing nonsensical or repetitive terms.

The strong point of this paper is its rigorous testing in a real-world setting. While many academic studies are limited to offline analysis, the authors here provide results from a two-week live A/B test. The findings show statistically significant gains not only in search relevance but also in crucial user engagement metrics like the add-to-cart rate, which offers compelling proof of the method's practical value and real-world impact.

However, despite these notable strengths, the manuscript has several weaknesses.

The entire approach hinges on a relevance model used to create preference data and filter the final output, yet crucial details about this model are missing. The paper only offers a vague description, calling it a multi-class classifier trained on human judgments. Important questions about its architecture and standalone performance remain unanswered, such as its precision and recall scores on the human-rated data. Without this information, the model effectively becomes a black box, making it impossible to assess how its inherent biases might influence the final QGDPO system.

A fundamental flaw in the methodology is the circular use of this same relevance model. It is used to generate the initial training data, to filter the model's output, and then again to evaluate the final results on a large test set. Consequently, the evaluation doesn't measure genuine relevance but rather how successfully the QGDPO system has learned to replicate the proxy model's own preferences. While a small-scale human evaluation was conducted, it isn't extensive enough to fully validate the main offline results reported in the paper.

Another questionable design choice that goes without justification is how the training data was constructed. The authors created learning pairs by sampling winning queries from an exact match category and losing"queries from an irrelevant category, while completely ignoring substitute queries. This decision discards a valuable intermediate signal. A more powerful approach might have taught the model that exact matches are better than substitutes, and substitutes are better than irrelevant queries. By throwing away the substitute examples, the model may have been forced to learn an overly simplistic and less nuanced understanding of relevance.

The experiment involving the Mistral-7B model feels disconnected. As presented, it reads like a simple comparison between two different base models rather than a true test of the QGDPO method on a more advanced architecture. A far more valuable experiment would have involved applying the entire QGDPO pipeline to the Mistral model. Such a test could have demonstrated whether the proposed optimization technique offers tangible benefits even when applied to stronger, more modern language models.

The paper's conclusion that beam search is the best decoding strategy is surprising, as it directly contradicts several prior studies cited by the authors themselves. Their brief justification, that stability is advantageous, is plausible but insufficient. A bold claim that goes against established findings requires a much more thorough discussion and analysis, exploring whether this outcome is unique to their specific model, the e-commerce domain, or the optimization technique used.

The paper's analysis would also benefit from a deeper qualitative review of the model's performance. The authors provide only a single positive example, which is not enough to understand the full picture. A more systematic analysis is needed to explore the model's typical failure modes. For instance, when does the system still produce inaccurate or nonsensical results? And does the impressive reduction in irrelevant queries come at the expense of diversity and novelty in the generated terms?

Finally, while the A/B test is a major strength, its description is disappointingly sparse. The paper omits key details, such as the size of the user groups, how web traffic was divided, and whether any novelty effects were observed. Moreover, the claim of a positive trend in Gross Merchandise Value feels overstated given its high p-value of 0.36. While not every metric must be statistically significant, a central result like this requires more transparent and detailed reporting.

title: Query Generation with Direct Preference Optimization for Document Expansion in E-commerce Search
review:
This paper extends the Doc2Query approach by introducing an additional DPO stage (QGDPO) and incorporating relevance filtering. The QGDPO pipeline consists of: (1) SFT training, (2) Relevance preference, (3) DPO, (4) Inference, and (5) Relevance filtering for document expansion.

Overall, the paper is well-written and easy to follow. The experiments, including ablation studies, are presented clearly. I also appreciate that the authors explicitly describe both the offline and online experimental setups, which greatly enhances the reproducibility of the work.

Since this is an industry track paper, I do not evaluate it based on novelty, but rather on reproducibility and contribution. From this perspective, the paper is clearly above the acceptance threshold.

title: Query Generation with Direct Preference Optimization for Document Expansion in E-commerce Search
review:
The paper presents an original method to improve the indexing of products in a large catalogue. The approach relies on fine-tuning transformer models to supplement product descriptions with relevant query examples (paraphrasing without repeating the product keywords). The method is applied both in vitro and in vivo, with performance improvements observed in each case, measured by relevance metrics and customer engagement, respectively.

**Strengths:**
- The paper is very clear and easy to follow
- It introduces an original approach
- Deployed on a large-scale real industrial use case
- Methodologically robust

**Weaknesses:**
- No significant weaknesses given the industrial application focus

**Typos/Miscellaneous:**
- An outline would be welcome at the end of the introduction.
- Line 86: "doesn't" should be "does not"
- Step 2: What happens if "exact" or "irrelevant" labels are not predicted?
- Line 168: "log sigma beta" -> perhaps the authors mean sigma raised to the power beta? If so, it should be "beta log sigma"
- Line 169: No indentation
- Section 3.2: Additional details would be helpful, especially since one might assume that a textual description usually accompanies the product, not just the title and attributes. Also, what are the statistics regarding the length of the Doc2Query inputs?
- Table 2: The performance difference is substantial compared to Table 1 -> what explains this?
- The online experiment protocol is somewhat unclear: Were different systems running in parallel (baseline and proposed method) for several months? If not, the experimental results may be confounded by natural growth in consumption over time.

title: DePPat: A Multi-Label Benchmark Dataset for Patent Classification with Technical Design Space Analysis under Real-World Constraints
review:
The paper introduces a patent dataset (1 million patents) labeled by domain, along with experiments involving various classification approaches (from logistic regression to LLM prompting) to illustrate achievable performance on this dataset. Discussions address potential trade-offs between computational resources and classification performance, with a conclusion highlighting the limited effectiveness of prompting methods.

**Strengths:**
- The topic has a likely significant impact on technological monitoring.
- A substantial volume with 1 million annotated patents.

**Weaknesses:**
- The article provides very (too) little detail about the proposed dataset. In practice, many of these details seem to be in the appendices (which are unfortunately difficult to read). The authors are encouraged to emphasize the quality and content of their dataset.
- The paper spends excessive time on the classification problem and classifier training, which is not the main focus (for example, the state of the art presents very general results on various text classification approaches).
- There is a wealth of existing work on patent analysis. It would be helpful to summarize this literature and position the contribution relative to it.
- The industrial aspect appears insufficiently justified. The data come from a public database (not cited). The problem does not seem specific to industry. Authors should better justify this aspect or submit to more traditional tracks if not.
- Having only one annotator is insufficient. It would be beneficial to measure uncertainty around annotations.
- Many claims about infrastructure and computational resources (standard GPU architectures in industry, resources per method) are underdeveloped or lack supporting evidence (what is the basis for these claims? resources per method are not quantified...).

**Miscellaneous remarks:**
- "foo - bar" should be "foo---bar"
- MLTC is used before being defined
- An outline at the end of the introduction would be helpful
- Which database is used for patents?
- "simsimlar" -> "similar"
- "Attention-Based Encoder Models" -> "Transformer-based Encoder Models"
- "Attention-Based Decoder Models" -> "Transformer-based Decoder Models"
- Section 6.1 is unclear
- Random performance of 0.5 seems suspicious given class imbalance
- Lines separating models would improve readability of Table 1
- "Prompt-Free SLMs" -> unclear or inaccurate (using SLM for RNNs or BERT is not appropriate)

title: DePPat: A Multi-Label Benchmark Dataset for Patent Classification with Technical Design Space Analysis under Real-World Constraints
review:
#### Summary

This paper introduces a multi-label classification dataset on patent documents. The authors also try various traditional ML and Transformers-based models for benchmarking.

#### Strengths

- As the paper introduces a new dataset for patent classification, the paper could have been an useful resource for future researchers and practitioners if it weren't for various weaknesses I have found (see below.)

#### Weaknesses

- There's a 'Future Work' section on Page 7, which should be counted towards the page limit.
- Table 1 and Section 6 do not specify which specific model variants and parameter sizes were used for each model types (encoder, decoder) The authors need to ensure that they are not comparing apples to oranges in their experiments.
- DePPat was only annotated by a single annotator, and the authors' excuse for this in the limitations section is that this expert knows everything and so there's no need for additional annotators. Even though this submission is for the industry track, I believe all papers to be accepted to EMNLP should have some level of scientific rigor. I don't think the argument of "I know this too well and I don't need a second or third annotator" is very scientific at all. Especially with the label descriptions in Section 4.5, I strongly doubt that the labels for this dataset do not need some level of inter-annotator agreement.

title: DePPat: A Multi-Label Benchmark Dataset for Patent Classification with Technical Design Space Analysis under Real-World Constraints
review:
The paper presents a large-scale patent data correction manually annotated with the International Patent Classification codes. Various multi-label classification methods are applied to evaluate their performance and efficiency. The main contribution of this paper is the construction of the dataset, DePPat, an expert-labeled patent dataset of over one million patent abstracts.

Although the characteristics of the proposed dataset, DePPat, are shown in the paper and the appendix, the important information on how the dataset is annotated and the quality assessment is not described. It is surprising that one million abstracts are manually annotated.

There are lots of inconsistencies and unclear points in the Evaluation section:

-	Table 6 is referenced three times in the paper, which should be Table 1.
-	In Table 1, weighted F1 is not defined. What weight was put on which score?
-	Lines 344-345: According to Table 1, Recall scores are much better than Precision. The Rec and Prec columns in Table 1 might have been misplaced.
-	Lines 355-357: This evaluation is strange since LSTM achieves very good performance, close to that of ENCODER in Table 1.
-	There is no explicit subsection for the ENCODER-based models. The BERT-based model is mentioned only in the first paragraph of Section 6.4 Prompt-free SLMs.

Section 6 should be intensively checked and revised.

title: More Data or Better Data? A Critical Analysis of Data Selection and Synthesis for Mathematical Reasoning
review:
This paper systematically analyzes and demonstrates that data quality is more important than data quantity in improving the mathematical inference capabilities of large-scale language models (LLMs). The authors design an integrated evaluation pipeline that mimics industrial training and deployment scenarios, validating the practical utility of various public datasets and data synthesis techniques. The study demonstrates that 1) even small amounts of well-cleaned data, distilled by high-performance models, are more effective. 2) Experimentally, the study demonstrates that in the SFT phase, complementing model weaknesses or training high-quality inference processes generated by superior models is crucial for improving performance.

Strength
- A Practical Approach from an Industrial Perspective: This study goes beyond academic performance evaluation and presents an integrated evaluation pipeline that considers the actual development and deployment of models in industrial settings. This approach bridges the gap between theory and practice.
- Systematic and Comprehensive Analysis: A consistent methodology was used to compare and analyze diverse datasets, including web scraping data, high-quality data, and model distillation data. Furthermore, the study distinguishes itself by dividing data generation into pre-training and SFT stages, and by deeply exploring effective strategies for each stage.

Weakness
- The effectiveness of a new dataset is judged based on a dichotomous criterion: "Is performance improved over the baseline model?"
- The ratio of validated data to new data is fixed at 80:20 during evaluation. Given that the paper emphasizes the importance of data mixing strategies, it's unclear how this fixed ratio impacts the experimental results, making generalizations difficult.
- While performance gains and losses are presented, validation (e.g., confidence intervals, p-values) is needed to verify whether these changes are statistically significant.
- Key experimental results supporting the main claims, such as model distillation datasets and weakness induction datasets, should be included in the main section.
- While the "weakness induction" method of generating similar data based on model failures is interesting, it lacks specific methodology, such as criteria for determining "similarity" or prompts used for data augmentation, resulting in low reproducibility.
- The study fails to provide an in-depth analysis of the data mixing strategy. This approach merely raises another research question rather than providing a conclusion. - Since the focus of the study was on mathematical reasoning ability, it is unknown whether the conclusion obtained here that ‘better data > more data’ can be generalized to other types of reasoning (e.g., common sense reasoning, scientific reasoning) or other domains.

title: More Data or Better Data? A Critical Analysis of Data Selection and Synthesis for Mathematical Reasoning
review: This paper presents a critical, practice-focused analysis of data selection and synthesis methods for training large language models (LLMs) in mathematical reasoning. By systematically evaluating open-source datasets and data construction approaches under a unified evaluation pipeline that reflects industrial settings, the authors investigate whether "more data" or "better data" most effectively improves LLM reasoning capabilities. Experiments span pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stages with various data curation strategies (such as model distillation, rigorous filtering, and weakness-guided augmentation), with quantitative results across multiple math and general benchmarks. Core findings demonstrate that careful curation and structuring of data—rather than blind data scaling—offer consistent improvements, and the study distills actionable strategies for the community and suggests RL-inspired future directions.

title: More Data or Better Data? A Critical Analysis of Data Selection and Synthesis for Mathematical Reasoning
review:
Strengths

Industrial Relevance: The evaluation pipeline explicitly mirrors real-world industrial training scenarios, enhancing practical applicability
.

Comprehensive Analysis: Covers both pretraining data refinement and SFT generation, and includes positive as well as unsuccessful experiments, increasing transparency.

Novelty in Perspective: Moves beyond “academic benchmarks” to practical deployment settings, addressing a gap in industry-focused LLM training research.

Clear Contributions: Provides actionable data selection strategies (e.g., favoring model-distilled reasoning data, principled large-scale generation, weakness-guided synthesis).

Balanced Discussion: Includes insights into limitations (restricted scope, small base models) and suggestions for future work (RL-inspired synthesis, curriculum learning, interference-aware data mixing).

Empirical Evidence: Multiple benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MathBench, HumanEval, etc.) are systematically used to validate claims
.

Weaknesses

Limited Scope: Focuses almost exclusively on mathematical reasoning. Claims about broader applicability (e.g., to NLP tasks beyond math and code) remain speculative
.

Small Base Models: The use of smaller models (DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Qwen2.5-3B) may underestimate the effectiveness of the proposed methods for state-of-the-art systems.

Mixing Strategy Unresolved: While data mixing interference is identified as a problem, the work does not propose concrete methodologies for resolving it.

Evaluation Depth: Some synthesis methods (e.g., RL-inspired) are only proposed conceptually without experimental validation.

Clarity: Certain sections (e.g., unsuccessful attempts with Long CoT and rule-based synthesis) could benefit from deeper diagnostic analysis rather than descriptive reporting.

Recommendation

Accept with Minor Revisions (Industry Track)
The paper provides valuable, practice-oriented insights into dataset quality vs. quantity trade-offs in LLM training. Its unified pipeline, empirical breadth, and industrial framing make it highly relevant. Strengthening clarity in unsuccessful experiments and offering concrete future methodologies for data mixing/curriculum learning would improve its impact.

Detailed Comments

Quality:
Solid experimental methodology with unified evaluation. Balanced inclusion of successes and failures increases reliability. However, the generalizability beyond math remains unproven.

Clarity:
The paper is well-structured and logically flows from introduction → evaluation → synthesis → failures → future work. Some sections could use additional explanatory depth, particularly around why rule-based or Long CoT synthesis underperforms.

Originality & Significance:
The focus on industrially-relevant evaluation and the “better vs. more” framing is both timely and significant. The insights into practical data curation could directly inform industry-scale LLM development.

title: CAPSTONE: Composable Attribute‑Prompted Scene Translation for Zero‑Shot Vision–Language Reasoning
review:
This paper presents CAPSTONE, a modular pipeline that translates outputs from multiple vision modules (detection, depth, pose, OCR, colors) into structured symbolic prompts for frozen LLMs. The aim is to decouple perception from reasoning, reducing training cost and improving interpretability.

The strongest contribution lies in the breadth of perception integration and the emphasis on human-readable, hot-swappable modules. Unlike prior prompt-based or tool-use systems that rely on one or two tools, CAPSTONE demonstrates a multi-channel composition. The deployment argument—that enterprises can integrate such a pipeline without retraining—adds practical relevance.

At the same time, several concerns remain. The novelty is incremental: the symbolic-prompt idea itself is not new, and the technical design mostly relies on straightforward engineering. The mention of a “trainable aggregation module” undermines the zero-shot claim and creates confusion. Empirically, the evaluation is too narrow: results are limited to POPE, which weakens the generality of the claims. Ablations on how much each module contributes would be essential.

Some minor comments: 
1) The comparison of deployment costs remains questionable. Many factors can be counted and carefully quantified in order to have a fair-enough comparison. I wonder love to see the authors disclosed detailed comparison calculation to make it more transparent.
2) While interpretability being a mentionable contribution is claimed by the authors, I don't actually see detailed benchmarking results to prove its effectiveness. The authors may consider present more results to prove its effectiveness. Furthermore, a contribution-attribution analysis would be a beneficial add-on to reveal the effectiveness of the choice of the module selection.

Overall, CAPSTONE is an interesting and useful engineering exploration. It shows a pragmatic path for interpretable, low-cost vision–language reasoning, but does not yet provide enough evidence or clarity to be considered a strong research breakthrough.

title: CAPSTONE: Composable Attribute‑Prompted Scene Translation for Zero‑Shot Vision–Language Reasoning
review:
**Overview**

This paper introduces CAPSTONE, a novel and pragmatic framework that enables LLMs to perform visual reasoning without direct access to image pixels. The core idea is to decouple visual perception from language-based reasoning by using a pipeline of off-the-shelf, specialized computer vision models to extract structured information from an image (e.g., object detections, colors, spatial relationships). This information is then "translated" into a detailed textual description, which serves as a prompt for a frozen, pre-trained LLM to answer questions or describe the scene, achieving impressive zero-shot performance that surpasses several fully trained VLMs.

**Strengths**

1. The modular, plug-and-play architecture is a highly innovative and practical solution to the high costs and opacity of traditional VLMs. 

2. The paper demonstrates exceptional results on the POPE benchmark, where the CAPSTONE framework paired with a 7B LLM outperforms several larger, fully trained VLMs.

3. The framework is inherently transparent, as the intermediate textual descriptions are human-readable, making it easy to debug and diagnose errors.

**Weaknesses**

1. The entire system's effectiveness is bottlenecked by the quality of the initial perception pipeline. If the object detector fails to see an object, or a classifier misidentifies it, the LLM has no way to recover from this error, as it never sees the raw image.

2. The process of converting rich, continuous visual information into discrete, textual descriptions is inherently lossy. Nuances like fine textures, subtle lighting effects, and complex, non-standard object poses are difficult to capture in text, limiting the depth of reasoning.

3. Figure 2 mentions a "Trainable Aggregation Module," which seems to contradict the paper's central claim of being a completely zero-shot, training-free framework. This creates significant confusion about the methodology.

title: CAPSTONE: Composable Attribute‑Prompted Scene Translation for Zero‑Shot Vision–Language Reasoning
review:
The paper addresses an industrially relevant objective—decoupling perception from reasoning by translating outputs of classical vision modules into structured prompts for a frozen LLM—but the core idea is not novel and substantially overlaps with prior work on tool-use and prompt-based pipelines. The related work section under-engages with these threads and omits key citations. Empirically, evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (POPE), where stronger models already exist; as a result, the reported gains are neither broadly demonstrated nor clearly state of the art. The comparison set excludes several competitive recent LVLMs, leaving SOTA claims insufficiently supported. The practical value proposition is also underdeveloped: the off-the-shelf perception stack (detector, depth, pose, OCR) still entails training and maintenance, yet end-to-end cost, latency, and infrastructure trade-offs are not rigorously characterized; the current cost table appears oversimplified relative to real deployment overhead. In addition, the paper would benefit from clearer system details, corrected technical descriptions, and a robust error analysis. Overall, the work needs a major revision focused on broadening evaluation, strengthening comparisons, and tightening technical rigor. For the revision, the following actions are recommended:

- Expand benchmarking beyond POPE to multiple, diverse tasks and datasets; report standardized metrics and confidence intervals.
- Include strong contemporary baselines under matched settings.
- Provide ablations isolating the contribution of each perception module and the aggregation stage, along with sensitivity to prompt structure.
- Present end-to-end cost, latency, and resource analyses with realistic deployment assumptions.
- Add thorough error analysis that categorizes failure modes across perception and reasoning, and links them to design trade-offs.
- Calibrate claims (including SOTA) to the breadth and strength of evidence, and strengthen coverage of related work with complete, up-to-date citations.

title: Finding Diamonds in Conversation Haystacks: A Benchmark for Conversational Data Retrieval
review:
This paper makes a substantial contribution to the field of conversational data retrieval by introducing the CDR benchmark, the first comprehensive framework designed to evaluate systems that retrieve conversational data for product insights. The authors have excelled in identifying distinct challenges inherent in conversational data retrieval, including implicit state recognition, turn dynamics, and contextual references—factors that are frequently neglected in traditional document retrieval tasks.

Strengths:

1. Its innovative approach to benchmark construction, including the multi-dimensional analysis framework and the systematic design of query templates.

2. The use of both real and synthetic conversational data ensures a balanced and comprehensive evaluation.

3. Furthermore, the detailed error analysis provides valuable insights into the limitations of current embedding models in conversational data retrieval.

Weaknesses:

1. Firstly, the benchmark is currently limited to English text-based conversations, which may restrict its applicability in multilingual or multimodal settings.

2. Secondly, the reliance on synthetic data, while valuable, may introduce subtle differences from real user conversations, affecting the generalizability of the findings.

3. Additionally, the assessment could benefit from the inclusion of more specialized retrieval models designed specifically for conversational data.

title: Finding Diamonds in Conversation Haystacks: A Benchmark for Conversational Data Retrieval
review:
Strengths

- Construction of a benchmark focused on retrieving conversational data, filling a clear gap in RAG research. A lot of description about how the benchmark was created.
- Three retrieval granularities (turn, chunk, session) and five distinct task areas.
- Error analysis highlighting interesting failures
- Query templates reflect real-world product use cases.
- Dataset and code to be publicly released.

Weaknesses

- The dataset is entirely open-source and synthetic.
- No demonstration of integration within/application to a deployed system or case study on proprietary data. That is, what has been learned from this benchmark that could be applied to an actual system? I definitely understand that this is the establishment of a benchmark dataset and that it may be too early to have learned anything useful yet. I ask merely because I'm looking for something practical since this is the industry track.

title: Finding Diamonds in Conversation Haystacks: A Benchmark for Conversational Data Retrieval
review:
This paper introduces the Conversational Data Retrieval benchmark, a comprehensive resource tailored for evaluation of conversational data. The construction of the benchmark involves a multi-stage process including data collection, query design and validation. Overall, the paper is well-organized and provides a valuable contribution to the industry community.

Strengths:
- The paper is clear and well-written, with a topic suited with the industry track theme.
- The proposed CDR benchmark dataset is the first of its kind to address the gap between traditional IR and the conversational context. This could be helpful to other industry practitioners working in a relevant domain.
- The methodology of the benchmark construction is also insightful. The multi-stage pipeline includes both automated and human-supervised components that improve the overall quality of the resulting resource.

Weaknesses:
- As a substantial portion of relevant query-conversation pairs are produced using LLMs as described in section 3, more details of how human evaluation is designed and conducted should be presented.

title: From Unstructured to Structured: LLM-Guided Attribute Graphs for Entity Search and Ranking
review:
This paper proposes a two-phrase framework, including an offline attribute graph construction and an online graph-based ranking in product searching task. The proposed method is evaluated on a public dataset Amazon Shopping Queries Dataset, using two evaluation pipelines (automatic LLM judgement and human evaluation). The paper also claims that the proposed method is deployed into production.

Strengths: 
1. Though the use of LLMs to guide graph-based reasoning is not novel, it is interesting that it is used in e-Commerce domain.
2. The paper is well-written with detailed prompt template, implementation details and clear figures.
3. The deployment into production makes this paper impactful for real-world applications.

Weaknesses:
1. The sample size for human evaluation is too small (only 40 samples) and lacks crucial details such as inter-annotator agreement, which raises the concern of statistical robustness and reproducibility of the results. 
2. There are still some parts need technical clarity. For example, since the proposed method is already deployed, what is the latency or efficiency trade-off for using LLMs at inference time? Why Claude is chosed as the LLM instead of other LLM models? What if the prompt is changed? Can the model still get robust performance?
3. Paper needs proofreading before submission. There are typos in line 197, line 268, oversize table 1, etc.

title: From Unstructured to Structured: LLM-Guided Attribute Graphs for Entity Search and Ranking
review:
As a type of entity search, product attributes are extremely important in determining relevant/similar products. This paper constructs a product-attribute graph via an LLM and then at inference time uses the graph to improve ranking precision. Evaluation is done on the Amazon shopping queries dataset with comparison to other rankers.  The baselines are a sparse and dense retrieval (dr) using just cosine similarity, the dr with an LLM to rerank the top candidates, and the dr with the proposed graph ranker to rerank the top candidates.  Human evaluation on precision is also provided and aligns with the automated eval results that use LLMs for evaluation.

Pros:
- Precision improvements across the board
- Attribute extraction could be useful for many features, not just reranking

Cons:
- The precision focus and the focus on hard/longer queries means that it is not clear how this performs overall; this needs to be discussed even if the decision is that this will only be used on, e.g., queries of 4+ words. In particular, how does this approach handle ranking factors such as cost, star-ratings, up-to-datedness (e.g. for fashion)?  Is the idea that this ranker would be an L2 and that an L3 would take care of these issues?
- The attribute definition step needs more detail to understand what was done.
- Baselines and their description could be improved: What is the embedding that is used for "dr"? What sparsification is used for "sr"? Why isn't lexical search + BM25 included (even if it performs really badly, this should be a baseline)?
- The conclusion says the method has "shown immense promise under a live deployment setting" but in sec 5.3, it appears that this is not live yet and no results (even with obscuring exact values) are shown. 
- The paper can be hard to follow at times For example, the introduction talks about recommendations but the evaluation is all about search. This can be relatively easily fixed and deleting some of the text would provide room for more technical details.

Comments in order of the paper (not including comments already covered above):
There are some typos in the paper; please proofread the final version.

l067: For general domain, the LLMs can work well for attributes, but specific domains (e.g. medical supply search) could cause issues. For those domains, some fine-tuning may be necessary but should be feasible.

sec3.1 attribute definition: How many levels re there and roughly  how many categories and attributes at each level? How are the names made consistent across subcategories if an attribute is in multiple of them but not enough for the super-category?  
l201 says "We curate these": Does this mean that every single list was human reviewed and edited? This is a fine approach for a production product but should be discussed more, especially for the industry track since it is important for the quality.

sec3.1 attribute extraction: How accurate is this (as opposed to the accuracy of using it for search)? Only text is mentioned, what about information already in structured data (e.g. a brand field)? How do you ensure the LLM does not hallucinate attributes and values (e.g. positing a brand when there is none)?

sec3.2 graph: Why was it decided to have the attribute values as the edges instead of the nodes? Entity related graphs usually are of the type where the edges map the relationship (e.g. is_brand, is_size, married_to, lives_in) and the nodes hold the values (and are generally typed as well).

sec5.1: what was the IAA for the annotators?  For a precision search task, I expect this was relatively high, but it should be reported.

sec5.3, line470+: Can rough numbers be provided for "slight latency increases"?  Even if just something like 10-50ms or 100-250ms would be helpful to know.  For "high-value or high-impact search scenarios" can you provide an example or two (e.g. long queries which would otherwise have null results or queries in electronics)?

title: From Unstructured to Structured: LLM-Guided Attribute Graphs for Entity Search and Ranking
review:
**Overview and pros:**
This paper reports on the efficacy of a two-stage method for entity search and ranking for product search and recommendation. During the first stage, an LLM is employed (by means of prompting) to define a set of attributes that's appropriate for supporting categorization of a wide range of products. Then, an LLM is used to extract the values of those attributes for a set of existing products. This first stage is done in an offline manner. The second stage is done online during the ranking of a set of retrieved products, where the LLM is prompted to rank a list of products where the attribute values are presented in a graph format. The experiments show reasonable improvement over the baselines by using stage of the method.

**Cons**:
The effects of how the models are prompted are not discussed. For example, how is this method susceptible to jailbreaks during ranking?

I also highlight the following writing and editing issues:
- line 197: ierarchical -> hierarchical
- line 274: "is computed" is repeated
- line 735: "xw" appears mistakenly
- Table 5 and Table 6 have the same caption, which I believe is wrong

title: LESER: Learning to Expand via Search Engine-feedback Reinforcement in e-Commerce
review:
**Summary**  
This paper addresses the one-to-many mapping challenge in query expansion and introduces LESER, a search-engine-in-the-loop reinforcement learning framework that uses real-time feedback for optimization. The method performs context-grounded query expansion by first fetching results for the original query, reasoning over those results (particularly leveraging metadata), and then generating a set of appended queries. The goal is to improve relevance and coverage of results beyond the original query. The reward is based on the relative relevance and result set size of expanded queries compared to the original query’s results. The system is evaluated against strong baselines, including GPT-based expansion, and shows measurable improvements.

**Strengths**
- Tackles a real, practical challenge in search relevance with an industrially applicable approach.
- Clever use of metadata from initial search results to guide expansion reasoning.
- Reward formulation explicitly balances relevance and coverage, which is important in real search scenarios.

**Weaknesses**
- The approach is reward-weighted regression rather than GRPO — lacks clipping and advantage calculation, which should be acknowledged also in Eq. 3 calculation the $i$th reward should be excluded as per standard GRPO formulation (see page 14 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.03300).
- Missing details on the warmup process (e.g., number of samples, selection criteria). Plz Provide details.
- Reporting only the % of improved cases can be misleading — does not convey magnitude of improvements. Plz report both aggregate improvement metrics and % of improved cases for a complete picture.
- Relevance improvements vs. GPT do not appear statistically significant as claimed in conclusion. Highly recommend reporting 95% confidence intervals to make the claims crisp.

**Questions for the Authors**
1. What was the rationale for using reward-weighted regression over GRPO?
2. How did you optimize $\lambda$?

title: LESER: Learning to Expand via Search Engine-feedback Reinforcement in e-Commerce
review:
This paper addresses the challenge of query ambiguity and underspecification in e-commerce search by proposing LESER that leverages real-time search engine feedback to fine-tune LLMs for query expansion. The problem tackled is practically significant as user queries in e-commerce are often short, vague, and represent diverse user intents that are challenging to capture via traditional retrieval methods. 

LESER introduces a novel framing of query expansion as a retrieval optimization problem. By incorporating Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), the approach directly learns from retrieval-oriented metrics such as relevance and coverage, which are critical for improving the alignment between expanded queries and platform objectives. The paper demonstrates how LESER is trained to reason over returned search results, thereby generating expansions that better reflect user intent while adhering to strict platform constraints.

However, it is important to note that the core innovations are somewhat incremental. The paper primarily applies known techniques rather than introducing new algorithms or frameworks. Additionally, the empirical comparisons focus mostly on relatively simple baselines such as embedding-based retrieval and basic prompting strategies. The paper would be strengthened by including comparisons against more recent and competitive query expansion or retrieval optimization approaches, such as those involving contrastive learning, learning-to-rerank models, or state-of-the-art instruction-tuned LLMs specifically designed for retrieval tasks.

Moreover, while the paper presents some ablation studies, a deeper analysis of LESER’s components, especially the impact of GRPO, the choice of reward signals, and the sensitivity to different search engine feedback types, would provide more insight into what drives performance improvements. 

Considering the real-time inference setting, a discussion or evaluation of computational efficiency, latency, and resource costs would also be valuable for assessing deployment feasibility at scale in commercial environments.

title: LESER: Learning to Expand via Search Engine-feedback Reinforcement in e-Commerce
review:
# Summary

The paper presents LESER (Learning to Expand via Search Engine-feedback Reinforcement), a novel approach for query expansion that leverages search engine results as reinforcement signals. The method employs a reward function that balances relevance and recall between expanded and original queries, utilizing GRPO for fine-tuning to optimize the generation of high-reward candidates. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach through comprehensive evaluations, showing improvements over existing baselines in both offline metrics and online customer engagement.

## Strengths

- S1: The approach of utilizing search engine signals for query expansion training is pragmatic and straightforward to implement.

- S2: The paper provides sufficient technical details, making the work reproducible.

- S3: The evaluation framework is robust, incorporating offline metrics, qualitative analysis, and online A/B testing to validate the method's effectiveness.

## Weaknesses

- W1: The core concept of using search engine feedback as reinforcement learning rewards for query generation has been previously explored in existing literature (e.g., [1,2]). The paper would benefit from acknowledging and comparing against these prior works.

- W2: The paper lacks detailed analysis of the reward function components (Equation 1), making it difficult to understand the relative importance of each term in the overall performance.

- W3: The method for determining query suggestion quantity and its impact on performance is not adequately explained or analyzed.

- W4: T: While the authors claim the generated queries are grounded in the product catalog, there is no systematic evaluation of potential hallucinations or verification of actual grounding.

## References
[1] Task-Oriented Query Reformulation with Reinforcement Learning

[2] CONQRR: Conversational Query Rewriting for Retrieval with Reinforcement Learning

title: Fishing for Answers: Exploring One-SHOT vs. Iterative Retrieval Strategies for Retrieval Augmented Generation
review:
This paper investigates two strategies to improve RAG performance in industrial QA settings: 

1) a one-shot retrieval method using a token-constrained chunk selection and lightweight filtering and cropping
2) an iterative retrieval strategy using multi-turn retrieval with fallback search and chunk deletion. 

The authors evaluate these strategies on a proprietary QA dataset categorized by reasoning complexity and report significant improvements over a baseline Top-k RAG setup.

Strengths: 
1) The paper is grounded in practical, real-world deployment settings for using RAG in enterprise contexts.
2) The strategies explore the design space for practical RAG setting thoughtfully including trade-offs between token budget and retrieval rounds, precision and recall.
3) The authors carefully designed a 4-level QA benchmark with nuanced differences in reasoning and retrieval needs.
4) The paper provides multiple ablation studies, comparisons across question types, and exploration of failure modes.

Weaknesses: 
1. The core ideas such as token-aware chunk selection, iterative retrieval are widely known RAG enhancements. The paper does not propose fundamentally new techniques, nor does it generalize the insights in a reusable way. Iterative, agentic retrieval with query reformulation, tool use, and reasoning steps has already been explored extensively (e.g., ReAct, AutoGPT-style agents, Search-RAG). It might help to reposition the paper as an applied case study with lessons from deployment, rather than implying research innovation.
2. Evaluation, while extensive, is difficult to trust and reproduce fully due to its closed nature of the dataset and lack of human validation. It would help to describe the dataset construction and evaluation process in more detail. If possible, release even a small portion of the dataset or evaluation rubric. 
3. The QA benchmark characteristics are well-known (e.g. single-doc vs multi-doc QA, look-up vs reasoning queries), but the writing seems to hint them as being novel. It is not clear how this closed benchmark is different from existing single/multi-doc RAG benchmarks.
4. The depth of analysis is a bit limited. While the paper discusses retrieval failure modes it is mostly superficial. It would help to extract deeper, more generalizable insights that can apply to other domains/datasets. For example, how chunking or LLM reasoning affects retrieval behavior in different data regimes.

title: Fishing for Answers: Exploring One-SHOT vs. Iterative Retrieval Strategies for Retrieval Augmented Generation
review:
This paper explores two retrieval strategies for RAG systems: a One-SHOT approach that maximizes token usage in a single retrieval ("casting a bigger net"), and an iterative approach that performs multiple targeted retrievals ("casting multiple times"). Through experiments on 1,000 industry questions, both strategies achieve similar accuracy (90-91%) but suit different scenarios.

Strengths: The paper demonstrates strong industry relevance through real-world deployment evidence spanning over 2 years of client service, along with clear documentation of RAG failure analysis showing 48% of failures due to missing golden chunks. It provides valuable negative results by revealing why combining strategies fails due to cognitive overload and identifying critical issues like query drift and retrieval laziness, potentially saving significant industry research effort. The paper also offers systematic comparison of retrieval strategies with concrete guidance for different resource constraints, supported by well-documented performance across various scenarios.

Weaknesses: The paper suffers from limited technical innovation, essentially just removing top-k constraints for One-SHOT and following existing frameworks for the iterative approach, without introducing novel algorithms or theoretical advances. The evaluation is problematic with a small dataset of only 1,000 questions from a single company, heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge, and limited SOTA comparisons. Implementation details are inadequate, featuring oversimplified query rewriting, vague chunk filter/cropping specifications, and no clear guidelines for strategy selection, culminating in a failed attempt at combining strategies.

While the paper provides some practical insights from industry deployment, its lack of technical innovation, limited evaluation, and implementation gaps make it unsuitable for publication. The work would benefit from substantial revision to include novel technical contributions, broader evaluation, and clearer implementation details.

title: Fishing for Answers: Exploring One-SHOT vs. Iterative Retrieval Strategies for Retrieval Augmented Generation
review:
Summary
=======
This paper tries to improve RAG for an industrial use case. The authors presents two retrieval strategies for RAG systems: a token-constrained retrieval approach and an iterative agentic method. The work addresses well established industry challenges but it has significant limitations in novelty and experimentation.

One-SHOT Strategy: This is the contrained retrieval approach. Instead of retrieving a fixed number of chunks, it dynamically selects as many relevant chunks as possible by optimizing for relevance-per-token ratios, formulated as a binary optimization problem. It has a rule-based chunk filter (based on some heuristics) and an LLM-based chunk cropping component for semantic filtering.

Iterative Agentic Strategy: This method implements a multi-turn retrieval framework where a reasoning LLM acts as an intelligent agent that autonomously decides when and how to retrieve additional information over up to 5 turns.

Review
======
The proposed strategies overlap a lot with existing work. The token constrained approach resembles work done in CORAG's (https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00744) and other adaptive methods, while the iterative strategy parallels Adaptive-RAG (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14403), Auto-RAG (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.19443) and recent agentic systems. The identified challenges of query drift (where autonomous query reformulation deviates from user intent) and retrieval laziness have been addressed previously as well. GraphRAG's DRIFT Search (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/introducing-drift-search-combining-global-and-local-search-methods-to-improve-quality-and-efficiency/) and multi-turn conversation research. Also, the chunk filtering components are similar to ChunkRAG's LLM-driven filtering methods.

The paper also has very basic baseline comparisons against the standard top-5 retrieval strategy. The experimental evaluation uses a L1-L4 difficulty framework (ranging from simple factual queries to complex multi-step reasoning tasks) but is limited by single-domain scope.
The paper provides some production insights from 2+ years of deployment but isn't exciting enough given the depth of work happening in RAG over the past few years.

title: Causal Learning with Language Model: Decoding HTE from ATE
review:

title: Causal Learning with Language Model: Decoding HTE from ATE
review: This work proposes an approach that leverages deep learning models (transformer architecture) to assist causal decision-making for business teams. Models were trained to predict treatment effects from observed behavior data. It is unclear if the proposed approach can train models to recover causal relationships. The experimental data was simulated and may be overly simplified compared to real-world data. Transformer architectures are highly non-linear. How is the linearity set up in Section 3.1 relevant to the practice in this study?

title: Causal Learning with Language Model: Decoding HTE from ATE
review:
NOTE: I have reviewed this paper in the past. Given that the paper doesn't seem to have changed
much, I include my original review below alongside new comment/thoughts marked with "UPDATE".

Summary:

The paper presents an approach to use an LLM to make "causal" predictions (or at the paper calls
them 'treatment effects") in a scenario that deviates from a typical training/prediction regime.
Training data only features aggregate predictions for a group of instances instead of each instance
(the "average treatment effects" setting). The other aspect of setting, that some feature values
may be rare in training data ("weak feature") is also noted as a distinction but it seems more
familiar to ML. The work discusses some details of this setting whose relevance escapes me and then
proposes to use an LM (GPT-2 in the experiments) to encode tabular features as text, to train that
LM, and to make it predict all "treatment effects" simultaneously. The results show it being more

Questions / Comments / Suggestions (see also the weaknesses section below).

    Multi-modal might be the wrong term to describe a text-only LLM. Perhaps multi-task (as used
