Again, the stakes are too high to try something like this and the results of the authors do not show the technology will work. Conceptually I do not expect it to work to the level required for the task.

The best part of the paper is the evaluation using synthetic documents and a Dungeon and Dragons data set. By virtue of using D&D they capture how LLMs "know" enough of the topic to provide answers even if the IR system has successfully blocked access to the relevant information.

Minor issues:

* If the main contribution of the paper is extending NeMo guardrails, then that approach should be described in some detail.
* This text:

> To evaluate system performance, we create a test set of 389 user
> queries generated manually with the assistance of GPT-4o.

If you created them using GPT-4o they are not created manually.

*  Table 2 is missing a baseline where the vectors have metadata and the filtering is done over the exact metadata. No cosine similarity approximation.
* The static filter numbers in Table 3 are different from Table 2.

title: ARBITER - AI-Driven Filtering for Role-Based Access Control
review:
Summary:

The work proposes a scheme that implements role-based access control using an LLM and several LLM
orchestration tools, specifically aimed at RBAC for retrieval-augmented generation systems (which
themselves are commonly written using some of the same orchestration tools). The goal is to make
sure information not accessible by a querying user/role as per policy does not become visible to
them in the various ways information flows in RAG apps. Initially adjustments to embedding system
to add RBAC information allows the system to possibly cut off inappropriate information before it
is even retrieved. Barring this, the system can further make sure that if a inappropriate (in terms
of access control) context is retrieved, it gets thrown out before it is seen by the LLM answering
queries. Finally, the final outputs that are to be sent to the user are checked once more against
policies which allows for handling the subtle case that the LLM itself might know things which are
not allowed by the policy to be shared with that user. With three phases of policy check, the hope
is that not only is the RBAC check accurate, it is capable of dealing with semantics-driven cases
not handled by traditional RBAC systems.

Experiments demonstrate the system relative to "static filter"-based RBAC systems using four
open-weights LLMs. These are also used to implement a RAG chatbot over which the RBAC system
presides. The results show small decrease in accuracy of the system relative to "static filters".

Strengths:

+ S1. Work attempts to navigate the subtle issue of access control over information that can be
  encoded not only in RAG retrieved contexts but also in the model weights (or effectively
  pre-training and fine-tuning data). This strength is not exploited though (see W1).

Weaknesses:

- W1. Lack of sufficient definition in the problem being solved. The idea that the LLM generate
  information which is governed by a policy, independent of it being shown that information in the
  context is both interesting and problematic. Some arguments need to be made to even accept this
  premise. The use of the D&D-based example complicates the matter in that the LLMs used likely
  have seen in the pre-training data, the same text that is now considered under the purview of an
  access control policy. The "traditional" view of access control does not have a "static filter"
  perform at less than 100% accuracy/f1 (these metrics themselves would not be even used to discuss
  RBAC).

  - Suggestion G1. Elaborate on and formalize what constitutes an access control violation. Argue
    that a violation can happen even if a system does not ingest any prohibited data and why this
    problem should be handled by an RBAC system as opposed to systems for memorization-prevention
    in LLMs. What if an LLM system never seen a particular piece of non-accessible data but
    hallucinates it; would revealing it still be an access control violation? In the context of the
    D&D-based dataset, is it OK for a character to learn about a spell they cannot use if the
    information comes from the description of something else that they can access (i.e. a different
    spell)?

- W2. No statistical validity considerations in experimental results. Many of the results in Tables
  2 and 3 are quite close to each other. The relative ranking of the systems could be up to
  non-determinism.

  - Suggestion G2. Repeat non-deterministic experiments and report some metrics of variance (i.e.
    confidence margins, IQR, or otherwise).

- W3. Evaluation and design mixes unrelated concerns which complicate or confound discussion and
  results beyond the core of the problem. This includes the use of a fact checker system, tuning of
  retrieval similarity thresholds, use of different LLMs to implement the RAG (as opposed to the
  access control checker). All of these things can be fixed removed/fixed in place across
  experiments to focus on evaluating the core part of the system, the access control itself (and
  not the quality of retrieval or query answering).

  - Suggestion G3. Limit number of variables in the system and experiments to as little as
    possible. E.g. fix the LLM implementing the app, and the embedding system implementing the
    retrieval, across all experiments. Vary only the LLM implementing the access control scheme.
    Separate out retrieval and generation failures from the system as concerns unrelated to access
    control or model some variety of them as overly conservative access control.

Questions:

- Q1. What is a "traditional RAG system" as opposed to a non-traditional one?

- Q2. Part of motivation is that static access controls are not flexible enough and systems need to
  handle "rapid role evolution". The experiments don't seem to be concerned about this? How would
  you evaluate such systems?

Other recommendations:

- Some cost estimates would be good in the experiments in terms of number of input tokens and
  output tokens needed to implement the various checks. Latency as well.

Smallest things:

- "NIM" not defined.

title: ARBITER - AI-Driven Filtering for Role-Based Access Control
review:
## Nature of the Contribution
This is primarily a deployed system architecture & evaluation paper, targeting Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in enterprise environments. The key novelty is the ARBITER system, a multi-stage, few-shot LLM-based filtering framework for enforcing RBAC without fine-tuned classifiers. It addresses an industry-critical deployment challenge: preventing sensitive information leakage in AI-driven retrieval systems.

## Real-world Impact & Novelty
### Impact:
- Tackles a genuine pain point in industry RAG deployments, access control with minimal retraining overhead.
- Supports dynamic policy updates via natural language role descriptions, lowering operational costs for role changes.
- Potential to reduce the lag between policy changes and enforcement compared to retrained classifiers.
- Addresses enterprise data sovereignty by supporting local deployment.

### Novelty:
- Not in the underlying idea of multi-stage filtering (cf. GUARDIAN framework), but in combining NeMo Guardrails with role-aware, prompt-driven few-shot LLM filters integrated directly into RAG pipelines.
- The synthetic testbed (D&D spells) cleverly avoids data privacy issues while still simulating role-permission constraints.
- The approach is notable for removing the dependency on fine-tuned classifiers, allowing faster deployment in evolving environments.

## Technical Quality & Clarity
### Strengths:
- Clear architecture diagram and component breakdown.
- Well-defined evaluation setup: synthetic dataset with ground truth, multiple open-source LLMs, comparative baselines (static filter).
- Multi-metric reporting (accuracy, F1, precision, recall) makes trade-offs explicit.
- Ablation study (input only, output only, combined) gives actionable insights for architecture choice.

### Weaknesses / Areas for Improvement:
- The dataset choice, while justified for reproducibility, may not capture enterprise complexity (temporal permissions, hierarchical roles, redaction scenarios).
- Latency implications are acknowledged but not measured, a key concern for interactive deployments.
- No security adversarial testing (e.g., prompt injection, role confusion attacks).
- The fact-checking layer’s contribution isn’t quantified separately.
Results are close to static filters but still leave a 6–8% gap in F1, with no analysis of the false negative cases where sensitive data leaked.

## Common Pitfalls Check
- Scope clarity: Very clear, focused on RBAC in RAG.
- Claims vs. evidence: Mostly well-supported, though "approaching enterprise maturity" could be toned down given synthetic dataset limitations.
- Ambiguous definitions: Minimal, but “dynamic policy updates” could be better quantified (e.g., how fast and at what operational cost?).
- Statistics: Metrics are reported correctly, but no statistical significance testing.

## Reproducibility & Transparency
- Positive: Code architecture described in detail; prompts provided; datasets described with licensing.
- Limitation: Proprietary enterprise datasets understandably absent; no latency or hardware cost reporting; ChromaDB threshold choice (0.5) “empirically found” but not fully justified or explored.

## Broader Context & Related Work
- Related work covers both traditional RBAC and LLM guardrails, including GUARDIAN and Elasticsearch RAG-RBAC.
- The distinction between static keyword RBAC and semantic few-shot RBAC is well-motivated.
Could cite more work on access control in semantic retrieval or prompt injection resilience.

## Strengths & Weaknesses Summary
### Strengths:
- Strong real-world relevance (enterprise deployment challenge).
- Architecture is modular and integrates existing open-source tooling.
- Multi-stage filtering validated against baseline, with ablation for insight.
- Supports natural language policy definitions, which could be a big operational advantage.

### Weaknesses:
- Synthetic dataset limits external validity.
- No latency/performance trade-off analysis.
- No explicit robustness testing against adversarial access attempts.
Performance gap vs. static filters remains unexplored in depth.

## Suggestions for Improvement
- Extend evaluation to include at least a small, anonymized enterprise-like dataset with real hierarchical roles.
- Measure latency and resource use for multi-stage filtering in realistic deployment settings.
- Add a security stress test (prompt injection, role spoofing) to validate resilience.
- Analyze failure cases in detail to guide future improvement.
Consider hybrid approaches combining static pre-filters with few-shot semantic filters to close the precision gap.

title: DASR: Distributed Adaptive Scene Recognition - A Multi-Agent Cloud-Edge Framework for Language-Guided Scene Detection
review:
This paper presents a framework for adaptive scene recognition in autonomous driving, addressing critical limitations in data collection efficiency. Some concerns are listed below:
1) The contribution of individual components (LLM coordinator, toolbox specialists, quantization) is not quantified.
2) DRAMA/HAD results (Table 3) show marginal gains (e.g., +4.14% over Qwen2VL-2B on HAD), but datasets were converted via "rule-based converters" (§4.2). No details provided on conversion fairness or potential bias.
3) Fine-tuning uses only 18k samples from Nuplan-QA-Eval (§4.1), raising questions about robustness. OOD tests (DRAMA/HAD) lack diversity (only Tokyo/San Francisco).

title: DASR: Distributed Adaptive Scene Recognition - A Multi-Agent Cloud-Edge Framework for Language-Guided Scene Detection
review:
Pros:
1. Clear and intuitive cloud–edge multi-agent design (GPT-4o coordinator + on-edge VLM + toolbox).
2. Robust OOD results (DRAMA 91.93, HAD 77.68). 
3. Strong motivation: replaces mass collection and rigid thresholds with an LLM–edge VLM pipeline.

Con:
1. Limited system metrics: no latency/FPS, memory footprint after AWQ, or on-vehicle energy usage.
2. Enterprise claims (time-to-market, review-time cuts) are projections without user studies.

Question for authors:
What are end-to-end latency, throughput, and energy on target edge hardware (pre-/post-AWQ)?

title: DASR: Distributed Adaptive Scene Recognition - A Multi-Agent Cloud-Edge Framework for Language-Guided Scene Detection
review:
This paper introduces DASR, a distributed adaptive scene retrieval framework for autonomous driving that partitions reasoning between a cloud-hosted large language model (GPT-4o) and an on-vehicle lightweight vision-language model (Qwen2-VL-2B) augmented with specialist perception tools. The framework aims to reduce storage overhead by selectively collecting relevant driving scenes in response to natural language queries. The work is motivated by clear industrial needs and demonstrates notable gains in precision and mAP compared to large VLM baselines on both the in-distribution Nuplan-QA-Eval dataset and the out-of-distribution DRAMA and HAD datasets.

**Strengths**

•	Clear industrial relevance – Tackles a real and costly problem in autonomous driving: storing and sending large amounts of unnecessary driving data.

•	Well-designed system – Combines cloud-based LLM reasoning with edge-side specialist tools and a lightweight VLM for final decisions.

•	Efficient in practice – Adapts tool and sensor use to the task and applies quantization for easier deployment.

•	Solid results – Delivers consistent improvements across multiple datasets and task types, including out-of-distribution scenarios

**Weaknesses**

•	Missing key details – The paper does not explain the cloud LLM’s prompting strategy, the query-to-tool selection process, or the exact mapping from task category and difficulty to activated tools and sensors.

•	No evaluation of the cloud step – The performance of the cloud LLM’s task classification and tool/sensor selection is not measured, so its reliability is unknown.

•	Unclear use of specialist outputs – The paper does not specify how the outputs from specialist tools (S) are integrated into the vision-language model input, i.e., whether S is serialized into text, embedded, or overlaid on video frames before being fed to the VLM. Formally: VLM Input = f(P, V, S), but the integration of S is not described.

•	Dataset limitations – The approach relies on a custom-labeled dataset that is not publicly available, which prevents external validation and replication.

**Clarity & Structure**

•	Writing is generally clear, with a logical structure from motivation → method → experiments.

•	However, the method section omits crucial implementation details, which breaks the flow for readers wanting to reproduce or adapt the system.

•	Figures are helpful, but one showing a full query → cloud → specialist → edge → output example with real prompts/outputs would greatly improve clarity.

**Novelty & Impact**

•	The novelty is more in system integration than in new model architectures — fairly acceptable for industrial track — but missing details prevent others from adopting the approach directly.

title: LP Data Pipeline: Lightweight, Purpose-driven Data Pipeline for Large Language Models
review:
This paper introduces the Lightweight, Purpose-driven (LP) Data Pipeline, a CPU-based framework for curating large-scale datasets for Large Language Models (LLMs). The authors address the significant challenge of high computational costs and resource dependency on GPUs in current data-filtering methods. The proposed pipeline focuses on efficiency and accessibility by employing CPU-optimized techniques for data extraction, filtering, deduplication, and domain-specific classification. The paper provides a clear overview of the pipeline's architecture and philosophy, supported by an empirical analysis of its performance on Common Crawl dumps.

Strengths:

- The paper tackles a timely and practical problem in LLM development: the high cost and resource barrier of data curation.

- The proposed CPU-only pipeline is a significant contribution, making large-scale data processing more accessible.

- The inclusion of purpose-driven dataset construction for specific domains like finance, law, and healthcare is a valuable feature for real-world applications.

- The empirical analysis of processing time and cost provides concrete evidence of the pipeline's efficiency and scalability.

Weaknesses:

- The paper would benefit from a more direct comparison with existing GPU-based pipelines in terms of final dataset quality and its impact on LLM performance.

- While the paper mentions the use of "qualitative assessments" to determine filtering thresholds, providing more detail on this process would strengthen the methodology.

- The limitations section acknowledges the lack of LLM training experiments; including even a small-scale experiment would have significantly bolstered the paper's claims.

Overall, this is a well-written and valuable contribution to the field. The LP Data Pipeline presents a practical and efficient solution to a significant bottleneck in LLM development. The strengths of the paper, particularly its focus on reducing computational costs and enabling purpose-driven data curation, make it a strong candidate for acceptance in an industry track. The weaknesses, while notable, are presented transparently and provide clear avenues for future work.

title: LP Data Pipeline: Lightweight, Purpose-driven Data Pipeline for Large Language Models
review:
The paper introduces a pipeline for creating large-scale training datasets for LLMs, which essentially helps to extract clean high-quality data from a larger crawled data like CommonCrawl. The novelty of the pipeline is that it utilises CPUs only, so that it's suitable for smaller industrial infrastructures and costs less than GPU-based data processing.

The paper is well-written and is easy to follow, it contains a good amount of related work and illustrative appendices. I think the paper would be helpful for the readers from industry who work on data curation for LLMs, which is quite a hot topic nowadays.

Pros:
- Relevant topic for the current industry, I think many will find this paper useful
- There's a clear practical use for the method introduced in the paper
- The pipeline's structure and the resulting stats of the datasets are quite convincing

Cons:
- The relation of the experimental results and methodology to related work (2.2. Quality filtering techniques) remained rather unclear to me. I think a reader might want to know:

- What kind of components in the pipeline were harder to adapt from GPUs to CPUs?
- How much approximately would a GPU-based data processing cost applied to the same raw data dump that you used? Some estimated numbers could've helped to understand the significance of the work better.

- Some CPU-based techniques mentioned in section 2.2 seem to have been integrated into your pipeline in different components. Pointing this out clearer would've also helped to understand the significance and novelty of the work better.

- You mention that the pipeline was run on 128 machines with 8 CPUs each. How many machines with GPUs would be needed for such processing? Cost / time estimates are really missing in my opinion (even approximate, without experimenting), when advertising your pipeline as lighter and more cost efficient than in the latest publications.

# Outline
This paper presents a CPU-based pipeline for processing large-scale datasets for LLM training. The framework reduces preparation time and computational costs through filtering and preprocessing steps.

# Strengths
- The framework demonstrates substantial reductions in processing time and computational costs compared to existing approaches, as shown in the empirical analysis section.
- Operating exclusively on CPUs makes the pipeline more accessible and eliminates the need for expensive GPU resources.

# Weaknesses
- The evaluation lacks quality assessment for the processed datasets. It focuses only on computational metrics without examining data quality preservation.
- The paper does not evaluate the effectiveness of domain-specific and quality filters in maintaining dataset integrity. No metrics are measuring only these two steps of the pipeline.

title: CHAD-LLM: Router-Guided Cost-Efficient Hybrid Anomaly Detection LLM
review:
# Summary

This paper presents a hybrid system for anomaly detection. A lightweight anomaly detection model serves as a router to identify easy and hard cases and also the detector for easy cases. An LLM finetuned with LoRA and augmented by RAG and Reflexion is used for hard cases. Experiments on five tabular datasets revealed effectiveness of the proposed method.

# Strengths

1. This paper presents a hybrid anomaly detection pipeline that involves query routing to balance efficiency and quality of detection. It proposes a cost-effective way to achieve on-par performance with LLM models while reducing LLM calls as much as possible.
2. The paper compared with 3 conventional models, 3 neural network based models, and 1 LLM model. Experiments show that it achieves better overall performance than baseline models.

# Weaknesses

1. The threshold in routing is fixed thus lacks adaptive mechanism to fit various scenarios. This work focuses solely on balanced datasets while in industrial applications anomaly cases are often extremely rare.
2. LLaMA 3.1-8B is the only LLM used in the pipeline, while it is valuable to have a comprehensive analysis on choices of LLM and verify whether SLM could achieve on par performances.

title: CHAD-LLM: Router-Guided Cost-Efficient Hybrid Anomaly Detection LLM
review:
## Summary

This paper presents CHAD-LLM (Cost-efficient Hybrid Anomaly Detection LLM), a framework that combines a lightweight anomaly detection model with an LLM to balance performance and inference cost. The system uses the small model as both a detector for "easy" cases and a router to identify "hard" cases that require LLM processing. For hard cases, the LLM is enhanced with LoRA fine-tuning, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and Reflexion for self-correction. The authors evaluate their approach on five tabular datasets and report achieving 83.3% F1 score while reducing LLM usage to 49.2% of queries.

## Strengths

1. **Practical Problem Addressing**: The paper tackles a genuine industrial challenge - the high cost and latency of LLM inference for anomaly detection while maintaining performance benefits.

2. **Well-Motivated Hybrid Architecture**: The router-based approach is intuitive and well-justified, leveraging confidence scores from lightweight models to determine query difficulty.

3. **Comprehensive Technical Integration**: The combination of LoRA fine-tuning, RAG, and Reflexion for the LLM component shows thoughtful system design to address different aspects (domain knowledge, retrieval, self-correction).

4. **Cost-Performance Analysis**: The paper provides quantitative analysis of the trade-off between LLM usage reduction and performance, which is valuable for practical deployment considerations.

5. **Reasonable Experimental Setup**: The evaluation covers multiple datasets and compares against relevant conventional, deep learning, and LLM-based baselines.

## Weaknesses

1. **Limited Novelty**: The core contribution is essentially combining existing techniques (confidence-based routing, LoRA, RAG, Reflexion) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods. Each component is well-established in the literature.

2. **Questionable Experimental Design**:
   - The balanced dataset construction (1:1 normal:anomaly ratio) is unrealistic for real-world anomaly detection where anomalies are typically rare (0.1-5%).
   - Using only 1,000 samples for the small model training vs. 10,000 for LLM fine-tuning creates an unfair comparison that may artificially inflate the benefits of the hybrid approach.
   - Limited to only 5 datasets, all from similar domains (fraud detection).

3. **Insufficient Analysis**:
   - Missing ablation studies on individual components (LoRA vs. RAG vs. Reflexion contributions).
   - No analysis of failure cases or when the routing decisions are suboptimal.
   - Limited discussion of how the method handles different types of distribution shifts.
   - No comparison with other cost reduction techniques (e.g., model distillation, early exit networks).

4. **Fixed Threshold Limitation**: The routing threshold (t=0.8) is fixed and determined empirically on one dataset. There's no adaptive mechanism or analysis of how this generalizes across different datasets or evolving data distributions.

5. **Scalability Concerns**: 
   - The RAG component requires maintaining and searching an external database, adding complexity.
   - The Reflexion mechanism with multiple optimization trials could be computationally expensive.
   - No analysis of system performance under high-throughput scenarios typical in industrial settings.

6. **Incomplete Evaluation**:
   - Missing evaluation on truly imbalanced datasets that reflect real-world anomaly detection.
   - No latency analysis despite claiming real-time applicability.
   - Limited analysis of explainability quality despite this being a claimed benefit.
   - No comparison of small model architectures beyond Appendix B.

7. **Methodological Issues**:
   - The confidence calibration assumption may not hold across different model architectures and datasets.
   - The paper doesn't address how to determine optimal routing thresholds for new domains.
   - Limited discussion of how the method handles temporal dynamics in real deployment.

## Technical Comments

1. **Routing Strategy**: While using confidence scores for routing is reasonable, the paper would benefit from exploring more sophisticated routing mechanisms (e.g., learned routers, multi-criteria routing).

2. **RAG Implementation**: The cosine similarity-based retrieval is simplistic. More advanced semantic matching or learned retrieval methods could improve performance.

3. **Reflexion Usage**: The iterative self-correction mechanism seems over-engineered for binary classification tasks and may not provide sufficient benefits to justify the additional complexity.

## Minor Issues

- Some experimental details are relegated to appendices, making the main paper harder to evaluate completely.
- The writing could be more concise in places, particularly in the related work section.
- Figure 2 could be simplified for better clarity.

## Overall Assessment

While CHAD-LLM addresses a practical problem and shows promising experimental results, the contribution is primarily engineering-focused rather than methodologically novel. The experimental design has several limitations that undermine the strength of the conclusions, particularly the unrealistic balanced dataset assumption and unfair training data allocation. The paper would be significantly strengthened by more rigorous experimental design, comprehensive ablation studies, and evaluation on realistic imbalanced datasets.

The work represents a solid systems contribution but falls short of the standards expected for a top-tier research venue due to limited novelty and experimental rigor.

title: CHAD-LLM: Router-Guided Cost-Efficient Hybrid Anomaly Detection LLM
review:
The paper presents a router-guided pipeline to perform anomaly detection, where a "small model", which is a lightweight anomaly detection model, acts as a router by the act of prediction. Samples which have a high confidence score from the small model are returned directly, and samples which have a low confidence score (below a threshold t- here, 0.8) are routed to an LLM which is supported by Reflexion and RAG. The LLM is also shown to mitigate temporal distribution shifts, and provides natural language explanations. They use an architecture from Zhao et. al as the small model, but show experiments in the appendix that the pipeline is sensitive to the exact small model that is used, with the need for confidence quality, which is essential to the routing. The Large Model is finetuned using LoRA to inject domain knowledge. RAG is not used during finetuning, but used at inference to improve generalization. Reflexion is used to feedback self-correction. Experiments are performed on five datasets from the fraud detection benchmark from Kaggle, by using subsets due to resource constraints.

# Questions for the authors
1. The small model seems to be trained with 1000 samples, but the LLM is trained with 10,000. Have the authors experimented with increasing the number of samples the small model is trained with, seeing as for the "easy" cases, the small model achieves 96% accuracy, even if there is a bit of imbalance in classes by doing the expansion? By evening out the playing field, the small model may have a higher confidence score for more number of examples, reducing the cost further. What was the motivation behind this choice? 
2. For finetuning the LLM, injecting domain knowledge, are each of the cells in Table 1 finetuned using a different set of samples, or the final training samples are a combination of samples from the different domains?
3. Table 3 in the appendix shows that with a threshold of 19.1%, only 19.1% of the queries get routed to the Large model, with a high F1 score. Although, in the experiments section, it is mentioned that 50% of the queries are routed to the LLM. Is this due to a single dataset having low confidence for most samples, which is increasing the average number of queries being routed to the LLM? 
# Strengths
1. The method demonstrates a reduction in reliance on the LLM, cutting down inference costs without sacrificing performance, and has good results on performance compared to the baselines.
2. The paper clearly outlines the architecture, with rationale for most design choices and system components (small model, LLM, reflexion, RAG). 
3. Appendix contains detailed empirical analysis of why the routing threshold was picked as such, showing transparency in decision making.
# Weaknesses
1. There is a notable disparity/imbalance in training sample sizes between the small model (1000 samples) and the LLM (10000 samples). This raises concerns about whether it is a fair comparison, and if the small model could have been further improved with additional training samples.
2. Experiments are not complete - they are limited in scope, and not compared against any of the state of the art anomaly detection methods, thereby lacking the motivation or need for such a pipeline as described in the paper. There are other non-LLM based anomaly detection methods, which would have also reduced the cost just as much, rather than having a router and both small and large models.
3. The paper would benefit from a thorough ablation study, especially showing performance at two extremes: 0% routing (only small model) and 100% routing (only LLM). It is unclear how sensitive the pipeline is to the data itself.
4. The need for 10,000 examples for the LLM is still an unrealistic expectation in practical deployments, to reach the level of performance.

title: A Compliance-Preserving RAG Framework for Aircraft MRO Task Retrieval
review:
This paper tackles a compelling and highly practical challenge: enhancing information retrieval for aircraft maintenance technicians, a critical function in a safety-sensitive industry. Bringing such a domain-specific application to the research community is in itself a valuable contribution, offering a glimpse into the real-world challenges and opportunities for LLMs beyond conventional benchmarks. The framework's "compliance-preserving" design, which acts as an assistive layer without altering certified systems, is a particularly thoughtful and commendable approach that acknowledges crucial industry constraints. Furthermore, the effort to build a new benchmark, that includes realistic noise, demonstrates a solid understanding of the operational environment and strengthens the evaluation's practical relevance. These elements make the paper an interesting case study on applying modern retrieval techniques to a high-stakes field.

However, the paper's overall contribution is undermined by a lack of methodological novelty and insufficient validation. 

- The core technical pipeline—combining dense retrieval with LLM-based re-ranking—is a well-established pattern, limiting the work's academic originality to its application in a new domain. 
- More critically, the paper fails to provide convincing evidence of its practical value. The reported Hit@1 accuracy of 70-80%  begs the question of whether a system that fails one out of every four or five times is acceptable in an industry where precision is paramount. To be compelling for an industry audience, the work would need rigorous user acceptance studies or quantitative comparisons against the traditional workflows it aims to replace. 
- From an academic perspective, the analysis is superficial, missing the opportunity to investigate deeper questions, such as whether a large LLM is truly necessary or what the minimal model requirements are for this specific task. 

Consequently, the paper reads as an interesting proof-of-concept but falls short of delivering the deep insights or rigorous validation needed to be a significant contribution.

title: A Compliance-Preserving RAG Framework for Aircraft MRO Task Retrieval
review:
This paper proposes a compliance-preserving RAG framework for aircraft MRO. The architecture combines offline knowledge structuring from Aircraft manuals, with online dense retrieval and LLM-based re-ranking. The authors have framed the problem statement and need for such a system very clearly. It is understood to be a high stakes, and compliance driven domain where errors in lookup can be risky and costly. They also highlight the need for a fast retrieval system, and outline the value their system adds to the real-world time consuming processes. 

Pros:
1. Study shows strong empirical results on synthetic benchmarks (90%+ Hit@5).
2. The authors include noisy/typo-inclusive queries showing awareness of real-world needs of industry technician.
3. While algorithmically standard, the work is pioneering as the first compliance-preserving RAG framework in aviation industry.

Cons:
1. There could have been more experiment-backed reasoning behind choosing dense retrieval + LLM re-ranking + VLM extraction. Algorithmic novelty is still thin. The pipeline is standard; the contribution lies in domain-adaptation and deployment.
2. Being a case-study/industry relevant work, the paper does not provide testing on real human data. It would have been great if a sufficiently larger validation set was created in collaboration with domain-experts, to capture their real, industry used semantic variety beyond typing-errors and language.  
3. Most importantly, validation of synthetic queries seems inadequate for such a compliance driven industry. Although the data generation queries were built with guidance of domain experts, there is no solid evidence that GPT-generated queries match the technical complexity of real technician queries. A lexical complexity analysis on queries or distributional comparison would strengthen credibility.

title: A Compliance-Preserving RAG Framework for Aircraft MRO Task Retrieval
review:
In this paper, the authors proposed a compliance-preserving retrieval augmented generation framework tailored for aircraft maintenance, repair, and overhaul.
The main process on the proposed methods contains 2 parts: offline knowledge structuring stage and an online task retrieval stage. The offline knowledge structuring step generated embedding representation for both structured metadata and PDF manuals, linked via unique ATA task ID. In online retrieval stage, relevant retrieval tasks are re-ranked using LLMs.
The work of the paper is very clear, but it seems lack of innovation in the current contents of the paper. The authors said that it the first work of compliance-preserving retrieval augmented generation framework tailored for aircraft maintenance, repair, and overhaul. But, representation of structed data, PDF representation by visual language model and re-ranking using LLM are general ideas used in previous works. There is not enough introduction on the difficulty on the application of these ideas in aircraft maintenance domain.
To improve this work, more detailed innovation must be described clearly before it can be an acceptable paper. Here are some potential directions for further improving
1) The structing embedding methods: how the embedding methods different from previous methods used for structed data. Dense embeddings for chapter, sub-chapter, and task title are too general to be technical innovation.
2) The visual language model extraction for PDF: is there any specific design in this part? Capturing verbatim text and layout information into structured JSON records is also too general.
3) If the core creative point is the structure and pipeline design. There should be more theoretical analysis and experiment results on this part.

title: RLHF Algorithms Ranked: An Extensive Evaluation Across Diverse Tasks, Rewards, and Hyperparameters
review:

title: RLHF Algorithms Ranked: An Extensive Evaluation Across Diverse Tasks, Rewards, and Hyperparameters
review:
This paper provides an overview of how different RLHF algorithms compare when applied to the same Gemma-2B model, with a variety of hyperparameter modifications. This is a well motivated study, as a better understanding of how different algorithms compare is needed, and the variety of hyperparameters studied is a valuable addition. However, the presentation and analysis of results is somewhat lacking. While the results in figure 1 and tables 1 and 2 are discussed somewhat, the analysis does not go into much detail considering the amount of experimentation that was done, and figure 1 in particular is challenging to interpret due to the amount of performance curves that overlap with each other. Despite this, there is some unused space in the paper that could have gone toward more discussion of the results. Given space constraints, I would also recommend moving the descriptions of each algorithm to the appendix and using that space to discuss the results. Overall, while I think this is a valuable study, the presentation of the results needs improvement before the paper is ready for publication.

# Questions
1. How do algorithms compare across tasks? It appears that the winning algorithms are somewhat divergent across tasks as shown in Table 2, is there any reason for this?
2. What properties of the best performing algorithms make them stand out over others? Could this be related to the tasks studied or the model architecture used?
3. What implications does this study have for future algorithms? What properties should be prioritized?

title: RLHF Algorithms Ranked: An Extensive Evaluation Across Diverse Tasks, Rewards, and Hyperparameters
review:
The paper presents an extensive benchmarking study of seventeen state-of-the-art RLHF algorithms. The authors evaluate various RLHF algorithms in terms of performance across two benchmarks: OpenAI’s TL;DR Summarization and Anthropic’s Helpfulness / Harmfulness tasks. The study explores a range of RLHF algorithms, such as PPO, REINFORCE, DPO, GRPO, and others, to provide a comprehensive ranking. The study identifies several top-performing algorithms, including IPO, DPO, Reinforce, and GRPO, and provides specific hyperparameter settings that yield optimal results.


Pros:
1. The paper is clearly motivated and easy to follow.

2. The authors revisit and rigorously evaluate several RLHF algorithms, including simpler alternatives like REINFORCE and DPO. This approach contrasts with the previous focus on more complex methods like PPO. 

3. The paper excels in its hyperparameter optimization by consulting with the original authors of the algorithms to select the most promising configurations. 

Cons:

1. The evaluation is conducted on two tasks (TL;DR Summarization and Helpfulness/Harmfulness), which might limit the generalizability of the findings. The inclusion of a wider variety of task are encouraged for comprehensive evaluation.

2. A discussion on the cost-benefit trade-offs of such large-scale evaluations, as well as the potential for smaller-scale evaluations to achieve similar insights, could make the paper more relatable to a wider audience.

3. The study uses a base model with 2 billion parameters for all experiments. However, it would be insightful to see how the algorithms perform when scaled to larger models.

 4. The authors mention the issue of mode collapse and the vulnerability of some algorithms to reward hacking. However, they do not dive deeply into how different reward models influence algorithm performance. 

5. The study provides hyperparameter settings for each algorithm based on their evaluation. However, one concern is whether these settings are universally optimal or task-specific. How robust are these configurations across different datasets or domains? Could a different set of hyperparameters yield better results on more specialized tasks or with different LLM architectures?

6. It does not discuss the interpretability of the algorithms themselves. How interpretable are the decision-making processes of the top-performing algorithms? Can practitioners trust these models to align with human values and preferences, or do they exhibit behavior that is difficult to explain?

title: CRAB: A Benchmark for Evaluating Curation of Retrieval-Augmented LLMs in Biomedicine
review:
**Summary**:

This paper presents CRAB, a novel evaluation framework targeting retrieval-augmented large language models (RAG LLMs) in the biomedical domain. Unlike traditional evaluation approaches that focus on response-level fluency or factuality, CRAB shifts the evaluation unit to citation-level, allowing a fine-grained assessment of how well models curate and integrate relevant references. The authors propose three interpretable and scalable metrics—Reference Precision (RP), Irrelevance Suppression (IS), and Curation Efficiency (CE)—to quantify curation performance via F1 scores. Experimental results across several mainstream LLMs show substantial performance variation, underscoring the need for improved biomedical curation capabilities.

**Strengths**:

1. The paper introduces a citation-level evaluation paradigm, addressing a critical blind spot in current LLM evaluation—how effectively models curate relevant references rather than merely generating fluent or factually correct text.

2. The proposed RP, IS, and CE metrics are both interpretable and scalable, enabling large-scale benchmarking of model performance in a more fine-grained manner than traditional approaches.

3. The experiments are thorough, providing detailed analysis of different models' performance across multiple languages and various query types. Additionally, metrics such as entity recall, entity precision, and query entity coverage are used effectively to assess how well the LLMs utilize the references.

**Weaknesses**:

1. The paper does not clarify whether the references used for evaluation appear in the LLMs' training corpora. If they do, the evaluation might overestimate model performance. The authors should discuss the risk of training data leakage and how it may impact the validity of the curation evaluation.

2. For each query, the setup involves selecting exactly 2 relevant and 3 irrelevant references. While this ensures consistency, it may be too rigid and not reflective of real-world scenarios. A more diverse sampling strategy, possibly varying the number or ratio of relevant/irrelevant references while keeping total numbers constant, could enhance robustness and generalizability.

title: CRAB: A Benchmark for Evaluating Curation of Retrieval-Augmented LLMs in Biomedicine
review:
This paper introduces the Curation of Retrieval-Augmented LLMs in Biomedicine (CRAB) benchmark, a significant contribution to the community. It addresses a critical aspect of RAG systems: their "curation" ability, defined as a model's capacity to discern relevant information from a set of sources while ignoring irrelevant content. This skill is vital in high-stakes domains like biomedicine. CRAB is the first multilingual benchmark (English, French, German, Chinese) designed specifically to evaluate this capability.

The authors propose a novel citation-based verification method to quantify relevance precision, irrelevance suppression, and overall curation efficiency. The reliability of this automated approach was confirmed by a human evaluation, which showed a strong correlation.

A wide range of LLMs were tested, revealing varied performance and language-specific strengths. Notably, models specifically fine-tuned for reasoning showed degraded performance, a phenomenon the authors attribute to "overthinking".

While the work is impressive, there is still room for further development. The evaluation uses a fixed ratio of relevant to irrelevant sources (2 vs. 3); studying variable ratios would be a valuable extension. Additionally, promising results on improving curation through fine-tuning, currently in the appendix, deserve more prominence in the main text.

Ultimately, this paper delivers a methodologically robust and significant benchmark. By giving the community a vital tool to measure source curation, CRAB directly supports the creation of more dependable RAG systems for biomedicine.

title: CRAB: A Benchmark for Evaluating Curation of Retrieval-Augmented LLMs in Biomedicine
review:
**Summary**  
The paper introduces a novel benchmark for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based large language models (LLMs) in the biomedical domain. The benchmark is multilingual and citation-based, aiming to assess how effectively LLMs utilize grounding data. The task is well-motivated, the methodology is clearly defined, and the authors commit to releasing source code and data to support reproducibility. Performance results for multiple state-of-the-art LLMs are reported, accompanied by detailed analysis and examples.

**Strengths**  

- The paper addresses an important and timely challenge: evaluating how LLMs leverage external grounding data in biomedical contexts.  
- The benchmark is multilingual and citation-based, which adds realism and diversity to the evaluation.  
- The authors provide detailed implementation information and commit to releasing data and code, enhancing reproducibility.  
- Performance comparisons across multiple LLMs are included.  
- A thorough error analysis is conducted, offering insights.

**Weaknesses**  

- **Reference Selection Criteria**: The method for selecting the top *N* references is unclear. The paper does not specify what *N* is, nor does it provide statistics such as the mean and standard deviation of *N* across queries. If the cut-off is based on the score threshold. It is not clear what the threshold is.
- **Realism of Dataset**: The benchmark assumes that each grounding set contains at least two relevant and three non-relevant references. However, the non-relevant references are retrieved using related queries, which raises concerns about whether they might actually be relevant in real-world applications. This could affect the validity of the benchmark.  
- **Minor Language Issues**: There are several typographical errors, such as:  
  - Line 132: “peresent the proposed...”  
  - Line 413: “Finally, We...”

**Suggestions for Improvement**  

- Clarify the reference selection process, including how *N* is determined and provide descriptive statistics.  
- Justify the construction of the grounding sets and discuss the implications of potentially relevant “non-relevant” references.  
- Correct typographical errors and ensure consistency in writing style.

title: Incremental Summarization for Customer Support via Progressive Note-Taking and Agent Feedback
review:
This paper proposed an incremental summarization system for agent-client conversations, where it takes chat messages and other contexts as input to incrementally add additional notes/bullets to previously generated ones. The system further take the agent edits as feedbacks to automatically improve the model performance via preference learning.  Experiments with offline model evaluation and online impact analysis show the effectiveness of proposed system compared to baselines. 

Pros:
1. The paper is well written and organized. The structure is very easy to follow. The details of the proposed method is well presented, raise it reproducibility and generalizability to other use cases. 

2. The proposed method was deployed and evaluated in real prod environment, show its practical success. 

Cons: 
1. The novelty of the proposed method is somewhat limited.  Incremental summarization, and learning from human feedback with preference learning are the two claimed contribution. The related work should discuss the related work of this.  The novel part could come from overall system design perspective. 

2. the motivation of automatic note taking in agent-client conversation is not clear.  The agent often have a good mental map of what has been communicated, not sure whether read, review/edit the summary notes would even slow down their response. title: Incremental Summarization for Customer Support via Progressive Note-Taking and Agent Feedback
review:
# Review
The paper presents a deployed architecture for generating summaries of customer support interactions. The proposed workflow, which uses two LLM agents and a classifier, offers an alternative to directly feeding entire customer interactions into a single model. The process decomposes summary generation into three iterative stages: 1) an LLM generates new bullet points or blanks for each input, 2) a fine-tuned DeBERTa classifier labels and filters these bullet points, and 3) a "review agent" revises the updated summary to correct any errors. This data can then serve as preference data for future model training.

The paper is well-written and contains interesting ideas. It demonstrates methodological rigour and provides lots of information for analysis. However, I find that the main contributions aren't fully supported by the evidence presented. It's unclear how the proposed approach is significantly better than the baseline fine-tuned model. In the offline experiments in tables 2-4 it indeed does score the highest, however, these scores fall within the confidence intervals of the baseline models - thus we have no statistically significant difference.

Similarly, for the online experiments I have some issues with the 2 main claims. **For the reported 3% reduction in working time** (9% for complex cases) lacks sufficient context to assess its significance - especially when simple inference changes yield 20% efficiency gains. It might be worth including metrics like cost reduction or token usage which might better illuminate the importance but as a reader it is not clear why this is a significant improvement. **Regarding user satisfaction**, I am missing some sort of comparison. The results in Section 5.3.3 don't appear to include a comparison with the control group, making it impossible to determine whether the high numbers are an improvement over an existing system.

Generally, I enjoyed reading the paper and reflecting on the proposed workflow. Despite my concerns about the evidence supporting the main claims, I found the analysis comprehensive. The paper would generally be improved if claims where clearly supported by evidence and written in a way that helps the reader understand the practical benefits of adopting this architecture.

title: IPR: Intelligent Prompt Routing with User-Controlled Quality-Cost Trade-offs
review:
## 1. Nature of the Contribution
- This paper is clearly in the deployed system/infrastructure innovation category. It addresses a real production challenge: automatically routing prompts to the most cost-efficient LLM while meeting user-defined quality constraints. The work combines:
    - A modular routing architecture with a quality estimator and model-specific adapters.
    - A user-tunable cost-quality trade-off parameter (τ).
    - An industrial-scale benchmark (IPRBench) with 1.5M annotated prompts.
    - Production deployment results on a major cloud platform with substantial cost savings.

## 2. Real-world Impact & Novelty
Impact: The deployment results are compelling, 25.5 to 43.9% cost savings while keeping quality comparable to the strongest model, sub-150 ms latency, and millions of live requests routed. This is a meaningful contribution to large-scale LLM service operations.

### Novelty:
- Not in creating a new ML model type, but in integrating scalable, latency-constrained quality prediction into production routing, with adapters for rapid new-model onboarding.
- The tolerance parameter offers explicit, continuous control to users, a gap in existing systems that often use fixed thresholds.
- The IPRBench dataset is itself an asset to the community (pending legal release).
- Compared to prior work like RouteLLM, HybridLLM, and GraphRouter, this system offers finer-grained quality prediction, better extensibility, and stronger real-world validation.

## 3. Technical Quality & Clarity
### Strengths:
- Solid formal problem formulation (constrained optimization with predicted quality).
- Clear separation of quality estimation, decision logic, and model registry modules.
- Detailed experimental setup and ablation studies.
- Transparent latency and deployment metrics.
- Clarity: The paper is well-structured, though some descriptions (e.g., reward model calibration and Bounded-ARQGC definition) could be shortened in the main text and moved to appendices to help readability.

### Methodology rigor:
- Uses large-scale supervised training with calibrated reward model labels, validated against human preference rankings (85% agreement).
- Provides multiple baselines, including static, random, and strong prior work.
- Evaluates both quality estimation accuracy and end-to-end routing performance.

## 4. Common Pitfalls Check
- Research question clarity: Very clear, optimize LLM routing for cost while meeting user-defined quality tolerance.
- Overclaiming: Generally avoided. Claims about cost savings and latency are tied to the presented metrics. Some generalization statements (e.g., applicability to “diverse business requirements”) could be slightly toned down until tested beyond Claude/Llama/Nova.
- Evidence support: Strong, though additional cross-platform or cross-domain validation would strengthen claims.
- Ethics: Data privacy and licensing considerations are mentioned indirectly (release pending legal approval), but no deep dive on potential biases in reward model labeling — worth at least acknowledging bias risks.

## 5. Reproducibility & Transparency
Positive: Architecture, training procedure, and evaluation metrics are described in detail. Integration process for new models is well-documented.

### Limitations:
- IPRBench is not yet released, reproducibility hinges on that.
- Reward model details are given, but if it’s proprietary or fine-tuned internally, replicating results externally may be challenging.
- Cost calculations are transparent (with Amazon Bedrock pricing table).

## 6. Broader Context & Related Work
- Related work section is thorough, citing major routing approaches from 2023 to 2025.
- Paper positions itself well in the context of prior routing solutions, highlighting differences in scale, extensibility, and latency.
- Could also briefly mention broader cost-aware inference literature outside LLM routing (to contextualize optimization frameworks).

## 7. Constructive Feedback
### Strengths
- Industrial relevance with production deployment results.
- Strong empirical evaluation on a large, realistic dataset.
- User-controlled quality-cost slider is both intuitive and impactful.
- Modular design that supports rapid model onboarding.
- Well-designed benchmark (IPRBench) that could become a standard.

### Weaknesses / Areas to Improve
- Dataset Release: The usefulness of IPRBench to the community is contingent on timely public release and clear licensing.
- Bias & Fairness: Need explicit discussion of possible biases from reward model–based labeling, especially since it guides routing decisions in production.
- Generality: Only tested on Claude, Llama, and Nova families; broader validation (e.g., mixing open-source and proprietary models, multilingual settings) would strengthen claims.
- User Study: While human preference alignment is tested, an evaluation of how actual end-users perceive the cost-quality slider in practice could be insightful.
- Session Context: The current routing is per-prompt; session-aware routing (noted in limitations) could be explored in future work.

title: IPR: Intelligent Prompt Routing with User-Controlled Quality-Cost Trade-offs
review:
We present IPR—a quality-constrained Intelligent Prompt Routing framework that dynamically selects optimal models based on predicted response quality and user-specified tolerance levels.

(1) a modular architecture with lightweight quality estimators trained on 1.5M prompts annotated with calibrated quality scores, enabling finegrained quality prediction across model families; (2) a user-controlled routing mechanism with tolerance parameter τ ∈ [0, 1] that provides explicit control over quality-cost tradeoffs; and (3) an extensible design using frozen encoders with model-specific adapters, reducing new model integration from days to hours.

The paper also curates an industrial-level dataset IPRBench1, a comprehensive benchmark containing 1.5 million examples with response quality annotations across 11 LLM candidates.

Instead of optimizing the model accuracy, the proposed method (1) filter candidates meeting quality tolerance, (2) select the most cost-efficient qualified model.

Strengthes:

1. LLM routing with optimized accuracy and cost is an important topic.

2. The proposed method by setting a quality (model accuracy) tolerance, then route to the model with lowest cost is an interesting idea.

3. Many experiments are provided.

Weaknesses:

1. How is the router latency and inference latency? Where shows efficiency with sub-150ms routing decisions?

2. The experiments are mainly on family-specific routers. In Appendix H, Family-Specific vs. Unified Routing are provided but not very clear. Could the authors elaborate more on why not a router for all models?

3. An algorithm table to show the routing process can be very helpful.

4. How is the performance of the adapter to new models?

5. Why using Prompt Encoder + LLM Identity Encoder, then concat to a MLP?

title: Grammatical Error Correction via Preference Alignment in Large Language Models
review:
This paper proposes and experiments with a novel way to tune LLMs for GEC, improving on the limitations of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and seeing some promising results for Chinese, with more modest/unclear results for English.

I appreciated the very solid explanation of the state of research in this area, the reason why SFT is not ideal (overcorrections, etc.), and the reasoning for why the authors' approach to fine-tuning makes more sense. I also thought the experiments were thorough and the findings were well explained. The work is very good in terms of reproducibility, as well as clarity & structure.

In terms of novelty and impact, this work feels a bit lower. Is this a practical innovation that will have an impact on industry use cases? I'm not sure, as LLM-based techniques are still not close to state-of-the-art for English, and the results presented here for English aren't convincing that there's much improvement, despite what the authors say in the conclusion. See https://nlpprogress.com/english/grammatical_error_correction.html and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.14914, where LLM-based methods are shown to not be competitive on their own with state-of-the-art methods, and moreover the best LLM-based FT methods achieve in the low 70s in F-Score (Chat-LLaMa-2 with fine tuning). A small improvement of 57 to 58 F-Score using PRPO vs. the baseline is hard to see impact-wise. For Chinese, I appreciate that the results do show that this helps get closer to the state of the art.

While not something to penalize, I also didn't find this to paper to have a strong fit with the Industry Track, as it is a normal research paper that could have been submitted to a non-Industry track. There is no mention of impact to industry, use of industry-specific data, or an intent to build an application, etc.

title: Grammatical Error Correction via Preference Alignment in Large Language Models
review:
The paper claims to address the over-correction issue in grammatical error correction (GEC) that happens with the use of large generative language models which makes them lag behind in performance compared to traditional sequence labelling and encoder-decoder approaches. To this end, they propose a modification of the Odds Ratio Preference Optimization (ORPO) technique, named Probability Ratio Preference Optimization (PRPO) along with a two-stage inference framework that does correctness judgment followed by correction only if the input is deemend in correct. The paper shows improvement in Chinese and English GEC tasks.

**Strengths**

* The paper addresses a relevant problem related to over-correction of LLMs in GEC

* The two-stage inference strategy is interesting and saves significant inference time for GEC in scenarios where the errors are sparse.


**Weaknesses**

* The learning objective of PRPO is strikingly close to Contrastive Preference Optimization (CPO) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08417). Details of differences to this has to be explained and a comparison be made to this method.

* It is not clear how replacing odds ratio with probability ratio addresses the over-correction issue. While results show that there is an increase in Precision and Recall compared to ORPO, there is not much difference compared to SFT baseline.

* Other popular preference optimization like DPO is not included in comparison and also other work that used a similar detection-correction paradigm and those that addresses reduction of over-correction (e.g. https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.96.pdf). 

* GEC papers have used LLama3 and other recent LLMs as baselines. This paper relies on older and possibly weaker baselines compared to those that have been used recently

* The manuscript has numerous typographic and writing errors that needs careful revision.

title: Grammatical Error Correction via Preference Alignment in Large Language Models
review:
The paper presents a fine-tuning approach for LLMs for GEC named Probability Preference Optimisation (PRPO). The approach combines the standard SFT loss with an odds ratio between the fluent and ungrammatical sentence and splits the training into a 2-stage approach of first detecting grammatical errors and then correcting them. The papers shows empirical experiments on several GEC datasets an shows improvements of the method over SFT.


Strength
========
- The motivation to split GEC into a detection and correction approach, similar to human processing, is intuitive
- The odds ratio in PRPO reflects the intuition that a sentence should be corrected if there is sentence which is relatively "better" than the uncorrected sentence but the sentence should not be overcorrected 
- The experimental results show an improvement of the PRPO method over SFT, resulting in results similar to SOTA for Chinese


Weakness
=========
- The paper is submitted to the industry track but there is no industry flavour, except the general relevance of GEC to language learning apps. There are no reports about real-world usage or practical challenges in practice. In its current form, the paper would better be suited to the general track

title: Leveraging Product Catalog Patterns for Multilingual E-commerce Product Attribute Prediction
review:
This paper introduces PatternRAG, a retrieval-augmented system designed to improve the prediction of missing structured attributes (like color, material, etc.) in multilingual e-commerce product catalogs. Instead of relying on general knowledge or external sources, PatternRAG strategically retrieves similar products from within the same catalog using a BM25 search engine. These retrieved examples are then used as in-context prompts for a large language model (Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct) to accurately generate missing attribute values.

Strengths:
- Leverages Internal Catalog Knowledge:
By retrieving similar products within the same catalog, PatternRAG makes use of existing attribute patterns and conventions that are highly relevant for accurate attribute prediction.

- Scalable:
PatternRAG is built on scalable, production-ready technologies (BM25, Lucene, and open-source LLMs), ensuring feasibility for large, real-world catalogs with millions of entries.

- Significant Improvements in Data Quality:
The approach demonstrates gains in attribute recall, catalog completeness, and overall data correctness, especially in non-English markets where LLMs often struggle.

Weaknesses:
- Over-Reliance on Simple Heuristics:
The system’s heavy reliance on glance views (popularity) and brand alignment for reranking assumes that popular or same-brand products are always the best references. This may not generalize well to other domains or catalogs where popularity does not guarantee attribute correctness, potentially limiting broader applicability.

- Lexical Retrieval Limitations:
By relying exclusively on BM25 for retrieval, the system can miss semantically similar products whose titles use different words or phrases. A more meaningful evaluation would include a comparison of different retrieval approaches, such as sparse (BM25) versus dense (neural embedding-based) retrieval, as well as an exploration of different retrieval models, to assess which strategies yield the best examples for attribute prediction.

- No LLM Fine-Tuning or Domain Adaptation:
The use of an out-of-the-box Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct model, without any domain-specific fine-tuning or adaptation, may constrain the ultimate accuracy of predictions. Fine-tuning on catalog data or in-domain examples could potentially yield stronger results. It would be particularly valuable to show a direct comparison between the untuned baseline and a fine-tuned version of the model, to clarify the added benefit of in-domain adaptation versus prompt engineering alone.

- Dependence on Catalog Size and Density:
The approach is effective only in mature, dense catalogs with many well-annotated entries. In new categories, niche markets, or sparse catalogs, the method will have poor coverage, as few or no suitable few-shot examples may be available. It would be valuable to see experiments that explore system performance across catalogs of different sizes and annotation densities, to better understand its limitations and scalability.

- Overall, narrow experimental scope:
The experiments are narrowly focused, primarily comparing PatternRAG to a single base prompting approach, rather than exploring the performance of different system variants or retrieval strategies. The analysis would be more meaningful if it included ablations such as comparing various retrieval methods (e.g., BM25 vs. neural retrieval), assessing the impact of LLM fine-tuning versus prompt engineering, and evaluating performance across catalogs of different sizes and annotation densities.

title: Leveraging Product Catalog Patterns for Multilingual E-commerce Product Attribute Prediction
review:
Summary -
Products with missing important structured attributes is a practical challenge in real world information retrieval systems. This paper discusses a multi-stage retrieval framework for predicting such missing attributes using few shot examples of similar products from the catalog. Proposed design is evaluated against a basic prompt based approach showing improvement in attribute level Precision, Recall and catalog level Completeness and Correctness.

Strengths -
1. Paper demonstrates a practical approach for knowledge retrieval systems by providing relevant few shot examples generated using hybrid search.
2. It provides concise, easy to follow explanation of system design, experiment set up and results.
3. Paper provides a novel approach for missing attribute prediction problem which is potentially generalizable beyond discussed E-commerce problem space.

Areas of improvements / Weaknesses -
1. Paper provides an incremental improvements over existing RAG based methods. Integration of external knowledge from trustworthy, latest knowledge sources is not a novel idea anymore. Instead, retrieval of relevant, accurate external knowledge backed by thorough ablation studies could have been novel and helpful. It discusses basic retriever methods followed by heuristic-based reranking with no detailed analysis, ablation results of effectiveness of these components.
2. Paper explains effectiveness of this system in multilingual environments as one of the contributions. However, it lacks more details on this. Multistage retrieval seems to be localized for each language (US, DE, ES) using language specific search indices. It doesn't seem to collect few shot examples from other languages if necessary.
3. Results show better improvement in Recall compared to Precision. FR seems to show significantly better results compared to other two languages. More explanation on these results and metrics would be helpful to understand root causes and future improvements.
4. Decision to use BM25 for operational efficiency is understandable but some commentary on whether it's at the cost of search quality could be useful.
5. Paper can be further improved with experiments with open source datasets and related research, eg, MAVEQA. It would help to reproduce similar results and reuse proposed system design in other problem spaces.
6. Minor feedback - Paper sometimes make a confusing claim that PatternRAG is not dependent on external knowledge bases. From RAG perspective product catalog is also an external knowledge base separate from model's implicit knowledge, isn't it?

title: Node-Level Uncertainty Estimation in LLM-Generated SQL
review:
This paper introduces an error detection model for LLM-generated SQL queries through estimation of uncertainty at the node level of the tree structure converted from the generated SQL. By automatically constructing the training examples from the generated SQL queries and their corresponding gold SQL queries, the paper presents an algorithm for matching those structures and estimating the correctness of the queries at the node level. Experimental results show better performance of the presented method than the baseline uncertainty model based on log probabilities.

While the overall ideas are well-motivated, there are lots of uncertain points in the paper:

-	The objective of the method is to estimate the uncertainty of each node in the generated SQL, and on lines 160 – 161, there is a mention of “node-level probability”. However, what is estimated by the proposed method is whether a node is correct or incorrect. It is not clear what is really estimated.
-	The semantic equivalence of nodes is first defined on page 3, lines 203-239, then the details are explained on pages 3 and 4, lines 242-292. The item numbers of those parts do not correspond to each other, which makes it quite puzzling.
-	On lines 236-237, it is first explained that no penalty is put on the generated query when there are omissions. There is no explanation why no penalty is given. Is it fine that fewer generative results are estimated with fewer errors? Please explain the rationale behind this.
-	Lines 238-239: This sentence is difficult to understand. There is no “new” in the given example. It is also not clear why it is labeled as correct in the later step.
-	Lines 293-318: The details of the post-processing are not clear. If it conducts context-agnostic matching between the nodes in the given SQLs, it will produce a larger number of matches, and all the correct matchings will cover all the matched nodes in the first recursive matching process. It is not clear why “the first pass is not redundant (lines 304-305)”.
-	After defining the features, it is not clear what model is used to train the estimator of the node correctness in the LLM-generated SQLs. There is no description of the training process.
-	The paper is premature in the current format as it ends with the experimental section, and no concluding section is presented.

title: Node-Level Uncertainty Estimation in LLM-Generated SQL
review:
The paper presents a practical framework for detecting errors in an LLM-generated SQL query by estimating uncertainty at the level of individual nodes in their Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).

**strengths**: The node-level probability serves as a direct measure of uncertainty, pinpointing the specific parts of the query that are likely incorrect. 

**weaknesses**: A comprehensive framework diagram may be required to illustrate the complete methodology.

title: Node-Level Uncertainty Estimation in LLM-Generated SQL
review:
The paper proposes a practical framework for detecting errors in an LLM-generated SQL query by estimating uncertainty at the level of individual nodes in their Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) consisting of 2 steps: 1) a semantically aware algorithm for labeling nodes in a generated SQL as correct or incorrect given a ground truth SQL, and 2) featurizing individual nodes based on a rich set of schema-aware and lexical features, and use them to train a model to identify erroneous nodes. This approach yields significantly better AUC (+27.44%) than log-probability.

- The paper does NOT have a Conclusion section, what is the take-home message?
- Parsing generated SQL and ground-truth SQL to AST representation and compare their tree structures are not novel (see https://github.com/eosphoros-ai/sqlgpt-parser, https://openreview.net/pdf?id=0XBuaxqEcG )
