title: Predicting Recurring Trends in Microblogs
review:
The paper reports on experiments on a task of "trend recurrence" prediction in microblogs, and encompasses: (a) detection whether a trend will reappear, and (b) predicting when it will re-emerge. A method is propsed which exploits a hybrid set of features, including: temporal dynamics, text content features, external signals, user profile characteristics, query logs, etc. The authors compare this method vis-a-vis other approaches on a dataset sampled from X platform in Japanese language. An ablation study is provided too.
  
Strengths:

- in general the manuscript is clearly written and well structured

- motivation of the industrial use case is well explained

- meaningful comparison of other type of approaches for the task at hand is provided

- the findings, although not too influential, might constitute information which might come in handy for practitioners 

Weaknesses:

- given the experimental set up, including one specific dataset and one language, little is said about generalizability of the approach (this aspect is embraced in the Limitations section, but the main findings in the introduction/conclusions should be played down accordingly)

- some details related to experiment set-up are not fully clear

- no information on the performance on specific classes/labels for ALL approaches is provided (only for the "Proposed" approach)

- sometimes the claims made sound bigger than the evidence provided in the paper

Some questions and suggestions:

1) For the sake of completeness I would suggest to include the performance figures for all classes, and in particular for the "recurring" class, for all methods tested. Macro-averaging that you use to compare all methods does not constitute the best indicator of what is best
in my opinion. The focus should be on the recurring class.

2) It is a known fact that LLMs may underperform vis-a-vis other methods on text classification tasks, however, you make a statement in line 417/418 that based on your experiments "LLMs do not perform well in classification tasks", which sound stronger than the evidence you provide. You only explored one model, namely, gpt40.

3) It is unclear from the manuscript how you split the dataset into train/test and whether you run cross-fold validation, etc.

4) You mention rule-based approaches being ineffective. Could you provide a reference to support this claim?

5) I would clarify a bit more how you define that a trend re-emerges. How did you compute it? It is just a technical detail, but some more information on this apsect would benefit improved readability

title: Predicting Recurring Trends in Microblogs
review:
This paper proposed a new task of predicting "recurring trends" in microblogs, specifically X (x.com), to identify trends that are useful for business planning in various industries. The authors attempt to solve this problem by reducing it to a classification task. Given a trend name, their approach is to devise several features for the classification including temporal frequency of posts in X, textual content of the posts, user profiles of X for the posts, and features from search queries on a proprietary search engine related to the trend name. Experimental results show that the proposed classifier outperforms several baselines including in-context learning by GPT-4o.
    
The problem setting itself is likely to be interesting to practitioners in many business domains. The first and biggest concern is that the problem setting heavily depends on a specific platform, that is, X, in terms that when a word appears as a trend is determined by the proprietary algorithm of the platform, as the authors write in the subsection 3.1. This means that the authors try to predict trends words as if they were stocks expected to rise in the future. Since there would be many factors that affect the trend words and are not observed directly, for example via advertising strategies by companies, I wonder if this task should be regarded as anomaly detection rather than classification.

The reason why both the proposed approach of using a classifier with various features and baselines including an LLM (GPT-4o) work to some extent may lie in the balance of positive and negative examples. According to Table 1, the ratio of positive (recur) and negative (non-recur) examples is $9810:42103$ $\\fallingdotseq$ $1:4.3$, which is imbalanced but not to a significant degree. If, as the authors pointed out in the bottom of the subsection 4.4, some words are strong signals of trend like update, next week, etc., then the task would be easy for a sophisticated classification algorithm (such as gradient boosting trees that the authors use) to find those clues from training data as there is a certain amount of positive data to learn it. So, I think it would be beneficial to readers of this paper if more information is provided as to how many trends are associated with such strong signals and how many are not.
  
In practical terms, the classifier cannot be considered very useful unless the performance for positive (recur) cases is sufficiently high. From Table 4, (Precision, Recall) = (66.15, 52.74). I would like to understand if this performance is sufficient for the use cases that the authors have in mind.

As for reproducibility, I would say that this work cannot be reproducible because search query logs are not available at all. From Table 5, search queries play an important role in performance as the authors claim.

title: AI Agent for Abbreviation and Acronym Expansion Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models and LLM-as-a-Judge
review:
Lack of Clear Contributions:
The paper does not explicitly define its novel contributions, making it difficult to assess how the work advances the field. The authors should clearly articulate what distinguishes their research from prior work.

Insufficient Evaluation of Proposed Framework:
The framework is introduced but not rigorously analyzed. A systematic comparison with baseline methods (e.g., through ablation studies or theoretical justification) is needed to demonstrate its advantages and limitations

Weak Empirical Validation:
The results lack robust scientific evaluation. Key metrics, statistical significance tests, or comparative benchmarks are missing and inadequately discussed. 

Other Issues:
There is significant confusion of term datasets vs data samples throughout the text.

title: AI Agent for Abbreviation and Acronym Expansion Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models and LLM-as-a-Judge
review:
**Summary**  

The paper presents an approach for exact mapping between acronyms/abbreviations and their corresponding longforms using a large language model (LLM) combined with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). While the task is relevant and the use of LLMs is promising, the paper suffers from significant clarity and completeness issues. The definition of the AI agent is vague, many methodological details are missing, and the experimental results lack both qualitative and quantitative depth.

**Strengths**  
- The task of extracting and expanding acronyms/abbreviations from domain-specific corpora is important and well-motivated.  
- Leveraging LLMs for this task is a novel and potentially impactful direction.

**Weaknesses**  
- **Lack of Baselines and Analysis**: The paper does not include comparisons with existing methods or baselines. There is also no detailed qualitative or quantitative analysis to support the claims.  
- **Missing Component Analysis**: The impact of individual components (e.g., RAG, post-processing) is not analyzed.  
- **Insufficient Methodological Detail**:  
  - The process for creating and representing RAG data is unclear. For example, Appendix A provides a JSON snippet, but the method for generating such data is not described. E.g. Term: "RL and AGG, and Context: "AGG_SCORE_FOR_RL, This column represents ..."; however, it is not clear how these RAG data are prepared.
  - Section 3.3 mentions a post-processing step, but its implementation and motivation are not explained.  
- **Clarity and Terminology**: The paper is difficult to follow. Key concepts, such as the definition and role of the “AI agent,” are not clearly introduced or explained.

title: AI Agent for Abbreviation and Acronym Expansion Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models and LLM-as-a-Judge
review:
The paper describes a framework for the automatic identification and expansion of abbreviations and acronyms in legacy and closed-system environments.
The authors argue in favour of a RAG style prompts using the term RAG in an inappropriate way. Rather, they provide a context for their prompts.
Some simple rules for postprossessing are provided. A second LLM prompt is used to assess the previous results.
The authors used 377k records from the most commonly used data tables and documents from a financial organisation and, using the Oxford 3000 word list as a reference, identified 185k records that contained at least one word that was not included in the Oxford 3000 list. The authors extracted abbreviation-related content from these records. In the 185k records, a total of 522k words were found that could be considered abbreviations or acronyms.
Although there is a part on methodology, it is very simple. Far more sophisticated mathematical methods can be used to solve the problems described by the authors. In addition, the financial dataset is copyrighted and the work presented cannot be replicated.
The authors are aware of some limitations of their work, as only a single financial dataset and only the Llama 3.1-8b model were used, so no real comparison is possible. Haoeevewr, awareness has not mitigated the limitations.
Most likely, the work presented is a real application, but hardly reproducible. Also, the practical innovation and applicability in industry is not clear.

title: GRAFT: A Graph-based Flow-aware Agentic Framework for Document-level Machine Translation
review:
well-written paper that uses an agentic, lower-cost LLM pipeline in an industry-applicable setting for machine-translating entire documents, including discourse structure.

strengths:
* important problem: how to better machine-translate entire documents with correct pronoun resolution and terminological consistency, etc.
* thorough experimentation and analysis
* provides the entire code and data already on an anonymized platform

weaknesses:
* a lot of sections (like related work, further results analysis and important examples) are put to the appendix. normally not too worrisome but this case is a bit extreme and could be regarded as "cheating" around the paper page limit. 
* while there is quite thorough analysis already, i would have wished for details around error propagation, e.g. what happens for a translation if there is a mistake already in the discourse graph representation etc.
* how many iterations and tuning did the few-shot and other prompting take? how robust are they?

typos:
* page 1: figure 1 is not referenced from the text, while figure 2 is? and/or maybe also mention that figure 2 is only to be found in the appendix; i was surprised by that
* page 6: the results of the En -> Ru analysis on discourse phenomena is presented in table 3, not 2

title: GRAFT: A Graph-based Flow-aware Agentic Framework for Document-level Machine Translation
review:
The authors propose GRAFT, a graph-based framework for document machine translation framework (DocMT). The framework models a document as a graph of interdependent sentences, so that the translation process can account for document-level context and coherence.


GRAFT is evaluated against both sentence- and document-level baselines and is shown to have higher BLEU scores, especially for language pairs, such as English to Chinese, with complex discourse phenomena.




Originality


Envisioning DocMT as a graph flow framework is novel.




Clarity


The motivation, of why sentence-level MT fails to capture document-level discourse, is strong.






Pros


Novel approach to DocMT.
Strong evidence shown that GRAFT improves DocMT




Cons


Lack of related work. Without the limited work and a comparison of GRAFT with latest DocMT models, it is difficult to properly evaluate the claims of the paper.
Limited analysis. .The interpretation of results is brief and a more linguistic error analysis (e.g., pronoun resolution, NER translation) would be beneficial.

title: GRAFT: A Graph-based Flow-aware Agentic Framework for Document-level Machine Translation
review:
This work introduces a framework for improved document-level machine translation. 
The framework consists of multiple agents. Each of these agents has a different task, such as segmenting the document into smaller chunks, modeling the dependencies between those chunks and translating the resulting graph into a target document. 
The last step additionally employs a memory agent for extracting local memory from each discourse. 
All agents are LLM-based using a few-shot prompting strategy. 

The authors provide many details and ablations (in particular in the appendix), including a human evaluation.
I also appreciate that results beyond BLEU and COMET are provided. 
While comparisons of non-LLM-based segmentation and edge construction strategies are provided, an ablation for the translation agent is missing. In general, I am wondering how GRAFT compares against an LLM which has been fine-tuned for document-level machine translation (e.g. based on Qwen and Llama).
Furthermore, I would appreciate significance tests (e.g. Table 1, best performing system 1-7 vs. GRAFT).

title: Conformal Guardrails: Building Safer AI in Low-Resource Indian Languages
review:
## Summary
The authors examine the use of automatic pipelines for pseudo-labeling combined with conformal prediction to enhance guardrail systems for low-resource Indian languages. Their experiments indicate that applying more advanced filtering methods improves performance across all tested languages.

## Strengths
- The writing is generally clear, particularly in the earlier sections, where the authors situate their work well within the context of existing research.

## Weaknesses
- Based on my understanding, the test set appears to be drawn from the same distribution as the training data. For a more robust evaluation, the authors should also include datasets from outside the distribution to measure generalization.
- The authors claim that their results are significant (Line 351). However, it is unclear how they reached this conclusion, as no statistical significance testing is reported.
- The novelty of the work is limited, and the results are somewhat expected, especially when using an in-distribution test set. A deeper investigation into questions such as dataset quality, and evidence that the improvements are due to better data quality rather than unrelated factors, would strengthen the work. Discussion of potential shortcomings of the proposed system is also missing.

## Comments and Suggestions
- The text should remain understandable even if all citation parentheses are removed. For example, in Line 099, using `\citet` would be more appropriate. In Line 159, placing two parentheses side-by-side is awkward; consider using `\citealp` and adjusting the formatting as needed.
- The quality of Figure 1 is low; consider using a higher-resolution or alternative file format.
- In Line 302, there is an incorrect table reference that should be fixed.

title: Conformal Guardrails: Building Safer AI in Low-Resource Indian Languages
review:
This paper proposes combining pseudo-labeling with conformal prediction to develop guardrail models for content moderation in low-resource Indian languages. The authors create a multilingual benchmark dataset from existing English safety datasets, apply pseudo-labeling to expand training data, and use conformal calibration to filter high-confidence instances. 

Strengths：
1. The paper directly addresses the practical challenge of building safety systems with limited labeled data for Indian languages.
2. The approach of translating established English safety datasets using IndicTrans2 is pragmatic and creates a valuable resource. 
3. The consistent improvements across six languages demonstrate the robustness of the approach. 

Weaknesses:
1. The core contribution is applying existing techniques (pseudo-labeling and conformal prediction) to a new domain. While the application is valuable, the technical innovation is incremental. 
2. The entire benchmark relies on machine translation from English, which may not capture culturally-specific harmful content patterns in Indian languages. There's no validation of translation quality or discussion of how translation errors might affect labels. The paper also lacks analysis of the pseudo-labeled data quality.
3. The evaluation uses only IndicBERT, a relatively small model. No comparison with larger multilingual models or recent LLMs is provided.

title: Conformal Guardrails: Building Safer AI in Low-Resource Indian Languages
review:
This paper introduces a framework to combine pseudo-labelling with conformal-based uncertainty calibration with the aim of optimizing guardrail model performance in 6 low-resource Indian languages - Gujarati, Kannada, Nepali, Sindhi, Punjabi, Urdu. 
The starting point is the dataset construction, and for this, the paper takes 4 existing datasets and translate them into the 6 respective Indian languages. There aren't enough details in the paper with respect to the collation of the 4 datasets. In total, 5,777 samples are translated from these 4 datasets, resulting in a total of 34K samples. The translation is done using IndicTrans2.
In the next part of the data creation, the mC4 is used. However, there are no details on how this is used. The samples are automatically labelled using a system that is trained on a system fine-tuned on the initial 5,777 samples. 

Finetuning is done using IndicBERT. V1 is the 5,777 samples in each of the 6 languages (I am guessing that a single model is trained to cover the 6 languages, rather than a model per language). V2 description is rather confusing, and due to the lack of details in the data creation from the previous section, I do not understand what this is trained on. Is it the Conformal Filtering row in table 2? And is V1 further finetuned? This is not clear at all. This is similar for V3 - referencing to a specific row in Table 2 would be very helpful. Also a clearer description of the data and the different finetuning steps is needed. 

The results are reported per model. An appendix is needed with more detailed results, including Precision and Recall for each language, confusion matrices, and a clear table indicating the training size for each language for each version.

From my perspective, I miss an analysis of the results from a "language" perspective. Why are there misclassifications? Usually these point to problematic scenarios in the data - either it is not representative enough, or there are certain complexities in the language that are difficult to process. This is an especially important step - nowhere in the paper do I see any effort to try to understand the data, both from a creation perspective or an evaluation perspective. 





Q1. Did you analyse the performance of IndicTrans2 on this type of data? Although the system might have overall good performance on translation metrics, it might be the case that the output on these specific datasets degrades. 

Q2. Do you have access to native speakers for all 6 languages within your group? This would tie in to the first question to understand how good the data that you produced and making available to the community is.

Q3. Can you provide details of the 4 datasets used? Did you always use the full dataset? In the case of a multilingual dataset like Aya-Redteaming, did you use the English portion or the Hindi portion? Why if either one and why not both?

Q4. Did you consider whether certain types of harm are more relevant to various Indian cultures and how well this is represented in the data? 

Q5. When using existing datasets, did you randomly select X number of instances from each dataset? Did you consider the different types of harms represented? 

Q6. How exactly did you use the mC4 dataset? 

q7. Did you consider manually checking a portion of the data? 

q8. Can you report the confusion matrices in an appendix? In such a classification task, it is not the accuracy/F1 that counts, but rather the precision. Understanding and discussing the misclassifications is very important.

title: Bidirectional Reasoning Supervision for Multilingual Financial Decision Making
review:
This paper addresses the challenge of multilingual financial sustainability classification. The authors propose a fine-tuning approach that incorporates bidirectional reasoning alongside traditional classification labels. Their method is evaluated across four languages—English, Hindi, Bengali, and Telugu, which covers high, medium, and low-resource settings. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms conventional and unidirectional reasoning approaches.

Pros:

- The methodology is clearly defined, and the experimental setup is robust, covering multiple languages and model sizes
- The method enables smaller, more efficient models to match or exceed the performance of much larger models

Cons:

- While a single ablation on hate speech is presented, further experiments on additional domains would solidify the method’s applicability beyond finance.
- It would be great to add more qualitative examples or case studies, especially for error analysis.

title: Bidirectional Reasoning Supervision for Multilingual Financial Decision Making
review:
The paper titled Bidirectional Reasoning Supervision for Multilingual Financial Decision Making explores the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in multilingual financial sustainability classification. The study focuses on four languages—English, Hindi, Bengali, and Telugu—spanning low-, medium-, and high-resource categories. The authors propose a novel fine-tuning approach that integrates bidirectional reasoning (positive and negative rationales) alongside classification labels to enhance model performance. Their method is evaluated against conventional label-only and unidirectional reasoning approaches, demonstrating superior results across all languages and model sizes. The study also highlights the cost-effectiveness of the proposed method, as smaller models achieve performance comparable to larger models trained with traditional methods.

The introduction of bidirectional reasoning (positive and negative rationales) is a significant contribution. This approach not only improves classification accuracy but also enhances interpretability by aligning model decisions with human-like reasoning.The inclusion of low-resource languages like Bengali and Telugu addresses a critical gap in financial NLP research, promoting inclusivity and broader applicability in global markets.

There are some comments:
While the study covers four languages, it excludes other underrepresented languages, which limits the generalizability of the findings to a broader multilingual context.

The reliance on GPT-4o for generating rationales may introduce biases or limitations inherent to the model. The paper briefly compares GPT-4o with DeepSeek-R1 but does not explore alternative or open-source models extensively.

The use of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) due to resource constraints may limit the exploration of full fine-tuning, which could potentially yield better performance.

Although the method is validated on a non-financial task, the primary focus remains on financial sustainability classification. Further validation across other domains would strengthen the claims of generalizability.

title: Bidirectional Reasoning Supervision for Multilingual Financial Decision Making
review:
The paper presents a reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning approach that incorporates bidirectional rationales into LLM supervision to improve multilingual financial sustainability classification. The idea is both interesting and practical, and the authors conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate its effectiveness. The paper is also well written and easy to follow.

I have two main comments:
(1) Limited novelty – The work does not introduce new algorithms, and fine-tuning LLMs has been extensively studied in prior research.
(2) Clarification needed – Certain technical details require further explanation. For example, in Section 3.3 (Reason Generation), it would be valuable to discuss the quality of rationales generated by GPT-4o, especially given that they are not based on human annotation.

title: AMAS: Adaptively Determining Communication Topology for LLM-based Multi-agent System
review:
Summary
This paper introduces AdaSwarm, a dynamic graph selector that adaptively identifies the optimal graph structure for each input instance through parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs).

Strengths

The paper is clearly written and well-structured.

The problem of modeling and understanding interaction flows among agents is both timely and important.

Weaknesses

While the work is solid, the empirical evaluation could be strengthened by considering models beyond the LLaMA family.

Although the authors provide a reasonable computational justification for not including extremely large models (>300B parameters), incorporating additional models of comparable scale to LLaMA would significantly enhance the robustness and generality of the results.

title: AMAS: Adaptively Determining Communication Topology for LLM-based Multi-agent System
review:
Summary:

This paper proposes a new dynamic graph selector that, through minor parameter adjustments, can select the appropriate multi-agent collaborative graph structure for each input sample in real time, breaking away from the limitations of traditional fixed architectures. In large-scale experiments on three tasks, AdaSwarm significantly outperforms existing single-agent and MAS baselines.

Pros:

1. The paper is well written: (1) The introductory paragraphs are clearly divided, and the paper is summarized in a clear structure of background + related methods + introduction of this method + experiments + contributions; (2) The overall structure of the paper is clear, the process in Figure 1 is clear, and the structure of the method section is clearly divided.

2. The query is used to select the structure of the graph, and the method introduction is intuitive, which is easy to understand and implement.


Cons:

1. The proposed method is a general method and is not targeted at a specific industrial scenario. This paper is more suitable for the main track of EMNLP rather than the Industry Track.

2. The experiments are not sufficient, with only a simple comparison of performance and a lack of in-depth analysis, such as visualization of the effects of key models.

3. There is a lack of testing in actual industrial scenarios, which is more critical for papers submitted to the Industry Track.

title: AMAS: Adaptively Determining Communication Topology for LLM-based Multi-agent System
review:
This paper focuses on the collaboration structure of multi-agent systems. It proposes AdaSwarm, a dynamic graph selector to adaptively select optimal graph structure for each input sample. The core observation is that there is no graph structure that can perform better than other structures on every input. The experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The strengths include:
1. Reasonable idea developed for multi-agent systems, an important architecture of LLM applications.
2. Detailed description of the proposed method which helps the reproduction of this method.
3. Paper is well-structured and clearly written.

The weaknesses include:
1. It seems that this paper only produces the ranker of candidate graph structures, which means previous graph structure generation methods should be integrated for a complete pipeline. Although this approach is acceptable for industry, the authors may consider if it possible to generate a unique graph structure according to each input via a single graph structure generation model.
2. Some typos. Line 322 missing period at the end of the sentence. Line 324 "infrastures" maybe "Infrastructures"?

title: PCRI: Measuring Context Robustness in Multimodal Models for Enterprise Applications
review:
### **Summary**
This work explores how robust VLMs are to visual changes such as irrelevant information such as the background for 15 different multimodal tasks. They introduce the Patch Context Robustness Index (PCRI), a metric for measuring this robustness. PCRI works by evaluating MLLMs per task on two inputs: (i) the full image and (ii) NxN patches of the image, with N controlling the granularity. The paper finds that models nearly always performs better with an image patch instead of the whole image, suggesting that they are quite brittle to background/irrelevant information.

### **Novelty & Impact**
* This paper introduces a clear and usable metric, PCRI, for measuring VLM robustness. The metric is straightforward and can be used for essentially any model and most multimodal tasks. It contributes to the field by being a usable tool for industry and research when selecting models.
*  I’m not sure PCRI is comparable across tasks with different #/options. Let’s say that patch performance is 100% and whole image performance is chance. For 2 options (e.g. yes/no), that means PCRI = 1 - (1/ 0.5) = -1. For 4 options (e.g. MCQA),  that means PCRI = 1 - (1/ 0.25) = -3. In both cases, the model is equally bad on the full image task but the magnitude of the scores is very different. Therefore in Section 4.1.3, these task types are directly comparable.
* A more minor con is that PCRI has a limited range of tasks it’s applicable for. For tasks that require compositional reasoning (e.g. CREPE, Winoground), the patch evaluation will likely fail. As an example, “white dog left of brown dog” versus “brown dog left of white dog”. This is just relevant in the PCRI ≈ 0, where this would likely not imply robustness.

### **Reproducibility**
* All datasets and models+sizes are listed in the paper. The specific hyperparameters are not included, though I imagine these would be released with the code. The authors could include a footnote describing whether they use the best released/suggested parameters for each model.

### **Clarity & Structure**
* It’d be nice to say early on (~L73) that the goal scenario is performance on the whole image > performance on a patch. I didn’t immediately glean that this is the goal until looking more at Table 1 and Section 4.
* Table 1 can be described in plain text in Section 3 as well.
* For the graphs in Figures 3,4 and 5, can you add an arrow on the y-axis indicating that lower is better? It’s a bit confusing at first that these are negative numbers and that higher is not better.

### **Questions**
* I love the human baseline and I’d be curious to see the captioning results in particular. The things humans describe in images differs culturally (see “Semantic and Expressive Variation in Image Captions Across Languages”) and so I’m curious the extent to which variant from just captioning a patch of an image may parallel real-world variations.

title: PCRI: Measuring Context Robustness in Multimodal Models for Enterprise Applications
review:
**Paper Summary**:
- This paper proposes quantifying the robustness of MLLMs to visual context via the Patch Context Robustness Index (PCRI), which highlights performance variation over localized and global visual contexts.

**Strengths**:
- The evaluation is comprehensive regarding diverse MLLMs and tasks.
- The proposed index provides insights into the performance disturbance over the patching granularity.

**Weaknesses**:
- This paper explores different granularities $n \in$ {1,2,3,4,5}, but they are all a bit coarse. For example, it's common for Vision Transformers (ViTs) to have a patch size of 16 * 16 pixels, which means an image of size 224 * 224 pixels will be divided into 16*16 separate patches, i.e., granularity $n=16$.

title: PCRI: Measuring Context Robustness in Multimodal Models for Enterprise Applications
review:
This paper proposes the Patch Context Robustness Index (PCRI), a novel, interpretable metric for quantifying how sensitive multimodal large language models are to changes in visual context granularity. The authors benchmark 19 SoTA MLLMs across 15 datasets and show that many models perform better on localized image patches than on the full image, which is a behaviour diverging from human reasoning. The work is motivated by clear real-world needs, such as robustness in noisy or cluttered environments, and provides a standardised evaluation that could meaningfully inform industrial model selection.

Pros:
- Introduces a clear, interpretable, and practical metric (PCRI) that appears to fill a gap in current evaluation methods
- Broad scope, with benchmarking on 19 MLLMs across 15 datasets 
- Conducted a human study to validate interpretability and identify divergence from human reasoning
- Practical relevance for model selection and deployment in industry

Cons:
- [Addressed in rebuttal] Limited scope w.r.t. other non-spatial dimensions, e.g., only evaluated on English-language, static image benchmarks (although there is an allusion to this in future works)
- [Addressed in rebuttal] Using the best-performing patch per sample may hide some failures
- Questionable application to EMNLP industry track as despite the use and evaluation of LMs, the focus is on the visual aspect

title: Unsupervised Open Intent Discovery in Production Contact Center Systems
review:
This paper seems to be the continuous improvement on the OID Framework from the SIGDIAL paper "An Open Intent Discovery Evaluation Framework". On top of the previous work, it added an extra decision tree classifier to decide which configuration to use. And it provided some improvement. But this work seems so incremental, like the entire section 3 of introducing OID Framework is already presented in other paper. 

I think having multiple improvement for an existing system, and provide analysis on how those improvement works will make the paper having enough scope. With this configuration classification system and a few more improvement I think it will contain enough knowledge to be a proper paper.

title: Unsupervised Open Intent Discovery in Production Contact Center Systems
review:
*Summary:*
- the authors introduce an approach to predict the best configuration in open intent discovery leveraging a multi-label decision tree.
- the authors extend the prior work of Anderson et al (2024) "An Open Intent Discovery Evaluation Framework" replacing the human selection of the best configuration with a prediction model. However in the proposed system the user chooses the target intent type and an estimated number of intents.
- the predicted configuration performs close to the optimal configuration identified in Anderson et al (2024)

*Reproducibility:*
- the authors evaluate their approach on publicly available datasets making it easy to replicate their results
- the authors mention that "we categorise all datasets used in our experiments as one of Action-Object, Topic or Mixed.". Given this is one of the user chosen intents, it's not clear to me how this categorisation is done.

*Novelty/Impact:*
- the authors extend the previous approach and introduce a multi-label decision tree to predict the best configuration. 
- the authors report the model to be used in a real commercial use case
- while it is an extension of Anderson et al 2024, the application of decision tree for hyper-parameter optimization is not novel (e.g. "Auto-WEKA ..." by C. Thornton et al 2013)
- the proposed approach achieves close to best performance in Anderson et al 2024. However it's not directly compared to the state of the art approach by R. Kumar et al 2022. While the two approaches are not directly comparable, limiting the evaluation of open intent discovery to cosine similarity does not provide enough information on the classification performance

*Clarity & Structure:*
- the paper is well written and easy to follow 
- when authors mention "we categorise all datasets used in our experiments as one of Action-Object, Topic or Mixed." it's not clear to me how. No model is mentioned.
- the evaluation follows closely Anderson et al (2024), however assessing the performance in terms of F1-score as in Marinelli et al 2019 and R. Kumar et al 2022 would provide more information about the effectiveness of the approach

title: Unsupervised Open Intent Discovery in Production Contact Center Systems
review:
#  Summary

This paper presents a system for fully automating Open Intent Discovery (OID) in production contact center environments, aiming to remove the need for manual configuration selection and reduce labeling effort. The authors propose a Configuration Prediction System that analyzes features of a new, unlabeled dataset and predicts the optimal combination of semantic representation, clustering, candidate intent extraction, and label selection methods via a multi-output decision tree classifier.

# Strengths
- The problem is well-motivated and has strong industrial relevance. Contact centers face constantly evolving customer intents, making manual labeling costly and unsustainable.
- The proposed pipeline supports a single-run, fully automated OID process, including automatic label generation, which is valuable for real-world applications
# Weaknesses
- The configuration prediction model is trained on only five datasets, which raises concerns about robustness and generalizability. From Table 2 in the paper, the “predicted” configurations are highly repetitive: clustering algorithm is always KMeans; semantic representation is mostly all-mpnet; candidate extraction is mostly Action–Object; label selection is mostly Most Frequent. This raises two major questions: 1) Is the prediction model necessary? If outputs are so skewed toward a single choice for most components, a simple heuristic or majority-rule baseline could produce almost the same configurations without training a model. 2) What happens with alternative configurations? 

- The decision tree classifier for configuration prediction is quite simple, lacking comparison against more powerful alternatives such as gradient boosting, random forests, or neural models.


- The evaluation uses cosine similarity and BART score for generated labels, which measure semantic and textual similarity but do not directly capture label utility for downstream tasks, especially under the proprietary datasets

title: An Address Intelligence Framework for E-commerce Deliveries
review:
This is a well written paper describing a well designed system to validate user inputs of addresses as well as use them to detect user and delivery issues concerning product orders. The address sanitization task is divided into completion, correction, and ordering sub-tasks with independent task-specific modeling that allows for independent evaluation of the sub-task and aggregate evaluation of the sub-tasks together. In the next stage, a converse approach of co-dependent modeling to include implicit dependencies across e-commerce issues concerning addresses, is achieved using a form of Pareto multi-task learning. Reported evaluation of each of these stages and sub-tasks within also indicate that this is a system that can be deployed in production with some confidence. Appendix details are also concise yet useful to consult while reading the main sections of the paper.

Nit: Some spelling mistakes in pages 1-3, and I think in the MTPOT section, tasks are labeled as Di but in table 1 listing evaluation results, they are identified as Ci. 

Some areas where more details or future work could further strengthen this publication:
1. Scaling and runtime considerations - I suppose MTPOT would be an 'internal' service with fewer number of users, vs address validation being a 'user-facing' service.
2. Examples across tasks and stages, where the system works very well - expected and surprising; and where the system does not - expected and surprising.

title: An Address Intelligence Framework for E-commerce Deliveries
review:
The paper is well-structured and clear. The methodology is well-detailed, and the results, based on large-scale experiments with real-world data, demonstrate significant business impact.

Pros:
The paper presents an end-to-end framework that tackles both address validation and operational loss prediction, which is more comprehensive than prior research focusing on isolated problems.
Novelty: The geographical attention mechanism and the MTPOT multi-task learning architecture are innovative contributions.
Strong Results & Business Impact: The large-scale experiments on real-world data and the reported millions in annual cost savings provide compelling evidence of the system's effectiveness and commercial viability.
Clarity and Detail: The paper is well-written and provides sufficient technical details and mathematical formulas 
​ to understand the methodology.

Cons:
Dataset Specificity: The study is based on an emerging market like India and a specific commercial system. The generalizability of the model, particularly the geographical attention mechanism and the MTPOT's performance, to other regions or e-commerce platforms is not explicitly discussed.
Lack of Code/Data: While not mandatory, the absence of code or a publicly available dataset makes it difficult to fully verify the results and reproduce the work.

title: An Address Intelligence Framework for E-commerce Deliveries
review:
The paper addresses two connected problems: delivery address normalization and address-based operational loss prediction in an e-commerce domain. Address normalization is implemented as a user suggestion and consists of address auto-completion, spelling correction, and address component sequence standardization. The second component of the proposed "address intelligence" framework is a predictive model that estimates likelihood of operational issues based on the delivery address.

The components of the address normalization pipeline are implemented as transformer models and a modified noisy channel model that incorporates both phonetic distance and edit distance. The operational loss prediction model, on the other hand, makes use of Multi-task Pareto Optimal Transformer (MTPOT). The performances of the address models were evaluated using BLEU (1 & 2) and SAR (suggestion acceptance rate), the MTPOT was evaluated using ROC-AUC. While no comparisons were made for the address models, the MTPOT model was compared to other models such as BERT. The experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach on 2 out of 3 tasks. The paper is well written and easy to understand.

The strength of the paper is in detailed description of the components, it is clear what is being used. However, a lot of important information is located in the appendices. 

The weakness of the paper is in its density and disconnect in the experimentation. Since the authors present a complete framework for "address intelligence", the experimentation is limited to independent components. For instance, there is no clear information on the impact of address normalization on operational loss prediction; even though, as the authors state, the correct address is critical. An explicit connection between 2 task settings would be appreciated (e.g. the MTPOT predictions on permuted addresses).
Another missing critical information is the proper dataset description with distributions; as well as significance tests for MTPOT comparisons.

Other comments:
1. Table 1 task labels make use of 'C' while in text it is 'D'. 
2. lines 060 and 155 contain spelling errors.

title: R3D - Reasoning for Search Relevance using Reinforcement Learning and Distillation
review:
This paper proposes R3D, a two-stage training framework for search relevance reasoning that combines reinforcement learning and distillation. First, inference-based distillation transfers both the labels and CoT reasoning trajectories from a strong teacher model to a student model. Second, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is used to further fine-tune the student model with verifiable rule-based rewards. Experiments on the ESCI dataset show that simple CoT distillation reduces performance, but R3D with GRPO compensates for this gap. These results challenge the view that interpretability must come at the expense of accuracy.

Strengths:

The experiments are thorough, and the conclusions are interesting—namely, that interpretability does not necessarily require sacrificing model accuracy.

The paper is relatively easy to follow.

Weaknesses:

In terms of effectiveness, the improvement of R3D over simple SFT after two-stage training is limited, which greatly reduces the practical value of R3D.

I suggest redrawing Figure 1, as it is rather confusing and difficult to understand.

Overall, this is a solid paper.

title: R3D - Reasoning for Search Relevance using Reinforcement Learning and Distillation
review:
Submission 321 presents work into building a small language model distilled from a CoT from a LLM teacher model to produce a query-relevance system with improvements over two reasonable baselines with a small model - which is good for fast, industrial purposes.

The motivation for the work is straightforward and sensible and appropriate for the industry track at EMNLP.  

My main concerns were around the evaluation.  While this is not a major complaint they are worth addressing:

1. There should be a description of the dataset and a motivation on why this one is being used as it seems there are more recent similar datasets.

2. First place leaderboard system: it is unclear if the public leaderboard has closed or open.  If open, then the top system should be noted with the date and the team name in the offchance others have improved on it.  

3. While the evaluation is about F1 performance, one of the aspects of the paper is constructing a smaller model.  It would be good to know how large the leaderboard 1st place model is (if possible), and whether other query relevance work delves into optimizing for model size.


Other:

1. Include a section on query-relevance work in general as it is unclear from the paper what the state of the art methods are and the size of the models involved.  

2. It wasn't clear to me what exactly slow and auto modes were.

title: R3D - Reasoning for Search Relevance using Reinforcement Learning and Distillation
review:
This paper proposes a two-stage framework to enable efficient and interpretable query-product relevance classification. Reasoning-based Distillation to transfer labels and CoT traces from a 32B teacher LLM to a 1.5B student SLM. GRPO for RL fine-tuning with rule-based rewards (accuracy, format, consistency, "no-think") to mitigate accuracy degradation from CoT distillation. This paper addresses a critical industry pain point—balancing latency, accuracy, and interpretability in search systems. The solution is deployable (1.5B model) and includes a customer complaint investigation tool.
Some weakness are listed below:
1) Rule-based rewards require tuning (e.g., accuracy rewards per class). Include sensitivity analysis of reward weights in Appendix.
2) Slow Mode lags Fast Mode by 0.48% F1. Discuss architectural tweaks (e.g., early exit) to close this gap.

title: GPT-Legal: Scalable Summarization of Long Legal Judgments with Trustworthy, Domain-Tuned LLMs
review:
This paper studied a timely topic and an important problem for real-world scenarios. However, there are some **key weaknesses** of the paper: 

1. **Missing Key Details**: The paper misses many important details, which makes it quite difficult to understand. For instance, what are the section-aware rules for document segmentation? What are the prompts used to prepare the dataset for fine-tuning and for the LLM Judge? Moreover, the paper also lacks justification for the different parameters that are selected (e.g., ratio). 

2. **Weak Baselines**: Only used LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct as the baseline, which is a zero-shot model and expected to perform poorly on in-domain datasets for not being tuned. Why not other LLMs are evaluated as a baseline that have higher context length?

3. **Evaluation Bias**: While the authors stated that GPT-4o performing better in terms of SAM metric because of being evaluated by GPT-4-Turbo, then why not the authors used other strong LLMs-as-the-Judge (e.g., Gemini/Claude)?

4. **Missing Key Ablation Tests**: The Authors did not conduct proper ablation tests of the different components used in their training procedure.

5. **Deployment Issue**: This part does not contain sufficient details. What type of computing resources are needed? Is this more expensive than using long-context closed-source models? What is the latency? How is the overall cost?

6. **Missing Human Evaluation Details**: What was the instruction for the human-evaluation? On what criteria was it done?

7. **Missing Qualitative Error Analysis**: Why joint summarization outperforms stage? This part requires qualitative error analysis. 

8. **Issue with Metrics**: Why ROUGE Recall was used but F1/Precision was ignored? Are there not some risks, such as high recall compromising precision?

9.  **Reproducibility Issue**: The paper lacks details on training parameters, as well as the dataset (e.g, length of the dataset). This makes reproducibility a big issue. 

10. **Presentation Issue**: Section 3.5 is difficult to understand. For instance, how to get the values of To and Expected Summary Length?

11. **Ethical Concerns**: Finally, the mention of the 2024 Minister Award for Sectoral Transformation with GenAI (and endorsements by Supreme Court Justices, government-affiliated institutions, etc.) directly risks anonymity.

title: GPT-Legal: Scalable Summarization of Long Legal Judgments with Trustworthy, Domain-Tuned LLMs
review:
This paper describes a domain-adapted LLM pipeline for automated headnote generation.  Headnotes are short legal summaries that distill case opinions to a holding and the material facts.   While headnotes enable legal researchers to skim case law, their creation requires manual effort by highly qualified legal professionals.   

The key contributions are as follows:
- Section-aware document segmentation that preserves legal discourse
- Separate generation of facts and holdings; facts often require a broader context than the holding
- Dynamic length of the summaries based on the size of the judgement 
- Long context generation using rotary positional embeddings, enabling processing of entire legal judgments without truncation

The approach resulted in +23.5% ROUGE-1 recall improvement over GPT-4o on gold summaries.  

Strengths:
- The approach implements a domain-specific architecture with section-aware segmentation and dual-stage summarization (facts vs. holdings) tailored to legal structure.
- Ablation tests on the segmentation and summarization strategies.  Both ablation tests focus on long legal texts and evaluate key design decisions.
- User-facing features like highlighting unmatched entities and linking to the source segments that enable human validation 
- The pipeline has a significant impact on a real-world task that requires skilled professionals to create. 

Weaknesses:
- Human evaluation only focuses on preference judgements, with few details on the number of evaluators or inter-annotator agreement.
- No human evaluation on fact extraction.  The paper relies on an entailment-based method, FactScore, instead.  Given the precise nature of legal language, entailment might not be sufficient.
- The completeness metric, SAM, is an automated method for counting the number of key points using an LLM.   The metric doesn't correlate to the ROUGE metric, and the eval provides no human judgments on completeness.
- The evaluation focuses on the LLM for the baseline model.  There isn't a comparison with other Legal-based models or extractive summarization.

title: GPT-Legal: Scalable Summarization of Long Legal Judgments with Trustworthy, Domain-Tuned LLMs
review:
The paper proposes GPT-Legal, a domain-adapted LLM pipeline for summarizing legal judgments into structured headnotes. The approach includes section-aware document segmentation, separation of factual and legal holdings, summarization strategies (e.g., join/stage summarization), dynamic length control, and instruction tuning. 

While the system is presented as a novel and general-purpose legal summarization solution, it is in fact specifically fine-tuned on Singapore Law Reports, and its broader claims are overstated. Many of the techniques described as novel such as summarization strategy, chunk-based segmentation, and fine-tuning have been explored in prior legal summarization work but are neither cited nor compared against. The paper also contains multiple incorrect or misleading citations, methodological gaps, lack of clarity on key components, and weak evaluation design (detailed below).

- The model is trained exclusively on or for Singapore law, yet the paper presents it as a general solution for legal summarization. This claim is overstated. The system’s jurisdictional overfitting risk should be acknowledged more transparently, and claims should be localized to the Singaporean context.
- Line 53, Line 184 - 186:  The claim of factual alignment and structural adherence  is not well supported. ROUGE scores, especially ROUGE-1, are insufficient proxies for these properties.
- Related work on existing summarization systems are poorly discussed. I see lexglue and legal bench being cited as summarizaiton benchmarks when there is lexsumm [1]
- Recent methods which arglegalsumm, coperlex, relexed, etc have not been discussed 
- Summarisation strategy detailed in here has been explored in LexSumm paper [1] for legal summarization, inspired from [5] has not been acknowledged but provided an innovation here. 
- Document segmentation and rhetorical role based content summarization are explored prior in [3]. 
- Moreover, the paper does not clearly explain how the facts and holdings are identified and segmented from the legal judgments, especially since such annotations are typically not available in standard datasets. If these components were derived from specific data artifacts, that dependency should be acknowledged. Alternatively, automated approaches such as semantic mapping [4] or rhetorical role labeling could be used, but these are neither employed nor discussed.

- Line 198: How is alignment on chunk to summary done?
- Dynamic length control mentions it in prompt - but it is not sure how much is the length mentioned in prompt in abided by model. 
- The role of instruction tuning in improving performance is unclear. Is it necessary in this solution for just enabling longer context windows? or does legal dataset based instruction tuning necessary here? 
- Domain adaption with SLR summaries just make it similar to fine-tuning. This step might erode generalisation capabilities of model and reduce it to fine-tuned model. How does this fine-tuning affect general summarization performance on other domains would be a point to discuss. Then the apples-to-apples comparison would be smaller domain fine-tuned models rather than such large models. I wonder why the comparison being done to general gpt-4-0 model here where the provided solution is explicitly tailored on singapore corpus. If the training is being done on singapore corpus again, why not use smaller models like long former etc with join/stage summarization strategy?
- Chunk level alignment and fine-tuning has been explored in Shukla et al 2022 but not acknowledged but presented as a novel strategy here.
- Overall, the claims seem to be out of place, where the authors stress on coherence, factual accuracy etc, though factual accuracy is captured by fact score to some extent, how’s coherence evaluated?
- Section 4.3: The authors just note importance in rouge-1 and highlight that, but that does not convey any meaningful takeaway as lexical improvements at 1-gram levels can be achieved without improvement in quality.  I am not sure if evaluation is any meaningful in terms of rouge - as the fine-tuned models on this corpus know the stylistic and lexical terminology used in gold summaries, thus resulting in inflated values in lexical measures like ROUGE, which on comparison with GPT-4-0 would be generally lower. So, rouge improvement is not really convincing that the performance increased. 
- One could argue, if you prompt GPT-4-0 with join/stage summarization strategy + structure based approach, that might achieve better or comparable performance even. No ablation to confirm the same.
- I would not discard evaluation bias in coverage metric based on GPT-4-0, may be that model is indeed better; as we cannot rely on lexical metrics (as I described above) + facts core is not presented; so I would not discount that data point rather present a more reliable metric to showcase the point.
- Section 5.2.1: I am not convinced domain specific fine tuning and parameter optimisation itself can help mitigate these hallucination issues. Overall, for a task like summarization where the knowledge is present in source document itself - does domain-specific fine-tuning help in anything? A model with good long content understanding and summarization capabilities can perform this well. No ablation to prove the point of domain-specific tuning as a mitigation strategy is indeed helpful to reduce hallucinations? Given the paper frames for general legal summarization, one would argue domain-specific fine-tuning might even erode general capabilities and might even overfit on singapore corpus. So, those claims on general task have to be scoped for model for singapore case law summarization etc  
- Section 5.2.2. - Entity matching and entailment checks (Section 5.2.2) are under-specified: how the entities are extracted, how the summary content is mapped to source segment. 
- Section 5.4: Human Evaluation is Underdetailed. The 99% preference for GPT-Legal over GPT-4o lacks detail: What criteria were provided? Who were the evaluators (background, training)?Was there inter-annotator agreement? No examples or qualitative feedback is provided.
- Section 6:  In Line 410–412, the paper suggests that ROUGE and SAM can be exposed to end-users. This is misleading, since these require gold reference summaries and cannot be computed at runtime in production systems.

Problem with citations: I feel that the citations are generated with some LLMs. There are lot of wrong references to the claims in the document.
- Line 34: How is grusky et al related to the claim made on LLMs for legal summarization. Grusky et al 2018 neither deal with LLMs nor legal summarisation
- Line 72: how is chalkidis et al 2021 which deals with legal judgement prediction has to do with the claim made here on abstractive summarisation 
- Line 77: Chalkdiis 2023b is lexglue and has nothing to do with legal summarization as lexglue is language understanding encoder based evaluation tasks; even guha et al citation there is arguable as it does not deal with legal summarization per se.
- Line 82-85: I am not sure how legal bench emphasize on legal adequacy and factual consistency
- Line 94-96: the claim says the context length extended from 4k to128k, however the cited ones like big bird, long former still deal with 4k and do not specifically talk on LLMs based adaptation 
- Line 132: How is chalkidis et al 2023 an and Zheng et al 2021 related to summarisation to be cited here.
- Line 192: How is chalkidis et al 2023b related to the claim?
