title: Quantifying the Robustness of Evaluation Metrics under Controlled Factual Errors in Table QA
review: The paper is well written and organized, and studies an important problem in deploying real-world QA systems. Specifically, the paper introduces two evaluation metrics, namely Numerical Precision and Query Entity Recall to assess the numerical faithfulness of generated answers in Table QA. This study has a good potential of real-world applications. However, the major limitations of the paper are (1) there is no empirical comparison with existing metrics such as Number Recall or similar metrics, but only with BLEU (there was a typo of 'Blue Scores' in Table 1)and Rouge. (2) the experiments are conducted only on systematic data but not on any real-world dataset. This make it less persuasive to use the proposed metrics to replace BLEU and Rouge, although they are sometimes misleading. The methods of numerical corruption or sentence dropout make sense for generating the corruption-based evaluation datasets, which however may not be well aligned with real-world datasets.

title: Quantifying the Robustness of Evaluation Metrics under Controlled Factual Errors in Table QA
review:
This paper talks about the downsides of using ROUGE and BLUE scores for metric computation for Information Extraction. The paper particularly focuses on use cases involving tabular data (I.e. TableQA). The paper says that these metrics don’t do well for entity and numerical extraction. But they are still widespread used. The authors introduce a simple parametric mechanism to corrupt the data, and measure its effect of the performance.

This is not a novel finding. It is very well known that these metrics fail to capture specific entities of high value in extracted text. The corruption scheme introduced basically perturbs the numbers found in the text by a small value (x becomes x +- delta). For most practical tasks, particularly RAG type approaches this corruption would be very hard to detect in this manner. Even good LLMs might fail to capture this nuance, let alone ROUGE and BLUE like metrics.

The authors propose a "framework" to do this corruption and use entity level Precision, Recall for measurement. That is also not novel. The paper doesn’t discuss the type of problem space they are working on to highlight their contributions. No context about the size of the dataset is also provided.

There’s not much one can do to improve their industrial systems based on the content of this paper. I would have liked to see some mechanism to use the learnings here and adapt it to a practical scenario. Given the high standards for EMNLP this is a weak submission.

title: Quantifying the Robustness of Evaluation Metrics under Controlled Factual Errors in Table QA
review:
This paper designs experiment to show case that common methods used in table to text task have poor performance in fact checking and proposes 2 metric that help evaluation factualness.

Additional points that can improve the paper are:

* Soundness: the 2 metric are particularly designed for the 2 ways of corruption, thus making the improvement in performance less sound.
* Generalizability: the NP are using coexistance, making it less not applicable for QA cases where calculation using numbers in the table is required.

title: MiLO-LoRA: Adaptive Low-rank Adaption Allocation on Large Language Models via Mixed-Level Optimization
review:
### Summary

This paper builds upon prior work in improving LoRA-based Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) by employing non-uniform ranks across different LoRA adapters attached to transformer modules. Several existing approaches aim to identify and retain the most impactful ranks while removing less significant ones. This strategy offers two key benefits: enhanced model accuracy and improved runtime efficiency due to reduced computational overhead.

The core idea involves training on a dataset while simultaneously optimizing both the LoRA parameters and auxiliary system parameters that assign weights to each rank in every module. LoRA weights are optimized on one half of the dataset, while system parameters are optimized on the other, using interleaved gradient updates. After training, ranks with the highest weights are selected, and those with the lowest weights are discarded to meet a predefined budget. Finally, standard LoRA is retrained on the full dataset using only the selected ranks.

While other works have adopted similar methodologies (AutoLora), the authors propose a more precise optimization technique that achieves superior model quality at comparable computational cost.

### Strengths

- The authors conduct comprehensive comparisons with baseline methods across a variety of datasets. This includes both running original implementations and performing ablation studies using their own codebase, modified to replicate other algorithms. Both approaches yield consistent  results.
- The appendix provides an in-depth background on the problem domain, previous methods, and the key distinctions of the proposed approach. This serves as a valuable resource for readers seeking to deepen their understanding.


### Weaknesses

- The paper does not reference an alternative method presented in *“FanLoRA: Fantastic LoRAs and Where to Find Them in Large Language Model Fine-tuning.”* That approach gates entire LoRA adapters rather than optimizing specific ranks via gradients. Adapter importance is assessed by comparing model performance with and without each adapter. While FanLoRA reports a 1% improvement over AdaLoRA, the current paper achieves a 2–4% improvement, making the comparison relevant and worth discussing.

### Reproducibility

The authors clearly define their algorithm and have committed to releasing the code, which supports reproducibility and transparency.

title: MiLO-LoRA: Adaptive Low-rank Adaption Allocation on Large Language Models via Mixed-Level Optimization
review:
This paper proposes MiLO-LoRA, a neural architecture search method for pruning LoRA modules applied to the self-attention and feed-forward network components within each Transformer layer. It achieves this by weighting each rank-1 component of the LoRA matrices with a learnable scaling factor, which is optimized using a new mixed-level optimization (MiLO) algorithm. The method operates in a two-stage fashion. First, it performs the neural architecture search on a large-scale instruction dataset to find an optimal sparse architecture. Second, using the discovered architecture, the method fine-tunes the remaining LoRA parameters on downstream task data. Experiments using the open-weight Llama-3 8B, UltraChat for instruction fine-tuning, and a wide variety of downstream tasks such as ARC, BoolQ, GSM8K, and proprietary HSM10K demonstrated that MiLO-LoRA outperforms baselines including vanilla LoRA, AdaLoRA, DoRA, and AutoLoRA.

Strengths:
* They proposed a neural architecture search method called MiLO-LoRA.  
* Experiments with a variety of downstream tasks showed the superior performance of MiLO-LoRA over the strong baselines.  
* The overall structure is easy to understand.

Weaknesses:
* The manuscript's motivation is weak. It lacks a clear industrial application and instead relies on claims about a potential flaw in existing methods (L058-061, L132-134) that are not substantiated with experiments or analysis, making them appear subjective.
* The chosen methodology, neural architecture search, seems unnecessarily complex for the task of pruning LoRA modules. The paper would be stronger if it justified why such a complex approach is required over simpler pruning heuristics.  
* The experiments focus on claiming superior performance over baselines rather than providing a rigorous evaluation of the pruning method itself. Such a strong claim requires more robust verification.

Comments:
* I recommend comparing against more methods dedicated to LoRA pruning, such as LoRAPrune and LoRA-drop, in addition to the current use of AdaLoRA which also prunes.  
* Also, if possible, I would like to see experiments closer to SOTA results. For instance, by using a more powerful LLM than Llama-3 8B. While I understand the academic budget limitations, the very low scores in Table 2 indicate that the presented results are weak overall and are insufficient to substantiate the strong claim of outperforming the baselines, which would represent a significant advancement in the community.  
* The reference to GPT-3.5 (L253-255) is unclear. Please clarify its role, as the experiments seem to focus on Llama-3.  
* Consider restructuring the sections before the main results. Sections 4.1 and 4.2 could be integrated into Section 4.3 as subsections to improve the organizational flow.  
* Details such as the GPU name (L284) could also be moved to the Appendix to save space in the main text.  
* The reference to Table 2 seems missing in the main text (L328-340).  
* Typo: "b-level" -> "bi-level" (L015)  
* Typo: "we propose" -> "We propose" (L087)  
* Typo: "Related works" -> "Related Work" (L102)  
* Typo: ".For each" -> ". For each" (L151).

Zhang et al. Findings of ACL2024. LoRAPrune: Structured Pruning Meets Low-Rank Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning.  
Zhou et al. COLING2025. LoRA-drop: Efficient LoRA Parameter Pruning based on Output Evaluation.

title: MiLO-LoRA: Adaptive Low-rank Adaption Allocation on Large Language Models via Mixed-Level Optimization
review:
The paper introduces MiLO-LoRA, a novel framework for adaptive LoRA in large language models. The core idea is to dynamically allocate LoRA ranks across different layers and modules using a mixed-level optimization method called MiLO, which draws gradient information from both optimization levels. The proposed method claims to improve performance on downstream tasks while maintaining a comparable number of tunable parameters. The key contributions include the design of a learnable architectural parameter for each LoRA rank, a mixed-level optimization algorithm, and comprehensive empirical evaluations across multiple tasks.

Pros:
1. The paper presents a novel approach to adaptive LoRA rank allocation, addressing a significant gap in existing methods that rely on unreliable importance measures.

Cons:
1. In Table 1, the proposed method outperforms the SoTA baseline "AutoLoRA" by 0.6% on the BoolQ task. However, the authors do not report standard deviations or conduct significance tests. The authors must report the results over multiple runs (e.g., 3-5) with different random seeds and include standard deviations. A t-test should be performed to validate the statistical significance of their results against key baselines.
2. The paper mentions that the MiLO-LoRA method has a comparable number of tunable parameters to the baselines, but it does not provide a detailed analysis of how the performance gains compare to the computational overhead.
3. There are several typographical errors throughout the paper, such as "optmization" instead of "optimization".

title: TTD-SQL: Tree-Guided Token Decoding for Efficient and Schema-Aware SQL Generation
review:
This paper is to address inference latency and schema hallucinations in LLMs for NL2SQL. This paper propose Tree-Guided Token Decoding (TTD-SQL), that integrates SQL grammar and database schema constraints into the decoding process without modifying the underlying LLM. TTD significantly improves valid SQL generation. Codellama’s exec rate rises +17.7% on BIRD (57.6% → 67.8%), Granite improves +6.3% on BIRD.

**Core contribution**: TTD enhances SQL generation through schema aware decoding. The token chain transition tree embeds schema information to facilitate dynamic data injection during the decoding process.

title: TTD-SQL: Tree-Guided Token Decoding for Efficient and Schema-Aware SQL Generation
review:
This paper introduces TTD-SQL, a method to improve the decoding efficiency of LLM for SQL query generation. It uses precomputed token-level decision trees to deterministically "auto-fill" SQL keywords, and schema elements, when possible, saving in the process calls to the LLM inference. It has the advantage of being directly applicable to the LLM without finetuning or costly process.

This approach leads to:
- Faster inference: Up to 19.96% token-rate speedups.
- Fewer errors: A +17.7% reduction in hallucinations and improving executable SQL rates.

This method can directly and easily be integrated to current LLM generation framework for improved inference speed in an SQL query generation context.

I do not see any strong weakness in this work. The authors mention that the token-level decision tree need to be updated as the database schema evolves, but it seems that the decision tree build process is not that expensive and the update could be done on the fly. This aspect could be clarified if you elaborate more on the cost of build process.

title: TTD-SQL: Tree-Guided Token Decoding for Efficient and Schema-Aware SQL Generation
review:
The paper proposes Tree-Guided Token Decoding (TTD-SQL), a lightweight framework that integrates schema-aware constraints into LLM decoding without modifying the model itself. This work attempts to solve simultaneously two persistent challenges in text2sql: Inference Latency and Schema Hallucinations.

The work archives better performance than baseline Standard autoregressive decoding (AR), and sometimes marginal improvements over other approaches GCD, CoT, CoD on 2 popular datasets Spider and BIRD (Minidev).

*** Although this approach seems to reduce inference latency and schema hallucinations by providing auto-fills using scheme tree, there is no data or description shows:
1) the cost for constructing such schema trees, and
2) the actual inference latency including the auto-refill; note that token-rate does not directly mean latency but refers to the speed at which an LLM generates subsequent output tokens after the first token is produced.
3) in an enterprise setting, how does this approach work given many existing schemas, how does the auto-fill select correct schema?

*** Some questions for authors:
- Lines 009-012 and 055-058: what is the reference/citation?
- Lines 012-014 and 062-065: what is the reference/citation?
- Lines 358-360: which model? where is this number "improvements in token-rate (TR) upto 359 19.96% over autoregressive decoding"?
- Lines 362: where is the number "Llama-70B: +12.3% TR"?

title: DACIP-RC: Domain Adaptive Continual Instruction Pre-Training via Reading Comprehension on Business Conversations
review:
### Original Review

This paper introduces DACIP-RC, a method for adapting smaller LLMs to business conversation tasks using a instruction pre-training technique based on reading comprehension. The approach is highly relevant for industry applications, and the paper clearly details a replicable methodology for creating domain-specific training data. While the limited novelty is acceptable for an industry track, the experimental evaluation could be more robust.

Key strengths:
- Practical industry value: Addresses the real-world need for cost-effective, specialized LLMs for business-specific tasks like meeting summarization and call analysis.
- Clear methodology: Provides a well-structured framework for generating instruction data from transcripts using reading comprehension tasks.

Recommendations for improvement:
- Strengthen baselines: The comparison is limited to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Including a larger model or other similarly sized instruction-tuned models would better contextualize the performance gains. A comparison against standard next-token prediction pre-training would also more directly validate the instruction-based approach.
- Enhance generation evaluation: The improvements on generation tasks are not always significant based on the reference-based eval scores. Given the known limitations of these metrics, a qualitative analysis with side-by-side output examples is highly recommended to better demonstrate the model's improvements in quality and conciseness.
- Provide direct evidence for forgetting: The claim of mitigating catastrophic forgetting needs stronger support. Evaluating the model on general NLP benchmarks (e.g., MMLU) before and after training would provide direct evidence of knowledge retention.

Overall, this paper presents a promising and relevant methodology, but the current evaluation lacks the rigor needed for acceptance. Addressing the recommended improvements regarding baselines and qualitative analysis would be necessary to elevate the work to a publishable standard.


----
### Revised Review After the Rebuttal
This review has been updated based on the author rebuttal. The new experiments have sufficiently addressed the initial concerns.

- Baselines: The newly added baselines, including a larger model and a direct next-token prediction comparison, provide the necessary evidence to support the effectiveness of the proposed method.
- Generation Evaluation: The addition of a reference-free LLM-judge evaluation successfully addresses the limitations of the original metrics and indicates a qualitative improvement in the model's output.
- Catastrophic Forgetting: The new experiments testing the model on out-of-domain tasks provide the required evidence to substantiate the claim that the method mitigates forgetting.

The paper remains borderline because the method's effectiveness has only been demonstrated within a limited industrial domain, which restricts the broader impact and proven generalizability of the work.

title: DACIP-RC: Domain Adaptive Continual Instruction Pre-Training via Reading Comprehension on Business Conversations
review:
Overall the paper provides an interesting approach for adapting smaller language models to industrial applications by using reading comprehension tasks and their effectiveness on conversational applications.
The paper is mostly clear and allows reproduction of the ideas without major difficulties.
The novelty of this approach itself is not very high though especially with its closeness to "Adapting large language models via reading comprehension."
I also see issues with the baseline comparisons and the claims done in the paper.


Strengths:
- the paper addresses the issue of adapation of large language models to industry specific use cases of conversations
- it shows an easy to reproduce approach and is thorough enough for readers to follow and reimplement
- the provided results suggest effectiveness of this method over a not adapted baseline.


Weaknesses:
- The claims about non-catastrophical forgetting in this regime are not really supported, due to lack of experiments going further and showing the robustness on more datasets and any experiments testing loss of capabilities that existed before.
- Especially the baseline is weak. The authors should have at least provided a comparison to an NTP based continuation from Llama8B(-Instruct). Comparing the continued pre-training with the baseline Llama8B is not enough to show that this approach is superior to a simple NTP continuation.
- the novelty over Cheng's paper is also limited and consists mainly in the application to the conversational domain.
- The presented scores on the generative part are also not as conclusive as it seems. The working used is misleading, since the "slight" degradation in the support call summarization is actually higher than most of the gains in the other generative tasks (except for one).


Overall I think the paper has a good idea and foundation, however it should be more explicit in the benefits over Cheng's paper, as well as it should use different baselines, to really show the benefit of this methodology over other existing methods. Furthermore the claims that were made (like no catastrophic forgetting) should also be supported by explicit experiments. At the current state I would suggest the authors to revisit these parts and work on them to then hand it in again.


EDIT: given the supporting experiments I’m raising my judgement to marginally above acceptance. Well done.

title: DACIP-RC: Domain Adaptive Continual Instruction Pre-Training via Reading Comprehension on Business Conversations
review:
Summary:

The paper presents DACIP-RC, a continual pre-training method designed to improve the zero-shot performance of small to mid-sized language models (≤8B parameters) on business conversational tasks. Instead of traditional next-token prediction (NTP), it uses reading comprehension-based instruction generation from real-world conversation transcripts to pre-train models. This enables better instruction-following across various NLP tasks in business domains. Experimental results indicate that DACIP-RC significantly improves zero-shot generalization across a wide range of business conversational tasks including meeting summarization, action item generation and call purpose identification.

Strengths:

1.	Novel Methodology:
        * Introduces reading comprehension as a driver for instruction pre-training on business transcripts—an underexplored domain.
        * Generates multi-style, task-diverse instruction-response pairs using closed-source LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o Mini) to train smaller open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.1-8B).
2.	Dataset Creation:
        * Compiled a dataset of 26M+ instruction-response pairs (~25B tokens) from anonymized business transcripts.
        * Categorized into reading comprehension styles like skimming, scanning, active/analytical reading, and more.
3.	Performance:
        * Significantly improved F1 and ROUGE-2 scores in text classification (e.g., call purpose, call outcome) and generation tasks (e.g., meeting summaries, action items).
        * Demonstrated superior performance on both internal tasks and external benchmarks like QMSUM.
4.	Structured Output Compatibility:
        * Shows that DACIP-RC models work well with JSON-constrained decoding, important for real-world deployment.

Limitations

1.	Scalability to new corpora is questionable: Concept identification & categorization are manual
2.	Evaluation is limited to business conversations—generalizability to other domains (e.g., legal, healthcare) is untested.
3.	No release of datasets due to privacy concerns, limiting reproducibility for external researchers.
4.	The contribution of individual task types (e.g., skimming vs scanning) in the dataset isn’t isolated via ablation studies.

title: LegalMidm: Use-Cases Considering Legal Domain Specialization for Korean Large Language Model
review:
This paper lays out a systematic method for creating LegalMidm, a specialized large language model for the Korean legal field. The authors root their approach in practical needs by analyzing existing legal tech services to define key tasks. Their process involves curating high-quality datasets with expert guidance, generating synthetic data from legal statutes, and conducting a series of ablation studies. These experiments test the effects of mixing legal and general data, formatting legal references, and using system prompts. The resulting 11-billion-parameter model outperforms much larger general-purpose LLMs on Korean legal benchmarks while remaining competitive on general tasks.

While the paper's premise is strong and its systematic approach is valuable, the promising results are undermined by a weak evaluation methodology. The claims of providing a general framework are not well-supported, largely due to a lack of human evaluation and an over-reliance on a single, opaque base model.

A glaring omission for a paper targeting real-world legal applications is the lack of evaluation by actual legal experts. The study depends entirely on automated metrics and another LLM as a judge, both of which are poor substitutes for assessing genuine utility. The legal professionals who helped create the data should have been brought back to assess the final model’s accuracy, usefulness, and trustworthiness against the baselines.

Basing the entire framework on a single proprietary model significantly weakens the paper's claims of generality. For this to be a true recipe for domain adaptation, the authors need to show that their findings on data mixing and system prompts apply to other model architectures and sizes.

Furthermore, the paper offers almost no information about the underlying Mi:dm model beyond its size. Its architecture, pre-training data, and baseline capabilities remain a black box. This opacity makes it impossible to determine whether the performance gains come from the proposed framework or simply from a strong, undisclosed base model.

The primary metric for generative tasks is an L-J score from GPT-4o, which is not a reliable measure of legal or factual correctness. This evaluation method is known to have biases related to position, verbosity, and stylistic preferences. Including the prompts in the appendix does not fix the core problem of using another model to judge nuanced legal text.

The authors also fail to address the risk of test set contamination. They held out 100 human-curated samples for testing but also generated a large synthetic training set from legal statutes. It is unclear if they took steps to prevent the legal principles from the test set from appearing in the synthetic training data, casting doubt on the evaluation's validity.

The description of the data creation team is also a concern. The expertise among six law majors, four legal industry professionals, and two attorneys varies widely. A first-year student's ability to curate legal data is not comparable to that of a senior lawyer. The paper needs to detail the specific roles, quality control procedures, and how disagreements were handled.

The claims about document drafting proficiency are based on a narrow subset of the task. The authors identify it as a key capability but only test the model on generating complaints and petitions, which does not reflect the complexity and breadth of legal drafting.

The paper reports only aggregate scores, offering no insight into the model's failure modes. A qualitative analysis of common errors is needed to understand where LegalMidm struggles, such as making subtle factual mistakes or misinterpreting complex statutes.

The method for generating synthetic data is presented as a key part of the pipeline, but it is a standard technique. Using an LLM to create question-answer pairs from a text is a common practice, and the paper should acknowledge that its application here is not a novel contribution.

title: LegalMidm: Use-Cases Considering Legal Domain Specialization for Korean Large Language Model
review:
# Overview

This paper focuses on training a legal-specific LLM to address everyday tasks in legal research and transactional law systems. The authors surveyed 20 legal tech companies to determine the use cases: question answering, document-based QA, document summarization, and document drafting. They curated a dataset based on the use cases to perform continual pre-training and instruction tuning. Their 11B parameter model outperformed larger general models (Qwen2.5-32B, Llama3.3-70B, etc.) on legal-focused tasks with maintained general performance. The authors execute several ablation studies on data composition, format optimization, and system prompting strategy to guide their design decisions.

This paper presents a methodologically sound and impactful contribution to legal LLM development. The use-case focused approach and the ablation studies are strengths. However, the evaluation methodology has some gaps in addressing the precise nature of legal language. The analysis relies on automated evaluation approaches without additional human validation. Additionally, there is insufficient treatment of citation validation in the testing.

# Strengths

- Rigorous experimental design with systematic ablation studies on design decisions for the pre-training data composition, the synthetic data format, and when to use system prompts
- Strong reproducibility with complete hyperparameters and computational details
- Professional collaboration with legal experts throughout dataset creation for the training and evaluation dataset
- Comprehensive task coverage for question answering, document-based QA, document summarization, and document drafting.

# Weaknesses

- Over-reliance on GPT-4o evaluation without human expert validation is concerning for the legal domain
- No systematic human evaluation of final model outputs despite domain criticality
- No verification that GPT-4o judgments align with legal expert assessments
- Insufficient treatment of citation hallucination issues in the final output, given that judges tend to censure legal professionals for these mistakes. Granted, the synthetic data generation did attempt to address the issue.

# Questions

- How do you validate that GPT-4o evaluations align with human legal expert judgments?
- The system prompt in Appendix B instructs the user to check citations. Citation accuracy is essential for a legal LLM, particularly for the drafting use case. Why wasn't citation accuracy systematically evaluated? What metrics could demonstrate the effectiveness of your mitigation strategies?
- Can you provide detailed methodology for the human curation process, including inter-annotator agreement scores and quality control measures?
- Have you conducted any real-world deployment studies or gathered feedback from legal professionals using the system?

title: Harmonizing Diverse Models: A Layer-wise Merging Strategy for Consistent Generation
review:
The paper proposes a method to improve consistency in the output generation that involves synthetic data generation, triplet loss for embeddings, and a layer-wise model merging approach to merge the models that are finetuned with different variations in phrasing. The authors identify many inconsistencies and variations in the output of a RAG based generator, and find indications that the generator is more sensitive than the retriever, so that is where they focus the effort on. By analysing the production queries, the authors categorize the inconsistencies stemming from a few key variations in input phrasing - how to/how do, singular vs plural, omission of articles (a phone vs phone). They focus on these three particular variations, and use this as a guideline to do synthetic data generation for these variations, to finetune the models. They incorporate triplet loss at the finetuning phase, and show in the experiments that it improves performance. A model merging method, building on DARE-TIES, then assigning dynamic weights based on consistency of each LLM layer, is used to merge the final model.

# Strengths
- The paper clearly describes the method and the problem that is being solved, which is model output inconsistency with minor variations, which is a real problem in industry settings
- The synthetic data generated could be useful in the industry setting to finetune models on consistency
- The results show that the triplet loss does improve the performance compared to just the finetuned model (no additions), and the merged model (with the novel merging) overall has the best results for Exact Match and Response Similarity.
# Weaknesses
- The work seems focused on a very narrow set of variations, which is not a good representation of the kinds of variations that are possible in a real industry setting
- The scope of experiments are limited, since it is limited to one model and very narrow data generated
- The results show a good performance improvement over a baseline, un-finetuned model, but the improvement over normal finetuning method seems very minor - as small as 0.02 in improvement, which does not seem like a lot
- The experiments could have been extended to public datasets to show the impact of the method, which could have been better established, and may actually show good improvements

title: Harmonizing Diverse Models: A Layer-wise Merging Strategy for Consistent Generation
review:
This paper addresses the issue of response inconsistency in RAG systems when faced with semantically equivalent but syntactically different queries. The authors propose an approach combining synthetic data generation for common query variations, triplet loss training for better embeddings, and a consistency-aware layer-wise model merging strategy.

Strengths:
1. The three-pronged approach (synthetic data generation, triplet loss, layer-wise merging) is well-motivated and systematically designed.
2. The consistency-aware layer-wise merging approach is innovative, using intermediate layer activations to derive consistency weights.
3. The experiment result shows consistency improvements of the proposed approach.

Weaknesses:
1. The evaluation uses only 2,738 queries from a single industrial dataset without enough details. The lack of public benchmark evaluation limits reproducibility and generalizability assessment.
2. The EM metric seems unnecessarily strict for evaluating consistency which might cause misleading improvements, as users care about semantic consistency, not character-perfect identical outputs.
3. Missing ablation on the contribution of each component, and comparison with other consistency improvement methods beyond self-consistency.

title: Harmonizing Diverse Models: A Layer-wise Merging Strategy for Consistent Generation
review:
This paper presents a method for improving the robustness of RAG model generations under varying inputs, assuming that the output from the retriever remains the same. They perform synthetic data generation to improve models' ability to generate consistent outputs in response to perturbed inputs. They then demonstrate that consistency can be improved by applying a model merging approach by merging layers that show similar activation patterns. Though I have some concerns about the generalizability of the synthetic data generation, overall the method seems relatively straightforward and applicable to other industry settings.

# Strengths

The testing of the method is thorough, and the explanations provided throughout are clear. The authors demonstrate the different forms of synthetic data used contribute to model performance, and that the merging method is effective at maintaining performance. The method is straightforward, and well described.


# Weaknesses and Questions

1. While many of the synthetic data examples generated are not domain specific, I can imagine some settings where they would not apply (e.g. a coding setting). Do you believe the method used to generate the data holds up in these settings as well?

2. What settings are used for ROUGE and BLEU scores? For comparison's sake it's best to list the settings used to generate these scores.

title: EventTempEx: A Tool for Interpreting Event-Anchored Temporal Expressions
review:

* a framework for event and temporal expression extraction

## Cons:

* The extraction system is a combination of mostly known technology and not novel
* the architecture includes web calls even though the authors describe these calls as a disadvantage of current LLMs claiming they lead to high latency

The motivation for this work is well written and made me excited for the rest of the paper, but the solution presented falls short on different levels. While the distinction between the different classes are well explained, the methods for the extraction and derivation of the temporal representation are not described in detail making it difficult to reproduce this work. The experiments in 3.1 lack important details such as size of the training/test set. How was the data curated etc. I also question whether the validation accuracy is the best metric and would have expected Precision and Recall for a multi-label classification task.

## Minor comments:
- the  paper doesn't seem to confirm to the required LaTeX package (missing numbers in the margins)
- missing white spaces before citations at several places 
- recognition of ambiguous temporal references: provide examples
- multilingual temporal expression normalization (PDF): what does this abbreviation refer to?
- Claude Sonnet (The): wrong citation command?
- UIE format (do you mean ISO)?

The proposed framework, EventTempEx, can normalize temporal cues and handle both real-time and emerging events, making it applicable to timeline construction, event tracking, and decision-making in complex, agentic systems.

title: Can Argus Judge Them All? Comparing VLMs Across Domains
review:
## Summary:

This paper presents a well-organized benchmark study of three widely used VLMs, introducing the Cross-Dataset Consistency (CDC) metric as a measure of robustness. CDC is conceptually promising and theoretically justified, but its practical value would be strengthened by explicitly specifying which metrics feed into it, how heterogeneous task scores are normalized to a common scale, and by providing empirical comparisons with alternative stability measures (e.g., coefficient-of-variation, rank consistency).

## Strengths:

- The Cross-Dataset Consistency (CDC) metric is a relevant and well-motivated addition to VLM evaluation, with clear mathematical definition and direct applicability to assessing cross-dataset robustness.
- Evaluation scope is broad, covering three architecturally distinct models (CLIP, BLIP, LXMERT) and multiple task types like retrieval, captioning, reasoning which supports a nuanced performance comparison.
- Dataset selection is balanced, combining structured/synthetic (CLEVR, VCR) and unstructured/natural (COCO, Flickr30k, Visual Genome) benchmarks.
- Consistent experimental protocol like unified preprocessing, model-specific tokenization, and identical hardware ensures fair and reproducible comparisons.
- Results are interpreted in context of architectural design choices helping the reader.

## Weakness:

- Clearly define CDC inputs, normalization procedures, and benchmark it against other stability metrics to demonstrate added value.
- Include error bars, variance estimates, and statistical tests to assess the significance of performance differences.
- Augment high-resource A100 results with at least one realistic low-resource or edge-device evaluation to support “edge AI” claims.
- There are discrepancies in code availability statements and clarify ambiguous configuration details (e.g., tokenizer choice, dropout settings).

title: Can Argus Judge Them All? Comparing VLMs Across Domains
review:
### **Summary**
* This work probes how consistent VLMs are across tasks, including captioning, retrieval and visual reasoning. They introduce a new metric called CDC, cross-dataset consistency, and also score each individual task. They find performance differences across task types, where a single model is not consistently the best and therefore conclude generalization is not consistent. Additionally, they provide some hypotheses such as model architecture to explain why models show performance differences.

### **Novelty & Impact**
* The chosen evaluation metrics all seem clear and reasonable for each task (e.g. BLEU for captioning, R@k for retrieval). The additional efficiency metrics are also helpful because they bolster the importance of industry usage.
* This work would really benefit from at least one more recent model. It could definitely be a smaller one like Qwen 3B or Llava Chat 7B.
* The evaluation tasks are also all older, which isn’t a bad thing, it just means that performance is very high and the many newer reasoning tasks are excluded. When performance is nearly saturated, it makes comparative analyses like this difficult because so many examples are already correct.
* I disagree with some of the claims, for instance: “However, most evaluations remain task-or dataset-specific, focusing on zero-shot classification (Radford et al., 2021), VQA (Goyal et al., 2017), and image-text retrieval (Faghri et al., 2018), with limited cross-dataset analysis relevant to real-world applications.” There are datasets like MMMU that intentionally test on different aspects of visual understanding and reasoning. Additionally, this work only uses existing datasets that are not any more grounded in the real-world. Addiitonally, some of the datasets are completely saturated such as Clevr.

### **Reproducibility**
* This work provides a link to all of their code. The models are also open-source. The experiments should therefore be completely reproducible.

### **Clarity & Structure**
* In Section 3.1, can you please cite each paper instead of only using the footnotes to the websites?
* There’s a lot of equations and notations, some of which can go. Here are some specific examples: L150-159 and Eq. 3 can be removed because batch evaluation is essentially always done to improve throughput, so it feels a bit redundant.
* Overall, the related work seems dated. The most recent citation is one from 2023 and everything else is 2022 and earlier.
* I’m trying to understand how – if at all – different chance performances for each dataset plays a role in interpreting the CDC score. If tasks A, B, C have a chance performance of 50% and task D has a chance performance of 25%, does that mean the random chance CDC score is different than if tasks A,B,C,D all have a chance performance of 50%? If so, can you include what the chance CDC score is in Table 5?

title: Can Argus Judge Them All? Comparing VLMs Across Domains
review:
The paper compares several vision-language models on a range of benchmarks. 

The promise of evaluating the "state-of-the-art models" isn't quite fulfilled by this paper. Salesforce's BLIP (as evaluated) was succeeded by BLIP-2, which was succeeded by InstructBLIP in 2023, which now features at rank 261 in HF's Open VLM Leaderboard. If you look at only models < 10B, it's at rank 138. There is a variant of CLIP at rank 128 (among <10B models). An evaluation of state-of-the-art models would have been the main source of utility for readers of this paper -- two years ago.

Perhaps there is utility in demonstrating how to evaluate a VLM, and I cannot reasonably comment on the choices the authors made here. But, I submit that in the past two years, many of the mainstream foundational models have become "routinely" multimodal, with synergies emerging between modalities. Thus, looking at just the VLM space might not be very useful.

The paper reads well, and clearly much competent work went into the project.

I assume this paper has been submitted and rejected previously, and it's simply no longer up-to-date. My suggestion would be to leave it on the preprint server, and move on. (Sorry for the short review, but it's a fast-moving business, and one needs to look at scientific insights gained and practical utility for the audience when selecting papers, and in this case I do think it's best to move on.)

title: DRAFT: Demonstration RerAnker Fine-Tuning for Multi-modal In-context Learning
review:
The authors empirically demonstrate the ineffectiveness of selecting in-context examples based on the similarity scores calculated by dual-encoder models like CLIP. They argue that selection should be based on the surface and semantic similarity (BARTScore) between the response generated from the query example and the response generated from a particular in-context example. In order to close the gap, they propose a new in-context example selection strategy called DRAFT that trains an MLP that calculates a ranking score that’s close to the BARTScore from the dual-encoder embeddings. Their evaluations show that DRAFT outperforms dual-encoder-based ranking strategies. They also conduct ablation studies to show the impact of each component of DRAFT has in the downstream VLM performance.

Strengths
- Effective in-context example selection strategies are an important area of research, especially for practical applications.

Weaknesses
- The whole premise of the paper is that in-context examples chosen based on the similarity calculated using dual-encoder models like CLIP are not as good as those chosen based on the BARTScore similarity between the response generated from the query example and the response generated from a particular in-context example. Then the authors go on to train an MLP that calculates a ranking score that is close to the BARTScore from the dual-encoder embeddings. My question here is: why do we need to train this separate MLP model? Can we not just use the BARTScore ranking? Are the authors concerned by the compute cost of running the LVLM multiple times? If so, that point is not discussed or shown empirically at all. At the very least, I believe they should present the BARTScore ranking as a baseline.
- The writing and overall organization are not clear and hard to understand with some mathematical notation typos. For example, in equation 2, I think you meant to write $\{z_j\}^n_{j=1}$ ($j$ is what should be initialized to 1, not $i$). Similar typos are seen in equation 5, 6 and 9.
- Missing discussions about prior works in in-context example selection for LVLMs by Yu, et al. [1] and Kim, et al. [2]. [1] studies the distributional properties of in-context examples in training data that elicit in-context learning in VLMs, and while [2] proposes another in-context learning selection paradigm. These approaches should also be presented as baselines.

[1] Keunwoo Peter Yu, Zheyuan Zhang, Fengyuan Hu, Shane Storks, and Joyce Chai. 2024. Eliciting In-Context Learning in Vision-Language Models for Videos Through Curated Data Distributional Properties. title: DRAFT: Demonstration RerAnker Fine-Tuning for Multi-modal In-context Learning
review:
Contributions: 
-----------------
- This paper introduced a method to fine-tune a demonstration reranker (DemoReranker) head on top of multimodal LVLM (CLIP) to rank ICL (demonstrations) based on the “influence” of the demonstration on the generated output. This is achieved by computing quality scores (BARTScore between the response generated with a similarity ranked demonstration set (response_q) to the response generated with one particular demonstration). Their pilot experiments shows that the quality score seems to be a better criteria to rank demonstrations than using embedding based similarity from open source and commercial embedding models and is consistent with previous findings.
- The benchmarking results show effectiveness of the fine-tuned reranker against text only, image only, and bi-encoder models across visual question answering, image classification, and image captioning benchmark. 
- The ablation results seem to suggest that the individual components in DRAFT (choice of embedding, and how to combine embeddings from visual and text modalities, the ranking, the weight coefficient selection) seems to marginally contribute toward DRAFT performance.

Clarity: 
-----------------
- The paper follows a standard publication format
- The figure and table captions are very terse in general, requiring the reader to jump back and forth between the main text and the data in the table to fully understand the results. The definition of tasks and evaluation metrics should have been included in the table captions but are currently embedded deep in the Appendix requiring the reader to have to dig through the paper to find that information. For example, the description of the different embedding strategies Table 3 caption is at the end of the Appendix.
The reasoning behind some of the parameter selection (e.g. number of demonstrations at training and inference times) are not included in the paper. 
- The reasoning for the loss function formulation (e.g. squared errors vs. absolute error) is empirical and doesn’t provide insight into whether this loss expression is generalizable beyond the benchmasking done in this study.
- Algorithm 1 in the Appendix refers to Equation 5 and 10 which was included in the main text. It’d be easier to read if those equations were also included in the Algorithm1 itself.

Originality: 
-------------
- The use of “feedback” from LM to improve reranker in RAG has been seen in previous work. Specifically, Li et al 2023 (UDR) uses list-wise ranking formulation similar to this paper although UDR uses a different loss function. 
The main novelty of this work are
- The quality score formulation derived from comparing the response generated using a larger list of demonstrations ranked by semantic similarity with that generated with using a single selected demonstration.
- The incorporation of the quality score in the loss formulation used to fine-tuned the reranker
It is encouraging to see that the DRAFT fine-tuned reranker transfers well to commercial LVLM without additional fine-tuning and outperforms other methods. 
- The ablation studies could have been more insightful. For example, exploring different reranker architectures and sizes would allow the reader to understand whether the training has been saturated or there’s room for improvements. Exploring the number of demonstrations used during training and at inference time and whether optimal number of demonstration may differs between different tasks and domains (datasets).

Reproducibility
-----------------
- The algorithms and the prompts used in the different tasks are provided in the Appendix. To make the work more reproducible, it’d be helpful if the authors could provide the code (and the fine-tuned reranker).

Significance: 
---------------
This idea of building a lightweight fine-tuned reranker for specific application domains that’s transferable to different LVLM is appealing to industry applications. The paper shows an effective way of training reranker that works well for VQA, Image CLS, and ImageCap using very simple domain specific prompts.

title: DRAFT: Demonstration RerAnker Fine-Tuning for Multi-modal In-context Learning
review:
This paper proposes DRAFT (Demonstration RerAnker Fine-Tuning), a parameter-efficient framework for improving ICLin Large VLMs. The core idea is to fine-tune a lightweight demonstration reranker head on top of a frozen CLIP embedding model, enabling the system to select more effective demonstrations for multimodal ICL tasks. The reranker is trained using list-wise ranking losses, leveraging LVLM feedback via response-based quality scores (using BARTScore). Extensive experiments across seven datasets and three task types (VQA, image classification, image captioning) show sound performance gains over multiple baselines.

### Pros

The use of response-based quality signals (i.e., leveraging the actual LVLM outputs to assess the utility of a demonstration) is well-motivated and, to my knowledge, under-explored in prior multimodal ICL work.

I like the list-wise ranking loss, which is a nontrivial technical contribution. The ablation studies clearly show its importance and superiority over regression or pairwise losses.

The evaluation is extensive and compelling, spanning three major task types and both public and proprietary datasets. This broad coverage increases the impact and trustworthiness of the results. Meanwhile, the baselines are strong and relevant (including CLIP, BM25, DINO, BGE, UDR), and the improvements are consistent and significant (often >3-5 points absolute over CLIP/UDR). Transferability to commercial LMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus) is an excellent touch—showing industrial relevance and practicality.


### Cons

The paper would be stronger with a qualitative investigation: What kinds of demonstrations are being promoted by DRAFT vs. CLIP? Are there systematic patterns or failure modes? Are some task types or dataset domains harder than others?

The correlation study in the pilot experiment is useful, but the paper could delve deeper into why CLIP-based similarity diverges from LVLM utility. Is it due to visual vs. textual mismatch, or to interaction effects in multimodal reasoning. 

While the parameter efficiency is clear, the end-to-end inference and retrieval cost could be discussed more. For each test query, does the need to re-score 32 candidates with the LVLM for training scale well? What about latency at inference time?

The demonstration selection problem in ICL overlaps with broader data selection and curriculum learning research. A more direct comparison or positioning against this literature (e.g., in active learning, curriculum-based selection, meta-learning) would clarify DRAFT’s novelty.

### Questions for the Authors
Can you provide illustrative examples where DRAFT selects demonstrations that CLIP misses, and vice versa? What are the semantic or structural differences?

1.  How does the fine-tuning process scale with larger support sets or more expensive LVLMs (e.g., GPT-4o)? Are there any tricks to reduce training-time LVLM calls?

2. Have you tried DRAFT on other multimodal tasks (e.g., visual dialog, document QA)? If so, how does it generalize?

3. Did you observe any cases where fine-tuning the reranker for one LVLM hurt transfer to another (e.g., Deepseek-VL2 → Claude)?

4. Are there task types, domains, or dataset conditions where DRAFT’s gains are smaller or inconsistent?

title: JSON Whisperer: Efficient JSON Editing with LLMs
review:
# Summary of contributions
This paper presents a set of experiments and evaluation that show that LLM-queries using patch-based editing of JSON can achieve comparable JSON output as LLM-queries which edit JSON via full object generation, while also reducing cost a latency by way of reduced token generation.  This improvement centers on using a combination of few-shot examples and EASE (Explicitly Addressed Sequence Encoding), a key-based transformation of JSON lists.  Evaluation is conducted on a synthetic dataset of JSON manipulation queries and outputs based on interactions from a film production platform.

## Core contributions
1. Background and overview of patch-based editing of JSON for LLM queries
2. EASE - the introduction of this representation demonstrates how to workaround limits of LLM understanding of JSON structure
3. Evaluation of patch-based and full-generation based editing of JSON


# Strengths

The paper does a good job of introducing patch-based JSON to the reader, and I appreciate how it is grounded in the authors' (presumably) very real context of supporting edits of films.  This description was enough to show how it could be used, but also gave enough that it teased the imagination for how it could apply elsewhere where core reseources or states are represented as structured data like JSON.  For example, I could see how a Mechanical CAD system could benefit from this approach.

The EASE representation is elegant in its simplicity. The approach reminds me of how backend engineers will transform JSON data payloads to make it easier to reference and render aspects of the data.  It addresses a very-real, still unsolved limitation of LLMs which do not have a mechanism for understanding array indices.


# Weaknesses / Areas of improvement

The limitations section already mention that the data are synthesized via LLM and part of the evaluation hinges on LLM as a judge.  While the choices made be that author make sense, it would still be useful to create a small, hand-coded dataset to validate LLM data looks similar to authentic inputs, and that LLM evaluation is aligned with expert or end-user judgment.

## Small fixes
Line 342: few shots learning --> few shot learning

title: JSON Whisperer: Efficient JSON Editing with LLMs
review:
**Author Anonymity**
- **Assessment:** No breaches detected.
- **Details:** The paper contains no explicit author names, affiliations, acknowledgments, or self-revealing citations.  
  No direct links to non-anonymized code repositories or preprints were found.  
**Anonymity preserved**.

**Limitations**
- The authors rightly called out the limitations of having evaluated only synthetic datasets. They did not include a real dataset, or provide any references. Even though the problem is relevant to industry, the lack of comparisons with any relevant JSON datasets makes the paper weak for an industry track.


**Overall Review Summary**
- The paper introduces **JSON Whisperer**, a schema-guided, incremental LLM parsing framework designed to reduce token usage and improve efficiency when extracting structured data from unstructured inputs. The method is well-motivated and addresses a real industry need for cost-effective JSON parsing, with optimizations like query narrowing and selective subtree retrieval. The paper is clearly organized and includes useful diagrams, but lacks reproducibility artifacts, detailed parameter settings, and stronger positioning against existing schema-guided decoding and function-calling approaches. Overall, it is a **practically valuable work that needs more rigorous evaluation**.
---

**Strengths:**
**Novelty & Impact**
- Proposes **JSON Whisperer**, a framework for efficiently parsing and extracting JSON fields using large language models, with a focus on **reducing token consumption and execution latency**.
- Addresses an important and **practical industry challenge**: enabling **edits to** structured data generation from unstructured inputs without expensive end-to-end LLM invocations.
- Introduces an **incremental parsing approach** where the LLM retrieves only relevant subtrees of the JSON schema on demand.
- They proposed an alternative design to array indexing issues when elements from a row are deleted. However, they did not explore a code generation mechanism to deal with the structured objects, which may have been relevant.

**Reproducibility**
-  The methodology is described with sufficient clarity to understand the pipeline: schema pre-processing, incremental LLM calls, and field extraction.

**Clarity and Structure**
- The paper is structured well, the writing is concise and the paper is easy to read. I liked the definitions that were clarified at the beginning of the paper. However, it is ** noticeably missing a Related Work section**, which redacts from clarity. It is hard to understand the contribution with respect to earlier research. 

--

**Weaknesses:**
**Novelty and Impact**
- While the efficiency focus is relevant, the approach’s novelty is hard to gauge due to lack of comparison with the state-of-art approaches.
- Industry applicability is clear, but the evaluation would be stronger if it included case studies beyond synthetic benchmarks.

**Reproducibility**
- No public code or sample schema/queries are provided, making it harder to reproduce results exactly.
- Lacks a breakdown of LLM parameter settings (e.g., temperature, max tokens, stop sequences) and API call counts.
- The experimental setup omits hardware/environment details and cost analysis, both important for validating claimed efficiency gains.
- Would benefit from publishing a small **demo dataset** and example parsing runs.

**Clarity & Structure**
- The **related work** section is brief and could better connect this approach to prior schema-guided decoding, streaming JSON parsers, and function-calling APIs.
- Some terms (e.g., "query narrowing") are introduced without immediate definition — a glossary or formal definitions would help.
- The motivation section would be stronger with **concrete examples** of the types of JSON parsing failures or inefficiencies seen in baseline methods.
- Minor grammatical errors and occasional awkward phrasing could benefit from copyediting.

title: JSON Whisperer: Efficient JSON Editing with LLMs
review:
JSON Whisperer proposes an LLM-based JSON editing method that generates RFC 6902 diff patches rather than rewriting full documents. The framework includes a synthetic few-shot dataset generation pipeline and introduces EASE, a representation that replaces positional arrays with key–value maps plus an explicit ordering string to eliminate index-shift errors. Patches are applied using standard JSON Patch algorithms, and the method is evaluated on ~400 synthetic scene-editing tasks spanning simple edits, creative additions, complex multi-field changes, and list manipulations.

Results show the approach maintains quality within ~5 % of full regeneration while reducing output tokens by ~31 %, yielding cost and latency savings. To the best of my knowledge, the combination of LLM-driven RFC 6902 patching with EASE is novel.  A limitation is that all evaluation uses synthetic test sets, so generalization to real-world data remains unproven.

I find this paper relevant to the industry track and the efficiency gains convincing so lean towards accept at the time.

title: eSapiens’s THOR Module Transformer Heuristics for On-Demand Retrieval
review:
The paper presents THOR (Transformer Heuristics for on-demand retrieval), a module designed and implemented by eSapiens (links are shared to the exact product). THOR is a module that performs text-to-SQL, in two stages: orchestration and execution. The module contains a supervisor agent to route queries, a schema retrieval component and a SQL generation agent which emits the output SQL query. There is also an error-correction loop to catch errors and exceptions, and triggers regeneration. The output SQL execution also comes with a Result Interpretation text, and some visualizations. While this is a standard setup of a text-to-SQL workflow, with limited novelty in the pipeline itself, the module does seem to be deployed and used in a production setting, and is used to enable non-technical users to interact with live data. While the paper is well structured and the components are explained, there is no novel contribution, and a lack of experimental results apart from a case study.

## Strengths
- The system is deployed in a production setting, and seems to be useful in providing insights to a non-technical user on finance, sales and operations domains. The visualization of insights is a useful step in the flow to ensure enabling of non-technical users
- Queries are enforced as read-only, and has guardrails for unauthorized column requests, therefore supporting data governance
- The benefits provided in the industry setting in the case study shows that there is an improvement of time spent on manual effort, by a large margin, compared to not having an AI agent at all. 

## Weaknesses
- The authors mention that, during an introspection loop at error correction, the full list of instance level data is revealed anyway - in order to perform this error correction - does this not violate the assumption that the instance level data is protected from the LLM, ensuring data governance?
- There is limited novelty in the pipeline itself, since it employs all components of a standard text-to-SQL workflow, and does not contribute any innovative new component or pipeline.
-  The insights that are generated with charts - how are the charts designed? Is that an automated process, or only available for specific headers and columns? 
- The experimental evaluation in this paper seems to be over 7 natural language queries, and compared with 3 anonymous baseline agents. That is extremely narrow, and does not motivate the need for such a system, or establish usefulness by good metrics.
- Currently, although it is a productized system, there seems to be no particular way to handle domain specific rules or nomenclature. For instance, most of the errors in these scenarios seem to be handled only on retry loops without any explicit direction.

title: eSapiens’s THOR Module Transformer Heuristics for On-Demand Retrieval
