title: eSapiens’s THOR Module Transformer Heuristics for On-Demand Retrieval
review:
Paper Summary:

This paper describes a system that takes as input natural language questions from users and generates verified read-only SQL for enterprise databases. The system implements an agentic approach that consists of an orchestrator that determines which tools (agents) to call and refine the generated query, iteratively to produce a final version that is sent to an "insight generation" and "answer delivery" module. An assessment of the system over a small dataset of presented to illustrate the effectiveness of the system.


How this work can benefit the community:

* The agentic system described in this work, combines several recent advances in LLM-based systems for NL to structured output generation. This system would be a great reference for the community of a practical agentic implementation of robust NL-to-SQL.

* Impact of this system on efficiency, as discussed in Table 2, would be of great interest to enterprise engineering teams.


Areas that can be further strengthened:

* This paper is clearly not anonymized and very obviously embeds author organization information in the title and text -- esapiens, esapiens.ai

* While the approach taken in this work is super interesting, very few details of the system are provided to be able to reproduce this work. The paper would greatly benefit from having more implementation details.

* The evaluation of the system is quite minimal. Only seven data points are used for assessment, and no system output quality metrics are discussed. Evaluation over standard datasets and metrics would give the readers more confidence in the effectiveness of the system.

* Much of the description of the approach is presented as an engineering overview. Given that EMNLP is a scientific conference, some focus on scientific learnings/insights would greatly strengthen this work.

title: Revisiting Large Language Models for Ranking
review:
This paper evaluates LLM ranking capabilities using three novel datasets covering temporal, numerical, and conceptual complexity. The authors show that pairwise ranking consistently outperforms listwise methods, with performance gaps increasing as input size grows. To address computational overhead, they propose using BERT cross-encoders trained on LLM-generated pairwise labels, achieving comparable quality with reduced inference time.

The work addresses a practical problem with clear industrial relevance. While the technical contribution primarily combines existing methods, the systematic evaluation of ranking approaches and practical efficiency solution provide useful insights for industrial applications.

title: Revisiting Large Language Models for Ranking
review: The paper explores the applicability of LLMs to the problem of text ranking. This problem is, a bit surprisingly, treated as though it has hardly been tackled before, even though a lot of work has been done on LLMs for, e.g., news recommender systems and other types of recommendations. The authors argue that prior work is deficient as it is based on the relevance of the target to a particular query, instead of "other important ranking scenarios... such as sorting items by preference, importance, difficulty, or chronological order". It can be argued that this task is either essentially the same (ranking is ordering by distance from some target) or not well defined. In the paper, the authors seem to rely on general reasoning capabilities of LLMs in some contexts (the set of troubleshooting transcripts corresponding to user issues of various difficulty) and their ability to extract a number from a text (for chronological and preference ordering, the texts are preprocessed so as to include the diagnostic value explicitly), in others. The main methodological choice tested in the paper is that between ranking based on pairwise comparison and "listwise" ranking, where a model outputs a ranked list in one go. The authors note that while "pairwise approaches may seem advantageous... this intutition lacks robust empirical support in the context of LLMs". They then provide this empirical support, showing that listwise ranking performance worse overall and considerably worse as input lists grow longer. To implement the pairwise approach, the authors use "the MergeSort algorithm" with the comparison operator implemented using an LLM. They do not discuss the case then pairwise rankings may lead to inconsistent ordering. They further show that these pairwise comparisons may be implemented efficiently by distilling the knowledge of an LLM into a BERT-type model.

title: Revisiting Large Language Models for Ranking
review:
This paper addresses the insufficient evaluation of ranking capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) by proposing a new method for constructing datasets and releasing three ranking datasets. Experiments demonstrate that pairwise ranking outperforms listwise ranking, with the gap widening as the scale increases. This paper proposes an efficient BERT cross-encoder, which significantly accelerates the process while maintaining performance and demonstrating strong robustness to noise, thereby providing support for the implementation of efficient ranking systems.

**Strength:**

1. By introducing a novel approach to create diversified ranking datasets, the paper provides three new datasets to evaluate the ranking capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in terms of temporal order, numerical order, and conceptual complexity.
2. To address the high computational cost of LLM-based ranking methods in industrial applications, the paper develops a BERT-based cross-encoder model that significantly reduces inference time while maintaining performance comparable to that of LLMs.

**Weakness:**

1. "Empirical analysis showing pairwise ranking outperforms listwise approaches across all datasets. (§4)"This finding is indeed interesting, but is it a generalizable conclusion? The experiments were only conducted on the News Chronology dataset using two advanced models (claude-3-haiku and llama-3.1-8B-instruct). By appropriately increasing the variety of models or using models with different parameters, this conclusion might be generalized.
2. While the three proposed datasets (news chronology, product ratings, troubleshooting difficulty) cover meaningful and distinct ranking dimensions, they represent a limited scope of real-world ranking tasks. The authors should acknowledge this limitation. It is recommended that the authors extend the domain data types to include statistical data types (ordinal, nominal, ratio, and interval data) to more comprehensively validate the generalizability and robustness of the method.

title: How to Fine-Tune Safely on a Budget: Model Adaptation Using Minimal Resources
review:
This paper examines the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting of safety behaviors when a language model undergoes supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on benign data. The authors hypothesize that the effectiveness of safety examples is governed by two factors: the instruction–response behavior type (e.g., refusal vs. explanation) and semantic diversity across harm categories. Through systematic evaluation of sampling strategies along these axes, they show that a structured, diversity-aware sampling approach can significantly improve model safety—reducing harmful outputs by up to 41% while adding only 0.05% more data to the fine-tuning set.

Strengths:

Introduces a combined framework of behavior type and harm-category diversity for sampling safety examples, filling a gap in understanding which examples most effectively prevent safety forgetting.

Compares multiple sampling strategies—including random addition, behavior-only, diversity-only, and combined methods—under controlled data increments, clearly demonstrating the superiority of the structured, diversity-aware approach.

Achieves up to 41% reduction in harmful outputs with just a 0.05% increase in data, highlighting excellent data efficiency and practical value for real-world deployment.

Weakness:
 
The method relies on classifying examples by response behavior type (refusal/explanation), but the paper does not clarify the annotation costs or feasibility of obtaining these labels—potentially raising practical deployment barriers if manual labeling is required.
 
 While emphasizing harm‑category diversity, the paper lacks deeper discussion on defining and measuring finer‑grained semantic diversity (e.g., subcategory distinctions or latent intent variation).

The experimental setup lacks variety in tasks and datasets; additional benchmarks and real‑world scenarios would strengthen confidence in the method’s general applicability.

All results are demonstrated on a modest‑sized model, raising uncertainty about how well the sampling strategy scales to larger, production‑grade language models.

title: How to Fine-Tune Safely on a Budget: Model Adaptation Using Minimal Resources
review:
This paper presents a data-efficient sampling framework for maintaining safety alignment in large language models during supervised fine-tuning. The authors systematically explore how instruction-response behavior (particularly refusal behaviors) and semantic diversity across harm categories affect the efficacy of safety examples. They propose stratified and prototypical sampling methods, along with behavioral variants, and demonstrate performance gains over random baselines, especially in low-data regimes. The work is relevant to industry deployment of LLMs, as its focus on reducing harmfulness with minimal safety data augmentation, and it provides a reproducible methodology for safety-preserving fine-tuning.

Weakness:
1. While the two-dimensional sampling approach is a useful insight, the paper doesn’t deeply analyze why T1 behaviors outperform other types.
2. Novelty side is more methodological refinement, not really a fundamentally new algorithm. But since the paper is submitted to industry track, this might be ok.
3. LLM-based harm labeling step could vary significantly depending on model and prompting, however the exact prompts not provided. No code or scripts are shared either, which may slightly hinder replication for practitioners.
4. The paper could benefit from a more explicit motivational example of a safety erosion case to help readers visualize the practical impact.

I would suggest authors to:
1. Add qualitative examples of harmful prompts and model outputs before/after fine-tuning with each sampling strategy.
2. Release code and labeling prompts for full reproducibility.
3. Investigate combinations of behavior types beyond T1 to understand potential synergistic effects.
4. Include a human-in-the-loop evaluation to cross-check automated scorer reliability.
5. Provide a cost-effectiveness analysis for industry practitioners (e.g., GPU hours vs. safety improvement).

title: How to Fine-Tune Safely on a Budget: Model Adaptation Using Minimal Resources
review:
This paper proposes a sampling method that can select effective safety-alignment data in the general fine-tuning, hindering models from forgetting their safety complication. The proposed method leverages two straightforward yet sound signals: semantic diversity and complication behaviors. Particularly the complication behaviors indicate that models have learnt to refute that harmful query therefore they should not forget this in the course of downstream fine-tuning. 

Pros: a straightforward yet engineering-driven method

Cons: There is a lack of analysis about the learnability of the selected safety data for example what if the fine-tuning data are very different from the selected safety data, can the models still learn from both fine-tuning and safety? Another analytical dimension is are there any gradient conflicts?

title: Mitigation of Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models via JABA
review:
This paper introduces JABA, a training methodology intended to reduce cognitive biases in Large Language Models when they function as automated evaluators. The authors' central claim is that their technique improves a model's resilience to common biases, such as those related to position or authority, without degrading its judgment quality compared to the baseline model. However, the manuscript is plagued by significant methodological and analytical weaknesses that undermine its conclusions.

The paper's primary assertion, that its Q-JABA model enhances bias robustness while maintaining judgment quality, is immediately challenged by its own results. The data shows that Q-JABA actually achieves a slightly lower score for alignment with human judges than its base model. While the authors dismiss this as comparable,"any decline in human alignment is a significant trade-off. The fundamental purpose of a judge model is to reflect human preferences, and sacrificing this for better bias resistance is a critical compromise that the paper fails to properly justify or explore.

The proposed methodology consists of a two-stage pipeline, yet the paper offers no analysis to separate the effects of each stage. It's unclear how much of the bias robustness stems from the initial fine-tuning versus the more targeted DPO training. It is quite plausible that the first stage alone is responsible for most of the effect, which would greatly diminish the claimed novelty of the DPO-based mitigation technique.

Furthermore, the study's findings are presented in general terms, even though the models and datasets are exclusively Russian. This is a significant overstatement, as cognitive biases can manifest differently across languages and cultures. The paper’s findings are strictly limited to Russian, a constraint that is only mentioned briefly at the end but should have been acknowledged as a central limitation throughout the work.

The authors openly state that their measurement of the halo effect is not entirely accurate, explaining that they only use it as a preparatory step for another experiment. Incorporating a bias into the core framework only to discount its evaluation as flawed and instrumental is a major methodological weakness that casts doubt on the rigor of the entire evaluation system.

Similarly, the experiment designed to test the decoy effect appears to be heavily confounded by positional bias. The results show that reversing the order of the models dramatically shifts the outcome. Adding a decoy option only pushes the preference for the first model to an extreme. This suggests the experiment reveals more about a massive positional bias than it does about the decoy effect, making the conclusions unreliable.

In another part of the study, an alternative scorer methodology is found to have a higher correlation with human judgments than the side-by-side approach used for the main experiments. The authors note this indicates instability, but it's a critical finding that undermines their entire evaluation setup. If a different format aligns better with humans, it raises the question of why the side-by-side method was chosen for the primary experiments and training in the first place.

The paper's experiments on using reasoning prompts also yield confusing results, showing that they offer minimal benefit and can even be harmful by increasing positional bias in one model and decreasing a key reliability score in another. The study fails to provide a clear explanation for this, leaving the reader with a contradictory and unresolved issue.

Finally, the DPO training stage relies on functions that are described in frustratingly vague terms, making them impossible to reproduce. For instance, the method for creating flawed answers involves asking another LLM to add n spelling mistakes, but crucial details, like which LLM, what prompt was used, and how 'n' was determined, are missing. This lack of transparency makes a core part of the methodology impossible to assess or replicate.

Although the paper references other methods for addressing biases, the experiments only compare the new model to baselines, not to these alternative techniques. The study demonstrates that its method has an effect, but it fails to prove that its pipeline is any more effective or efficient than simpler approaches that already exist.

title: Mitigation of Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models via JABA
review:
## Summary
This paper examines how cognitive biases affect large language models (LLMs) when they are used as evaluators ("LLM-as-a-judge"). The authors show that Claude Sonnet 4 is more resistant to these biases than most other models. They also measure the agreement between models and human annotators using Cohen's kappa, finding that most models have weak correlation with human judgments. Finally, they propose a training pipeline (JABA) to reduce bias. Their results show a small positive effect, although the improvement is limited.  

## Strengths
The paper addresses an important and timely problem in the evaluation of language models. The idea is relevant to many current AI applications, and the experiments are interesting. The work could help raise awareness about potential issues in automatic evaluation with LLMs.  

## Weaknesses
- Although the experiments are interesting, the discussion sometimes focuses on less critical findings. For example, Table 2 contains results that could reveal deeper problems with LLM-as-a-judge compared to human annotations, but this is not explored in detail.  
- The proposed training method does not produce a strong improvement in model performance, and even it slightly reduces the Cohen's kappa score. While the authors claim that the model becomes "significantly more robust" (line 364), the experimental results do not convincingly support this statement. No statistical significance testing is reported to confirm the robustness of the results.  
- Table 4 is poorly structured and difficult to interpret. It is unclear what the main takeaway from the table should be.  
- How do the authors ensure that the human annotations are not influenced by the same biases? Were there specific guidelines or control measures to reduce bias in human judgments?  

## Comments and Suggestions
- Some citation style issues should be corrected. The text should remain self-contained even if the parentheses with citations are removed. For example, in line 072, use `\citet` instead of `\cite`. In line 099, combine citations into a single `\cite{key1,key2,…}` rather than multiple separate commands.  
- In line 179, "section" should be capitalized.  
- In Section 3.4, the formula for Cohen's kappa could be omitted, as it is widely known in NLP.  
- In line 256, fix the reference to the relevant table.

title: Mitigation of Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models via JABA
review:
Summary:
- This paper looks at a common problem in AI: using LLMs to judge other LLMs. 
- These judge models can be biased, like preferring one answer just because it comes first (positional bias) or being influenced by spelling mistakes (halo effect). 
- The authors propose a new method called JABA, which trains a better judge model that is less affected by these biases.
- They train their model, Q-JABA, in two steps: (i) First, using real human-labeled examples; (ii) Then, using changed (perturbed) examples that test different kinds of bias.
- They test Q-JABA and compare it with other models like GPT-4 and Claude. Q-JABA gives results similar to strong models, but it is more fair and consistent.

Pros:
- The paper focuses on an important problem (bias in LLM evaluations).
- It introduces a clear and new training method.
- Many types of biases are tested (e.g., positional, anchoring, halo, etc.).
- Results are well explained with helpful tables.
- The new model, Q-JABA, performs better in resisting bias.

Cons:
- The dataset is only in Russian, so it may not work the same in other languages.
- Human annotators may also have bias, but this is not studied.
- It does not test demographic biases (like gender or race).
- The model’s performance still depends on how you write the prompt.
- It is unclear if the model or data will be shared publicly.
- References/citations could be expanded and improved - e.g., missing but highly relevant work to cite: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03907

Overall Evaluation:
- This paper is useful and brings a smart solution to a real problem in AI evaluation. 
- It is well-organized, with good ideas and strong testing.

The two solutions proposed, QuestionRAG_ICL and QuestionRAG_SFT/GRPO can effectively address the problem and improve performance. Experiments are also reasonable. I can see the solution can be applied generally in multiple fields that are related. Some suggestions:

title: Knowledge-Augmented Question Error Correction for Chinese Question Answer System with QuestionRAG
review:
### Summary
This paper introduces QuestionRAG, a framework for handling input errors (such as grammatical errors or ambiguous phrasings) in Chinese Question Answering. 
The paper specifically aims to tackle misinterpretation and overcorrection issues of LLMs to erroneous input questions by 1) leveraging RAG for retrieving essential context for error correction, and 2) RL-based training for the question error correction task to avoid over-correction.

The authors perform ablation experiments on different Chinese Question Correction datasets to demonstrate:
- The impact of different types of knowledges in RAG (combined with non-fine tuned model)
- The effectiveness of the full pipeline provides the best results over baselines such as directly using just original question, QuestionRAG-ICL (QuestionRAG without fine-tuning) and QuestionRAG-SFT (QuestionRAG with SFT fine-tuning) .


### Strengths
- The paper is well-written, the approach is interesting, and experiments are well-carried out.

### Weakness
- As the authors acknowledged, the effectiveness of the system depends on retrieval system. What if search results are irrelevant? In case of long-tailed entities, what if the majority of the top results favor a wrong, more popular entity?
- The experiments are done on Qwen-3B model. It’s hard to conclude whether the effectiveness scales across model sizes.
- The pipeline may add significant latency in deployment

title: Knowledge-Augmented Question Error Correction for Chinese Question Answer System with QuestionRAG
review: This paper introduces QuestionRAG, a framework for correcting input errors in question-answering systems. The approach addresses two key problems: misinterpretation of user intent and over-correction that unnecessarily alters question structure. The solution combines external knowledge augmentation with reinforcement learning alignment to improve correction accuracy. It's technically solid. The evaluation metrics need to be added to Tables 3 and 5. More qualitative analysis would be beneficial.

title: AutoFineEval: Evaluation of enterprise RAG QA with interplay of reference-free, fine grained automated metrics
review:
The paper presents a collection of reference free metrics (AutoFineEval) for evaluating RAG QA systems. The metrics are designed to give insights on different dimensions providing guidance on which components of the RAG systems to improve.

The paper also shows results from a study that assessed how similar the ratings of human judges are to AutoFineEval's ratings in comparison to ratings by another set of referenceless metrics, RAGA. The authors claim that their metric behaves more similar to human judges.

Novelty & Impact:
It is not entirely clear to me from the paper what the main difference between RAG and AutoFineEval is.

In addition to the metrics, the authors also develop a monitoring system that provides an overview of metrics over time and feedback that can be used to guide further development of the RAG QA system being monitored. The monitoring system will be made available and could be useful for others who are developing or maintaining a RAG QA system.


Reproducibility:
The monitoring system will be made available, but it is not clear whether that will also include the data used for the evaluation, which is an augmented subset of WikiEval. Furthermore, not all details for the comparison with RAGA and the collection of human judgments are given. In particular, which RAGA metrics exactly were used and the exact instructions given to human judges.


Clarity & Structure:
The paper is very hard to read for several reasons: First, the paper is not self-contained as a lot if important information is only given in the appendices. E.g. the equations in Sec. 4 cannot be understood without the explanation in the appendix. Similarly, Table 2 and Figure 2 are not mentioned in the paper itself. Only the appendix refers to them. Second, many details are not explained.

- Sec. 3: What is the RAG triad?
- How are the decompose and match modules implemented?
- Table 1: The labels (SD, RP, etc.) are not introduced.
- What are the RAGA metrics that were used? How do they differ from the metrics proposed here? Were the instructions to the human judges formulated in such a way that they were neutral wrt. the difference between the RAGA and AutoFineEval metrics? That is, can we be sure that the judges weren't biased toward a rating behavior that is more similar to AutoFineEval?
- Sec. 5: What is the "precision-coverage trade off metric" described here?

Third, the writing contains a lot of grammatical errors and awkward formulations that impact the flow of the paper and make it hard to read.

Here are some typos and grammatical issues from the introduction. I did not continue to note these for the rest of the paper:

l. 030: "to a generator model(LLMs) tasked with generation of the response." --> missing space before the opening parenthesis; "tasked with generating the response"

l. 031: "Given that RAG enables ..., they present ..." --> "Given that RAG enables ..., it presents ..."

l. 035: "RAG based QA has been widely used in automation of customer care services (Xu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a) operations and as ..." --> Missing comma after the closing parenthesis?

l. 043: "Evaluating and improving retrievers and generators components individually don’t necessarily have effect on overall performance of downstream RAG QA applications." --> "Evaluating and improving [the] retriever[] and generator[] components individually [doesn't] necessarily have [an] effect on [the] overall performance of downstream RAG QA applications."

l. 056: "Existing metrics either demanded reference responses and annotated sources or LLM-as Judge metrics quantified errors in concepts like relevancy that does not provide interpretable scores ..." --> "Existing metrics either demand[] reference responses and annotated sources or LLM-as Judge metrics quantif[y] errors in concepts like relevancy [in a way] that does not provide interpretable scores ..."


Strengths:
- The authors developed a monitoring system that provides an overview of metrics over time and feedback that can be used to guide further development of the RAG QA system being monitored. The system could be useful for others who are developing or maintaining a RAG QA system.

Weaknesses:
- The paper is lacking details (especially about the comparison with the RAGA metrics).
- The paper is not self-contained. It relies on information in the appendix.

title: AutoFineEval: Evaluation of enterprise RAG QA with interplay of reference-free, fine grained automated metrics
review: This paper discusses the difficulties of measuring RAG QA quality and proposes.   AutoFineEval is "a ground truth free, fine grained framework we have operationalized for evaluation. The framework utilizes interplay of metrics to identify specific areas of improvement in RAG QA pipelines."  While the metrics discussion is useful, I am not sure that much new ground has been broken here.  It also fails to discuss some of the most significant problems with RAGs: how the RAG deals with contradictions between parametric knowledge of the LLM and material in the retrieval cache, and contradictory material in the retrieval cache.  While there are some useful metrics here, I don't see that they are compelling enough to replace human-in-the-loop evaluations, which are what really matters for real world deployment of RAG solutions.

title: AutoFineEval: Evaluation of enterprise RAG QA with interplay of reference-free, fine grained automated metrics
review:
# Overall Assessment

The paper's primary contribution is the proposed set of metrics for online evaluation of RAG systems. These metrics, centered on query coverage and precision for both retrieved passages and generated responses, aim to provide a more granular assessment by using an LLM assisted decomposition technique.

# Key Contributions & Strengths

The most significant strength lies in the demonstrated high correlation between the proposed LLM-estimated coverage and precision metrics and human preference data. This finding suggests that these metrics can indeed be meaningful proxies for human judgment, which is crucial for automated evaluation in production settings.
The paper also provides LLM assisted metrics to asses the response distinctness and grounding 

# Areas for Improvement

## Metric Novelty & Substantiality

The proposed trade-off metrics (query precision and query coverage for both source and response) are not a substantial novel contribution. It would be beneficial for the authors to elaborate on what makes their specific formulation of these metrics unique. The concepts themselves are familiar to the research community.

## Ablation Experimentation

A significant omission is the lack of an ablation experiment. To fully understand the impact of the LLM-assisted decomposition of queries, retrieved passages, and responses on the metric's performance, an ablation study is crucial. This would involve comparing the proposed granular estimation with a more standard, non-decomposed approach to demonstrate the value added by this specific methodology.

## Human Evaluation Comparison

While the high correlation with human preference data is a strong result, it would be beneficial to compare the proposed metrics with human scores on a Likert scale, as opposed to preference alone. A Likert scale offers a more nuanced measure of quality beyond simple preference, providing a richer dataset for validating the metrics' ability to capture different degrees of performance. This would strengthen the claim that the metrics are truly meaningful and not just reflective of a binary preference.

## Presentation and Clarity 

The presentation of the paper could be improved for better readability. Specifically, Section 4, which introduces the core metrics, suffers from a multitude of notations and indices that make it difficult to follow. Understanding the notation requires frequent cross-referencing between the main text and the Appendix, which disrupts the flow of reading. A clearer, more streamlined explanation of the notation, perhaps with a dedicated table or more intuitive naming conventions, would significantly improve the paper's accessibility.

title: Leveraging LLMs to Streamline the Review of Public Funding Applications
review:
Summary: This paper presents two real-world deployments of LLM-assisted systems for reviewing public funding applications in Portugal: (1) IExp: Corporate applications for international business expansion, focusing on summarization, inconsistency detection, and preliminary scoring of long-form proposals (~50 pages each), and (2) ReClaim: Citizen reimbursement claims for energy-efficient home improvements, focusing on document parsing, consistency checks, and checklist pre-filling for ~80,000 applications. Both deployments integrate GPT-4o into human-in-the-loop workflows, yielding measurable improvements in reviewer productivity (e.g., +20.1% for ReClaim). The authors provide qualitative reviewer feedback, highlight integration challenges, and discuss organizational barriers.

Strengths:
1)	Real-world deployment and scale: The paper describes two substantial operational deployments in public-sector workflows, processing tens of thousands of documents.
2)	Clear workflow integration: The work carefully considers human-in-the-loop design, GDPR compliance, and organizational constraints, which are often overlooked in research papers.
3)	Quantitative and qualitative evaluation: Productivity gains and reviewer agreement metrics are provided alongside subjective feedback, offering a multi-faceted view of system impact.
4)	Transparency in design choices: The authors detail why GPT-4o was selected over alternatives, and outline prompt design and cost-performance considerations.

Weaknesses:
1. Limited algorithmic novelty: The core technical approach is a straightforward application of commercially available LLMs (GPT-4o) to summarization and information extraction tasks, with prompts designed based on reviewer guidelines. No new model architectures, fine-tuning strategies, or adaptation methods are introduced. The novelty lies primarily in the deployment context, not in NLP methodology. Similar pipelines are well-documented in prior applied works for legal, administrative, and financial domains.
2. Repackaging of known techniques: The use of relevant section selection to avoid the lost-in-the-middle problem is known from retrieval-augmented prompting literature. The hybrid OCR + VLM approach for document parsing is standard in many document AI systems; the contribution here is largely the operational tailoring for Portuguese-language data. The prompt design patterns (structured outputs, XML/JSON schema constraints) are widely used and already reported in earlier industry and government pilot deployments.
3. Evaluation limitations: Reported productivity gains are compelling but lack baselines against alternative automation tools (e.g., fine-tuned smaller models or rule-based systems). The 20% improvement is context-specific; it is unclear how transferable these numbers are to other domains or languages. Some key metrics (e.g., false-positive rates) are measured on small test sets without statistical significance analysis.
4. Overemphasis on operational narrative: While integration challenges and regulatory constraints are important, the paper spends significant space on descriptive deployment details without translating them into generalized methodological insights for the research community. The lessons learned are mostly managerial/organizational, limiting the paper’s impact for an EMNLP-style audience expecting linguistic/algorithmic contributions.

title: Leveraging LLMs to Streamline the Review of Public Funding Applications
review:
The paper proposes a system to use LLM + Humans to streamline application for public funding in EU context. 

Strengths:

* There is no detail about how these applications were sampled from the general pool  
* Since the paper mentions 80K applications, it would be great to see results on a larger corpus:  how much did LLM and Humans agree on those (even if humans were verifying LLMs vs. doing independent assessment) .

review:

title: Domain-Specific Reranking: When is Adaptation Worth the Cost?
review:
The paper describes experiments in adapting the re-ranking component of a RAG system to different domains. The paper experiments with a ColBERTv2 architecture – using RoBERTa-base – for the re-ranker. Methods for domain adaption applied are domain-adaptive pre-training and fine tuning.

The experiments presented in this paper are relevant and interesting for the reader.
However, the reading experience could be greatly improved by improving the structure and narrative of the paper.

Many of the essential information is scattered throughout the paper, and the reader needs to piece together these pieces of critical information from different parts.
It would be better for the reader if you would state in one place the set-up of your re-ranker, and how you are going to evaluate. E.g., state once very early, that you are using a ColBERTv2 architecture that uses RoBERTa-base.
When you write in Section 3.2 that for fine-tuning you focus on ColBERTv2, it is confusing to the readers, and leads them to believe, that there are also other re-rankers that you worked on, when in fact you have only worked on one.

Also state early, that you are only going to evaluate the result of the re-ranker, but are not using it in combination with a downstream LLM and downstream tasks.
Since you are showing a downstream LLM that is using the RAG result in Figure 1, and also mention the different domains you are working, rather early, the readers wonders for a long time what the actual tasks are that you are going to work on, to find out that you are only evaluating the re-ranking result, using information retrieval metrics.

Data:
When you describe the data Section 4 you make it sound, as if you are only describing the fine-tuning data. But it then turns out that you are also using the same data for the testing (by inference from the headings in Table 2). However you are not describing how you split the test data from the fine-tuning data.
It would be necessary to state also the size of the test data sets, and how you split them from the underlying base sets. Ideally you would have a table for the different data sets, split in train, development and test sets, and what the different sizes of the sets are. The way you are describing it, it almost sounds as if you are fine-tuning and evaluating on the same data.

Metric
When it comes defining the metrics, it would be better to do that in Section 4, instead of Section 3. Further, a discussion on the difference in the metrics would be good. Since this is RAG for LLMs, in my opinion the hit rate would be a much more important metric, than mAP.
You can have an mAP of 1, but still have bad RAG for the downstream LLM, e.g., if your first RAG entry is a relevant one, and the rest of the entries is irrelevant. That would be excellent for mAP, maybe good enough for a human doing a search, but could be really bad for use in a downstream task.

Why is ColBERTv2 with RoBERTa-base not one of the baselines, but only appears in the base experiments?

Given the sometimes comparatively small difference in hit rate between the base models and the fine-tuned versions, it would be interesting to see what the impact on the improvements in the RAG results are on down-stream tasks. I.e., do the improvements in the information retrieval scores actually translate into improvements in downstream tasks making use of the RAG result?

Additional comments:
Section 4 does not make proper use of subsections. Instead it goes directly to subsubsections.

Figure 1 is way too small and hard to impossible to read, especially on a printout. But even in the electronic version, one as to zoom in a lot to be able to read the figure.

Line 048: corpuses -> corpora

title: Domain-Specific Reranking: When is Adaptation Worth the Cost?
review:
Summary

The paper is devoted to the domain adaptation of rerankers used for RAG. The authors claim that fine-tuning on small labelled datasets allows for improving the performance over the baseline.

Strengths

- Figure 1 elegantly demonstrates the difference of the proposed method from the related works.
- The motivation of the work is clearly presented.
- The paper is well-structured and easy to follow.

Weaknesses

Presentation

title: Domain-Specific Reranking: When is Adaptation Worth the Cost?
review:
This paper discusses a modification in the use of ColBERTv2 in which the model is adapted to particular domains.  The paper examines if any adaptation is helpful, and if so, should it be done at pre-training time (DAPT, domain-adaptive pre-training) or should it be done at post-training time (called fine-tuning, FT, in this paper).  In addition the authors explore if fine-tuning is effective with synthetically labeled data instead of human-annotated data.  The authors find: 1) DAPT + FT is not more effective than just FT unless there is large amounts of data to pre-train on, 2) domain-adaptation doesn't help re-rankers when the domain is close to general text, and 3) synthetically annotated data can provide the same benefit as human-annotated data (especially if the domain is niche).

This paper is quite niche in application and the set of experiments is quite limited.  The findings about data size, domain distance from "general text", and human vs. synthetic annotation may not apply even to another set of domains in the same application, much less extend to other areas.  However it is generally well written and easy enough to understand, and presents an interesting case study in domain adaptation (if limited), so I lean towards recommending this paper for publication.

Pros:
- well written and easy enough to understand
- domain adaptation of embeddings is an interesting and relevant topic

Cons:
- range of experiments is small, claims are stated more broadly than perhaps merited based on the experiments
- limited application of the ideas and findings

title: Unlocking the Edge deployment and ondevice acceleration of multi-LoRA enabled one-for-all foundational LLM
review:
This submission presents a hardware-aware framework for deploying a multilingual, multi-use-case LLM on resource-constrained mobile devices (Samsung Galaxy S24/S25, SM8650/SM8750 chipsets). The system integrates multiple LoRA adapters as runtime-switchable inputs within a single, frozen LLaMA-based inference graph. Innovations include: (1) efficient multi-LoRA management without graph recompilation, (2) on-device quantization and architecture optimizations, (3) concurrent multi-stream stylistic decoding, and (4) Dynamic Self-Speculative Decoding (DS2D) for accelerated token generation. The authors claim up to 6× latency/memory reductions and 2–3× decode speedups across 8 tasks in 9 languages, with accuracy comparable to server-side baselines.

### Pros

The paper addresses a critical and timely bottleneck: deploying adaptive, powerful LLMs on consumer-grade hardware, moving towards private, low-latency, always-available AI. Commercial deployment on devices (S24/S25) underlines real-world relevance and engineering maturity.

Treating LoRA weights as runtime inputs to a frozen graph (assuming fixed dimensionality) is elegant, allowing dynamic task/style switching without memory or compilation overhead. This design is convincingly benchmarked against less scalable approaches.

The concurrent multi-stream decoding strategy for stylistic variation (e.g., formal, jovial, etc.) reduces redundant passes, a clear improvement for user-facing mobile apps (e.g., Smart Reply).

DS2D achieves semi-autoregressive token generation without draft models, crucial for constrained devices. The dynamic, use-case-aware branching configuration for speculative decoding is technically sound and well-implemented.


### Cons

The manuscript omits details about the base LLaMA model training and LoRA construction (“proprietary,” refer to Touvron et al. 2023 and Hu et al. 2022). While understandable for commercial reasons, this reduces reproducibility. I urge the authors to include at least:

- Specific LoRA rank, dimensions, task selection criteria, and adaptation data size.

- How task/Lang-specific LoRAs are evaluated for coverage, overlap, and interference.

While baselines like MobiLlama, Flash Attention, and Eagle/Medusa speculative decoding are discussed, experimental quantitative comparisons are mostly absent. Including direct, apples-to-apples on-device benchmarks against these open baselines would solidify the claimed gains.

While G-Eval/ChatGPT 4.5 metrics and accuracy rates are reported, some user study or human-in-the-loop assessment (e.g., latency tolerance, stylistic output satisfaction, edge-case failures) would give a more holistic view of practical utility.

The main text sometimes defers too much to the appendix for technical details (especially for CTG and DS2D). A more self-contained core description would improve readability.

Figures referenced (e.g., Fig. 1–3) are essential to understand the system but are not always clearly integrated in the main body. Consider making key system diagrams more prominent.

While the framework is “a practical blueprint for broader AI workloads,” most contributions are tightly tied to LLMs and LoRA-style PEFT. Discussing the boundaries of generalizability (e.g., to vision transformers, multi-modal models) would temper expectations.

title: Unlocking the Edge deployment and ondevice acceleration of multi-LoRA enabled one-for-all foundational LLM
review:
This work introduces a framework for deploying LLMs on edge devices by using a multi-LoRA approach. The paper focuses specifically on experimenting and deploying multiple LoRAs from Llama foundational models on devices from the Samsung Galaxy series that come with specific Qualcomm chipsets. 

They experimented with three different approaches for deploying multiple LoRAs on an edge device: (1) a weight-sharing approach that reduces memory usage, (2) a masking approach that has a tradeoff between increased memory usage but faster inference, and (3) a LoRA-input based approach where the LoRA weights and primary input tokens are both sent as inputs to the model, which the authors claim have latency and memory benefits. Some additional strategies are also used, including accelerated token generation, a multi-stream decoding mechanism for being able to concurrently generate stylistic variations, and much more. 

The authors conducted several experiments across various tasks and many languages (even if it is limited to a particular family of devices with a specific chipset alongside additional constraints on the deployed foundational model). The findings may be interesting to an industry track audience who may also be looking to deploy larger language models on edge devices. 

However, there are several issues with the current state of the paper: 

- The paper's presentation would benefit from a more comprehensive related works section. The authors cited a mere 9 related works. The research problem of deploying larger language models on edge devices has been fairly explored, and there may be overlaps with existing work. This work obviously has its own unique findings and perspectives, and citing more previous related works will help readers understand why this work is different and important in its own way. 

- A number of related works are missing, such as:
   * Liu et al. 2024. MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for On-Device Use Cases. ICLR 2024. → This work demonstrates how smaller models can perform as well as LLaMA-v2 7B, and one can argue that smaller models that are on par with larger models can then be deployed on edge devices.
   * Hu et al. 2024. MiniCPM: Unveiling the Potential of Small Language Models with Scalable Training Strategies. COLM 2024. 
   * Xu et al. 2024. On-Device Language Models: A Comprehensive Review. 

Obviously, there are a lot more, but given the lack of a strong argument for how this paper distinguishes itself from existing work, it is hard to judge the contribution of the work within the broader research field. 

- Additional write-up issues:
  * Line 88: "...stylistic variants often are driven by the first token,..." There are other factors that determine stylistic variants… 
  * Line 259: "For example, Smart-Reply provides 8 diverse prompts for users to choose from." What is "Smart-Reply"? Is that a method from another paper? Which paper?
  * Line 286: What is d? It is never introduced formally, but it is defined in Figure 3 (d refers to the features of a token). All notation must be properly defined in the main text as well. This also goes for p and q (m was defined in Line 276). Same goes for notation in Figure 2.

title: Unlocking the Edge deployment and ondevice acceleration of multi-LoRA enabled one-for-all foundational LLM
review:
#Quality
This is a well-written paper about engineering.  It talks about the real-world problems of putting big multilingual LLMs on mobile and edge devices with strict limits on memory and latency.  The suggested framework combines multi-LoRA runtime switching, INT4 quantization, architecture-aware optimizations, concurrent token generation (CTG), and Dynamic Self-Speculative Decoding (DS2D).  The tests were done on Samsung Galaxy S24 and S25 devices, showing that they can work in the real world..

## Strengths in quality:
Showed real-world use on commercial smartphones, not just in tests.
 Results in numbers for 8 tasks and 9 languages, including memory and latency tests.
 A well-designed mix of several optimization methods, such as LoRA as input, quantization, operator fusion, and speculative decoding.

# Clarity
The paper is mostly clear and well-organized, with separate parts for related work, methods, experiments, and limitations.  The technical story is backed up by figures and tables.  But because of the hardware-specific details, the paper is more useful for people who are already familiar with Qualcomm NPUs.

## Strengths in clarity:

Clear explanations of three alternative strategies for multi-LoRA enablement.
Figures (e.g., CTG pipeline, DS2D branching) provide intuition.
Well-defined limitations section increases transparency.

# Originality
Systems innovation is very original: treating LoRAs as runtime inputs instead of static merges is new for mobile deployment.
Multi-stream decoding for stylistic changes in a single forward pass is a smart engineering solution.
DS2D speculative decoding doesn't need an extra draft model, which is one of the main things that sets it apart from Medusa/Eagle-style methods.

# Significance

The importance is very high:
The work goes beyond just testing in a lab and shows that on-device foundation models can work without relying on the cloud in Galaxy S24/S25 smartphones.
Results show that latency, memory, and throughput have all improved by 2 to 6 times, which shows that multi-use-case LLMs can be used on devices with limited resources.
This has direct effects on AI that protects privacy, AI that works offline, and AI that works at the edge and saves energy.

# Pros
Real-world deployment on flagship smartphones (not just benchmarks).
Novel LoRA handling (runtime inputs to frozen graph) enabling plug-and-play adaptability.
Comprehensive optimizations (attention parallelism, conv reinterpretation, quantization, speculative decoding).
Strong results across 9 languages and 8 tasks with consistent efficiency gains.
Transparent discussion of limitations and future directions.

# Cons
My feedback on Accessibility barrier: heavy reliance on hardware-specific engineering knowledge.

title: Unlocking the Edge deployment and ondevice acceleration of multi-LoRA enabled one-for-all foundational LLM
review:
Strength:

The paper is clearly structured

The method reduces the memory and latency for the LLM inference, which is useful for industrial application.

Weaknesses:

The motivation of designing three separate multi-LoRA enablement approaches is not clear. If they are targeting different application scenarios, the application scenarios should be stated clearly. In Section 3.1, the authors proposed three approaches (Figure 1a, 1b, 1c) for multi-LoRA enablement on device, but they do not give any information about their corresponding application scenarios, i.e., when to use which approach or they are used as some kind of combination? In addition, there is no comparison between them to demonstrate the pros and cons of a specific approach over the others and the motivation behind designing each one of them is also absent.

Moreover, some essential details are missing when describing each approach.

For the first approach (Figure 1a), it says in line 185-186 “During run-time, the corresponding graph is triggered.” There is no detail about how the graph is triggered and what statistics are used to determine which graph should be triggered.

For the second approach (Figure 2a), missing details about the one-hot encoded mask. Specifically, is the mask determined by user or the model itself? If it is determined by the model, how is it computed?

For the third approach, line 197-198 states “passing LoRA weights as inputs along with tokens.” Could you elaborate in detail how do you organize the LoRA weights with tokens to form your input?

title: DAST: Difficulty-Adaptive Slow-Thinking for Large Reasoning Models
review:
# Paper summary
This paper introduces Difficulty-Adaptive Slow-Thinking (DAST), a framework that enables large reasoning models to autonomously adjust their Chain-of-Thought length based on problem difficulty. By proposing a novel Token Length Budget (TLB) metric and employing budget-aware preference optimization, DAST effectively reduces overthinking on simple problems while preserving high accuracy on complex ones.

# Positive points of the paper
1. The paper is well-written, well-organized and easy to understand.
2. The paper squarely tackles the real-world pain-point of “overthinking” in LLM—excessive latency and cost—by letting the LLM decide how much to reason based on problem difficulty instead of always going deep. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that shorter answers need not come at the expense of correctness. This is a very encouraging result.

# Negative points of the paper
1. The performance of the proposed  DAST framework depends heavily on the chosen truncation threshold δ, which must be tuned via grid search on held-out data. This will bring additional computing costs and makes it difficult to implement a plug-and-play implementation in real applications. I'm somewhat concerned about the robustness of this approach in real-world scenarios.
2. The paper reports only the results of automatic evaluation metrics, and does not include any human evaluation or readability assessment. This omission might make it unclear whether the compressed DAST outputs remain coherent, interpretable, or free from hallucinations, especially in complex reasoning steps.

title: DAST: Difficulty-Adaptive Slow-Thinking for Large Reasoning Models
review:
This paper dives into improving LRMs that tend to "overthink" simple problems by producing overly long explanations, which wastes time and resources. The authors introduce a framework called DAST that lets models automatically adjust how deeply they think based on how tough the problem is. They define a metric called Token Length Budget to encourage the model to be concise on easy tasks but thorough on hard ones. Their experiments show this approach cuts down unnecessary computation while keeping accuracy high on complex questions.

Strengths:
1. The DAST framework introduces a novel mechanism that dynamically allocates reasoning resources based on problem difficulty. By enabling models to adaptively adjust their reasoning depth, the approach effectively reduces unnecessary computation, which is crucial for real-world industrial applications where inference latency and resource consumption are critical concerns.
2. The introduction of the Token Length Budget (TLB) as a measure of problem difficulty and response length offers a principled way to quantify and control model behavior. 
3. Extensive validation across multiple benchmarks and model scales demonstrates that DAST can maintain or even improve reasoning accuracy while significantly reducing response length and inference costs. This balance between efficiency and performance is a notable achievement relevant to industrial settings.

Weaknesses:
1. This paper is submitted to the industry track. But this paper fails to clarify the connection to industry. It looks more like a research paper.
2. In Table 1, the authors compared their DAST with many baseline methods. However, these baseline methods performed even worse than the original LRM. So, what's the point for these baselines as they lost much accuracy to achieve less tokens.
3. The training process involves several steps, including calibrating reward scores, constructing pairwise preference datasets, and fine-tuning with SimPO. This complexity might hinder straightforward integration into existing industrial pipelines without further optimization or simplification.

title: DAST: Difficulty-Adaptive Slow-Thinking for Large Reasoning Models
review:
This paper introduces a framework that aims to dynamically adjust the reasoning depth of LLMs based on task difficulty. The method rewards concise reasoning for simple problems while encouraging thorough reasoning for complex ones by applying TLB and budget-aware preference optimization. Evaluations across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that DAST offers significant token savings while maintaining or improving accuracy compared to SOTA methods.

**Highlights**

- The introduction of the TLB as a difficulty-aware control signal is effective.

- Ablation studies and fine-grained analyses provide useful insights into the contributions of different components.

- The method demonstrates adaptive behavior, with longer reasoning preserved for harder problems and concise outputs for easier ones.

**Limitations**

- Lack of real-world runtime analysis: Although there are extensive benchmark results, the paper fails to provide concrete measurements of runtime improvements or actual inference time comparisons. Given that the primary motivation is computational efficiency, this omission weakens the argument for practical impact.

- Limited model diversity: DAST is only evaluated with DeepSeek-R1 variants. It would be beneficial to see results on more diverse backbones such as GPT-4 and Claude to demonstrate generality.

- I would appreciate it if authors could add a comparison to early-exit or speculative decoding techniques, which are also designed to reduce unnecessary computation.

title: GenTradeX: Dynamic and Trackable Trade eXtraction from Financial Chats
review:
Problem: Extract structured, trackable trade events (explicit entities: ticker, coupon, maturity, ISIN, price, volume; implicit: direction, trade_status) from free‑form client–sales chats where attributes change over time and multiple trades co-occur.

Method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) Construction concatenates role‑masked messages and prefixes relative message numbers; (2) Extraction fine‑tunes decoder‑only LLMs via PEFT/LoRA to generate a linearized string of entity triplets with message indices; (3) Decode transforms strings into trade tables while preserving traceability.

Metric: GOATS greedily pairs predicted/gold trades using per‑pair F1 to compute a composite Similarity = mean(F1effect, F1avg, F1trade), designed to handle unordered sets and differing trade counts efficiently.

Data/Experiments: 1,186 annotated IB chats (≈48k messages; avg 40.35 msgs, 3.7 trades/chat), 80/20 split; 5‑fold cross‑validation reporting means±sd. Baselines: production RuleTrade (multi‑task BERT + rules) and GPT‑4/4o zero/few‑shot ICL. Models: Mistral‑7B, Llama‑2‑7B, Phi‑3 mini/small with LoRA; some 4‑bit quantized variants for deployment constraints.

Results: Best fine‑tuned Mistral‑7B achieves Similarity ≈0.77 vs RuleTrade ≈0.63 and GPT‑4/4o few‑shot ≈0.62–0.64; consistent gains across sub‑metrics; stronger performance on single‑message vs cross‑message trades; ablations on LoRA rank and LR. Greedy pairing is orders of magnitude faster than brute‑force permutations with negligible Similarity drop at high trade counts.

The paper type seems to be system/engineering report with benchmarking/production evaluation.

Strengths:
Clear, practical framing of a complex industry task with evolving attributes and implicit intents; message‑number traceability is a strong design choice for auditability and post‑validation.
Demonstrates meaningful gains of fine‑tuned, mid‑size open LLMs over both a production BERT+rules pipeline and GPT‑4/4o prompting on a realistic dataset.
GOATS offers an efficient, task‑aligned way to handle unordered/variable‑cardinality outputs; the composite metrics are easy to interpret.
Useful engineering details (LoRA settings, context length, training hardware; pre/post‑processing steps; quantized deployments).
Solid industry alignment: deployment plan on AWS GPUs, domain constraints discussed, and pre‑production expert feedback.

Weaknesses and Limitations:
Reproducibility gaps: proprietary data without release or synthetic substitute; incomplete reporting of seeds, sampling strategy for few‑shot exemplars, annotation protocol and inter‑annotator agreement, and decoding settings beyond max length.
Evaluation scope: limited stress tests for long‑context tracking, robustness to domain shift (other asset classes, counterparty styles), and error analysis on implicit intents; no statistical significance testing beyond fold variance.
Metric design: GOATS relies on greedy pairing that is not globally optimal; while efficiency is shown, formal analysis of worst‑case errors, ablations on the F1>0 threshold for “effective pairing,” and comparisons to bipartite matching (Hungarian) are light.
Industry ops metrics: latency/throughput, memory footprint, and dollar cost per chat are not quantified; hallucination handling is only briefly mentioned.
Anonymization/privacy: the paper notes masking but lacks explicit procedures for PII handling, retention policies, and regulatory review artifacts.

Industry relevance and impact
Strong fit: directly targets a high‑value pain point in sell‑side/buy‑side workflows; the traceability design aids audit/compliance; pre‑/post‑validation hooks are practical.
Deployment: Running on g5.24xlarge with quantized 8B models is plausible; however, provide concrete throughput (chats/hour), SLOs, fallbacks on failure, monitoring/alerting, and an A/B or shadow‑mode validation plan with real users.
Business impact: The claim of “capturing previously missed trades” is compelling; quantify lift (precision/recall of trade detection end‑to‑end, incremental revenue or time saved) and show at least a pilot‑phase evaluation.

Writing Suggestions:
Move the formal definition of GOATS and Algorithm 1 to the main paper earlier and show a small numeric example inline.
Provide a concise table mapping implicit decision rules (e.g., how Buy/Sell is inferred by role and phrasing).
Tighten Related Work to separate generative IE, event extraction in dialogue, evaluation metrics, and industry systems.

Questions for authors:
GOATS details: Why was F1>0 chosen to define “effective pairing”? Did you try optimal bipartite matching (Hungarian) and can you report the accuracy/time gap on your test sets, not just synthetic counts? Any failure cases where greedy pairing clearly mismatches? (arxiv.org)
Long‑context robustness: How does performance vary with chat length and number of interleaved trades? Please report metrics binned by context length and a memory/latency profile.
Implicit labels: Provide explicit, deterministic rules/examples for Buy/Sell and trade status inference (e.g., speaker role + verb patterns). How often are implicit labels wrong relative to explicit spans?
Data/annotation: What are the guidelines and inter‑annotator agreement for entities and statuses? Are ISIN/ticker normalizations standardized? Any annotation drift across time?
Reproducibility: Can you release a synthetic/de‑identified sample dataset and the linearization/decoder code to facilitate external validation?
Baselines: Did you evaluate RAG‑style prompting or constrained decoding (schemas) with GPT‑4/4o or open LLMs? If so, how close did they get?
Deployment: Please share measured end‑to‑end latency per chat, average GPU memory usage, throughput under concurrency, and approximate cloud cost per 1k chats; include monitoring and fallback plans.
Error analysis: Provide a confusion breakdown for direction/status labels and common entity errors (e.g., price updates vs final price). Any systematic failures for low‑liquidity bonds or unusual notations?
Generalization: Have you tested on other asset classes (FX, rates, loans)? What re‑training cost/labels would be needed to port GenTradeX?

Typos and minor comments:
Figure 1 caption: “An single example” → “A single example”; “an Client and Agent” → “a Client and an Agent”; “Trade flowing process are” → “Trade flow processes are”.
Table 1: Ensure consistent spacing for ± and significant figures.
Section 3.3: “batch size of 1 per GPU” — clarify gradient accumulation steps, if any.
A.3: “g5.24xlarge instance” — specify exact GPU model (A10G) and CUDA/cuDNN versions.
Misc.: Standardize capitalization of “LoRA”; fix a few line-break artifacts in references; ensure all acronyms are expanded on first use.

title: GenTradeX: Dynamic and Trackable Trade eXtraction from Financial Chats
review:
The paper presents an innovative framework for extracting structured trade information from unstructured financial conversations, such as those occurring on platforms like Instant Bloomberg (IB). The authors address the challenges of dynamic trade attribute extraction and traceability in client-agent chats, proposing an end-to-end solution based on fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). The paper also introduces a novel evaluation metric, Greedy Optimized Average Trade Scoring (GOATS), to handle the misalignment between predicted and ground-truth trade data.

The paper tackles a critical yet underexplored problem in financial markets: extracting dynamic trade details from unstructured chats. The task is complex due to the fluid nature of trade negotiations (e.g., changing prices, volumes, and implicit intents) and the need for traceability.The GOATS metric is a significant contribution, offering an efficient and effective way to evaluate trade extraction performance, especially given the challenges of cardinality mismatches and unordered predictions.

There are some comments:
The model performs notably worse on trades spanning multiple messages, indicating room for improvement in long-context understanding and noise filtering.

While LoRA reduces fine-tuning costs, the deployment on high-end AWS instances (e.g., g5.24xlarge) may be prohibitive for some organizations. The paper does not explore lightweight alternatives for smaller firms.

The paper lacks a detailed analysis of why certain entity combinations (e.g., "maturity, price, volume") exhibit higher variability in performance. Interpretability tools could help diagnose these issues.

The dataset is limited to English IB chats, potentially biasing the model toward specific linguistic patterns and trading profiles. The authors acknowledge this but do not propose solutions for multilingual or multi-platform adaptation.

title: GenTradeX: Dynamic and Trackable Trade eXtraction from Financial Chats
review:
Formatting: Does this paper follow the EMNLP template? The first page reads “Anonymous ACL submission,” which suggests it was prepared with the ACL template. Adherence to the venue’s formatting guidelines is a basic requirement, and noncompliance alone can warrant rejection. Nevertheless, I will provide some feedback.

Summary: The paper examines extracting financial attributes and trade outcomes from market sales and training transactions—an important yet understudied facet of financial-system modernization. Its primary contribution is a data model and end-to-end pipeline that enable large language models (LLMs) to learn transaction structure and generate structured outputs.

Comments:
First, while the paper explains the importance of the task, it does not clearly articulate (i) the limitations of recent LLM-based financial applications and (ii) the additional contributions this work makes beyond them. Consequently, the value of the paper and how it differs from prior approaches remain unclear. In Table 1, the tuned model outperforms a zero-shot baseline, but its advantages over existing financial methods are not demonstrated.

Second, the proposed GOATS approach offers limited novelty in its greedy pairing strategy. Similar one-to-one matching heuristics are widely used in various areas. Moreover, while the paper introduces the averages of three scores for the similarity metric, it provides no ablation studies to quantify the contribution or sensitivity of each component.

Recommendation: Reject at this time. The paper tackles an important problem, but the current version lacks clear differentiation from prior work, strong baseline comparisons, and ablations to substantiate its technical choices.

title: BioSynthRL: A Parameter-Efficient Biomedical Reasoning Model Through Synthetic Data Curation and Reinforcement Learning
review: This work presents BioSynthRL for transforming pre-trained foundation models without reasoning capabilities into ones capable of handling complex biomedical reasoning tasks. BioSynthRL utilizes systematic synthetic data generation and advanced reinforcement learning. Was Llama3-8B-R1 used as the pre-trained foundation model in the implementation? Since it is claimed as a framework, has it been applied successfully to other pre-trained foundation models? The symbols used in the equations require clarification to significantly enhance their clarity and comprehensibility. What baseline was used in the claim “Real-world industrial deployments demonstrate 78% total cost reduction and 23% diagnostic accuracy improvement”? It was also claimed that “BioSynthRL achieves 70-80% of large model performance at only 10% computational cost.” In critical application domains, like medical/healthcare, is this kind of trade-off between computational save and performance well justifiable?

title: BioSynthRL: A Parameter-Efficient Biomedical Reasoning Model Through Synthetic Data Curation and Reinforcement Learning
review:
Summary:
The authors present BioSynthRL, a biomedical reasoning framework consisting of three main steps: Synthetic Data Generation using Source2Synth, supervised finetuning with this data, and finally reinforcement learning with hybrid reward functions. The model has been evaluation with integration score to measure performance guarantee across all capabilities and balance score. Human evaluation of randomly sampled outputs was included for medical accuracy, reasoning quality, and clinical relevance.
While the solution may be impactful, the problem solved is unclear and the results need to be contextualized with better writing.

Pros:
1. Cost analysis provided for the framework which is helpful when assessing whether to implement the proposed model.
2. Ground truth evaluation with humans included. Ablation studies show the performance drop for excluding each of the three components.

Cons:
1. The literature review section is very limited, just a few sentences. Reasoning models cited and considered are old. There are other ones such as ReAct, Reflexion, and agentic solutions.
2. The paper is written poorly and there are incomplete sentences. For example section 5.4 ends with “We conducted human evaluation with 3 medical experts who assessed 200 randomly sampled outputs across three dimensions:” without stating what the dimensions are.
3. The goal of the paper is unclear. While the contributions list the steps of the framework, I’m unsure what the problem being solved is. 4. Is the task to create a biomedical-specific foundational model? Is it a reasoning process to be used on a generic LLM? Is the goal to create a chatbot? This is important to assess the relevance of experiments and understand the scope of the work being done.
Few baseline models are used for comparison. Even reasoning models listed in the related work section such as “Chain-of-Thought” are not compared against.

Details and questions:
1. Why are more synthetic data generation methods not considered? It would also be good to include a measure of synthetically generated data quality apart from the drop in performance in the ablation study.
2. Please include some qualitative insights as well as examples of what BioSynthRL gets correct compared to baselines and why.
3. Also, it might be beneficial to run the draft through a spell/grammar check. Some of the issues flagged below.
    a. Capitalization missing in section 6.1: biomedical reasoning Achievement:
    b. Missing space after period: “remains consistently high.Expert Consensus Patterns”

title: BioSynthRL: A Parameter-Efficient Biomedical Reasoning Model Through Synthetic Data Curation and Reinforcement Learning
review:
This paper introduces a parameter-efficient biomedical reasoning framework that converts 7B-parameter foundation models into domain-specific experts using synthetic data curation and reinforcement learning, achieving 70-80% of large model performance at 10% computational cost. Its deployment in healthcare and pharmaceutical settings demonstrates significant cost savings (78%) and accuracy improvements (23%), making it ideal for resource-constrained environments.


Key points:

Efficient Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art results within its parameter class while dramatically reducing computational costs.
Practical Applications: Validated in real-world scenarios with measurable improvements in diagnostic accuracy and cost efficiency.
Innovative Framework: Combines synthetic data (Source2Synth) and reinforcement learning (GRPO) to develop balanced multi-capability models.
Domain Expertise: Excels in biomedical-specific benchmarks like BIOMED-MMLU with 80.95% accuracy.

Overall, I think this is a solid paper, giving good contributions, experiments look correct and well-listed. The paper is well-written, easy to follow and I recommend for the conference.

title: AutoCVSS: Assessing the Performance of LLMs for Automated Software Vulnerability Scoring
review:
This paper proposes to use LLM for automatic CVSS prediction. The authors and prior work has established that this is an impactful task, enabling quicker turnaround for prioritizing certain CVE on the day it is published, reducing the risk of exposure to the high-severity vulnerabilities.

Given the quick advances of LLMs, application in various domains will have to catch up. This paper is one of them, applying it to CVSS task amidst existing non-LLM-based automatic CVSS predictor.

Strengths:
* Paper is clear, well-motivated, and justification is sound.
* Experiment code is provided, including all the prompts used
* Experiment setup and baseline chosen are sound
* Positioning of result is reasonable, baseline-level on high-data context, competitive on low-data, and leading in very limited data context

Weaknesses:
* Although prompts used were provided in the submitted code, there is little to no discussion on how the prompts were chosen. There could be more work on how the various kinds of prompts may affect the performance of AutoCVSS

title: AutoCVSS: Assessing the Performance of LLMs for Automated Software Vulnerability Scoring
review: The paper focuses on the relevant problem in software security of automatically, promptly assessing the criticality score for novel CVE records once they are published. The method focuses on generating prompts to several LLM systems, in order to let them assess such scoring. The paper is clear with wide, adequate background of the target task, and showing legitimate empirical methodology. While the paper is based on LLM application, the target task is into a software-security specific niche. I have some issues about its relevance and appropriate venue. In a strict language research track, the results would be arguably weakish, basically stating that: 1) LLMs mostly/somewhat work, and 2) reducing data hurts trained/tuned models. Now, coming to actual submission in the present Industry Track, after carefully checking the call for papers, I am slightly concerned about the actual relevance here as well, because the paper does not address, or addresses weakly, the key points required for an industrial setting. Its general focus should be industry-related issues (architecture, scalability, infrastructure, performance, etc.) of system deployment. Given the present paper content and organization, it would be best addressing directly the research-oriented communities of software engineering and software security. Nonetheless, the paper shows sound experimental methodology. As a practical benefit, software implementation is made available.

title: AutoCVSS: Assessing the Performance of LLMs for Automated Software Vulnerability Scoring
review:
# Summary

The manuscript introduces AutoCVSS, a RAG-based vulnerability assessment tool. The authors compare AutoCVSS against fine-tuning small language models (SLMs) under both low-resource and limited-resource settings (specifically for CVSS 4.0). Their findings suggest that AutoCVSS is the only viable solution during the industry’s transition from CVSS 3.x to CVSS 4.0, although it appears less competitive for CVSS 3.x scenarios.


# Questions, Comments, and Suggestions

 -   Prior work [1] shows that the different aspects of CVSS scores are correlated. My own experience assigning CVSS scores to CVE records aligns with these findings. This raises concerns about framing vulnerability assessment as an entirely independent multi-class classification problem (L215). A more suitable approach could be to construct a hierarchical structure that reflects the dependencies among CVSS aspects. Such a design would allow AutoCVSS to evolve beyond a straightforward prompting method into a more neuro-symbolic framework, potentially improving both accuracy and interpretability.
