title: Bias Amplification and Model Collapse: Large Language Models as Increasingly Biased and Degraded Media
review:
This paper looks at bias amplification as LLM is fine-tuned on synthetic data, with a focus on political bias. It uses the Webis-Bias-Flipper-18 dataset. 1518 articles (506 left, center, right, respectively) are used to fine-tune GPT-2 to then generate synthetic data. The remaining articles in the dataset (around 5K) are used to train a political bias classifier (details about the distribution of this portion of the dataset are missing in the paper). The paper states that it introduces the test quality index based on the Giberish Detector, but it is unclear whether it is the same metric but simply applied by calculating the score for each sentence and then averaging over all sentences in an article, or whether this is an extended version of the Giberish detector. Various mitigation strategies are used to observe the impact on quality over different data generation iterations. Moreover, an interesting 


Whilst the ideas of the work are good, there are a number of weaknesses in the paper. From the outset, this paper appears to have been repurposed for the Industry Track without sufficient consideration. For instance, Appendix K simply provides an expanded version of the related work. Several key details are placed in Appendices when they should belong in the main text (please note that the guidelines state "The paper should be readable by itself, and any details important for understanding the key aspects of the work should be in the paper rather than in appendices."). This reflects the 6-page limit in the Industry Track vs the 8-page limit in the regular track. Moreover, the paper does not provide enough context for the work's relevance to the industry track. The focus is more research-oriented, and I would highly recommend that the authors consider this, or else completely represent the research in a different mental framing. 

No justification is provided for using GPT-2 in these experiments. Considering that this is a 5-year+ model and a plethora of models exist, proper justification should be provided. It also becomes problematic since the same level of collapse might not happen with larger/more recent models. Moreover, the dataset covering news articles from 2012 to 2018 could already be part of the training data. A more interesting approach to data provenance might have been to use post-GPT-2 data to ensure that there is no data leakage in the model. 



Questions:

q1. From your Related Work section, a number of studies on political bias have identified left-leaning tendencies in a number of models. Yet, your results show that the generated data becomes more right-leaning. How do you explain this difference? 

q2. section 3.6 - why 6 rounds per training round? How long does each round take to train? 

q3. why not provide fig 2 with the iterative distribution change over the synthetic output? 

q4. why gpt-2 and why a dataset from the "same period"?

q5. given that you focus on gpt-2 as a model, what is the key application/contribution of your work on today's models?

q6. for synthetic generation, do you always use the original dataset? If so, how does it change in different iterations since "these predictions are made using a deterministic generation to enhance the reproducibility"?

q7. are synthetic articles not only the same number of articles as the original, but would also be similar in length given the 64-token blocks? 

q8. why is generation more prone to produce right-leaning articles if models are reported to be left-leaning? 

q9. there seems to be a correlation between text quality and right-leaning bias (shown in fig. 3), what are your thoughts about this?

q10. what should one make out of fig 4? I cannot see any emerging patterns or changes, and I am not sure what to make of it as a reader. 

q11. do you attempt to manually alter identified correlated neurons to see if the output can be influenced in one direction or the other? 



Recommendations:
- Include a proper reference for GPT-2 with clear details on the version used
- Use ` in latex for single open quote

title: Bias Amplification and Model Collapse: Large Language Models as Increasingly Biased and Degraded Media
review:
## Summary
This paper studies bias amplification and model collapse when training large language models on synthetic text in the context of political ideologies. The authors fine-tune GPT-2 on a balanced news dataset, then repeatedly generate new datasets from the model's outputs to further train it. They find that, although the original dataset is politically balanced, the model's outputs underrepresent left-leaning perspectives even after the first fine-tuning. This imbalance worsens with further iterations. They also observe that the quality of generated text decreases over time. Three mitigation strategies are tested. While these strategies can reduce model collapse, they do not stop bias amplification. Using a mechanistic neuron-level analysis, the authors show that the parts of the model responsible for bias amplification and for collapse are mostly distinct.

## Strengths
- Broad experimental setup with interesting and timely findings.  
- Clear focus on a socially important issue.  
- Well-structured and coherent paper.  

## Weaknesses
- The study uses GPT-2, which is outdated compared to current models such as LLaMA-3.  
- The choice to limit the source news articles to pre-2018 content is not well-explained.  
- Some sections lack clarity. For example, Figure 4 is difficult to interpret, and Section 4.4 does not clearly explain what the figure shows.  
- The conclusion mentions many experiments that are only described in the appendix. These should be moved to the main text or omitted.  
- The implications for industrial applications are not discussed in enough detail.  

## Question for the Authors
In the literature review, you mentioned that modern models are often criticized for a left-leaning bias. However, your results show that the model you tested tend to shift toward a right-leaning bias. How do you explain this discrepancy?

title: Bias Amplification and Model Collapse: Large Language Models as Increasingly Biased and Degraded Media
review:
This paper does not seem to fit well an industrial track, it is more suited for a research track possibly.

An obvious and somewhat surprising issue is that the paper focuses on GPT2. 
One could argue that the underlying technology is still very relevant and that the paper tries to uncover a behavior of a classes of models.
Assuming that that's the case and the work still applies, then I would expect a study that provides insights on what fundamentally leads these kinds of model to a certain behavior, not just that GPT2 has a certain behavior.

Therefore, I would encourage the authors to then experiment, for example, at what scale certain phenomena appear and whether that is dependent on pre-training, or on aspects of the model, or if it depends on a somewhat subjective assessment of what is right and left.
For example, many people on the left side of the political spectrum prefer the term illegal to undocumented. 


There are also many apsects that make the study hard to evaluate. For example, to have a politically unbiased dataset it's not enough to just have an equal number of articles for each category - other factors also matter. Lenght, strength of bias, etc. and this assuming that the bias assessment is... unbiased.
The statistical significance analysis seems to need Bonferroni-like corrections unless I am missing something, and needs to account for errors in the classifier and subjectivity in the ground truth - in summary, results suffer from a large set of limitations.

The article also states that "Our results demonstrate that bias amplification and
model collapse are driven by distinct sets of neurons, implying they are separate phenomena." but I am not convinced that there is evidence to support this claim.

You would also need to make sure there are no confounding factors the model is picking on, that have nothing to do with political leaning.
To have an unbiased study i'd recommend to put models in front of humans and perform a randomized controlled trials across models and subjects, trying to control for confounding factors.

Finally, I am also unsure as to what the paper contributes in terms of state of the art. There are lots of papers on political bias and on collapse - some of them indeed cited, but it is unclear which new insights are provided here.

title: RulePatch: Continual Rule Learning for Large Language Models to Reason with Tools
review:
In commercial settings, tool-using language agents are required to adapt to ever changing sets of tools and work-flows while remaining interpretable. This calls for continual learning, making incremental improvements without requiring retraining. Modern tool-using LLMs use rules to direct their behaviors, incorporating them into their prompts. The source of these rules is what distinguishes alternative approaches.

Here, the authors draw extensively on previous work in explanation-based learning. They present a neuro-symbolic system that adds targeted rules over time using failure-driven learning. Their goal is to incrementally learn natural language rules tailored to recurring modes. Rules are provided by an LLM in response to component-specific prompts. When a failure has been detected, it is taken as the need to adapt their rules. Retrieved candiate rules that have been validated (e.g. do not cause regression, are not too similar to the existing rules) are incorporated into a rule library and are incorporated into the prompt to guide that system in the use of the tools. Rules are retrieved by their semantic similarity to the current problem.

The paper is well written and its exposition is effective and flows smoothly. They include an extensive, if abbreviated, review of other systems looking at whether they require domain tailoring, learn from data, handle noisy data, and are doing  continual learning The components of their system are very thoroughly described, along with the prompts each one uses to identify rules, errors, and retrieve rules to be used in the prompts they formulate when running. 

Their experiments use two benchmark datasets, ToolHop and BFCL ("Berkley function calling leaderboard") which all involve multi-step reasoning with user-contributed documentation and queries. For their experiments they draw on two subsets ("Live-Simple" and "Live-Multiple"). They compare their system's performance against two baselines with complementary approaches to the problem, PhraseEvo and ReAct. They look at task results (percent correct) running on  commercial LLMs of varying strengths from the GPT and Gemini families, plus LLAMA. They thoroughly discuss the results looking at properties or the task and the different approaches. They emphasize that the rule knowledge their system, RulePatch, is persistent across run and reusable. I presume, though they do not say, that rules retain information about the failure(s) that motivated them. Their regression test restricting the number of rules that can be part of a prompt, is particularly interesting

As thorough as the authors are, this paper still leave much to the imagination. It will likely provide valuable insights to readers who work in this area. However to a neophyte coming from a completely different are of AI, it appears that all the 'good stuff' is provided by a black box. It would be of enormous value to have a few completely worked examples, perhaps working backwards from what you show in figure two. What are the failures that prompted these rules? What costs are we looking at (runtimes, space requirements, typical number of rules in a problem prompt, etc.? There is not room for a proper set of examples in this paper, but think of how you would organise the journal paper that comes next.

Question #1: How do you detect a failure? Your system diagram in Fig.1 only says "correct response" versus "incorrect response". You refer to comparing the 'final output' to "ground truth". How to you get any ground truth without any tailoring to the problem domain and tool set?

#2 Please provide more detail about how "semantic similarity" (line 201) is done. Is it the same thing as "embedding-based similarity"? (line 228). How do you bootstrap these procedure when your rule library is still small.

title: RulePatch: Continual Rule Learning for Large Language Models to Reason with Tools
review:
This paper introduces a method called RULEPATCH for LLMs improving tool-usage ability. This method enables LLMs learn from failures in test time, where the failures are summarized and generalized to rules stored in rule pool and then retrieved for future uses. It is called continual rule learning. Experiments on ToolHop and BFCL show the method outperforms traditional Act, ReAct and PhaseEvo method, and the ablation study reveals the effectiveness of the used rules and the rule retriever.

In overall, the proposed method is straightforward and shown effective. However, I have the following concerns:
1. The method needs an initial rule pool generated with a training set, where the compared methods, especially Act and ReAct, cannot leverage the training set. This results in an unfair comparison.
2. A more straightforward baseline is in-context learning, where the training set serves as the in-context examples and can also be retrieved with a retriever based on query similarity. But the paper did not compare with it.
3. The method is only tested on BFCL live simple and multiple categories. While the authors emphasize "multi-step" (line 245) for the reason of chosen, these two categories are only about single-turn single-step. The selection of test categories is not convincing.
4. The motivation for the design is not well clarified. For example, why using LLMs for rule retriever considering semantic similarity? When the rule pool is large, the context length for a retrieval should also be large and not friendly for LLMs. And why the rule generator is divided into two parts, explainer and generalizer? Given that these two parts are only two fixed different prompts, combining them to one fixed prompt is also feasible. Have the authors compare these two settings?

Given the above concerns, I think significant revision is needed and so recommend rejection.

title: RulePatch: Continual Rule Learning for Large Language Models to Reason with Tools
review:
### General Comment:

In the area of tool/function calling agents, this paper proposes to incrementally learn modular natural language rules from agent failures (to add one targeted rule each time from one failure). This rule learner is from a prompt-based LLM, and the learned rule will be added to a rule library, to be retrieved (based on a prompt-based LLM) and the retrieved rule will be added to LLM's prompt for inference. (A prompt-based LLM means the main contribution is lying on the prompt design of the LLM to let it work). So far, the whole pipeline is very moderate, which I personally see very limited industrial merits, nor methodological merits.

### Strength:

- S1: The paper is generally well written and easy to follow.
- S2: The paper also compares with a decent amount of models, from GPT-4o to LLAMA-3.3


### Weakness:

- W1:  So far, only two frameworks are evaluated, PhaseEvo and ReAct, and neither is the state-of-the-art (published in 2023 or early 2024). For example, there are also follow-up works after ReAct, such as reasoning agentic models, DeepSearcher.

- W2: I believe the recent Reasoning Language Model (such as Qwen-3-think, DeepSeek-R1) may easily solve the so-called "rule learning task" from their loop-like iteratively reasoning process; and if so, the motivation of this work is weakened. The authors should also compare Reasoning Language Model (such as Qwen-3-think, DeepSeek-R1).

- W3: How can we evaluate the quality of the learned rules? Table 4 did some ablation studies, but randomly selected rules for sure will perform bad. How can we evaluate, even if the rules are carefully selected, but there must be good-quality rule and bad-quality rule.

- W4: Another important missing point is: is there a golden ground-truth rule(s) for each query? if yes, the recall of the rule retriever is very important to do experiments about.

- W5: My biggest concern: what industrial merits can this paper offer to the users who really work in tool and function calling? In industry, we just put the error message from last round failure to the next around prompt, and most of the time, it works. We don't really wanna go through the tedious rule learning, and store the rule, and then retrieval

title: SLOT: Structuring the Output of Large Language Models
review: The paper shows fine-tuning LLMs is effective for developing models that transform free-form natural language output of language models into structured JSON. For fine-tuning and evaluation, they rely on SlotBench, which they also plan to release, that comprises a curated test sets and a training set. The test set relies on partial synthetic generation and the training data is fully synthesized. It's then filtered to ensure quality. Fine-tuning smaller language models on the synthesized data beats the very same larger models that were used for data creation. Given the importance and prevalence of needing structured data for many downstream tasks, the community benefits from the results.

title: SLOT: Structuring the Output of Large Language Models
review:
The authors contribute two major items in this work: (1) Slot, a post-processing approach for structuring the output of LLMs, specifically to JSON formats, and (2) SlotBench, a new benchmarking dataset that the authors created for evaluating the structuredness of the generated output. 

Underlying Slot is essentially a finetuned LoRA model that structures the output of LLMs and presents the work as an alternative to standard constrained decoding. The solution's approach itself is not novel; there is a breadth of non-research work that finetunes LoRA models for various industry tasks (a quick Google search shows a LoRA model for structuring outputs into JSON format: https://predibase.com/blog/lorax-outlines-better-json-extraction-with-structured-generation-and-lora). While the problem of structuring the output of LLMs is a known challenge in the industry, a LoRA model on its own is too widespread a solution to merit its own research paper in an industry track at ACL. 

On the other hand, the authors also introduce a new dataset, SlotBench, alongside an evaluation framework. The evaluation framework measures two aspects of the generated output: (1) schema accuracy and (2) content similarity. The proposed SlotBench dataset was curated using a combination of public datasets and synthetic data generation, resulting in a challenging and complex dataset, which the authors illustrate and describe in detail (which should suffice even if the dataset is not yet available to the public).  

However, in light of much recent work in this space, I would have expected that this paper also addresses other works that it might be overshadowed by, such as StructEval by Yang et al. (https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20139v1). StructEval covers a diverse range of structured formats beyond JSON, such as YAML. The paper does mention other existing benchmarks, such as JSONSchemaBench by Geng et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10868). Yet, one might argue that the JSONSchemaBench benchmark pretty much covers what SlotBench aims to do anyway, even if JSONSchemaBench's evaluations are focused on constrained decoding (the benchmark itself is quite comprehensive).  

The evaluation section shows results across a range of strategies for structuring the output. It showcases that finetuning a model for structuring outputs and also using constrained decoding improves the structuredness quality of the model's output. The finding itself is not novel; of course, any finetuning for a particular task would improve its performance on said task. 

Some of the claims in the paper are also inaccurate, such as in Line 124: "Our post-processing based method is flexible and does not require access to LLM model weights, making it suitable for the case of serving a diverse array of LLMs in a platform." However, the proposed solution uses an adapter model to post-process the generated output, which essentially means one would need access to some LLM model weights.

title: SLOT: Structuring the Output of Large Language Models
review:
The authors describe their SLOT system ("Structured LLM Output Transformer") which operates in the inference phase to convert the raw unstructured, text output of an LLM into an instance of a designated JSON schema for downstream applications to use. 

When LLMs are being used as a component of a larger system (e.g. building multi-step action workflows, function calling to answer questions) it is important to ensure that their structured output conforms to a stipulated format with accurate attributes and values given the text string input generated by the LLM. There are alternative methods of intervening during the inference phase to transform text to a target structure. but the authors argue that these are too cumbersome, require access to the LLM's weights, or add unneeded latency. This is unnecessary with SLOT, where user prompts specify the JSON Schema to be used for the structured output, and its trained model of text-to-structure mappings does the work.

They evaluate SLOT according to two criteria: Schema Accuracy, does the response string exactly match the schema that was requested in its keys and value types, and Content Similarity, does it include values for all the slots in the schema and are the values sufficiently close to ground truth. Content similarity is done using a pretrained Sentence-BERT model comparing produced values against the corresponding value with matching key in the ground truth.

To train SLOT, the authors collect a set of triples: the input text produced by the LLM, the schema that defines the structure specification, and the ground-truth structured output. These are drawn from five public data sets that all provide ground truth JSON. Three that have been used for natural language generation (data-to-text) challenge problems, a table-to-text dataset taken from Wikipedia tables where some cells are paired with descriptive sentences, and one drawn from Hugging face transformer issues chosen for their diversity and realism and the complexity of their schema. The input texts in the last two data sets do not cover all of the variables in their schemas. For these, the authors use Claude-3.5 to create synthetic texts that cover the missing data.

SLOT is trained to accurately transform unstructured text input in JSON according to a specified schema and satisfying their evaluation criteria. They build on a pretrained decoder language model, Llama-3.2 and Mistral-7N-v02, using Supervised Fine-tuning. 

They evaluate SLOT against its alternatives. Proprietary LLMs with standard prompting (Claude-3.5-Haiku and -Sonnet) to establish a baseline. And open-weight LLMs with constrained decoding (Qwen-2.5  and Llama-3.3) with two constrained decoding frameworks: Outlines, and XGrammar. They also evaluate SLOT combined with constrained decoding. The best results were SLOT plus XGrammar. 


The writing is fluent and clean. The exposition, particularly of the testing procedures, is effective and convincing. It does, however, make extensive used of its set of appendices, of roughly the same size as the paper proper. This additional material was extremely helpful to this reader to understand how their system works, particularly the review of other approaches and the details of the datasets they use.

title: FishFlow: A LLM-Empowered Dynamic Pricing Framework for Online Fleamarket Platform
review:
Brief Summary of the Paper: This paper tackles a relevant and underexplored problem: dynamic pricing in C2C online flea markets, where single-stock items and sparse, noisy data make standard pricing methods ineffective. The author's idea of leveraging LLMs to extract structured information and reference items from unstructured seller input is novel and well-motivated.
In this paper, the proposed FishFlow framework is well structured by fusing user preferences, retrieval of reference items (via LLM-based similarity scoring), and function-based price estimation. 

Below are a few key weak-points about this paper:
(a) While the framework is clean, the methodological novelty is somewhat incremental..
(b) The contribution is more of a system integration paper by leveraging LLMs in a easy use manner..
(c) Key comments about the Evaluation Metrics: The proposed metrics (PIR, PDR, PR-F1) lack strong grounding in economic theory;
No revenue uplift analysis is provided; and No statistical significance tests are shown for the online evaluation uplift.

Questions to Authors:
1. You modeled the demand curve as an exponential decay function. Could you explain why this specific form was chosen over other demand models (e.g., linear, logistic, or learned parametric forms)? Also, please explain how sensitive are your results to this assumption?

2. Your evaluation significantly relies on PIR, PDR, and PR-F1 as proxy metrics. Could you provide additional results showing the actual revenue impact (e.g., expected seller/platform revenue gains, etc.) or at least simulate revenue outcomes under different strategies?

3. FishFlow is tested on a specific platform that contains textual descriptions and search logs... how generalizable is your approach to other C2C or B2C marketplaces? Any quick comments do you have?

title: FishFlow: A LLM-Empowered Dynamic Pricing Framework for Online Fleamarket Platform
review:
The paper presents FishFlow, a compelling LLM-powered dynamic pricing framework tailored for online fleamarket platforms, addressing a critical industry need where traditional pricing models fail due to sparse data and unstructured item descriptions. Its hybrid approach (LLM + demand function) balances interpretability and competitiveness, validated by offline metrics (PR-F1: 59.39%) and real-world online gains (+3.03% exposure, +5.25% chat conversions).The paper is clearly written, with logical flow and sufficient detail. It has substantial practical implications.

Pros:
1) Novel Methodology: Combines LLMs with demand function modeling, addressing LLMs' numerical insensitivity while retaining interpretability.
2) Practical Relevance: Solves a real-world problem for fleamarket platforms (e.g., Xianyu, eBay) where sellers lack pricing expertise.
3) Strong Evaluation: Offline results show balanced performance (PR-F1: 59.39%), and online deployment improves exposure (+3.03%) and chat conversions (+5.25%).

Clear Design: The three-stage pipeline (user preference fusion, reference item collection, price estimation) is well-explained with prompts and case studies.

Cons:
1) Limited Multimodal Data Use: Focuses only on text, ignoring images/videos that could enhance item similarity scoring.
2) Computational Cost: Relies on a large LLM (Qwen3-235B) without fine-tuning, which may hinder scalability.
3) Simplified User Preferences: Categorizes preferences into three discrete types (0, 1, 2), potentially oversimplifying seller behavior.

title: FishFlow: A LLM-Empowered Dynamic Pricing Framework for Online Fleamarket Platform
review:
Pros:
1. The paper proposes a framework for dynamic pricing using LLMs. It generates reference items using search logs and then estimates price using both LLMs and demand functions. 
2. The paper is well organized and provides a comprehensive explanation of the model. 

Cons:
1. Section 3.2, page 4 mentions using top-k sampling on similarity scores generated by LLMs where similarity scores are discrete values {0,1,2}. How is the sampling performed exactly, like what are the tie-breaking rules? Was any experiment performed by generating top-k similar items directly through the LLM? 
2. It’s unclear when using search logs for the current target item listing, how long after the listing is the dynamic price generated and how often is it refreshed? 
3. It will be useful to define the “naive” baseline used and provide a reference for it if applicable. 
4. In the online experiment, some other metrics like increase in the number of items sold, diversity of the items in the experiment etc. will be helpful to strength the contribution. 
5. Please add definitions like list price, reserve price, etc in the revision.

title: Effective Performance Measurement: Challenges and Opportunities in KPI Extraction from Earnings Calls
review:
The paper reports on experiments of deploying different models, including transformer- and generative AI-based ones, for the task of extracting company KPIs from so called earning calls (i.e., conferences between management and investors). For the sake of carrying out the study three benchmark corpora have been created. The authors compare the performance vis-a-vis KPI extraction from SEC filings which serve similar purpose, but are more structured and apparently easier to extract information from. Examples showcasing the difficultry of extracting KPIs from call earnings are provided.

Strengths:

Questions/Details:

title: Effective Performance Measurement: Challenges and Opportunities in KPI Extraction from Earnings Calls
review:
The paper aims at extracting KPIs (traditionally known and novel ones) from earnings calls (transcripts). This task has already been explored on SEC Fillings but the authors stress that obtaining KPIs from earnings calls is also important as it impacts stock performance and other critical metrics. Given the earlier SEC fillings exploration, the authors first experiment with existing techniques from that literature. The authors also experiment with few-shot prompting on decoder models such as Gemma for the task. Further, they contribute with three novel benchmarks, two of which are on earnings calls and one which is manually annotated. The authors conclude that existing encoder language model based techniques are not at par with earnings call KPI extraction however large decoder based language models show promise for the task. They provide a detailed qualitative analysis as support.

**Strengths**

1) Given the impact of KPIs and details in the earnings call, this is an important task in the domain of financial information extraction.

2) The detailed qualitative analysis provides an insight into how difficult the nature of earnings call transcripts and extraction from them can be.

**Weaknesses**

1) The evaluation on ECB-A is conducted using the KPI Gap metric or in LLM-as-a-judge mode when there could have a better way given ECB-A has proper manual annotations of the KPIs and associated values. The extracted KPIs/values and the gold ones can be matched using word overlap or semantic similarity (lenient) which would be more appropriate for information extraction evaluation. Another associated gap is that in the caption of Table 3 it is mentioned that "Performance on ECB, LLM-judged win rates against human labels". This is contrary to the mentioned facts that ECB doesn't have human annotations (ECB-A has human annotations) and the LLM-as-judge prompts (Listing 2 in Appendix) use human labelled entities.

2) At several places (lines 218, 230, 231) the task mentioned is KPI classification. It is not clear that in those contexts the task is only of KPI classification (traditional vs non-traditional) or both extraction and classification. This should be made clear for proper problem understanding.

3) Particularly for the ECB-A dataset, details such as annotation guidelines and inter annotator agreements are not highlighted. Given the task of identifying KPIs and their corresponding values is complex, annotation guidelines provide necessary guidance on text segements to be considered as KPIs/values and such guidelines must be included.

4) In section 4, the detailed model details such as architecture etc are referred to Section A.1 in Appendix, however apart from company abbreviations there are no other details on model architecture, hyperparameters, etc. It is important to detail which are the existing encoder model architectures (atleast in the Appendix) to understand how the tags "B-revenues" get learnt and predicted. Further, it can be specified whether a Conditional Random Field (CRF) based decoding head was used or a simple token-wise softmax was used.

5) There are several gaps and confusing phrases in the paper. Some examples are:

- GAP: Lines 127-131, examples of Traditional and Non-traditional metrics should be highlighted

- GAP: Line 194, How is KPI extraction frequency defined?

- GAP: The different BERT variants such as BERT-SL1000, etc should be briefly explained in the Appendix

- GAP: In the ECB-A result analysis, class-wise (Traditional, Non-traditional, other) results can also be added for stressing whether the novel KPIs are better/poorly extracted in comparison to the Traditional ones.

- CONFUSING phrase: "zero-shot LLMs". Generally zero-shot prompting is a technique rather than LLMs being zero-shot. If there is any other semantic associated with this phrase, that can be explained.

- On lines 90/91, the citations of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo (AI, 2025) and Gemma-3 models (Team et al., 2025) have issues regarding the author name as only either "AI" or "Team" which is the second part of the name ("Meta AI" or "Gemma Team") is coming.

6) The paper is not well written and there are several issues with the sentence formation and grammar. Some examples are highlighted as follows:

- SECB Unlike HiFi-KPI (Aavang et al., 2025), that maximize information density. SECB maximize text extracted, including non-KPI text.

- Specifically, 94.76% of judged 4B wins with 27B losses on the same snippet is when the 27B model predicts no entities and 4B does.

- Zheng et al. (2023) showed that you could reliably use LLMs (GPT-4) to evaluate the performance of language models .

title: Effective Performance Measurement: Challenges and Opportunities in KPI Extraction from Earnings Calls
review:
This paper analyzes a challenging problem in a way that might be of value to other practitioners, but it's not exactly clear what the contribution is. I'd suggest clarifying exactly what the problem, proposed solution, desired outcome, and evaluation method are, e.g. what are we trying to do, how will we do it, what are the results we want, and how will we measure them, and to what end?

One potential angle that might be worth pursuing: tracking KPIs (traditional and non-traditional) over time and via extraction from SEC filings and earnings calls. For "traditional" KPIs this has obvious applications and value (e.g. profit has increased every quarter for the last 9 quarters) when evaluating a company. Similarly, if a company uses a custom non-traditional KPI (such as "fully autonomous miles driven") tracking that through time would be important. The traditional KPIs could be predefined, extracted, and tracked, then tested for accuracy. For experimental setup for non-traditional, it would be interesting to use an initial earnings call to identify KPIs, then track those on subsequent earnings calls, noting omissions and additions of new KPIs; this too could serve as a meaningful way to evaluate a company. Concretely grounding/apply the analysis the authors performed to a task like this would go a long way towards clarifying the purpose of this paper and increasing the value it provides to the community.

1. Limitations Section

No limitations section. As noted in reviewer guidance, no penalty assessed since this was added to the requirements after the CFP had opened.

2. Author Anonymity

No violations noted

3. Novelty & Impact

The authors clearly did a thorough analysis of a complex space (earnings calls and SEC filings), but apart from the conclusion that extraction is challenging, it's unclear to me exactly what the impact is. Other practitioners might be able to use the procedure laid out in the paper as a way to tackle their own use cases, and perhaps use the datasets the authors release as a way to validate them. I do greatly appreciate making a new data source available to the public.

4. Reproducibility

There is likely sufficient detail to reproduce the work, and it should be noted that all or nearly all of the models used in the paper are open-weight, which is highly appreciated (though not required).

5. Clarity & Structure

The paper is well written and structured logically.

title: JaCorpTrack: Corporate History Event Extraction for Tracking Organizational Changes
review:
This paper proposes a novel task called JaCorpTrack, which aims to automatically extract organizational change events such as ESTABLISH, CHANGE, MERGE, SPLIT, and LIQUIDATION from the “corporate history” sections of Japanese companies’ annual securities reports. The authors constructed a high-quality dataset consisting of 4,224 events by combining GPT-4o-based automatic extraction with heuristic processing and manual correction. This dataset was created using 210 companies’ reports disclosed via EDINET from April 2023 to March 2024.

Through comprehensive evaluations using both existing methods and large language models (LLMs), the study found that, first, GPT-4o with in-context learning achieves the highest accuracy. Second, there are significant differences in extraction difficulty and performance depending on the event type. Third, anonymizing company names leads to a substantial drop in GPT-4o’s accuracy, which suggests that its performance likely relies more on memorization than on true document comprehension. The authors also provide case studies that illustrate the challenges associated with different event types.

The automatic extraction and structuring of corporate history, especially events related to organizational change, may offer valuable opportunities for expanding knowledge bases and improving entity linking. In addition, these techniques could support more objective evaluation and visualization of corporate value and credibility, which may be of interest in both business and broader societal contexts.

## Pros
- This paper introduces a novel information extraction task for tracking organizational changes in companies, an area previously underexplored in event extraction research.
- The authors have created a new dataset and plan to release it.
- The paper evaluates both traditional methods and large language models, and offers valuable analysis of LLM memorization bias and differences in difficulty among event types.

## Cons
- The paper does not present concrete application examples using the extracted event data, so the practical impact of the task remains to be demonstrated.
- The dataset is currently limited to Japanese language and companies, which may restrict its immediate use. Nevertheless, this limitation does not diminish the value of the work, as the proposed methodology and task design are general and could be extended to other domains in the future.

title: JaCorpTrack: Corporate History Event Extraction for Tracking Organizational Changes
review:
## TL;DR

The paper introduces JaCorpTrack, a document-level event extraction task/dataset for tracking organizational changes (establish, rename, merge, split, liquidation) from Japanese corporate histories in annual reports. It defines a clear event schema and evaluates classic EE systems and several LLMs under finetuning and in-context regimes. Results show strong performance on ESTABLISH but large drops on CHANGE/MERGE/SPLIT, especially when arguments span lines or terminology is ambiguous. While the dataset is valuable, the baseline coverage, long-context modeling, and industry deployment evidence (latency, throughput, monitoring) are limited.

## Summary of the paper

* Problem: Extract temporally consistent events describing organizational changes in corporate histories; identify company names before/after the event and the date.
* Contributions: (1) Task & schema with five event types and argument roles; (2) Dataset of 210 corporate histories (EDINET, Apr 2023–Mar 2024); (3) Benchmarks with DMBERT, BERT+CRF, Llama-3 (8B) finetuned, and GPT-4o/mini in-context; (4) Analyses by event type and argument role; (5) Anonymization study to probe memorization.
* Method/Setup: Event table filling with three metrics: Event Detection, Event Table Filling, Event Record Identification; average over five seeds; 50 docs for training (or demonstrations), 160 for test.
* Evaluation: Tables 4–6 report main and per-type results; Table 11 shows anonymization impact; Table 10 lists hyperparameters; prompts are in Figures 3–7.

## Strengths

* Clear, useful task & schema for industry-relevant changes (name change, merge/split) with explicit argument roles (before/after companies, dates). Table 1.
* Grounded data source (EDINET) with time window (Apr 2023–Mar 2024) and sampling description; 210 docs; strong IAA details.
* Balanced evaluation design across classic EE and LLMs, with three metrics that probe detection vs full record correctness.
* Actionable analysis: Event-type F1 gap, argument-role errors when arguments are far from triggers, and ambiguity around spin-offs vs sell-offs with concrete examples, impact of memorization
* Industry-oriented transparency: Compute and cost details (single A6000; GPT-4o \$0.004–\$0.014 per example).

## Weaknesses / Concerns

* Baselines miss strong doc-level IE/long-context models (e.g., OneIE; Longformer/BigBird) that could directly address long timelines; current BERT baselines truncate to 512 tokens. 
* Limited industry deployment evidence: No latency/throughput on realistic corpora, SLAs, monitoring or drift detection; only per-example GPT-4o cost and single-GPU training time. 
* Risk of model memorization: Authors note GPT-4o performance drop under anonymization; however, scope is narrow (only GPT-4o and Llama-3) and anonymization specifics are brief.
* Reproducibility gaps: No dev split; unclear document/company de-duplication across splits; partial details on preprocessing (HTML→timelines) and test-time inference latencies; Not found in paper (except general description of HTML removal/normalization).
* Evaluation scope: Only two traditional pipeline baselines and two LLM series; missing recent document-level argument extraction methods (e.g., conditional generation or graph/tracker models) as competitive references.

title: Improving Factual Accuracy and Completeness in Long-form Table QA: A Modular Detection-and-Mitigation Pipeline
review:
The paper focuses on the factual and completeness errors (hallucinations and omissions) in long-form answers generated by LLMs for table QA. To this end, the authors propose a two-stage pipeline. The first Detection stage leverages existing evaluation frameworks (G-Eval for coarse-grained scores and MT-RAIG Eval for fine-grained claim analysis) to identify flawed answers. The second Mitigation stage introduces a prompt-based correction module that revises the flawed answers.

Strengths
- The inclusion of two distinct detection/mitigation pathways (G-Eval and MT-RAIG Eval) and a thorough human evaluation.
- The focus on a single-call mitigation step to minimize latency and cost, with the Deployment Considerations section discussing score-based routing and auditability.

Weaknesses and questions
- The pipeline's effectiveness is dependent on the upstream detection module. The error analysis discusses cases where the detector is wrong (false positives), make it Unchanged or Deteriorated outcomes. However, the impact of false negatives (the detector fails to flag a genuinely incorrect answer) is not discussed. How does the pipeline account for false negatives from the detection stage? What is the rate of such failures, and what is the potential risk to overall system reliability when erroneous answers are deemed correct and passed directly to the user without mitigation?
- The paper emphasizes the importance of efficiency and low latency, while lacks a quantitative dimension. The mitigation step, while efficient, still introduces an additional LLM call. Could the authors provide a more concrete cost-benefit analysis? E.g., what is the typical percentage increase in end-to-end latency and token cost when an answer is sent through the mitigation pipeline? How does this overhead compare against the significant gains in faithfulness and completeness, especially when considering different models like GPT-4o vs. GPT-4o-mini for the mitigation step?
- The human evaluation results in Table 11 show that a non-trivial fraction of answers (e.g., 6% for G-Eval and 14% for MT-RAIG on FeTaQA) were labeled as Deteriorated post-mitigation. While the error analysis attributes it to the inherent limitations of current LLMs, it is a significant failure mode. Could the authors provide a more detailed breakdown of the Deteriorated cases? Did the mitigation prompts themselves sometimes introduce ambiguity or lead the model astray, or was it purely an issue of the LLM failing to follow instructions for complex reasoning? Are there any potential safeguards, such as a final verification step, that could be added to catch and prevent such regressions?

title: Improving Factual Accuracy and Completeness in Long-form Table QA: A Modular Detection-and-Mitigation Pipeline
review:
Paper Summary:

This paper deals with the task of Long-Form Table Question Answering -- generating long-form answers based on a set of facts extracted from tables. Specifically, this research focuses on improving faithfulness of the generated answers to the source facts, and on improving the completeness of the facts in the generated answers. The key idea developed in this work is based on two modules... one that identifies faithfulness and completeness issues, and one that refines the generated answer to mitigate those detected issues. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the ideas, the system is evaluated over two separate datasets through an LLM-based eval as well as a human expert assessment. Additionally, the paper presents interesting analysis over the failure cases, providing the readers with deeper insights into the presented solutions.


How this work can benefit the community:

* This work introduces a practical and effective strategy for improving faithfulness and completeness of generative QA systems. The scientific community would benefit from this work, potentially influencing other similar QA tasks with these ideas.

* The insights from the error analysis were especially intriguing to me, presenting interesting directions for future explorations in this space. I expect analysis such as this is of particular interest to practitioners in the field.

* It was great to see that the ideas were validated over multiple datasets -- demonstrating the broader applicability of the key ideas.


Areas that can be further strengthened:

* The paper would be greatly strengthened by providing more details and clarity around the key system components. Specifically, the use of G-Eval and MT-RAIG Eval for both evaluation and for the detection module makes it confusing for the reader in how it plays these two different roles.

* Additionally, more details of the implementation would greatly benefit towards strengthening the paper in terms of reproducibility.

* Broadening the space of experiments over additional variables -- choice of LLM used, variation in system prompts -- would be provide the community with deeper insights and learnings.

title: Improving Factual Accuracy and Completeness in Long-form Table QA: A Modular Detection-and-Mitigation Pipeline
review:
This paper introduces a pipeline for improving faithfulness and completeness of answers in Long Form Table Question Answering (LFTQA).
The pipeline includes two components: 1) detection module that identifies faithfulness and completeness issues, and 2) mitigation module that addresses the identified issues and makes revisions to the original answer.
For detection module, they use existing methods for faithfulness and completeness detections such as G-Eval and MT-RAIG Eval.
For mitigation/correction module, they use LLM-prompting with the identified issues by detection module.
Experiments performs experiments to demonstrate that the proposed  pipeline consistently improves both faithfulness and completeness, measured by both automated and human evaluation.


Strengths:
- The paper aims to solve a real-world problems with long-form table question answering by proposing a pipeline and shows the effectiveness of the proposed pipeline via a battery of experiments.

Weaknesses:
- The main weakness of the paper is novelty. Detect-then-correct pipeline has been used in multiple previous work [1, 2]. Additionally, the components of the pipeline are also not novel (re-using previous approaches such as G-Eval).
- Using LLMs (such as GPT4-o or GPT4o-mini) for detection and correction might introduce significant latency in practical applications. Although the authors mentioned “Detection can use smaller or cached models depending on resource constraints”, the performance of the use of small detection models and the performance of the pipeline in resource-constraint setting aren’t evaluated in the paper.

Questions:
- Regarding the correlation of performance of detectors and instance-level human scores (Table 2 and 3), what kind of correlation metric was used? Isn’t correlation low for faithfulness, except for G-Eval GPT4-o on FeTaQA? 
- The detection module and automatic evaluation metric are the same in some cases (e.g. both G-Eval), will this bias the evaluation results?

References:
1. Peng et al, 2023 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.12813
2. Gao et al, 2023 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.08726

title: Universal Embeddings for Multimodal Multilingual Retrieval
review:
This paper presents NEWMODEL, a 3.8B parameter embedding model designed for both text and image modalities, supporting single-vector and multi-vector retrieval via a unified encoder. The authors also introduce NEWBENCHMARK, a new benchmark for visually rich document retrieval, featuring more diverse query types, languages, and formats than existing alternatives. The model is modularized through LoRA adapters for asymmetric retrieval, semantic similarity, and code search tasks.

The main strengths of this work lie in its unified and flexible architecture, which allows for both dense and late-interaction retrieval within a single model. This makes it versatile for real-world use cases. The introduction of NEWBENCHMARK is also valuable, broadening the evaluation of visually rich, multilingual retrieval scenarios.

However, the paper would benefit from a deeper discussion on the trade-offs between multi-vector and single-vector embeddings, including when and why to prefer one over the other. It is also unclear whether training both representations jointly brings tangible benefits, this aspect deserves more clarity. The main weakness is the lack of ablation studies, which limits our ability to understand which components (e.g., unified encoder, LoRA adapters, Matryoshka learning, late interaction) are most responsible for the improvements over baselines.

Overall, the model performs competitively across many benchmarks, but a more thorough analysis of where the gains come from would significantly strengthen the paper.

title: Universal Embeddings for Multimodal Multilingual Retrieval
review:
This paper presents a 3.8 billion parameter text and image embeddings model. The model provides both single vector and multi-vector embeddings as output. The intended use for these are retrieval tasks for conventional and late-interaction (for multi-vector) settings. The contributions of the paper can be summarised as the following which can also be counted towards strengths of the paper as they are all valuable contributions:

1. A multimodal and multilingual embedding model with dual output options (single and multi vector).  The authors tested the capabilities of this model with several benchmarks including CLIP benchmark for image retrieval tasks, MTEB, MMTEB and MTEB-CoIR  for text retrieval and  code retrieval tasks. They also report results on their own benchmark for some other tasks. 

2. Several modular LoRA adapters for tasks such as text similarity, code retrieval and information retrieval.

3. A Visually rich document retrieval benchmark which they report the results on. This benchmark extends an existing benchmark, ViDoRe, by including a diverse range of new data including legal texts,  Readme files from Github, hand annotated educational materials and more. It is also a rich inventory of documents types such as visual documents with charts, tables, manuals, printed text, maps). The documents are from 20 different languages and from various resources such as existing datasets, manually annotated or synthetic data. It is exciting that this benchmark will be made available to the public.

4. Addressing the modality gap. The model’s VLM architecture with a single processing path for both images and text significantly reduces the so called modality gap compared to dual-encoder  architectures like CLIP. Images are first converted into token sequences via a vision encoder, and then both image and text modalities are jointly processed by a shared language model decoder that includes contextual attention layers.


Strengths:

Overall the paper is interesting and well presented. The model achieves reasonable performance in with limited training. It has low memory and compute print compared to fully trained models given what it achieves.  
There are extensive experiments and tests on the performance of the model to the point where it might even be too much for one short paper. 

Weaknesses/Suggestions

1. The performance on the multilingual tasks seems to be somewhat limited and not comparable to the state-of-the-art in some languages. This suggests there is space for improvement in multilingual settings especially for low-resource languages. as noted when comparing it to nllb-siglip-large on the Crossmodal3600 benchmark.

2. The capabilities of the system is limited by the base models that was used as was also adressed in the limitations reported by the authors.

3. There are some errors in formatting of the paper especially in the references section where the line numbers are garbled up.

4. It would be useful to include more text containing explanations and discussion about the results included in the appendices.

5. It is recommended to include comparisons and results with ViDoRe2 as well.

title: Universal Embeddings for Multimodal Multilingual Retrieval
review:
This paper presents NEWMODEL, a multimodal and multilingual embedding model featuring a novel architecture that can generate both single- and multi-vector embeddings, suitable for various retrieval tasks. It also introduces NEWBENCHMARK, a diversified benchmark designed to test retrieval performance on visually rich materials, demonstrating that NEWMODEL surpasses existing models in this area. The architecture integrates text and image inputs into a shared processing pathway, offering significant savings over multiple models for different tasks and modalities. LoRA adapters are used for task-specific optimizations, and various benchmarks show NEWMODEL achieving competitive performance across multiple domains.

Some things could be improved or clarified.
1) The paper lacks details on many crucial aspects of the content. For example, the process of constructing NEWBENCHMARK, especially the selection criteria for datasets, the method of creating synthetic data, and query generation techniques, lacks depth. Insight into how this benchmark was validated and measures taken to ensure its comprehensiveness would be valuable. Furthermore, there is limited technical detail on how LoRA adapters are integrated and optimized within the architecture. More information on their specific function, how they interact with the frozen backbone, and their impact on model performance would enhance understanding.
2) The paper compares the retrieval performance with other systems, but it misses necessary ablation results on whether the improvement comes from new data, task-specific LoRA, or simply a more powerful base model.

title: LLM Agents Implement an NLG System from Scratch: Building Interpretable Rule-Based RDF-to-Text Generators
review:
This work proposes the automatic generation of a rule-based RDF-to-text NLG system using 'LLM agents'. The paper is well written and structured.

Starting with a knowledge graph as input, the system consists of the following agents, all of which are LLM based and use in-context learning:

1. Test agent: selects 50 random predicates (ideally with some coreference as illustrated in the example in the prompt of the appendix) from the input knowledge graph and generate input-output with at least 3 unit tests per predicate.

2. Software architect: is given the set of predicate in the knowledge graphs and is asked to define the code structure with functions signature.

3. Software engineer: codes each function specified by the SA.

4. Evaluator: executes the code with the unit tests and passes output to an LLM to evaluate whether the output correctly verbalized the input. As soon as 5 unit tests fail, the process is terminated.

5. Code analyst: receives the evaluation and check if problem stems from architecture or implementation of specific modules.

The whole workflow ('training') was run with a maximum number of 25 iterations (10 for GPT). 

The text generated with this approach is compared with zero-shot prompted and fine-tuned LLM baselines using ground truth and LLM-as-judge. Results are competitive and approach has better latency. Human evaluation shows system generates no hallucination in evaluated test set and omissions, repetitions and disfluencies that are comparable to the prompted LLMs.

Some more challenging baseline such as LLM with in-context learning and/or a manually crafted prompt could have been used for a fairer comparison.

Regarding the modification task of the interpretability evaluation, it seems to imply that the predicates are hard wired in the code which does not make much sense given that the system is said to be robust to out-of-domain triples: a snippet of code and modification would help understand better how this works.

You mentioned 168 lines of code but how many functions were produced? How does the unit testing influence the variations and robustness of the code? Does the code resemble a NLG architecture, i.e., content selection, ordering, etc? What was the size of input knowledge graph, i.e., number of triples and links between triples? Is the order of triple provided in the input random or corresponds to natural 'grouping' of triples, i.e., linked triples are contiguous? Also testing the generation at different iterations would be interesting, to see the effect the workflow has on the quality of the generated text? Basically a more in-depth analysis of the generated system and data used would help understand its impact and make the work more engaging/exciting to the community.

In the qualitative evaluation, you did not consider fluency/coherence. 

Have you considered using tools such as DSpy for prompt tuning?

title: LLM Agents Implement an NLG System from Scratch: Building Interpretable Rule-Based RDF-to-Text Generators
review:
This paper presents a novel approach to RDF-to-text generation. Specifically, the paper proposes to use a collection of LLM agents to generate a Python program which can generate text given a set of RDF triples. Five LLM agents with different specializations (such as architecture design, software engineering, test engineering, etc.) collaborate in an interactive process to write and refine the Python program. An evaluation using both automatic metrics and human judgments shows that the text output produced by the Python program is of largely comparable quality to output produced by a fine-tuned LLM or an LLM using zero-shot prompting. But the Python program is interpretable, doesn't need a GPU to run, and is much faster.

Novelty & Impact: The proposed approach is novel. Its advantages of not needed a large training corpus of reference texts, yielding a rule-based generation system that can be adjusted by hand, being fast and not needing a GPU might make it an attractive option to explore for many real-world applications of NLG.

Reproducibility: The code is made available. It seems largely undocumented, but with a bit of determination it should be possible to use it to replicate the results.

Clarity & Structure: The paper is structured well and clearly written.

Some questions:

- Sec. 2, ll. 148-151: Does training ever terminate early not because the NLG system has gotten good, but because the unit test are bad/ineffective?
- Sec. 3.1, ll. 194-195: The maximum number of iterations was set to 25 (10). How many iteration did training run on average?

Here are some typos and other suggestions:

- The paper uses abbreviations when referring to tables, figures, and appendices. I find that they disrupt the flow of reading. If the space allows it, I would spell those out.
- ll. 085, 110: "App." vs. "Appx."
- l. 284: "Tab 6" --> missing period
- l. 295: missing space after the closing parenthesis
- ll. 313-314: "the smallest number of repetitions ex aequo with [the] prompted LLM."
- ll. 316-317: "Since the result of training of our rule-based NLG approach is a Python code," --> "... is Python code"; no determiner

Strengths:
- The proposed approach is interesting.
- It produces good quality output with fewer hallucinations (than LLM generated text) and other advantages.
- The code is being made available.

Weaknesses:
- The paper does not show any example output.
- I would like to know more about the performance on the dialog dataset. It seems quite a bit lower according to the reference based metrics, but similar to the other test sets on the reference-less automatic metrics. It would be interesting to see some human judgments. Do the generated utterances make sense but are just not formulated appropriately for a dialog?

title: Product-Searcher: Real-World E-commerce Product DeepSearch via Reinforcement Learning
review:
**Summary**  
This paper proposed a reinforcement learning framework for product search using a two stage retrieval process. Stage 1 performed initial retrieval with the user query. Stage 2 used an LLM to expand the query based on the original query and Stage 1 results, aiming to improve recall. A scalable offline training environment enabled fast experimentation and transferred effectively to real world deployment. The reward function, powered by a judge model with a cache, checked extracted query properties in final results, rewarding increasing novel good items. The method delivered 53%  improvement over a strong baseline and outperformed GPT 4o. The authors also explored a two turn expansion setup, where the query was expanded iteratively twice, showing gains over both GPT 4o and the baseline.

**Strengths**
* The idea is simple: clear two stage retrieval pipeline that combines initial retrieval with LLM driven query expansion, leveraging extracted properties for targeted relevance improvements.
* Demonstrates substantial performance gains, 53 percent improvement over baseline, in both offline and real world settings, outperforming GPT 4o.
* Scalable offline training setup supports robust experimentation, generalizes effectively to deployment, and reduces deployment risk.
* Paper is well-written and easy to follow

**Weaknesses**
* Reward design focuses on novelty of results but does not penalize removal of relevant results from the original query, which could degrade user experience.
* No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the claimed improvements.
* Data and code are not released due to industry constraints, which limits reproducibility and further validation.

**Comments**
* Line 70: Add space before citations.
* Line 389: Remove extra apostrophe.
* Consider adding a penalty term in the reward function to discourage dropping relevant results from the original query.  
  For example: Novelty can be defined as $ \frac{|R(Q') \setminus R(Q)|}{N} $ and Loss as $ \frac{|R(Q) \setminus R(Q')|}{|R(Q)|} $.  
  The reward could combine both terms with appropriate weighting:  
  $ \text{Reward} = \alpha \cdot \text{Novelty} - \beta \cdot \text{Loss} $.
* Provide statistical significance analysis for the reported improvements, ideally with 95 percent confidence intervals.
* Include qualitative examples showing how query expansion in Stage 2 improved results compared to Stage 1 alone.

**Questions for the Authors**
1. How was the judge model validated for accuracy and bias?
2. Were the improvements over GPT 4o statistically significant?

title: Product-Searcher: Real-World E-commerce Product DeepSearch via Reinforcement Learning
review:
**Summary:**

This paper introduces Product-Searcher, a novel end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) approach specifically designed for e-commerce search. It presents a complete RL training pipeline, including the base policy model Qwen-7B, data collection process, evaluation system, reward definition, and the GRPO training algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that Product-Searcher outperforms baseline methods in both offline and online evaluations.

---

**Strengths:**

* This paper offers valuable guidance and reference for the industry.
* It demonstrates engineering optimizations of the search engine to ensure the stability and scalability of the training pipeline while maintaining core functionality.
* It introduces a rule-based evaluation system used to assess search performance.

---

**Weaknesses:**

* The paper lacks novelty, as it primarily applies the GRPO reinforcement learning algorithm to train the policy/LLM without providing sufficient technical detail. It resembles a technical report more than a research paper, focusing mainly on the overall pipeline. While individual components may have some engineering value, the work does not meet the standards typically required for publication.
* There are noticeable typos throughout the submission, indicating a lack of careful proofreading.
* The baselines used are overly simplistic, with minimal effort to construct strong or competitive comparisons, which significantly weakens the empirical validation of the proposed approach.
* The online experiments suffer from a lack of transparency, and the reported gains are marginal, offering limited evidence of practical effectiveness.
* The offline evaluations appear to offer little meaningful insight and do not contribute significantly to the overall assessment of the method.

---

**Questions / Concerns:**

* In Section 3.4, how is the set of valid product IDs retrieved by the query defined?
* In Section 3.4, why is the reward defined as the difference between R(Q′) and R(Q), divided by N? This choice is not explained in the text. (Q′ refers to the query generated by the LLM at the center of Figure 1.)
* In Section 3.5, the authors present only the GRPO algorithm, which is already well-established and should not be the sole focus of this section. They do not provide sufficient practical details on how GRPO is integrated into the overall training pipeline illustrated in Figure 1. It appears that several critical aspects are missing from the submission, particularly regarding training efficiency, the implementation of parallelism, and how variance within policy rollouts (i.e., the LLM) is managed, given that GRPO is an on-policy method.
* It is expected that in Table 1, the Product-Searcher significantly outperforms the other three models, as those models do not involve any training. However, in Table 2, the improvement is quite marginal. Besides, the training pipeline introduces additional overhead. It is recommended to include results from more open-source LLMs in Table 2 to better assess whether the performance gain remains marginal across different models.
* Since the pipeline uses a relatively small LLM, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, I’m a bit skeptical about the effectiveness of the “thinking” stage, as shown in Figure 1. 
* In Table 2, the two baselines have more room to improve, such as giving more rounds, more context and reflections, and more demonstrative examples with listed awards together with explanations. The baselines are prompting methods, and they have their advantage of flexibility and are easy to implement, compared to the RL training method, which is not stable and needs much more effort.
* Section 4.4 / Qwen vs. Llama: The findings of the further analysis of Qwen and Llama are not surprising, and it is not related to the research; needless to say that they have the same order of magnitude in terms of parameter.
* Section 4.4 / GRPO vs PPO: The conclusion that PPO and GRPO perform roughly the same cannot be drawn purely from the test reward shown in Figure 5. This comparison is too simplistic and hasty. PPO requires a separate critic model, while GRPO does not need it - instead makes comparisons across multiple rollouts. From this point, GRPO has the advantage of low resource requirement, but on the other hand, GRPO needs more outputs, which emphasizes the variance and diversity, and may therefore have an impact on the divergence. I do not see too much deep analysis about this kind of discussion, although it may not be the crux of the submission.

title: Product-Searcher: Real-World E-commerce Product DeepSearch via Reinforcement Learning
review:
## Summary

This paper proposes Product-Searcher, a query generation module trained via reinforcement learning (RL) within a custom environment comprising a mini search engine and an LLM-based product quality judge. The model is trained using Guided Reward Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based reward functions. Experimental results demonstrate that Product-Searcher can retrieve higher-quality products compared to baselines, both in offline and online settings.

## Strengths

- S1: The authors introduce an LLM-based product quality judge, which quantifies the quality of retrieved products and serves as the basis for reward signals during RL training.

- S2: Offline evaluations indicate that Product-Searcher retrieves more high-quality products than baselines. Online test results further show improvements in good rate and match rate.

- S3: The paper explores a multi-query generation setup and shows that the RL-trained multi-query model achieves the best performance.

- S4: The authors also explored different base models and RL algorithms, increasing the completeness of the evaluation.

## Weaknesses

- W1: The paper lacks comparison against alternative reward signals, such as ranking scores or click-based metrics. While the authors argue that query-document annotations are unavailable, implicit user feedback (e.g., clicks) could have been leveraged as reward signals for a more comprehensive analysis.

- W2: The generalization ability of the LLM-based judge is not evaluated. Given that product attributes vary widely across categories, it is unclear how well the judge performs across diverse product types.

- W3: The definition of "match rate" (line 373) is unclear. Additionally, there is inconsistency in Table 2: the caption refers to "excellent rate," while the table itself lists "good rate."

- W4: The improvements reported in Table 2 appear marginal. It is also unclear whether these metrics reflect real user engagement or are solely based on the LLM judge’s output.

title: STREAQ: Selective Tiered Routing for Effective and Affordable Contact Center Quality Assurance
review:
This paper addresses the highly specific yet practical domain of quality assurance in contact centers. The authors clearly outline the considerations within this domain: routine behaviors are consistently performed well, whereas key failures are rare but have significant business impact. I believe that the paper's strength lies in its precise definition of domain-specific issues and exploration of appropriate solutions. The authors provide a clear explanation of the domain's uniqueness and present a well-organized argument leading to their proposed solutions.

This paper clearly explains the background leading to the development of the proposed methodology. The authors experimentally demonstrate the method's performance and show its effectiveness in reducing costs in real-world applications.

However, I am concerned that the proposed methodology may significantly underperform compared to the baseline. Upon reviewing Table 1, the precision, recall, and F1 scores cast doubt on the actual effectiveness of the two-field framework, as it shows considerably lower performance than full inference. While it clearly reduces costs, the performance drop seems more significant than expected. 

- Is there a practical distinction between the 84% AOI precision of Claude-4-Sonnet compare to the 76% AOI precision of the two-tier Claude-4-Sonnet in real-world applications?
- Simply, consider two systems, one with a 16% error rate and another with a 24% error rate. Isn't it more preferable to choose the system with the lower error rate, even if it incurs higher costs? How does this apply in the contact center context discussed by the authors?
- Strengthening the argument about this performance difference could significantly enhance the paper's impact.

Additionally, consider addressing these minor comments:

- What are the specifics details of the Nova-Pro model?
- More detailed explanation of the "out-of-the-box" scenario and the “AOI” context would enhance readability.

title: STREAQ: Selective Tiered Routing for Effective and Affordable Contact Center Quality Assurance
review:
The authors explore a RoBERTa-based routing function that determines whether a response given by an in-house LLM should be accepted or rejected, in which case a larger but costlier third-party LLM is called. Their application scenario is automatically evaluating the quality of customer care agents, where an LLM answers a list of quality assurance questions about each dialogue.

Pros:
- The scenario is relevant and important in practice, especially for high-volume enterprise applications
- The method is sensible and novel for this specific practical application
- The experiments are sufficiently rigorous

Cons:
- Further analyses are somewhat lacking. For example, how do the recall-precision curves look? Are there patterns in the failure cases? How sensitive is the model? What do the scaling laws for dollars saved to model effectiveness look like?

These cons are addressed in the rebuttal.
