title: TechMatch: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Large Language Models for Recommending Innovative Technology
review:
This paper proposes an approach for recommending technologies, supported by a dataset of 48 queries and a method combining knowledge graphs (KG) and large language models (LLMs).

Unfortunately, the paper is not clearly written, which makes it challenging to identify the precise problem statement. The narrative is difficult to follow, in part due to inconsistent examples — for instance, the introduction begins with a case involving Germany’s use of a trade fair venue but later shifts to a mobile device manufacturer without clear transitions, making it hard to establish a coherent context. A consistent, visual illustration of the input and output throughout the paper would greatly improve clarity.

In terms of contribution, the dataset is limited in size (48 queries), which restricts its potential impact. The proposed approach, while incorporating both KG and LLM components, does not demonstrate novelty relative to existing methods. Furthermore, the work does not provide significant new insights into the industry setting, nor does it advance the field more broadly. The lack of clear positioning within the literature further obscures the paper’s unique contribution.

title: TechMatch: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Large Language Models for Recommending Innovative Technology
review:
This paper introduces TechMatch, a hybrid framework that combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with a Knowledge Graph (KG) to recommend emerging technologies and enterprises based on natural language user queries.

The proposed methodology is compelling, with a clearly defined two-stage pipeline (KG construction + LLM-enhanced retrieval). The authors report consistent and meaningful improvements over strong baselines across both public and private datasets. Moreover, they provide a curated, annotated dataset and release the accompanying code, enhancing reproducibility and practical utility.

However, I have several concerns:

- The range of baselines is somewhat limited. There is no comparison with KG-only retrieval methods or sparse-retrieval + KG hybrids, which would help isolate the contribution of each component.

- The term merging step lacks detail. Specifically, how terms are resolved to Wikipedia entries should be explained more clearly.

- While the combination of KG and LLMs is the core innovation, the interaction between them is not sufficiently detailed in the case study. It would be helpful to understand more precisely how information is expanded or connected.

- The KG construction process, though described in detail, may not need as much focus. However, the experimental setup, which arguably is more critical to evaluate the system, relies too heavily on the appendix. Some key information (e.g., number of queries, LLM parameters, evaluation splits) should be included in the main paper.

- The failure case analysis is insightful but somewhat shallow. It remains unclear whether the failures stem from LLM limitations, KG coverage gaps, or noisy/unstructured enterprise descriptions. A more systematic error analysis would strengthen the evaluation.

- The evaluation dataset is based on manually written queries, but there’s no evidence of user studies or real-world query logs. How well does TechMatch generalize to noisy, ambiguous, or multi-intent queries?

- An ablation study would help quantify the individual contribution of the KG, reranking, and LLM filtering stages.

- Since the system relies heavily on prompt-based LLM behavior, some discussion about prompt stability, sensitivity, or tuning effort would be valuable.

The field of combining LLMs and KG is very relevant, and this is a potentially strong idea, but in its current form, the paper may lack some clarity, completeness, and evaluation depth needed to support its claims.

title: TechMatch: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Large Language Models for Recommending Innovative Technology
review:
This paper introduces TechMatch, an approach that integrates knowledge graphs with LLMs to provide recommendations on technology topics. Main contributions include constructing a curated test set of emerging technology enterprises by collating descriptions of the tech via conference/tradeshow descriptions. The data is also human annotated for relevancy and quality. The authors demonstrate that the recommendation system using knowledge graphs and LLMs can improve accuracy on this test set when compared to using vanilla LLMs for recommendations. 

Strengths/Pros:
- Release of a new dataset to support additional research for recommendation systems and link between knowledge graphs and LLMs
- Evaluation and some ablation studies to determine performance differences between bare LLMs and LLMs using knowledge graphs 
- Case analysis shows why certain approaches (e.g., RAG + CoT) fared less well than others and in what circumstances 

Weaknesses/Cons: 
- Limited scale of the experiments; only one test set reported since the second test set needs to be kept private for company reasons, and only 2 LLMs evaluated. The paper would benefit with more breadth to support robustness of the TechMatch system. 
- Performance gains with TechMatch were sometimes modest (e.g., upwards 3-5%). Unclear where the delineation was where the tool is more helpful than the current LLM-only methods. 
- More details on knowledge graph would help substantiate the paper - why coud LLMs not transverse the KG? was it due to the KG construction or the LLM capability? How robust was the KG nodes? e.g., were there many false positives when tracing parent nodes back to a single Wikipedia page? The details on the KG construction were somewhat murky, and didn't instill complete confidence this was a robust approach.

title: FLOW-BENCH: Towards Conversational Generation of Enterprise Workflows
review:
This paper presents FLOW-BENCH, a dataset of 101 tuples: <NL utterance, input workflow, expected worflow> with user tasks and edit operations and an approach to generating those workflows using LLMs that consists in content selection (selecting the activities denoted in the NL instructions) and "demo" injection, that is including examples of <NL utterance, workflow> in the prompt. The approach followed in this work is to use pythonic code as a workflow itermediate language representation that can then deterministically be translated to the BPMN workflow language with the Py2BPMN tool.

Experiments are performed with different numbers of activities and demos, different kinds of retrievers (embedding similarity, cross encoder), different LLMs and independence or not of activities in the demo wrt ground truth (i.e., cross domain if independent, in-domain if dependent), achieving an F1 score of 86 and 90 respectively for cross domain and in domain activities with mistral-large.

The authors present two use cases and solutions to these: one which is to generate a workflow from scratch given an NL utterance and the other which is to update and existing workflow. In this latter case, the approach is to convert the object workflow to python code with the BPMN2Py tool. This workflow is used as additional information for the activity retriever and is included in the prompt to be used by the LLM to serve as input to generation. The resulting workflow is compared to original workflow with Diff2BPMN and edit operations are generated to modify the input workflow and obtain the final workflow.

The paper is clear and well written and the development of a dataset for NL-to-business-workflow generation is a nice contribution to the community. 

Having said that, the dataset is quite small, consisting of only 101 tuples and it should be better characterized wrt complexity, edit operations, domain, etc. The relatively high performance of the generation is probably skewed by the small dataset and careful manual curation: it is unclear how this would fare 'in the wild'. The authors do describe a deployment of their work. However there is no metric available in this production environment.

It is unclear whether the second use case is considered in the evaluation (NL instructions to modify existing workflow) and also in what proportion workflow update is present in the dataset: given that each dataset tuple includes input workflow, it is to be assumed that utterances are always to modify an existing workflow but this is not clear and also no metrics are given regarding the diffference between input and output workflow such as number and type of edit operations. 

Also given that the generation depends on access to activities from a 'catalog', some better characterization of mapping between utterances and activities is needed: simple one-to-one mapping, one-to-many, many-to-many, many-to-one, or unavailable mapping, for example.

Regarding related work, give that this work uses python-like code generation as a proxy to address this problem, then talking about any works that generate python-like instructions might be in order.

All these issues need to be addressed or clarified in the final version of the paper. Also discussion of challenges and errors how to address them should be added.

Note: authors are identifiable via a simple search as paper is available as preprint:

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11646

- https://github.com/IBM/Flow-Bench

- https://www.linkedin.com/posts/vatche-ishakian_github-ibmflow-bench-high-quality-dataset-activity-7330960241502674944-Ayrq/

Small details:

- Line 378: missing period

title: FLOW-BENCH: Towards Conversational Generation of Enterprise Workflows
review:
Summary: This paper discusses using python as an intermediary generation step for a LLM to create Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) flows from natural language instructions. The primary contribution is a dataset of 101 examples, and the second contribution is a system demonstrating generation of new and incremental workflows from natural language.

Quality & Novelty: The paper is well structured and clear, The design decisions and limitations are helpful. The work is early, but I think a valuable starting point.

PROs:
* this is an under-investigated area, and business process information is notoriously hard to obtain because of the confidential nature of the real data.
* the approach is solid and seems to have real world use.

CONs:
* the dataset is small
* the limitations of the IR affect the expressiveness of the resulting BPs

title: FLOW-BENCH: Towards Conversational Generation of Enterprise Workflows
review:
## **Summary**
The paper introduces Flow-Bench, a benchmark containing 101 test samples for NL-to-BPA (business process automation). Since LLMs were trained on limited BPA-related data, the authors propose Flow-Gen, which uses a Python intermediate representation to generate BPA through dynamic prompting with RAG approaches.

## **Strengths**
The use of an intermediate representation (Python) to generate BPA is a strong point. As the authors note, Python is more concise than BPA, reducing cost and latency.

## **Weaknesses**
- The paper lacks a clear introduction to business process automation (BPA). No examples are provided. What is the difference between BPA and SOP (standard operating procedures) ?
- No statistics are given for Flow-Bench. When proposing a new benchmark, it is important to include details such as average BPA length, domain/task distribution, or issue categories.
- The dataset is very limited (only 101 samples). Additionally, nested cases were excluded (Line 106), raising concerns about the dataset’s complexity and challenge level.
- The experiments feel incomplete. It is unclear whether tests were conducted without the Pythonic intermediate representation, making it difficult to assess its impact. While comparing different LLMs is useful, further experiments (e.g., structured vs. unstructured intermediate representations) would strengthen the paper. Additionally, (similar) baselines from related work are not included in the experiments.

## **Questions/Comments**
- In Table 1, recall reaches 99%. However, what is the total number of activities? Line 289 mentions that it "may contain thousands," but exact counts per case would be helpful.

## **Conclusion**
Overall, this work explores an underexamined area (BPA) and presents an interesting approach. However, the paper lacks clarity in describing the proposed dataset, and the experiments need further refinement to support stronger conclusions.

title: PARSE: LLM Driven Schema Optimization for Reliable Entity Extraction
review:
The study is on a topic with a lot of industry applications, which is extraction of information into JSON schemas that focus on being consumable primarily by LLM-based agents. Both improving information extraction and by-passing unnecessary restrictions in making JSON structures pleasant for humans, they make significant improvements over a reasonable baseline (especially on the SWDE dataset). There are latency trade-offs, which they describe and provide numeric information on. Their methods seem reproducible. They include prompts and a description of the process. They use 2 public datasets (and one internal one). 

The authors show examples of the schema improvements over iterations. While added context was the most frequent improvement, it’s also noticeable in the appendix examples how well they do regex, which would be rather error-prone if hand-written (especially trying to generalize over data). 

The paper is clear and well written, tables and figures are informative and are well explained in the document. 

This approach can be used by other companies that want to have multiple agents passing information and reduce the proliferation of inaccuracies, which is a highly relevant current topic. 

One concern I had was human readability and compatibility but they address this in that there is a RELAY module that can return the original form, if needed. 

Their baseline is clearly described, their  evaluation criteria are clear. 

Knowing what to extract and how to build good schemas is tedious, so having agents improve the process is a helpful application. 

The datasets and models tried were ample for the conclusions (5 models, 3 datasets). It’s a thorough, contained study that doesn’t overstate its claims.

title: PARSE: LLM Driven Schema Optimization for Reliable Entity Extraction
review:
This paper presents a refined LLM-based method for extraction of structured information from natural language instructions.  It is intended to support emerging HCI models, especially in the domain of software development, in which technical specifications are provided to the computational system in free text.  The approach of the paper differs from prior research in not taking the JSON output schema as fixed, but tasking an LLM agent with refinement and elaboration of the schema prior to extraction in order to optimize performance.

At a high level, the approach seems sensible, and the reported results seem to demonstrate its efficacy.  However, I did not completely understand how methods using different target schemas can be compared apples-to-apples in the evaluation phase.  The authors write of maintaining backward compatibility across the schemas “through code,” but I was not able to determine what is meant by this.  Generally, the presentation of the material could be improved - sections of the paper are unnecessarily wordy and repetitive, while core points are not sufficiently demonstrated or explained. (Figures 1, 2; Table 4 are complex and crowded - a well-chosen, simpler example of transformations and linkage for backward compatibility would be preferable.)

title: PARSE: LLM Driven Schema Optimization for Reliable Entity Extraction
review:
Paper presents the PARSE system with two synergistic components: ARCHITECT to autonomously optimize JSON schemas for LLM consumption while maintaining backward compatibility and SCOPE to perform extraction of structured information with combined static and LLM-based guardrails. Experimental results over three datasets demonstrate the benefits and practicality of the proposed approach. 

Paper has novel contributions in handling a practical problem, is well-organized, easy to follow, has supporting experimental results over three datasets and describes limitations of current work. Details of any production or learnings usage is missing.

Key contributions include 

C1: ARCHITECT a novel automated schema optimization framework that iteratively refines JSOM schemas for LLM performance, adding detailed entity descriptions and validation rules, and restructuring schemas for clearer representation while maintaining backward compatibility through integrated reverse engineering

C2: SCOPE a reflection based extraction framework that combines static + LLM-based guardrails for systematic error identification + correction

C3: Experimental results demonstrating the benefits of the proposed approach over three datasets (SGD, SWDE and Retail-Conv) - achieving 2-4% improvements for SGD, ~15% on Retail-Conv and  65% improvement for SWDE (where the baseline performs very badly). Additional experiments demonstrate generalization across models (schemas optimized using one LLM maintain benefits when applied with different models), SCOPE’s benefits over simple retry mechanisms and how the combination reduces latency penalty to ~10s vs. ~16s with just SCOPE (given baseline of 9s, latency doubles in many scenarios). ARCHITECT analysis describes key consistent patterns across datasets (entity description enhancements, structural reorganizations) with some examples in the appendix. 

Some questions to address include 

Q1: Error analysis on various subcomponents of ARCHITECT and SCOPE would be helpful - e.g., how often do bad constraints or pattern refinements get added in SCOPE, RELAY steps accuracy or types of errors introduced in this step. 

Q2: There are significant differences in how much performance improvements are achieved across the three datasets - additional analysis and insights into this aspect would be helpful. 

Q3: Computational expensive solution as highlighted under limitations section. Needs further work to improve broader practical adoption. Details of any production or learnings usage is missing.

title: Contextually Aware E-Commerce Product Question Answering using RAG
review:
The paper describes Product Question Answering system with Retrieval Augmented Generation for Conversational e-commerce. The proposed approach makes sense overall and it is clearly described. Moreover, the paper is well written and easy to follow. 

The proposed approach consists of a pipeline of LLM-based component for (1) Query Rewriting to convert conversation turns into stand-alone queries, (2) Search to retrieve relevant products, (3) query type classification model, (4) retrieval of relevant information & its reduction, and (5) response generation. All the components are properly described, omitting the actual prompts unfortunately, though prompt composition is explained. 

The components 1-4 are assessed using standard evaluation metrics. The intent model performance is assessed using weighted & macro-F1. Unfortunately, the data statistics are not provided.

To assess generation performance, the authors propose a set of "novel" metrics that are awfully similar in definition to the existing confusion matrix based metrics, with the added sub-classification of true positives as factually correct and complete (further on the 'good' response is defined as both factually correct and complete, so it becomes TP). Given that factual correctness (or grounded accuracy) is often used under the name of 'answer/response accuracy' and completeness is an aggregation of turn-level responses to provide a conversation-level score (rather than question-level), this hardly justifies as a novel metric.

title: Contextually Aware E-Commerce Product Question Answering using RAG
review:
Strengths:
1. Context-Aware Integration: The paper presents a robust framework that effectively integrates conversational history, user profiles, and heterogeneous product data (structured, unstructured, and semi-structured) to deliver personalized and accurate answers. This deep contextual understanding enhances user experience by reducing cognitive overload.

2. Scalable RAG Architecture: The proposed system leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with innovative components like the Standalone Query (SAQ) module and entropy-based intent handling, ensuring scalability and adaptability across diverse e-commerce queries. The two-stage retrieval process balances precision and coverage.

3. Novel Evaluation Metrics: The paper introduces tailored metrics (e.g., Context Coverage, Hallucination Rate) to rigorously assess RAG systems, addressing gaps in existing evaluation protocols. These metrics are broadly applicable and validated through both automated and human-aligned evaluations.

Weaknesses:
1. There is a lack of discussion and comparison of related work, such as ProductAgent.

2. The presentation of Figure 1 is so unclear that I can hardly make out the content of the figure.

3. It is uncertain how well the proposed method will be deployed, or whether the code and data will be open-sourced.

title: Contextually Aware E-Commerce Product Question Answering using RAG
review:
## Summary

This paper presents a scalable, end-to-end e-commerce Product Question Answering (PQA) system built using a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework. The system includes a standalone query (SAQ) rewriting module, an intent classifier, a retrieval and re-ranking pipeline, and a generation module. It integrates heterogeneous product data (structured, unstructured, and semi-structured) and leverages conversational history and user context to produce grounded, personalized answers. The system is deployed in production and evaluated both module-by-module and using a custom set of generation quality metrics.

## Strengths

- S1: The paper introduces a practical, modular architecture for real-world RAG-based PQA, combining product context, user history, and intent modeling effectively.

- S2: The implementation details and engineering considerations are clearly explained, making this work valuable to industry practitioners building conversational assistants.

- S3: Each component is evaluated individually, and the system as a whole is shown to improve user engagement metrics post-deployment.


## Weaknesses

- W1: The SAQ module is motivated by two specific goals (i.e., coreference resolution and product disambiguation) but the evaluation only reports restructuring accuracy, without directly assessing whether those two goals are effectively achieved.

- W2: The catalog search module’s effectiveness is described anecdotally, but lacks comparisons or deeper analysis (e.g., types of failures or edge cases).

- W3: A key contribution is the integration of heterogeneous product context, but the ablation only compares re-ranking methods. There is no breakdown or experiment on the importance of different types of context (e.g., structured vs. unstructured), limiting insight into what kinds of data most improve generation.

- W4: Although grounded accuracy and completeness are defined in the evaluation framework (Section 5.2.5), their actual values are never reported in the results.

- W5: While the paper positions the system as addressing challenges in handling diverse and heterogeneous contexts, it does not sufficiently analyze why this is difficult for existing PQA systems or provide comparative evidence to show how the proposed system improves upon them. This limits the reader’s understanding of the novelty and significance of the approach.

title: ProCut: LLM Prompt Compression via Attribution Estimation
review:
This paper introduces a framework that prompts LLMs to generate masks for prompt segments and estimate segment attribution with a small number of training set inference results for prompt compression. Results demonstrate a significant reduction in token usage with comparable or even slightly improved performance.

Strengths:
- LLM-agnostic, training-free framework.
- Fewer tokens in production while maintaining or even slightly improving task performance.
- LLM-driven attribution estimator achieves performance comparable to popular attribution methods, while offering lower end-to-end latency.

Weaknesses/Questions:
- It is less significant to perform compression only on the instruction prompt but not also on the {example QA} and {question} compared to prior works. With the needs of a training set for evaluating the generated masks, ProCut cannot be extended to these components.
- In Table 1, the test set contains only 100 instances, which is a small sample and may lead to unreliable evaluations.
- The baselines selected are too old, many works in the recent two years show significant improvement over Selective Context. More recent and stronger baselines would give a more meaningful comparison.
- More recent works should be cited and compared, e.g., C3oT, selection-p, EFPC, and DisComp.
- Is the word-level method like LLMLingua-2 also delete placeholders? I think experiments can still be conducted if forcing the {question} placeholder not to be removed and allowing the baseline methods to prune other tokens/words?
- Is the compression performed directly on the prompt templates presented in Table 5 or on the TextGrad prompts derived from those templates? Is a single compression used for all evaluated instances? It is somewhat confusing reading the compression with a short prompt in Figure 12 and the compression with a long prompt with TextGrad in Figures 9 and 10. Which subsection of the experiment do Figures 9 and 10 correspond to? In case compression is performed on the TextGrad prompts, it is clearer to also provide the performance with the initial prompt without TextGrad in Table 2. Also, the claim of “78% fewer tokens in production” would benefit from an example illustration. 
- In Section 3.2, the in-context example in Figure 6 guides the LLM to segment at the sentence level, which is similar to the structure-aware segmentation. An illustration on all three segmentation strategies would be helpful.
- It's better to align ProCut Steps' titles between Fig.1 and section 3.
- Is there a typo for the label [Y] and [N] in Fig.1? (Both are labeled as: Mask Label - segment retained)

title: ProCut: LLM Prompt Compression via Attribution Estimation
review:
The proposed framework ProCut addresses this with a flexible, LLM-agnostic, training-free framework that compresses prompts through segment-level attribution analysis. It decomposes a prompt into semantic units, quantifies each unit’s contribution to task performance, and prunes low-utility components. An LLM-driven attribution estimator accelerates the process, cutting compression latency by more than 50%. ProCut integrates seamlessly with existing prompt optimization frameworks, so teams can adopt it without retooling their stack. In production, ProCut achieves up to 78% token reduction while maintaining or improving accuracy--outperforming other compression methods by up to 62%. Real-world deployments have realized 73% and 84% token reductions, translating directly into substantial cost savings with lower latency and cleaner, more maintainable prompts.

The main contribution of this work is cost savings through significant reduction in token usage. Even with pretrained, off-the-shelf LLMs, inference remains costly in production because serving cost scales with prompt length. Reducing token count directly reduces latency and cost, making prompt compression valuable. 

There are few questions&/ suggestions:
* If one does very sharp token reduction it may cause sharp performance drops in some datasets (say SQuAD). Is it possible to think about a safe compression range, beyond what it harms the performance ?
* Of course the proposed method reduced the computational cost of attribution in comparison to the naive methods, but the attribution analysis still requires multiple LLM calls, which could be expensive at scale.
* The evaluation remains the main "Achilles hill". Is it possible to add one or a few experiments where ProCut still works with noisy/weak metrics? 
* Is it possible to provide a few qualitative example like before/after prompts and which parts were pruned? One could not find it, is it already there?

title: ProCut: LLM Prompt Compression via Attribution Estimation
review:
Summary: This paper presents ProCut, a selection-based framework for prompt compression. In this framework, prompts are divided into segments and analyzed for their relative contributions to performance. Prompts that contribute the most are selected for final inference. The proposed framework was tested against five benchmarks and two real-world use cases. The results suggest that the proposed framework could help reduce latency without impacting performance.

Strengths:
1. The experiments are well-designed.
2. The proposed method is highly interpretable.

Weaknesses:
1. The results are not rigorously compared to existing selection-based methods in the literature. An in-depth analysis is needed to reveal the strengths of the proposed approach.
2. The GPT models used in this study are not full-size models, so the impact of the proposed approach on full-size models is yet to be explored.

General feedback: The authors are strongly advised to work on comparison with existing selection-based approaches as well as experiments with larger models.

title: TOBUGraph: Knowledge Graph-Based Retrieval for Enhanced LLM Performance Beyond RAG
review:
Overall, a well written paper with an interesting implementation of a RAG pipeline using automatically extracted knowledge graphs. The application domain seems like a good place to use knowledge graphs in some form, and their implementation leverages KG extraction techniques with LLMs to represent user information about memories in a flexible and expressive way. The contributions of the paper are clear and their evaluation is thorough and mostly well explained.

In general, I think the authors do a good job of making their approach clear, but I think there are some elements that could be added or explained differently that would make the paper even clearer and give a stronger motivation to the specific design choices of their approach. Below, I will summarize the elements I found that might be improved, space permitting, and questions that came up in my mind while reading.


General remarks:
The structure they chose for their graphs is interesting and seems to make sense for their application, but more detail and explanation about the reasoning behind their choice of this specific graph structure and elements of the retrieval process would help considerably in understanding the motivation and logic of the design. Their introduction and motivation of the approach would be strengthened with some comparison to similar approaches to extracting or using KGs like e.g. GraphRAG, space permitting.

While the figures look nice, the text in many of them is small and hard to read. The boxes in Figure 1 and especially Figure 2 is quite small (e.g. ‘memory_id’), if the attributes are important enough to show, they should be clearly readable without a large amount of zooming in. Figure 4 could also have much larger labels within the horizontal space it takes up, and Figure 5 is very dense and has some space that could likely be used differently as well to make it more easily readable. Overall, it would be very nice if as much of the text as possible in the figures were made larger, particularly labels of elements more so than details in the example data/documents.

Another detail that would be useful is whether the relationship labels added to the relationship nodes have any preprocessing/text normalization or whether the labels are taken as is from the user. If no normalization is applied, it would seem that variations or spelling errors with labels risks obscuring connections between memories that should be linked on a path through the same relationship by creating multiple nodes for one semantic relationship. Have the authors accounted for this, or is this not a risk?

Additionally, what is the filter criterion in the retrieval step? Is it top-k, or is the LLM simply instructed to select an undefined number of most relevant labels for the context? Or is it something else entirely? At Line 231, the authors state “The system then traverses the RMG…”. How does it traverse the graph? What is meant by associated here? What is the procedure for collecting the memories once the relationship node filtering has been applied? This relates to g(R’,G’) in their formalization: how does the function g specifically select memory nodes?

In the generation process, they mention that once the system has sufficient details, it replies directly and otherwise asks clarifying questions. What details are sufficient, i.e. does the conversation aim to narrow the retrieval down to one unique memory or are multiple memories allowed to be retrieved per conversation or turn? If multiple memories can be used, how is it determined that the system has gathered sufficient details from the user?

I’m not sure that presenting a color scale table like they do in Table 4 is the best way to present the qualitative analysis, since it isn’t really an exact ordinal scale and the comparison is clear enough from the text, plus the space might be better used to discuss important details lacking elsewhere. At the same time, a quick visual summary of the models\ qualitative analysis is also nice, but maybe there is a different way to present it. I also imagine it isn’t accessible for colorblind readers.

Miscellaneous:

Line 37-40: “ RAG preprocesses documents by chunking text and storing the chunks 039 in a vector database. During retrieval, it retrieves the top-ranked chunks based on vector similarity…” -> Vector databases are not the only way to preprocess / store data for a RAG pipeline, this statement is too specific as worded to describe approaches to RAG as a whole. title: TOBUGraph: Knowledge Graph-Based Retrieval for Enhanced LLM Performance Beyond RAG
review:
**Summary**

This paper presents a graph-based retrieval framework called TOBUGraph. LLMs are used to extract knowledge graphs from unstructured text and form relations between different text documents. At inference time, a graph traversal strategy is used to retrieve information across multiple documents by leveraging the extracted relationships. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated using a real-world application named TOBU, with experimental results showing that TOBUGraph outperforms other alternative RAG approaches.

**Strengths**

1. The graph-based retrieval approach is well-motivated by the discussion of the limitations of existing query-chunk similarity retrieval methods. 
2. The application of the approach to a real-world application (including validation with real user data) supports the relevancy of this work to industry use cases. 
3. Extensive evaluations and analyses are provided in the form of user studies and interesting qualitative analyses. 

**Weaknesses**

1. While the evaluations on a real-world application are appreciated, focusing exclusively on TOBU for experiments makes the generalizability of this approach unclear. However, the authors at least acknowledge this in the limitations section.
2. The novelty of extracting knowledge graphs from unstructured text for use in retrieval pipelines is limited, as this has been explored in prior work (e.g., [1])
3. The results do not include any comparison of the efficiency of TOBUGraph to the baseline methods. It seems that TOBUGraph would be much more resource intensive than standard retrieval methods, both in terms of extracting the graphs with LLMs and retrieval at inference time through graph traversal.
4. The experiments lack comparison to other baseline methods that aim to automatically construct KGs from unstructured text using LLMs.
5. The scope of the evaluated dataset (as described in section 3.2) seems quite small – relying on only 80 queries raises questions about the generalizability of the results

[1] Choubey, Prafulla Kumar, et al. "Distill-SynthKG: Distilling Knowledge Graph Synthesis Workflow for Improved Coverage and Efficiency." arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.16597 (2024).

**Questions/Suggestions**
1. The text in the figures throughout the paper is too small to read
2. Where are the confidence intervals that are alluded to in the caption of Table 2? Only single values are provided here.
3. Typo on line 314: AAmong -> Among
4. Was any effort made to quantify the difference in hallucination rates among evaluated methods (I4 of Section 3.4)?

title: TOBUGraph: Knowledge Graph-Based Retrieval for Enhanced LLM Performance Beyond RAG
review:
This paper presents TOBUGraph, a novel graph-based retrieval framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to dynamically construct knowledge graphs from unstructured data, aiming to enhance retrieval performance beyond traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods. The authors have done a commendable job in addressing several key limitations of RAG, such as its reliance on text-to-text similarity and sensitivity to chunking strategies, by introducing a graph-based approach that captures deeper semantic relationships among data.

Strengths:

1. The innovative approach of constructing knowledge graphs automatically and utilizing graph traversal for retrieval is well-conceived and effectively implemented in the TOBU application.

2. The evaluation using real-world user data demonstrates significant improvements in precision, recall, and user experience over multiple RAG baselines, providing strong evidence of the method's effectiveness.

3. The paper is well-structured, with clear contributions outlined and comprehensive assessments conducted, including both quantitative and qualitative analyses, as well as user studies.

Weaknesses:

1. The dependency on OpenAI's GPT-4 API is a notable limitation, as it restricts the applicability of TOBUGraph in environments without access to this proprietary model. Exploring and evaluating open-source alternatives would enhance the method's accessibility and flexibility.

2. The dataset used for evaluation is domain-specific, potentially limiting the generalizability of the results. Expanding the evaluation to diverse datasets would strengthen the findings.

3. While the paper highlights improvements in retrieval accuracy, the scalability and computational efficiency of TOBUGraph on larger datasets are not thoroughly discussed. Addressing these aspects would provide a more complete picture of the method's practicality.

4. The descriptions about the graph construction are not detailed. The authors should list the semantic nodes in the appendix and describe how to extract the semantic nodes.

5. There are existing GraphRAG tools like: GraphRAG of Microsoft. The authors should discuss the relationship between the proposed framework and the existing tools.

In conclusion, TOBUGraph presents a promising approach to enhancing LLM-based retrieval systems through knowledge graph construction and graph-based retrieval. With some refinements to address the aforementioned limitations, this work has the potential to make significant contributions to the field of information retrieval.

Suggestions:

1. Line 182: missing reference link for ``Figure 1''.

2. Line 227: missing reference link for ``Figure 2''.

title: AgentPS: Agentic Process Supervision for Content Moderation with Multimodal LLMs
review:
**Overview**

This paper introduces AgentPS, a novel fine-tuning framework designed to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for complex content moderation tasks. The core idea is to integrate "agentic process supervision" by sequentially feeding ancillary questions and their corresponding answers into the model during training. This approach mimics a human-like, step-by-step reasoning process (Chain-of-Thought), guiding the model to make more accurate final predictions. A key contribution is the demonstration that these ancillary supervision labels can be generated by other MLLMs at scale, significantly reducing the reliance on expensive human annotation and making the framework practical for large-scale industrial applications. 

**Strengths**

1. The proposed AgentPS framework is a novel and effective method for improving MLLM performance on complex, policy-driven tasks. By structuring the fine-tuning process to mirror human reasoning, it achieves significant and consistent performance gains across multiple datasets and model sizes, as evidenced by the comprehensive experimental results.

2. The authors conducted a thorough evaluation, including experiments on both proprietary and public datasets (UCC, ANSA, HSD), an insightful ablation study separating the effects of process supervision and the CoT structure, and even an online A/B test. This multi-faceted validation lends strong credibility to the paper's claims.

**Weaknesses**

1. The paper admits that designing effective ancillary questions requires domain expertise but fails to provide a systematic methodology for their creation. I suggest to add a section or appendix discussing the principles for designing high-quality ancillary questions, perhaps with a flowchart or checklist for practitioners. 

2. The loss weights for ancillary questions were set to a default of 0.1 without justification.

3. The paper compares AgentPS to vanilla SFT and a multitask setup, but not to a more standard text-based Chain-of-Thought fine-tuning baseline. Such a baseline would involve fine-tuning the model to generate textual reasoning steps before the final answer, without the complex multi-head MLP structure.

4. The A/B test results are promising but lack crucial details. The baseline model used for comparison is not explicitly stated, and absolute metrics (e.g., raw ICVR values) are omitted.

5. The paper frames itself as a general solution for "content moderation," but the evaluated tasks (unoriginal content, nudity, hate speech) are relatively well-structured. It is unclear how AgentPS would perform on more nuanced moderation tasks like misinformation or harassment.

6. The term "Agentic" implies a degree of autonomy or tool use that is not present in the framework. The model is not an active agent but is passively guided through a structured fine-tuning process, so the term could be seen as misleading.

7. While showing MLLM-generated labels work, their accuracy (67-79% for process questions) is far from perfect. The paper's claim of "minimal performance degradation" might be an overstatement.

title: AgentPS: Agentic Process Supervision for Content Moderation with Multimodal LLMs
review:
In this work, the authors propose a framework called Agentic Process Supervision (AgentPS), which incorporates multiple intermediate question prompts into the input and uses their corresponding answers as process labels for multimodal large language model (MLLM) fine-tuning. This approach encourages the model to learn not only the correct final prediction, but also a structured, step-by-step reasoning procedure, with supervision applied at each stage. Such a method can be particularly beneficial for tasks where high-quality labeled data is expensive or difficult to obtain. However, I would encourage the authors to provide greater clarity on how the ancillary question–answer pairs were obtained for each dataset, as this is crucial for understanding the scalability and generalizability of the approach.

Typos/Suggestions

Add space in 063 and 423

title: AgentPS: Agentic Process Supervision for Content Moderation with Multimodal LLMs
review:
The paper proposes to enhance reasoning capabilities in classification tasks by introducing supervision to a reasoning process; the reasoning happens according to a predefined and fixed policy that asks a series of questions. This mirrors policy for many safety-relevant tasks and is not dissimilar to how human raters would be instructed to judge potential model output, or, indeed, processes that make judgments in real-world legal matters - to give some context.

The most relevant papers cited by this manuscript are (1) Ma et al. 2003, which it seems to improve upon by introducing supervision to each reasoning step during SFT; and (2) Wei et al's 2022 chain-of-thought prompting, which is more of an SI-controlled, inference-time method.

The proposed method makes a lot of sense, and it seems to improve upon the basic SFT baseline. That said, would it improve on the Ma et al. (2023) method?

Second, I wonder how large the stated improvement is. (0.22% decrease in ICVR, 1.3% decrease SSVR). What are the absolute numbers? If this is too sensitive to report, perhaps report relative error reduction instead of the decreases. Still, on the benchmarks, tables 1 and 2 report absolute gains, which are clear. So this leaves only the question about comparison with Ma et al.

I think that this method may be useful for many cases of content moderation, where practical policies can be defined as a series of questions. That said, what human raters are able to do is examine exceptions that haven't been foreseen by policy. Let's assume that this is desirable -- to remain a "reasonable person" as opposed to a "robotic" decision-maker.  A model with supervision only on the final outcome might gain similar intuition. If it is strongly guided by the question chain, will it still acquire such intuition? If not, could a scheduled learning process (using the question process first, followed by training on just the outcome) help?

Note; Section 2.1 (model architecture, page 2 right column) describes the integration of the vision portion in detail. I am not sure how his contributes to the understanding of the contribution; to make some space, this could be eliminated.

title: ECHO-LLaMA: Efficient Caching for High-Performance LLaMA Training
review:
The paper presents a neat trick: re-use the KV cache of an earlier LLaMA layer for the later half of the network, then fine-tune in small chunks. The result is faster training (up to 77 % tokens/s) and inference (+7 % throughput) while keeping accuracy flat. It’s simple, clearly explained, and directly useful for anyone who already has a LLaMA checkpoint and a tight GPU budget.

## Pros
1. No need to re-train a monster model from scratch; you start from any off-the-shelf LLaMA and just “patch” it layer-by-layer.
2. You decide how many layers share KV (25 % or 50 %). This lets engineers trade accuracy vs. speed depending on their product.

## Cons
1. Baseline comparison is limited – They compare only to vanilla LLaMA and TinyLLaMA. YOCO is mentioned but dismissed because “no official checkpoint”. A quick re-implementation of YOCO on TinyLLaMA would strengthen the claim that ECHO is the better choice.
2. Task breadth – All benchmarks are short-form QA / common-sense tasks. Large-scale generative tasks (e.g., long-context summarization, code completion) are missing.  It is very important to know the impact on long-context tasks, since short-context tasks are easier to be fit in fine-tuning

title: ECHO-LLaMA: Efficient Caching for High-Performance LLaMA Training
review:
The paper presets a detailed study of KV layer sharing, and proposes an incremental method of adapting a pre-trained standard Llama model to introduce the architectural change after the fact by further training iterations. The KV sharing makes the model more similar to encoder-decoder architectures (although a true encoder-decoder system would feed the autoregressive feedback not into the encoder). The paper is generally well-written.

I do, however, have one major concern about the evaluation. The paper shows that the presented method improves accuracy. It is not clear to me why that is expected. I can accept accuracy benefits when comparing under _constant budgets_, but I have doubts that a model would be _improved_ by introducing the KV sharing (unless the baseline is overtrained). Since the Echo adaptation involves additional training iterations, a fair comparison would apply similar further training iterations to the baseline model. I did not see a mention of such steps. I conclude that the accuracy gains are more likely due to the change of training data and/or additional training iterations applied only to the Echo model but not the baseline. This paper may still be of interest to the reader, but as a condition for publication, **I ask the authors to point this out or clarify this in the final paper**, even if it makes the comparison look less beneficial.

Also, I find the 77% speed-up surprising. Isn't normally the FFN the dominant component? And the O(N²) complexity of attention is still there. So isn't the only saving from the K and V transforms? The authors should add a note about this.

Because of these two concerns about the experimentation, I rate the paper a borderline accept.

Details:

* Figure 1: The wording "adaptive" is confusing, as that seems to refer to a training process, not the model architecture. Could you clarify? E.g. "The architecture uses shared KV caching. It is trained by layer-wise adaptation..."
* In the encoder/decoder interpretation, please clarify/point out that the model remains causal.
* L187: *share_d_
* L282, 283: I suggest avoiding variable names (num_worker). Maybe just use prose, "number of workers."

title: ECHO-LLaMA: Efficient Caching for High-Performance LLaMA Training
review:
The authors propose a method for using shared KV cache for high-performance LLaMA training. The main idea is to use shared KV cache for up to half of the layers in the transformer architecture. They also provide a method to adapt existing models like LLaMA and TinyLLaMA to their shared KV cache architecture with incremental updates. Their experiments show that their method achieve better MFU (model FLOPs utilization) compared to the base model without shared KV cache. However the main idea of shared KV cache comes from the YOCO paper (Sun et al 2024) and the extra contribution of adapting existing models are limited. 

Suggestions: 
- In Table 1, the last column should be throughput improvement instead of throughput (it's better to directly fix the column name than explain in the caption).

title: Computational Blueprints: Generating Isomorphic Math Problems with Large Language Models
review:
Summary:

The authors introduce the task of Isomorphic Math Problem Generation (IMPG) and propose Computational Blueprints for Isomorphic Twins (CBIT) to address it.

Strength:
The proposed method focuses on generating mathematical questions that are similar to the input questions, which is a good approach for building mathematical exercise sets for practice.

Weaknesses:

Limited novelty: The idea of changing numerical values in a mathematical problem to generate a new one seems to be an incremental contribution. Mathematics, in general, encompasses multiple types of problems, and the authors have not discussed in detail the subcategories of problems.

The paper is not well-positioned in comparison to recent works, making it difficult to assess its effectiveness.

One of the core contributions is the dataset, which contains 195 original problems—a relatively small size. Moreover, there is no detailed analysis or clear design criteria provided for curating such a dataset hindering the reproducibility.

title: Computational Blueprints: Generating Isomorphic Math Problems with Large Language Models
review: The line of work here is the automatic generation of mathematics problems at roughly the pre-college level.  (So this is not about research-level mathematics).   The new problem is to generated "isomorphic" math problems, and to do so efficiently (in a precise sense) and correctly.  The paper's definition of "isomorphic" is rather strict, and I doubt that everyone in the field would be happy with it: one can only change numbers, not 'ideas'.   So this limits the interest of the work.   But for what it is doing, the paper is quite good, and the writing is clear and easy to follow.   The overall idea of looking at the batch prompting strategy was also interesting.   (But personally I was not persuaded that the TPS measure is so interesting.)  The fact that the CBIT approach was deployed and tested on 6732 students, with a large number of generated problems, and also a good control group size, was the most impressive part of the paper; I would accept it for this EMNLP track based on that alone.  And the error rate in this was lower than slightly than the human-authored problem set.

title: Computational Blueprints: Generating Isomorphic Math Problems with Large Language Models
review:

The authors constrain LLMs in their generation process to achieve and present successful modifications to original math problems that are meaningfully different to assess students' knowledge.

title: Datasets and Recipes for Video Temporal Grounding via Reinforcement Learning
review:
**Summary:**
* The authors propose a novel two-stage training framework for Video Temporal Grounding (VTG) to enhance the capabilities of large vision-language models. 

**Strengths:**
* Video Temporal Grounding is an interesting problem with a wide range of applications.
* The paper is well-organized and provides the necessary details regarding their proposed framework.
* Their extensive experiments show that high-quality cold-start data and difficulty-controlled RL training are both crucial for improving model performance and generalization. 
* The authors also show that their approach is scalable and effective for real-world deployment.

**Weaknesses/Questions:**
* Why GRPO? How do you justify your choice of GRPO compared to its variants?
* Is this two-stage SFT and RL novel? Did you make any novel contributions?

**Typos:**
* Change "dose" to "does" in the query in Figure 1.

title: Datasets and Recipes for Video Temporal Grounding via Reinforcement Learning
review:
This paper proposes a two-stage training recipe to fine-tune a VLM to perform video temporal grounding. The first SFT stage involves fine-tuning the VLM on the reasoning traces and answers generated by Gemini. The second RL stage further trains the model, using the combination of an IoU reward and a reasoning format reward. The resulting model outperforms baselines on public benchmarks. Further analyses show that the quality of the SFT data and controlling the difficulty of the RL task are crucial to the model performance.

Strengths
- The data collection effort and the release training dataset is a valuable contribution.
- Analyses on how each stage of the proposed training recipe reveals interesting findings.

Weaknesses
- It seems like the proposed method basically distills knowledge from Gemini, i.e., Gemini basically performs the same exact task as the proposed model during the data collection phase. Why not just use Gemini then? What’s the advantage of the proposed model over Gemini? Does the RL stage allow the model to outperform Gemini? I think it’s important to include Gemini as a baseline.
- The two stage approach seems to have been borrowed directly from DeepSeek-R1 [1], even using the same terminology “cold start”. Despite this, the DeepSeek-R1 is neither referenced, nor discussed in terms of the relationship between it and the proposed work.

[1] Guo, Daya, et al. "Deepseek-r1: Incentivizing reasoning capability in llms via reinforcement learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2501.12948 (2025).

title: Datasets and Recipes for Video Temporal Grounding via Reinforcement Learning
review:
Pros:
1. Clear two-stage recipe (SFT cold start → difficulty-controlled RL) targeted at VTG; well-motivated in intro.
2. Competitive results on NExT-GQA, ReXTime, and Charades-STA; RL stage delivers large gains over SFT.
3. Ablations show high-quality cold start and RL data filtering both matter; longer cold-start CoT helps.

Cons:
1. RL budget is short (600 steps, β=0.0); unclear stability/variance across seeds or longer runs. 
2. SFT-only model underperforms base on some sets; perhaps there is some sensitivity to cold-start data composition?

title: LLM-as-a-Judge for Reference-less Automatic Code Validation and Refinement for Natural Language to Bash in IT Automation
review:
The paper proposes two evaluation metrics to enable LLMs more effectively evaluate automatically generated code. 

The paper lacks details that makes it hard to assess the practical usefulness of the proposed metrics -- See detailed comments below. 

Abstract is not informative, e.g., what type of automation is intended?
Use present tense in Abstract
Reported evaluation does not provide indications about findings

Providing an example in the introduction would be very useful
Provide citations or footnotes for APM tools 
Why verifying code is an important step?
Unclear what types of metrics are proposed by the authors, why do they make sense, and how do they compare (or address) limitations in existing work

Explain what it means “reference-less”
Why bi-directional evaluation is important? 

Figure 2 is misplaced and not properly referenced. 

Paper lacks sufficient details for enhanced readability and understandability 
Unclear whether Automatic code extraction is part of preprocessing the datasets used in the evaluation or part of the approach

Automatic code refinement was not highlighted earlier in the paper and appears out of the blue in Section 4.2.

Unclear what is the sections about “Self-reflection agent” and “Reflection agent with dedicated evaluator”

Unclear rationale behind thresholds used in the lexical similarity metrics like BLEU
What does “predicted positive” or “negative” mean in this context? 
Evaluation metrics should be properly defined, what is a true positive, false positive, and false negative in this context?
What does recall 1 or 0 entail?

Despite the emphasis on the limitations of lexical metrics, the proposed metrics are compared against them with little comparison against the other category (execution based).
 
The paper would benefit from including a proper “threats to validity” section 

The authors are encouraged to look for relevant work in the software engineering venues, such as ICSE and ASE conferences. 

Additionally, peer-reviewed references should be more cited instead of simple ArXiv papers (see guidelines on including a references with many authors — the one for GPT4)

title: LLM-as-a-Judge for Reference-less Automatic Code Validation and Refinement for Natural Language to Bash in IT Automation
review:
The paper introduces two LLM-as-a-Judge metrics for the automatic validation and refinement of Bash code. Taking into account that both metrics are merely custom prompts without any additional mathematical apparatus, I don't understand why the authors have decided to postpone the release of the actual prompts and detailed experiment configurations until paper acceptance (footnote 3). This decision harms the reproducibility of the results.

Furthermore, the paper contains claims that are not justified by the presented data. The authors state (lines 375–378) that, "Our metrics consistently achieved higher accuracy and agreement on binary judgments with the execution-based evaluation (ground-truth) than all other metrics", but it is clear from Table 1 that, for Bash-3, both BLEU and ROUGE-based metrics outperform their methods in terms of accuracy. Also, the precision results in Table 1 are bolded incorrectly. For Bash-1, ROUGE-L_0.9 outperforms the authors’ metrics. For Bash-2, BLEU_0.8 outperforms their metrics. Moreover, it is hard to agree with the authors that their metrics are "validating both functionality and logic correctness of the code" (lines 180–182), given that for Bash-3 they achieve precision ranging from 0.35 to 0.47.

I don't think that this paper, in its present form, should be accepted.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge for Reference-less Automatic Code Validation and Refinement for Natural Language to Bash in IT Automation
review:
The authors propose two metrics for LLM validation of NL2Bash task. The first metric, bidirectional functionality matching, extracts functionality description from both user questions and generated code snippet and compare them to get a binary judgement. The second metric, logic representation, converts question and code into pseudocode to eliminate the performance gap of LLM on niche programming languages like Bash. Experimental results on NL2Bash-EABench corpus show that the proposed method outperforms ICE-score method, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Here are some questions:
1. The experiment is only conducted on the NL2Bash-EABench dataset, which only has 150 samples in total. The small size of the benchmarking dataset makes the results insufficient and less convincing. Also, having only a single choice for both the Generator LLM and the Validator LLM raises concerns about the method's generalizability.
2. In Table 1, it’s not difficult to observe that the combined method only slightly outperforms the Func Match setting. This result diminishes the necessity of proposing the logic representation metric.
3. The paper mentions that the logic representation metric is intended to mitigate the issues caused by the obscurity of the programming language, but in my opinion, it doesn’t fundamentally solve this problem. The process of translating both the problem and the code into pseudocode still requires the LLM to understand the obscure language—this inherent flaw remains unresolved.
4. I’m hoping to see a case study on the code refinement task.

title: Thinking with DistilQwen: A Tale of Four Distilled Reasoning and Reward Model Series
review:
## Pros

* Practical, scalable KD pipelines with industrial value.
* Strong results across benchmarks. 
* Adaptive series are compelling.
* Reward-model distillation is useful.

## Cons

* Missing reproducibility details, e.g., prompts, configurations, hyperparameters, compute setup.
* Limited ablations isolating the contribution of each component.
* No clear accounting of data sources or safeguards against contamination.

## Questions

1. Line 179: Using DeepSeek-R1 as the long CoT difficulty scorer seems costly. Any particular reason for not using a non-reasoning model?
2. Table 1: R1-distilled model [1] performs better than the proposed slower-thinking models. Why do we still need them?
3. Section 3.2: What are the prompts used for the CoT difficulty scorer, re-writer, verifier, RV/CD scorers?
4. Line 186: Is the verifier rule-based outcome verification or LLM-based process verification?


## Reference:
[1] Guo, Daya, et al. "Deepseek-r1: Incentivizing reasoning capability in llms via reinforcement learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2501.12948 (2025).

title: Thinking with DistilQwen: A Tale of Four Distilled Reasoning and Reward Model Series
review:
This paper presents the DistilQwen models, a series of smaller, efficient reasoning models tailored for real-world uses. It highlights four types: slow-thinking models designed for accuracy; two adaptive-thinking models that change their approach based on the task to stay efficient; and reward models that help improve the reasoning through reinforcement learning. The models strike a balance between strong reasoning skills and fast responses, which is essential for industry needs.

The strengths of this paper include:
1. The introduction of four specialized DistilQwen model series, slow-thinking, adaptive-thinking, and reward models, demonstrates a comprehensive approach to balancing reasoning accuracy and efficiency tailored for industrial applications.
2. Extensive benchmarks and evaluation results showcase the models’ strong reasoning capabilities and inference efficiency, highlighting their practical advantage over larger models and existing approaches.
3. The development of an AI platform that supports training, evaluation, compression, and deployment emphasizes real-world applicability and scalability, facilitating easy integration into existing systems via RESTful APIs.

The weaknesses of this paper include:
1. There is insufficient detailed analysis of potential biases or data leakage propagating through distilled models and their impact on reasoning outcomes, which is crucial for responsible deployment.
2. The evaluation primarily relies on benchmark datasets which may not fully reflect complex, dynamic real-world environments, possibly overestimating models' operational effectiveness.
3. Regarding Sec. 4.4, it is confusing for the worse results in Table 4 in comparison to Table 1 and Table 2.

title: Thinking with DistilQwen: A Tale of Four Distilled Reasoning and Reward Model Series
review:
This paper describes the methodology followed for producing several distilled LLMs from Qwen models. The main focus of these distilled models compared to previous one is their ability to handle complex reasoning tasks. The core of the paper is the distinction between two series of models, a first series named “slow-thinking models”, and a second one called ‘adaptive-thinking models’. Both series are obtained through a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) distillation strategy where a CoT processor is defined for generating CoT from a large model, characterizing, selecting and correcting the CoT obtained to build an adaptation corpus on which small LLMs are fine tuned.

According to the experiment section, the distilled models show good performance with respect to previous ones, they constitute interesting resources for both academic and industrial studies.

Despite these strengths, the main weakness of the paper is the lack of novelty in the method proposed. This study is a follow up to previous studies such as ‘DistilQwen2.5: Industrial Practices of Training Distilled Open Lightweight Language Models’ and ‘Reasoning with OmniThought: A Large CoT Dataset with Verbosity and Cognitive Difficulty Annotations’.

On the overall this paper is more a technical report on the way these new distilled LLMs have been produced rather than a scientific paper.

In particular, the main contribution presented by the authors is the distinction between the “slow-thinking models” and the ‘adaptive-thinking models’. It is said several times that “Our slow-thinking models prioritize accuracy for demanding tasks, while the adaptive-thinking models dynamically optimize reasoning strategies to balance efficiency and performance.” However it is very hard to understand why the different CoT distillation strategies used for both types of models differ and will induce a different behaviour. First of all the terms “slow-thinking” and “adaptive-thinking” should be properly defined, then the different recipes used for both model should be better justified with respect to these definitions.

For example, it is said that one of the key difference in the distillation methods for the “adaptive thinking” is “The key difference is that we generate multiple CoTs for each problem using different teacher models.“ Why is that specific to “adaptive-thinking” and not “slow-thinking” models?

In the experiment section, it seems that the results obtained with “adaptive-thinking" are much better than those with “slow-thinking”, although the latter was supposed to be prioritizing accuracy. The authors need to justify with more details what are the differences between these 2 types of method, and the benefit of each of them.

title: Classifier-Augmented Generation for Structured Workflow Prediction
review:
This study is about a highly relevant industry topic which is the automation of workflows, in this case, using IBM DataStage. Starting from descriptions in natural language, they predict the workflow stages and combine them properly (determine edges between types) for the desired task. They try their approach with four models and report the accuracy against reasonable baselines. 

The presentation needs to be much more explicit on what the data is, what the prompts are, and how these are used. There is no appendix with full examples or with prompts, only a qualitative description of the prompts and a couple of data snippet samples in the text. Because of this, it’s very hard to understand what is going wrong (or right) with the evaluation. 

One less-central data source that linked is the documentation for IBM DataStage. But this is glossary information with some examples. Where are the 1010 natural language flow descriptions coming from? Are they from this or from an internal business use?

“For this evaluation, we sampled 1010 natural language flow descriptions for stage prediction. From this set, we annotated 308 flows with 1410 properties, and additionally sampled 54 complex non-linear flows (with up to 14 stages) for edge prediction.”

Can you be more explicit about what you mean by non-linear here and provide an example in an appendix? 

In the text of the paper, there are two examples of the natural language flow descriptions. Here is one: 

“I want to use teradata where my connection name is teradata-00, schema name is TM DS DB 1 and table name is EMPLOYEE2. then sort on the age column. then filter out pizza column. then postgres where my connection name is tristan postconn , schema name is public and table name is demoautotest, Also do the following, Decimal rounding mode is ceiling, Generate Unicode Columns, Row limit should be 50.”

Is this a permutation of the examples in the IBM DataStage documentation or did  someone to paraphrase things they do with DataStage in the workplace?

The main objective is to make dataflows easier to write and less error-prone. One thing that stands out is that these examples seem to expect exact names for tables, for example, which are highly idiosyncratic to a company and a code-base. It makes sense that it would be out of the scope of the task to try to disambiguate misspelled table names, but, from an end-user perspective, the drop-downs with table names (that don’t require users to go look for them) is one of the major benefits of the GUI. Is there evidence that natural language descriptions written in this way are a useful way for helping data scientists do their work? The phrasing is very cumbersome, run-on style and doesn't look like how an end user would complete the task of "use natural language to describe a workflow". 

This was stated, "For every property, we store its description, type, default value, and availability conditions in a structured format suitable for prompt generation and output validation."

Were there any generalizations made about licit workflows by the LLMs based on this information? That also seems to be something the IBM GUI controls for that could be complicating the decision space in how this approach was implemented. 

Small editorial notes: 
Lines 470-471 closer ? Missing a noun here. 

Line 485 (open quote is wrong character)

Comma on more than 3 digit numbers seems more standard (line 181 2,133).
