title: Classifier-Augmented Generation for Structured Workflow Prediction
review:
The paper proposes a Classifier-Augmented Generation (CAG) framework for generating executable ETL workflows from natural language descriptions, targeting tools such as IBM DataStage. The system decomposes user utterances into sub-utterances, uses a trained classifier to identify relevant stages, and then applies targeted few-shot prompting to generate stage predictions. CAG is compared against single-prompt and agentic baselines, showing higher accuracy, reduced token usage (~66% less), and improved interpretability. The evaluation covers stage selection, edge layout, and property generation, reporting up to 97.7% stage prediction accuracy and over 70% structural similarity for complex workflows.

### Strength
1. CAG outperforms single-prompt (96.4% → 97.7%) while cutting token usage from ~14k to ~4–4.7k per request.
2. Addresses token efficiency in large-context models—a practical deployment concern.
3. The three-stage pipeline—stage prediction, edge prediction, and property prediction—is logically organized and well explained

### Weakness
1. Multi-Label Classification is limited. The classifier is trained only on single-label utterance–stage pairs due to dataset constraints.
2. It can still produce granularity mismatches or missed trivial stages 
3. The author only compare to single-prompt and agentic variants within the authors’ pipeline. There is no benchmarks against recent tool-augmented LLM planners or retrieval-augmented generation frameworks for workflow synthesis, like AutoFlow, AFlow, etc
4.

title: Classifier-Augmented Generation for Structured Workflow Prediction
review:
The paper presents a system that translates natural language descriptions into executable workflows that conform to the ETL paradigm. The main contribution discussed in the paper is the CAG (Classifier-Augmented Generation), a prompt augmentation procedure proposed by the authors, that utilizes a classifier to select candidate ETL stages, which are passed to an LLM for further processing. As the name suggests, it is an approach inspired by RAG-based solutions. The approach is simple but effective, leading to a reduction of token usage by 60% while maintaining a high (97%) accuracy.

Summary of Weaknesses:

1, The authors focus on workflows for a specific ETL tool — IBM DataStage. While the tool is mature and widely recognized, it is not clear how the results presented in the paper would generalize to other ETL tools.

2. The description of the classifiers is almost hidden in section 3.2 and lacks details. How many labels are considered? What is their distribution? What are the precision, recall and macro-F1 scores of the classifier?

3. Edge prediction accuracy is very low, which suggests that the system is not production-ready — a major weakness for an industry-track paper. Remark: I'm not convinced that an LLM is the proper tool for edge prediction. Perhaps you should consider geometric deep learning methods such as graph convolutional networks for this task in the future.

title: RAILS: Reasoning Along Intended LineS for Agent Orchestration
review:
This paper shows the effects of two techniques on improving the performance of multi-turn agentic datasets, Retail-Conv and Tau-Bench.

The headline result, which is that these methods significantly help smaller models while achieving only marginal success on larger models, is buried, and deserves more consideration beyond a claim of "democratization". Perhaps RAILS acts as a kind of distillation -- but this is challenged by the offhand observation (that I find very counter intuitive, and which is presented without numbers reported) that "the best performance is typically achieved when the same model is used for both prompt optimization and execution". Why can't big models do well optimizing prompts for smaller models? Some more investigation/ablation here would be helpful.

My broader comment, though, is that the paper overstates the novelty of its approach, as well as the generalization.

(1) Structured thinking: The only baselines tried are "No Thinking" and "CoT", though Tree-of-thoughts and ReAct get mentions in the related work -- and entirely dismissed as "undirected", which is a bit harsh. Structured or guided reasoning is something of a sub-field, e.g., https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.14295v1 refers to "reasoning topologies" and shows several examples of directed reasoning in action. RAILS is, as the name aptly implies, not an exploration of a set of possible reasoning structures but a single, particular one that claims to be based on their sense of how humans structure their thinking (though, no citations from the psychology literature are provided that can back up their intuition on human cognition). As the authors acknowledge in the limitations section, it's not clear how well this particular structure will generalize to other tasks, so claims like "RAILS is designed as a drop-in enhancement for existing agent architectures" are overstated and should be modulated. Similarly, calling unstructured CoT the "current state-of-the-art" is really quite dismissive!

(2) Automatic Prompt Optimization: Here, too, the authors imply some degree of novelty with IRIS, where APO is also well established as a way to optimize prompting (see https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11560 for a review). Framing IRIS within the context of prior APO efforts would help to calibrate the paper's claims, namely, that the authors have applied the approach to good results on their use case. (Which is fine for an industry track applications paper.)

Granular comments:

- "RAILS decomposes each orchestration step into: (1) Context Understanding..." and "Our key insight is that human decision-making in complex scenarios follows predicable patterns" -- Seems like some implied domain assumptions here, as opposed to this list of 5 steps applying to all thought processes. A claim about all of "human decision-making" should be backed up with psychology literature.

- "Intelligent RAILS Instruction Synthesis" -- Does everything need its own name - can we not say that we applied a form of APO to the domain?

- Section 3.2: I notice an implicit closed-weight assumption. Post-training is not considered, but can apply just as well to optimizing reasoning traces as final answers. This may show that the particular set of 5 steps is not the one that a self-directed optimization process would discover for itself, i.e., the ML "bitter lesson". Also, please say something about how the necessary context (available tools, action schemas, response strategies, SOPs) are provided; schema adherence is its own huge problem and sub-field.

- "The updated prompt is validated on a held-out subset of the data" - thanks.

- Table 1: How many iterations does IRIS use in practice and for what reason does it terminate, in these results?

- The RAILS (Human) baseline is not described before results are presented for it. What were the humans asked to do? How many did you recruit? How many iterations were they allowed? These details are apparently omitted.

- The IRIS section seems to imply that only the most recent prompt is evaluated, based on how the Case Analyzer and Insights Aggregator interpret its results. A lot of optimization approaches look at the most recent n or best-performing n iterations in the past. This longer memory can help IRIS trying the same mistake over and over, getting caught in a local maximum.

- "consistent improvements across all datasets" -- "both" datasets? "All" implies 3+.

- "our five-step framework represents one possible decomposition--alternative structured approaches merit investigation." I'd also suggest using IRIS without RAILS (see above comment about "bitter lesson").

- "This uses the RAILS format but retains the base prompt structure." Why?

- Thanks for including the entire prompts in the appendix.

- What is Pass^k? I thought this meant Pass@k (meaning any one of the most likely k samples is correct), but performance goes down, not up, with k in Table 4. (Pass@k should always be flat or go up as more options are considered.) Does it mean k correct agent turns in a row in a sliding window method of counting (since a trajectory can have dozens of turns)?

title: RAILS: Reasoning Along Intended LineS for Agent Orchestration
review:
# Main contributions:

This paper proposes a reasoning along intended lineS framework, called RAILS, which constrains the thought process of LLM agents into structured 5 steps.

Besides the RAILS, authors introduce an intelligent RAILS instruction synthesis called IRIS, which is an automated system that effectively generates RAILS-based instructions.

The RAILS involves context understanding, request analysis, action planing, validation and response generation steps.  All of the steps are explicitly defined in the input instructions.

The IRIS  is a prompt optimization system with a pipeline of case analyzer, insights aggregator and prompt optimizer. The optimizer results directly refine the input instructions

# Strengths

1.  Readers can easily catch the main idea, and follow the  instruction format.
2.  The experiment results compared with CoT exhibit the proposed method is useful for tool calling reasoning tasks.

# Weaknesses

1.  More comparisons with LLM reasoning methods, such as ToT, GoT,  are needed.
2.  Will the instruction get longer and longer after iteratively updating the instruction?
3.  The authors claim that RAILS mirrors human096problem-solving strategies, which needs some references.

# Typo

line 331: "Prompt Optimizer" should start in a new line.

title: RAILS: Reasoning Along Intended LineS for Agent Orchestration
review:
The paper presents RAILS, a method for integrating explicit reasoning steps into instruction-following models to improve reliability and transparency in safety-critical domains. The model is trained to output both a reasoning trace and a final answer, with the idea that the intermediate reasoning can be inspected, audited, or verified before use. The approach is motivated by industrial needs for oversight in high-stakes scenarios and is evaluated on multi-step reasoning tasks. Results show gains in correctness and reasoning faithfulness compared to direct instruction tuning and vanilla chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, though the improvement varies across datasets.

The work is relevant and well-motivated for industrial application, but I am ambivalent about the degree of novelty. The method combines established components — supervised instruction tuning and explicit reasoning — rather than introducing new modeling techniques, and its distinctiveness lies more in its application framing than in algorithmic innovation. The baseline choice of vanilla CoT is somewhat basic, given that more advanced reasoning-augmented methods (Self-Consistency, Plan-and-Solve, Tree-of-Thoughts) are now common and could offer a stronger point of comparison. ReAct is cited in related work but not included in the experiments, even though a reasoning-only adaptation could have been tested.

Another limitation is the narrow range of models tested (mainly Qwen, OpenAI, and Mixtral). With more recent flagship models, the improvements appear smaller, possibly because these models already integrate internal reasoning mechanisms through prompt templates or architectural changes. This raises the question of how much RAILS still adds when used with state-of-the-art LLMs. The paper also does not compare against “thinking” models explicitly designed for reasoning, which would be a natural and important benchmark. Finally, there is no discussion of computational cost: adding explicit reasoning steps may increase latency and resource use, and many production systems already trade off reasoning depth for efficiency.

On reproducibility, the method is described clearly and the use of open benchmarks is positive, but more detail on the annotation process for reasoning traces would help assess viability and cost in real applications. The paper is well written and structured, with effective diagrams, though some minor presentation issues remain (e.g., commentary before tables). Overall, this is a solid industrially relevant contribution with promising empirical results, but the modest novelty, limited baseline coverage, and absence of cost analysis leave open questions about its comparative advantage, especially with the newest generation of reasoning-capable LLMs.

title: GSID: Generative Semantic Indexing for E-Commerce Product Understanding
review: This paper showcases the application of the GenRet document tokenization learning to a consumer-to-consumer e-commerce platform (the details of the platform are not disclosed right now for the sake of anonymity). The results are reported against reasonable baselines and also in terms of improved CTR. As a downside that can be improved, the paper claims that it "optimizes the GenRet training framework to overcome the challenge of its difficulty in training on large-scale datasets." However I had a difficult time understanding where those optimizations lie exactly. I was not able to detect the differences between the paper's method on GenRet. So that part needs further clarification. Otherwise the novelties there are hard to assess. But I still find the application to and results on an e-commerce platform valuable.

title: GSID: Generative Semantic Indexing for E-Commerce Product Understanding
review:
In this paper, the authors propose Generative Semantic Indexing (GSID), a data-driven approach to generate discrete, hierarchical structured representations (semantic IDs) for products in e-commerce. Specifically, they aim to address poor coverage of long-tail products and misalignment with buyer preferences. GSID leverages GenRet to learn tokenization and derive short and discrete representations, as well as guide product structure with real-world user queries. 

Strengths:
* Data-driven approach can better avoiding manual curation and addressing long-tail products.
* Effectiveness in product understanding
* Real-world deployment

Weaknesses:
* Lack of multi-modal integration when images and other data could be important in e-commerce
* Inflexible hierarchical structure of semantic ID
* Lack of experimental details for the reproducibility

title: GSID: Generative Semantic Indexing for E-Commerce Product Understanding
review:
This paper deals with structured product organization in an e-commerce platform, specifically the one which is consumer-to-consumer (second hand sale). The paper motivates the problem by describing the current status in which such consumer-to-consumer scenarios lead to a long tail, and the product organization is done manually. 

The paper proposes a generative approach in which they train a T5 model for this task. The paper goes into great details about describing the various parts of training (namely pre-training on e-commerce data and then progressive training). The paper shows the efficacy of their approach by comparing them to traditional baselines used in this domain, as well as showing the results of online A/B testing. 

Major strengths: 
1. The paper delineates in depth the whole training pipeline, including the various objective losses, sampling strategies, and the modifications in loss function done to make the training more stable. All these point to a very well thought out system. 
2. For evaluating the model the authors present three very distinct and valid evals (those on retrieval, those on interpretability using hierarchical clustering, and A/B test). 

Weakness:
I am not 100% sure of the baselines are strong, and if there should have been a manual baseline as well.

title: Depression Detection on Social Media with Large Language Models
review:
The paper proposes a medical knowledge-guided approach for detecting depression from social media posts, comparing both traditional ML methods and LLM-based classifiers. Experiments report performance in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. However, Table 1 reveals strikingly poor precision for LLM-based methods, which is neither discussed nor justified. The related work section omits several key deep learning studies on depression detection, and the dataset description is vague, with unacknowledged limitations regarding the use of translated Chinese social media posts.

Strengths
1 - Tackles a socially significant and clinically relevant problem: automated depression detection from social media.
2 - Attempts to integrate domain-specific (medical) knowledge into the classification process, which is conceptually interesting.
3 - Evaluates across multiple model categories (traditional vs LLM-based), which could provide insights into performance trade-offs.

Weaknesses / Areas for Improvement
1. Unexplained Low Precision in LLM-Based Methods
In Table 1, the reported precision for the LLM-based method is 0.0899, drastically lower than all traditional baselines. This is a severe anomaly such low precision suggests that the LLM is producing an overwhelming number of false positives. The paper does not acknowledge or explain this result, which raises questions about: The quality of prompt engineering. Whether label imbalance is affecting the metric. Whether evaluation settings differ between methods.

2 - Omissions in Related Work: The related work section is missing several recent and relevant studies that use deep learning for depression detection.
Notably absent is:
Sarkar, S., Alhamadani, A., Alkulaib, L., & Lu, C. T. (2022). Predicting depression and anxiety on reddit: a multi-task learning approach. IEEE/ACM ASONAM, 427–435. 
This work is directly comparable, as it uses multi-task deep learning for mental health prediction from Reddit data, and could serve as a strong performance baseline.

3 - Vague Dataset Description: The paper fails to specify the exact social media platforms used in the dataset — e.g., Twitter, Reddit, or others. From reviewing the cited source, it appears that most data originates from Chinese social media, later translated into English. This introduces translation artifacts and potential semantic loss, particularly for sentiment and mental health cues. The paper does not mention this limitation or describe any quality control measures for the translated text. Dataset details are largely outsourced to the referenced paper rather than being described in full here, reducing transparency and reproducibility.

title: Depression Detection on Social Media with Large Language Models
review:
This paper presents a highly compelling and well-executed study. The authors propose DORIS, a novel framework that effectively addresses two critical challenges in AI-driven mental health detection: the integration of robust medical knowledge and the necessity for high explainability. The hybrid architecture, which leverages LLMs for feature engineering and explanation generation while relying on a Gradient Boosting Tree (GBT) classifier for robust prediction, is both innovative and pragmatic. The work is substantiated by rigorous experimentation, including comprehensive comparisons with strong baselines, detailed ablation studies, and thoughtful analyses of hyperparameters and component efficacy. The results are impressive, demonstrating a significant and meaningful performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods. The paper is well-written, the methodology is sound, and the ethical considerations are thoroughly addressed. This work represents a substantial contribution to the field and has strong potential for real-world impact.

There are some comments:
The authors rightly acknowledge the limitation of using a single dataset (SWDD). While the dataset choice is excellent (real-world prevalence, includes non-self-disclosing users), a note on plans for future validation on additional datasets (even if not performed yet) would further strengthen the paper. This is already mentioned in the limitations section, so it is adequately addressed.

The process of generating T_MC is described, but the prompt (in Appendix D) is quite high-level. A brief example of an input (a few timestamped posts) and the resulting LLM-generated summary output would make this powerful component even more tangible for the reader.

Was any calibration performed on the GBT classifier's output probabilities? Given the severe class imbalance, well-calibrated probabilities could be very important for a clinician interpreting the "confidence" of a prediction.

title: Depression Detection on Social Media with Large Language Models
review:
This paper introduces DORIS, a framework to improve early depression detection using social media data. Their framework uses large language models to annotate user-generated content based on medical diagnostic criteria and summarize users' mood changes over time. These features feed into a Gradient Boosting Tree classifier for prediction.

Strengths:

Uses established diagnostic criteria for feature extraction.

Incorporates mood patterns over time rather than relying on isolated posts.

Weaknesses:

Relies heavily on LLMs, which may introduce bias or errors in symptom interpretation.

It may lack validation in real-world clinical settings beyond the experimental dataset. 

Comments:

Figure 1 -> I did not find the figure mentioned anywhere in the main text. The figure is also not very clear about what it describes.

Contributions -> I don't understand the difference between the first two contributions since they seem to say the same thing, but are said differently and vary in content.

Lines 238-239: "For each emotion template, we generate a representation using a pre-trained embedding model:" -> Embeddings of which model?

Lines 246-247: "For each emotion j, we retain posts within the top m% of similarity" -> What is the value of m, and how was it determined?

Lines 404-406: "Due to space constraints, we present the experimental results for RQ3, RQ4 and RQ5 in the Appendix." -> Why not consider this paper in the main conference instead of the industry track?

I am not sure that the paper is suitable for the industry track. It does not present any real-world deployment, not even at the demo level.
This is combined with the previous point that most of the descriptions, analyses, and experiments are not even in the main part of the paper.

**** Comments after rebuttal: I thank the authors for taking the time to answer my comments. After reading and reconsidering them, I adjusted my score accordingly; however, I still believe that the paper is more suitable for the main conference than the industry track.

title: Generative Reviewer Agents: Scalable Simulacra of Peer Review
review:
This paper describes a multi-agent generative AI approach to peer review. Each paper to be reviewed goes through a pipeline which constructs a knowledge graph from it, then to "select" a set of appropriate AI agent reviewers, then each reviewer agent generates their review, and finally a final meta-review agent generates the final paper review. The result is a set of scores, sub-scores, and qualitative paper review.

There's a lot going on in this paper -- which the authors themselves acknowledge in the Limitations section -- but that makes it difficult to follow since each phase in the pipeline could be a separate paper in its own right. Some questions I have are:

1. There seem to be a lot of prompts used throughout the entire process; where can I find them?
2. How and why were the LLMs used selected for this system? Which LLMs were used in which phases of the pipeline?
3. How many possible AI agent reviewers are there?
4. What kinds of reviews are being generated? Do the reviews include grammar and style checks (this may be answered when the prompts are shared)?
5. Do all of the reviews use the same points and reviews system, and if not, how do you adjust for that? What's the distribution accepted/rejected/borderline papers in each data set and how might that have affected the performance of your system?
6. In the evaluation, it's hard to tell when actual humans are being used compared to another LLM. Sometimes it seems like "LLM Evaluators" (line 396) are being used but then the metrics are being shown as coming from "Human" so, which one is it?
7. What's the difference between a "win" and a "preferred" review? Wouldn't a preferred review be considered a win and vice-versa?
8. What is "GAR>"?
9. In table 3, it seems like results are averages, but I can't figure out what they're averages of.

Typos etc.:
* On lines 104 - 106, move the citations towards the end of the description, e.g. "Furthermore, LLMs can generate research concepts (Wang et al., 2024a; Baek et al., 2024), and..."
* On line 142: "reviewer" should be "reviewed".
* On line 203, "algorithms" should be "algorithm".
* On line 379, "Openreview" should be "OpenReview".
* On line 444, "f1" should be "F1".
* In the citations, try to preserve proper capitalization using { } e.g. `{LLM}`.

title: Generative Reviewer Agents: Scalable Simulacra of Peer Review
review:
I thank the authors for working on this exciting topic. The addition of the four components for agent instantiation is a novel idea, with memory, profile, novelty, and review modules. The notion of graph creation and a graph-based paper representation that links claims, evidence, and technical details, is also novel for this use case. I next look at strengths, weaknesses/ questions.

Strength:
- The paper consists of many modules and each of them are explained well. The simulation of the review process with multiple agents is also spot on.
- Evaluation is complete: With automatic quantitative metrics and human comparisons with preference pairs. 
 - The paper presents very interesting results: Humans prefer LLm generated judgement compared to human generated ones in preference pair evaluations.

Weaknesses: 
- The paper has some un-explained uses of LLM as a judge without human evaluation (for example section 4.4); which introduces some circular evaluation.
- (minor) While very hard to account for, it would have been interesting to know if the models already had information about the paper in their pre-training datasets.
- It is hard to spot how the authors attribute performance gains to persona parts (example lines 446-448). Addition of such details would make this easier to read.
- A quick question is how much previous review information is available to the LLM? Would there be an increase in performance if few shot reviews were given as baselines?
- The choice for graph based similarity as compared to semantic similarity needs greater motivation. Additionally, the graph creation process is non-deterministic due to the nature of LLMs. How does that impact your findings?

Update: I thank the authors for the reply, I will keep the scores as is with a high rating. Despite the considerable variance in the scores, I believe that the authors have also made a good faith effort to respond to all reviewers. I wish them the best.

title: Generative Reviewer Agents: Scalable Simulacra of Peer Review
review:
**Summary**

This paper introduces Generative Agent Reviewers (GAR), an LLM-based framework for automated peer review. The system employs a graph-based manuscript representation, reviewer personas derived from historical data, memory-augmented reviews, and multi-round evaluation processes. The authors evaluate GAR on ICLR and NeurIPS datasets, claiming performance comparable to or exceeding human reviewers.

**Strengths**

- Technical Innovation: The graph-based manuscript representation with community detection (Section 3.1) offers a novel approach to structuring complex academic papers, potentially improving upon linear text processing methods.

- Comprehensive Architecture: The four-module design (profile, memory, novelty, review) demonstrates thoughtful system engineering with clear separation of concerns.

**Concerns**

1. Ethical Concerns and Evaluation Metrics:
- There appears to be a disconnect between the stated goals and the evaluation methodology. Lines 487–491 explicitly note that the vision is to “enhance the review process” and “support” human reviewers, yet the evaluation framework relies entirely on replacement metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1 scores, preference rankings). To address this, the paper could shift its emphasis towards examining how the proposed segment modules can effectively *facilitate* the human review process. This could be demonstrated through smaller-scale experiments that assess how the novel aspects (e.g. graph-based representation of the manuscript, retrieved similar papers B_sim) could contribute to improving the review process when provided to human reviewers.
- Other than accuracy, it would be valuable to investigate whether reviewer Agent driven by an aligned LLM could amplify or mitigate systemic biases in peer review compared to human reviewers, such as "preferential treatment toward well-established institutions or underestimating novel but unconventional ideas" as mentioned by author.

2. Insufficient Details
- Missing Prompts: Core prompts (Qmerge, Qsum, Qcomp, Qfocus, etc.) are referenced throughout but only one example is provided (Appendix). These are fundamental to reproducing results.
- The statement in lines 410-418 that "GAR-generated reviews stem from their depth, resulting in high preferences" is somewhat vague and speculative. It would be helpful to provide more detailed examples and clarify the evaluation criteria used to determine the "depth" of reviews. The claim that human reviews are "more shallow" should also be substantiated with specific examples or a clearer definition of what constitutes shallow versus deep reviews, as these terms are subjective without clear evaluation standards.
- For the human-likeness analysis, should clarify the number of samples and participants involved.
- For Table 4, it would be informative to include real human review scores as a reference, even if the GAR model does not surpass human reviews. This would provide a clearer benchmark for understanding the model's performance.

3. Presentation Clarity:
- The paper would benefit from illustrating the graph-based manuscript representation using a concrete example, potentially demonstrating the approach on the submitted paper itself to enhance reader comprehension.
- Minor typographical error on line 142 ("reviewer r has reviewer the paper p" should read "reviewed")
- The “GAR>” notation appears throughout multiple tables but lacks a clear definition. Is it in any way related to the “RAG>” notation mentioned in Line 373?

title: COLAS: A Fair and Automated Programming Lab Assessment System Using an Adaptive LLM and Metric-Driven Evaluation
review:
Authors developed a modular, AI-powered system for "secure, fair, and pedagogically grounded" in-person programming lab assessment.

The solution generates custom programming problems, solutions, and test cases based on instructor prompts. It analyzes multiple versions of student code to highlight logical differences, strategies, and optimizations. It was deployed at code.cognistorm.ai and trialed in over 10 lab sessions with 100+ students, reporting reduced grading time and improved fairness perceptions.


- My main concern is the lack of human/automated evaluation: there is no empirical evidence showing that COLAS’s constraints, monitoring, and analytics improve conceptual understanding or problem-solving skills. Most reported benefits (e.g., "4.2 hours saved per session" or "improved fairness") are self-reported and lack statistical rigor. There’s no objective analysis of grading accuracy, false positives/negatives in plagiarism detection, or actual improvements in student learning outcomes, or rigorous human evaluation experiments.  While related work is discussed, the paper doesn’t provide direct head-to-head performance or usability comparisons between COLAS and well established platforms like CodeRunner or Gradescope.


- The tool is based on quantized 3B LLaMA model to save resources, which may produce suboptimal or inconsistent problem statements and analysis. The paper admits this but doesn’t quantify the drop in quality or provide error analysis of generated content compared to stronger models.

title: COLAS: A Fair and Automated Programming Lab Assessment System Using an Adaptive LLM and Metric-Driven Evaluation
review:
Summary:

The paper describes an automated programming lab assistant (called COLAS). It has the following modules - 
1. Problem-set generation and Submission Analysis
2. Code Execution
3. Plagiarism Detection
4. Constrained Primitives
5. Activity Monitoriing
6. Analytics

Novelty and  Impact:

While similar systems (Eg. Hackerrank, Codeforces, Topcoder, etc.) are already present, this system claims to add LLM problem generation as an added impact. This feature can be particularly useful for creating problem sets for smaller groups like school / college students, as opposed to open-to-all like many coding platforms.

The system also has a plagiarism detection mechanism, which can be useful for detecting similar submissions.

The system has been deployed and 100+ users have already used the system.

Clarity and Structure:

1. Are the LLM-generated problems correct? Hallucination is a known challenge in LLMs, and this should be addressed in the paper. For example, what if the test cases generated are wrong? Or what if the expected solution is incorrect?

2. The appendix should come after the references, not before.

3. A user study of the system (Eg. user feedback) will strengthen the submission.

Anonymity Issues:

The submission has a non-anonymized URL in the abstract and the paper itself, compromising the anonymity requirement.

title: COLAS: A Fair and Automated Programming Lab Assessment System Using an Adaptive LLM and Metric-Driven Evaluation
review:
## Strengths
An LLM powered implementation to support and enabled better learning experiences for students in introductory programming courses. Instructors can generate programming assignments at scale

Presents several quantifiable metrics to present the benefit offered by the system. Figure1 shows the different actors. This work is a great detailed workflow discussion of a closed-source system for anyone interested in the internal mechanisms

## Weaknesses
But that is where the work stops . For a typical work at EMNLP, my understanding is that there should be more comparisons absed on the unederlying NLP models such as open source /closed source systmes that power the tasks enabled by the system are the authors able to provide a revised version of this work that includes these details? title: Talk2Data: A Multimodal Agentic Framework for Conversational Data Analysis
review:
This paper introduces an assistant framework for data analysis over multi-modal inputs and outputs, including voice, image and text. The proposed system integrates a speech recognition engine, code generation-execution engine and text-to-speech engine into a unified framework, enabling users to explore and analyze data in an interactive environment. The authors carried out experiments with the proposed framework on 48 sample use cases based on three tabular datasets, and their system achieved 95% success rate measured manually.

### Strengths
- The paper presents an interesting integration of existing components (ASR, TTS, LLM-driven code generation) into a unified multi-modal framework for data analysis, which could be valuable for industry applications.
- The proposed framework provides a complete pipeline from voice input to multimodal output which could address practical needs for hands-free data interaction, especially conversational interfaces for data exploration.

### Weaknesses
- **Insufficient motivation and problem justification**: The paper does not clearly articulate the specific technical challenges being addressed or provide compelling justification for why this particular integration is needed over existing solutions.
- **Unclear production impact**: The paper fails to quantify expected benefits for end users or demonstrate measurable improvements over existing approaches.
- **Missing technical depth**: Key technical decisions, such as the routing component design and the trade-offs between unified vs. separate processing paths, are not well justified or analyzed.
- **Lack of baseline comparisons**: The evaluation lacks comparison with baseline systems, making it impossible to assess the actual effectiveness and added value of the proposed approach.
- **Weak experimental evaluation**: The test sample size (48 cases) is too small for robust evaluation, and the manual success rate measurement lacks reproducibility.

### Comments and suggested revisions
- Clearly articulate the specific technical challenges and limitations of existing approaches that your system addresses. Provide concrete use cases where existing solutions fall short.
- Comparisons with relevant baseline systems (e.g., existing voice assistants, separate code generation tools, or simpler integrated approaches) are required to demonstrate the value of the proposd approach.
- The authors may want to provide clear reasoning for the routing component design. Also, please discuss the trade-offs between separate code generation/chat paths versus a unified approach, and analyze when routing decisions might fail.
- Consider increasing the test sample size significantly and including quantitative metrics beyond manual success rate.

#### Minor comments
- At line 204, consider replacing "whitelisted" with "allowlisted" to use more inclusive terminology.

title: Talk2Data: A Multimodal Agentic Framework for Conversational Data Analysis
review:
- This paper described a system: Talk2Data. The system can accept voice input to analyze the data, and then respond with voice too.
- The system is implemented using ASR from OpenAI Whisper, Coqui TTS for TTS, a LLM for routing and QWen for code generation, and code is generated with within a security sandbox.
- The system is evaluated with 3 datasets, with 48 tasks in total, and resulted only 2 tasks were wrong, with 95.8% accuracy. The paper also reported the latency per stage.
- The idea of adding voice input and output to the current text data analysis NLI is a step forward. The paper implemented the system end to end, and produced a test result that has a high performance.
- The weakness of the paper:
    - (1) It reads like a PoC system implementation paper, instead of a research paper. It’s good to put some additional components to an already commercialized type of products. Though I don’t see too much research contribution into this paper.
    - (2) Th evaluation: while 95.8% is amazingly high result. I wonder what is the baseline accuracy for systems without voice input & output? I would imagine adding voice input and output would simply reduce the performance. In another way, the author can do apple to apple comparison without the voice components. Then the result can focus on features of the voice. Also, the system has considered context, memory, and multiple turn, I would like to see evaluation around these too. Maybe it is because the accuracy is already 95%+, there isn’t much to add. If it is the case, it might be a problem of the evaluation set is too simple to show the impact of these, then I would suggest to update the evaluation set up.

title: Talk2Data: A Multimodal Agentic Framework for Conversational Data Analysis
review:
This paper describes a modular pipeline for automating conversations about tabular datasets designed to answer a user's questions about the datasets and generated plots, calculations, etc. to assist with analyzing the data. The framework works with both speech and text input using third-party services for the modular components in the pipeline (ASR, LLM, TTS) and it dynamically determines whether the system should respond directly to the user's query based on the conversational context and available metadata about the dataset or if it should run a Python coding tool to generate numerical / graphical results.

Strengths
* The framework combines several features (speech input, code execution, visual feedback) that have typically existed separately in similar systems that have been developed.
* The system is able to correctly respond to well-structured, straightforward queries.

Weaknesses
* The paper seems more like a description of a demo than an EMNLP Industry Track submission. There is no product based on the framework (Section 5.1 speculates about some hypothetical use cases for the tool) and there is no real-world deployment.
* The main intellectual contribution of the work is the prompts, since the development of the framework simply involves chaining together pre-existing tools. However, very little information is provided in the paper about how the prompts were developed. Additional practical information about the prompt development process would make the paper more useful for industry researchers, such as answers to the following types of questions: What was the nature of the iterative process that was used to test out different versions of the prompts? What prompting approaches seemed to work better or worse for different types of data sets and queries? How did the authors decide on the final versions of the prompts?
* The evaluation section is quite weak. 48 evaluation queries were generated by the authors, but no information is provided about how they were generated. The authors clearly had knowledge of the system's capabilities while they were generating the queries, so it is impossible that they weren't at least subconsciously biased about the types of queries that the system can support. A more valid evaluation would have involved eliciting questions from users who were not familiar with the system prior to interacting with it. Ideally for an EMNLP Industry Track submission, the evaluation would be with actual end users of a deployed product; however, at a minimum, it should include actual interactions with the system from human testers, not static queries that were defined by the authors.

Here are some additional comments about specific sections in the paper:

* p. 3, line 158: "For large datasets, row-level sampling is used to keep prompt context within LLM limits." -- More details about this sampling procedure would be helpful and interesting (how are the rows sampled? how is it determined whether a dataset is "large"?)

* p. 3, line 172: "The decision is made using a structured LLM prompt that classifies the user query into one of two paths: code_generation or chat_response" -- It is helpful that the authors provide the specific prompts that were used in the system (https://github.com/ml-dev-anonymous/talk2data/blob/main/talk2data-fastAPI/prompts.py); however, as mentioned above, it would be much more impactful if the authors described how the prompts were designed.

* p. 4, line 272: "Each dataset was evaluated with 16 natural language tasks, totaling 48." -- As mentioned above, it is unclear how valid these queries are. I.e., do they represent the types of queries that actual users of the system would make for these datasets? As shown in the files containing the queries (https://github.com/ml-dev-anonymous/talk2data/tree/main/talk2data-fastAPI/evaluation_benchmark), all of them are complete, grammatical sentences, which is unlikely to be the case in an actual deployment. Also, they are all decontextualized, isolated queries and don't represent the types of questions that would actually arise in a conversational session. Finally, how do we know that these are tasks that users would want assistance with? Ideally, this framework would be used in an actual product prototype for collecting real-world queries.

* P. 4, line 279: "A query was marked correct if the output chart or response was accurate and aligned with expectations (based on manual ground truth calculations)." -- The data set also contains queries with subjective questions, such as "What do you think we should do as data‑cleaning step before modeling? please explain it." How was accuracy evaluated for these types of queries?

* p. 5, line 305: "We measured end-to-end latency per query (excluding ASR time)" -- Why is ASR latency excluded from the analysis?

* p. 5, line 322: "In multi-turn dialogues, the agent maintained context and decision accuracy." -- It's not very convincing to evaluate the quality of the contextual conversational responses with just a few hand-picked examples.

* p. 5, line 347: "Talk2Data shows that combining voice input with LLM-driven analysis makes data exploration more natural. Users can ask open-ended questions (e.g., “What does this mean?” or “Show me X”) as they would a human analyst." -- I don't understand how the second sentence provides evidence for the claim in the first sentence, since open-ended questions can be asked just as well using text input.

* p. 5, line 353: "suggests current LLMs are capable of handling diverse, realistic data queries" -- This claim is not supported by the paper, since there is no evidence to confirm that the queries used in the evaluation are "realistic".

title: Beyond IVR: Benchmarking Customer Support LLM Agents for Business-Adherence
review:
The paper presents a benchmark and an approach to assess "business" AI agents.
I believe authors make importa point about the need to encode some aspect of business logic that are supposed to drive the agents.

There are however several aspects that are unclear or that i feel do not apply to real life situations.

First and foremost, if a logic has to be scripted, it can be that Ai is not the right way to implement. 
If we want a system to follow a specific path we can just code it.

Second, what the authors basically discuss is the notion of conformance to a process. 
This topic has been studied for a long time in the BPM community, and so have representations of processes that provide the balance between flexibility and prescribed behavior.
It sounds like for a business agent you do not necessarily want to follow a process, but you want the execution to have some properties.

Last but not least, my experience with generated traces is that they lack the nuances of real data.
Generating "raalistic" data, and particularly in the domain mentioned by the authors (customer support) is really hard.
I do not see evidence in the paper that the benchmark - intended to represent actual business cases - actually reflects real data.
Also, custumer support is often not an easy a straightforard process, which is why sometimes we do need AI and some deviation from a prescribed path.

I suggest the authors to
1. clearly define what they expect from a benchmark
2. define a trace representation that allows for flexibility
3. add evidence that the generated data reflects the nuances of real data
4. Test agents on real scenarios and show the usefulness of the benchmark in taking decisions

title: Beyond IVR: Benchmarking Customer Support LLM Agents for Business-Adherence
review:
### General Comments:
I read the paper carefully. This paper creates a benchmark named JourneyBench to evaluate the customer support ability of business-aware LLM agents. This is an overall interesting domain:  JourneyBench uses SOPs as workflow graphs to create diverse scenarios, covering domains of telecom, e-commenter, and loan application. 

### Strength:
- S1: The paper is well written

### Weakness:
- W1: All the key three steps: 1) SOP graph structure generation (generated by LLM with prompt shown in Appx. B), 2) user journal generation (based on step 1, generated by Breadth-First Search), 3) scenario data generation (didn't specify, but I guess also generated by LLM): are all generated and synthetic. So my biggest concern is: can we really use a fully LLM-generated and synthetic dataset to benchmark LLMs?
- W2: Sim-2-Real gap:  Since the data is also synthetically generated, how real is it, and what will be the potential sim-to-real gap? I suggest that the authors add some actual proof to justify that the synthetic data is close to the real one (e.g., some statistical metric, embedding similarity, etc)
- W3: Since it is a benchmark paper, I will expect more statistical description about the benchmark dataset, in the form of bar charts or pie charts, and a deeper analysis, e.g., the distribution of the difficulty/complexity level of the SOP tasks.
- W4: only two frameworks are tested, Static-Prompt-Agent and Dynamic-Prompt-Agent, which are not common nor well-known choices for agentic framework

title: Beyond IVR: Benchmarking Customer Support LLM Agents for Business-Adherence
review:
The authors propose an interesting and likely valuable method to address a challenging problem, better controlling behavior of LLM agent systems. The framework they propose appears well thought out and widely applicable.

One note: there appears to already be a different thing in the data science world called JourneyBench: https://journeybench.github.io/
This submission is different, so it's worth considering the title of this paper and the name of the software.

1. Limitations Section

Limitations are noted. Discussion of cost is greatly appreciated; this is especially important in this era of highly-performant but paid proprietary models.

2. Author Anonymity

No violations noted.

3. Novelty & Impact

The use of journey graphs to test LLM-based agentic frameworks is not entirely novel, but this appears to be a meaningful contribution nonetheless. In addition, the inclusion of a software package to implement their methods makes the potential impact high.

4. Reproducibility

Sufficient details and software are included to make the results reproducible, and - equally important in an industrial setting - allow a practitioner to apply the methods to their own use case.

5. Clarity & Structure

The paper is well written and logically structured. Full details are included on the key components and thorough results and analysis are included.

title: Has Fine-Tuning Reached Its Limits? Prompting vs. Fine-Tuning for Diagnosing Automotive Issues
review:
Overview:
The objective for the paper seems to be to investigate the performance of large language models (LLMs), in a low resource setting, for domain-specific classification in the automotive sector. Two complementary approaches to improve out-of-the-box performance of LLMs were focussed on: fine-tuning and prompting.

Comments on Paper's Contribution:
- There is no focussed contribution of the paper. The ideas and contributions are scattered all over the article. For example, the Abstract starts with an overview of vehicle service reports and how LLMs can be used to extract information from them. Then in the abstract only the authors digress by mentioning that they are motivated by claims on fine-tuning limits reached. Then the authors talk about the new dataset, which they mention later that it cannot be shared of explained in detail. So, as a reader of the paper, I am confused as to what is the real contribution here. And there is no outcome either that could help me figure out. Another constraint on low resource availability also suddenly appeared in the middle of the paper.


Seems like the authors started an experiment and completed it with some outcomes which they would like to share. This may be good for an abstract but not for a paper in the Industry track of a prestigious conference such as EMNLP.

Formatting comments:
- Citations need to be narrative. For example, "In another study, the authors in Chen et al., (2023) propose a framework....." instead of "In another study, the authors in (Chen et al., 2023) propose a framework". Correction needed across the paper.

title: Has Fine-Tuning Reached Its Limits? Prompting vs. Fine-Tuning for Diagnosing Automotive Issues
review:
# Summary

This paper investigates the effectiveness of fine-tuning and prompting for classifying vehicle service reports. Using both a proprietary in-house dataset and a larger public dataset from the NHTSA, the authors conclude that prompting is more effective with limited data, while fine-tuning performs better with a larger, more abundant dataset.

# Questions, Comments, and Suggestions

-   The purpose of the topic modeling section (Section 3.2) is not clear. The connection between this section and the paper's main conclusion about fine-tuning versus prompting should be more explicit. How do the results from topic modeling directly support or influence the conclusion
-   The authors could significantly accelerate their experiments by using a dedicated GPU for fine-tuning, as noted in lines 287-290. The reported runtime of 103 hours on a MacBook is a major bottleneck; a gaming laptop with a dedicated GPU, which may cost less than $1,000, could reduce this time dramatically and make the research process much more efficient.

title: Has Fine-Tuning Reached Its Limits? Prompting vs. Fine-Tuning for Diagnosing Automotive Issues
review:
The authors investigate the problem of categorizing automotive issues on the basis of service reports. They compare the performance of fine-tuning versus prompting on a proprietary dataset of truck service reports and an open dataset of complaints. They find that both approaches improve performance, but prompting is much more effective. 

The paper is clearly written. The exploratory data analysis and visualization of topic model outputs are a nice addition and motivate the category taxonomy fairly well. 

In presenting the results of their experiments, it feels like the authors downplay the magnitude of the improvements achieve via prompting; they develop a domain-specific system prompt that performs at or near ceiling (in terms of F-score) across nearly all categories, far outperforming the fine-tuning results. There is an experiment using a back-translation to handle cases where service reports or complaints are written in a different languages. The translation impacts performance, but this is surprising given that translation introduces non-trivial distributional shifts to the texts that compose the corpus. This latter experiments feels superfluous and probably could have been omitted.

A few specific notes/concerns:
- final sentence of abstract (line 22) has awkward wording and perhaps a missing word
- the knowledge that the proprietary data are from a Swedish automative manufacturer, combined with the upper-middle wordcloud in Figure 2, potentially results in partial deanonymization
- footnote 4 (line 373); why not release the code for this experiment via anonymized github (https://anonymous.4open.science)
- I appreciate that precision and recall are presented, since the authors acknowledge that class imbalance is a factor, but in that case it would be good to also give the support for each class in the eval set

title: Enhancing Foundation Models in Transaction Understanding with LLM-based Sentence Embeddings
review:
$\textbf{Novelty and Impact}$:
Using LLM sentence embeddings to initialise tabular ID fields for sequential transaction modelling is a practical twist on recent “semantic-ID hybrid” ideas. The one-word prompt constraint is simple yet original, and the industrial relevance is high. Nonetheless, methodological novelty is moderate because similar hybridisation has appeared in prior recommender-system work.

$\textbf{Reproducibility}$:
Methodological exposition is generally clear, but critical details are missing. The data are proprietary and no synthetic substitute is offered; hyper-parameters, training schedules, and hardware specs are absent; the “relative-improvement” metric is described narratively but not formulated, and raw scores are withheld. Without these elements, independent replication would be difficult.

$\textbf{Clarity and Structure}$:
The manuscript reads well and follows a logical flow. Figures and tables aid comprehension, though Table 1 is dense and visually hard to parse in grayscale. Code listings spill over the recommended length, and a few typos (“attibutes”) remain.

$\textbf{Strengths}$:
The work tackles genuine industry pain-points such as cold-start and semantic loss in large-scale payment data. Its hybrid design cleverly keeps inference costs low while preserving semantic richness. Evaluation spans multiple tasks, showing ≥ 3 % relative lift in many settings, and the authors are commendably candid about limitations. 

$\textbf{Weaknesses}$:
Reproducibility suffers from the absence of public data, code, hyper-parameters, and a formal definition of the proprietary metric. There is no ablation on prompt design or embedding size, and no latency or throughput numbers, despite cost being a primary motivation. Reported gains lack variance measures or statistical significance tests. Conceptually, the contribution is incremental relative to prior hybrid embedding approaches.

title: Enhancing Foundation Models in Transaction Understanding with LLM-based Sentence Embeddings
review:
The authors propose to improve the existing "foundation model for tabular transactional data in the payment industry" by initializing the model's embeddings with the embeddings from LLM. The models initialized with the LLM embeddings show modest improvement on the metrics authors provided. 


## Weakness

Since they hid the paper of the "foundation model for tabular transactional data in the payment industry", the paper lacks the details of their framework especially on how the embeddings from the LLMs are utilized in their foundation model (how the dimension reductions are done) and how the vainilla model initializes its embedding without them.
I believe the authors could have hide their identity while still citing the paper. 


While improvements are consistent across some tasks, they are modest in absolute terms (e.g., ≤ 0.3 MAE for Next Amount, ≤ 0.01 absolute in Acc/F1 for classification). The authors should test the statistical significance of these gains to show that there was meaniful enhancement. 

Also, based on the provided information in the paper, one cannot automatically assume that the embeddings from the LLM "enhanced" the foundation model or just an unfortunate seeding of the vanilla model caused it. The authors should provide more evidence to support that claim, especially when the reproducibility is limited.
Also, the operational significance of such gains should be better motivated, perhaps with business-impact metrics.

title: Enhancing Foundation Models in Transaction Understanding with LLM-based Sentence Embeddings
review: The paper suggests an improvement on the previous neural model for tabular data proposed by the same authors. (A bit confusingly from a general NLP perspective, general models for tabular data are called "foundational models" in the manuscript, while text-embedding models are called "LLMs".) The core innovation of the proposed method is to replace learned embeddings for categorical data types (such as merchant-category codes, locations, etc.) with embeddings of their extended textual descriptions. These embeddings are argued to be more informative and therefore more helpful for downstream tasks of transaction-feature prediction and fraud detection. The authors propose a prompting methodology for extracting such embeddings, which first combines all relevant information in a short text and then asks the model to summarise it in a single word. The embedding of this word is the embedding used later; this methodology also makes it possible to fine-tune the LLM and the tabular-data model end-to-end. I couldn't understand, however, how exactly this approach "avoids costly runtime LLM inference, while preserving semantic richness and sequential context" -- the learned LLM-based embeddings seem to be static, which saves on LLM inference time but likely reduces sequntial context to the usual type. The method seems reasonable; however, the results on the public datasets (Table 1) are less impressive than those from the private dataset (Table 2), and a lot of content in Section 3 is repetitive.

title: Beyond Generation: Multi-Hop Reasoning for Factual Accuracy in Vision-Language Models
review:
**Background**
The paper addresses a well‑defined and highly relevant problem in the domain of VLMs- produce factually inaccurate captions (hallucinations) even when their descriptions are fluent and plausible. While fact-checking via external knowledge has been explored in text‑only LLMs such structured reasoning is underexplored in VLMs, especially for multi-step, multimodal factual verification. This is done using a 5 stage multi-hop reasoning framework
1) Vision–Language Understanding – Initial caption generation using Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct.
2) Entity Extraction Hop – Identify named entities from the caption (e.g., “Lalbagh Fort”, “Dhaka”).
3) Knowledge Graph Navigation – Match these entities to a curated graph of landmarks via exact and fuzzy matching.
4) Fact Verification 
5) Caption Correction – Replace or adjust hallucinated details with verified facts while preserving fluency.

**Results**
The authors evaluate their prototype on a small but diverse landmark-focused dataset from a mix of Google Landmarks v2 , Conceptual Captions  and COCO Captions. About 100 images are used for evaluation where the evaluation is between the Baseline Caption(generated by VLM before the multi-hop stage) and Factually corrected Caption. The framework reduces hallucinated entities by ~31.8% compared to baseline captions.

**Pros**
1) The five-hops are interpretable and modular, meaning each stage’s output can be independently inspected and improved. Modularity enables plugging in future, larger KGs or more advanced entity recognition without redesigning the pipeline.
2) Extending KG-based multi-hop reasoning to multimodal captioning is a novel and non-trivial step.
3) Using triples, hierarchies, bullet-points is a intelligent choice because each sub-method excels at different reasoning types

**Cons**
1) Evaluation is on only 100 images. One can't claim strong generalization.
2) All experiments are with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct only limiting generality
3) While multi-hop might improve performance, computational-tradeoff is not discussed as this approach can slow down the inference

title: Beyond Generation: Multi-Hop Reasoning for Factual Accuracy in Vision-Language Models
review:
**Main content**

This paper addresses the critical issue of factual inaccuracy in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), which often produce confident but incorrect assertions about entities and relationships in images. To mitigate this, the authors propose a multi-hop reasoning framework that leverages a structured knowledge graph to systematically verify and correct image captions. The framework operates in several steps: it first generates a base caption with a VLM, then extracts named entities from it, matches these entities against a domain-specific knowledge graph to identify verified and potentially hallucinated information, verifies the factual claims, and finally generates a corrected caption. A core part of the study is the exploration of three different knowledge representation formats—triple-based relations, hierarchical trees, and bullet-point facts—to perform this verification. Experiments conducted on a curated dataset combining Google Landmarks v2, Conceptual Captions, and COCO captions showed that the framework significantly improves factual accuracy, achieving an approximately 31.8% reduction in hallucinated entities. The work demonstrates the potential of integrating external knowledge to advance reasoning and create more reliable multimodal systems.

**Strength**

1.	The research targets the critical issue of factual inaccuracy, or "hallucination," in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). This is a key limitation that hinders the reliability of VLMs in domains requiring high factual precision.

2.	The paper introduces a novel multi-hop reasoning framework that systematically verifies and corrects facts.

3.	A key strength is the systematic comparison of three different knowledge representation formats: triple-based, hierarchical, and bullet-point facts. The study analyzes their effectiveness and finds that a multi-representation approach significantly improves the robustness of the fact-verification process.

**Weakness**

1.	Limited Capability for Verifying Complex Facts: The knowledge representation formats presented in the paper, such as triples and hierarchical trees, are well-suited for validating direct attributes and hierarchical relationships (e.g., "(A, located in, B)"). However, the framework may struggle to validate more nuanced and complex real-world facts that involve temporal, conditional, or causal relationships, such as "it was formerly the capital" or "its architectural style was influenced by...".

2.	Limited Scale and Scope of Experiments: The evaluation was conducted on a small, manually constructed dataset focused on a specific domain (landmark images). This raises questions about the generalizability of the findings, as the framework's performance in broader, open-domain scenarios remains unknown.

3.	Constraints of Knowledge Graph Construction: The current knowledge graph is manually curated, which fundamentally limits the system's scalability. While the appendix details the construction process, this manual approach is impractical for large-scale applications. The authors acknowledge that future work will need to integrate large-scale, dynamic knowledge sources.

4.	Reliance on a Single Evaluation Model: All experiments and analyses were conducted using the Qwen family of models, specifically the 2B variant. The lack of evaluation on other mainstream Vision-Language Models (VLMs) makes it difficult to determine the framework's universal applicability across different model architectures.

title: Beyond Generation: Multi-Hop Reasoning for Factual Accuracy in Vision-Language Models
review:
**Overview**

This paper presents a modular, multi-hop reasoning framework to address the critical issue of factual inaccuracies in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). The proposed system operates as a pipeline: it first generates an initial caption with a VLM, then extracts named entities, verifies these entities and their relationships against a structured knowledge graph, and finally prompts the VLM again with the verified facts to produce a corrected, more factually accurate caption. A key contribution is the systematic comparison of different knowledge representation formats, triples, hierarchies, and bullet points, to evaluate their impact on the fact verification process.

**Strengths**

1. A standout contribution is the empirical evaluation of how different knowledge representation formats (triples, hierarchical, bullet-points) affect fact verification. This analysis provides valuable insights for designing future knowledge-grounded multimodal systems, moving beyond a one-size-fits-all approach to knowledge integration.

2. The proposed pipeline is inherently interpretable, as each reasoning step (entity extraction, graph traversal, correction) produces intermediate outputs that can be inspected. This modularity not only aids in debugging and understanding failure modes but also allows for the flexible integration of different components or knowledge sources in the future.

**Weaknesses**

1. The knowledge graph is manually constructed and domain-specific (landmarks), which severely limits the system's scalability and generalizability. It is unclear how this approach would perform in an open-domain setting without a pre-existing, high-quality knowledge base.

2. The evaluation is conducted on a small dataset of 100 images. While described as preliminary, this sample size is insufficient to draw robust conclusions about the framework's effectiveness. The evaluation should be expanded to a much larger and more diverse dataset to validate the findings more rigorously.

3. The framework's performance is only compared against the baseline VLM's original output. There is no comparison to other existing methods for knowledge-grounding or fact-correction in VLMs, such as RAG approaches.

4. The confidence threshold for fuzzy matching is set to 0.85 without any justification or sensitivity analysis.

5. The paper introduces custom metrics like Entity Accuracy and Fact Verification Rate. While useful, they are not standard, making it difficult to compare this work with others. Moreover, the human evaluation of coherence lacks detail on the number of annotators and inter-annotator agreement.

6. The final correction step relies on prompt engineering and templates. This may lead to corrected captions that are factually accurate but sound unnatural or formulaic, a weakness hinted at by the slight drop in coherence scores.

7. The authors should discuss the trade-offs of this pipeline approach versus end-to-end fine-tuning and position the work as a practical, post-processing solution.

title: COTE: Chain of Thoughts for Embedding
review:
# Facets
- Quality: Good
- Clarity: Mostly clear
- Originality: I haven't seen this before, though I find similar recent work in a quick Google search. That work did not affect my score because it's so recent
- Significance: Small-medium

# Areas to improve
It'd be helpful to contextualize the results more so that I can gauge the significance of the results. Is it worthwhile to implement this, given the added complexity for an approx. 1% gain? That depends on the context!

Additionally, it'd be helpful to provide more interpretation of the results. Are there categories of recommendations that are improved more than others? Explaining the trends in the actual changes would give me more confidence that this approach might generalize to other datasets or situations.

The use of "slow mode" to provide explanations for customer complaint investigation is interesting. My main concern is that the model behaves differently when in fast vs slow mode, so the explanations in slow mode may not align with the output of fast mode and may mislead customer service agents. I'd like to see a basic human evaluation of the explanations provided for investigation. Are they useful or just interesting? What changes have they led to?

# Notes
- 125, 267: It's jarring to see T5 and Palm called "large" and then Qwen 1B called "small". Personally I find the small/large nomenclature unhelpful though I understand it's common. It didn't affect my review, just noting that it's weird.
