To name a few: (1) name of the LLM used for the slow taxonomy classifier, how it is trained/finetuned, and where the training data comes from/how it is constructed, (2) how the suitability function \Phi exactly works when the predicted labels and the LLM-claimed labels are different, (3) how exactly all the threshold values are determined, (4) how exactly the rule-based verifier works, and (5) name of LLM used as a judge, whether its validity for judging the task has been verified, the exact prompts used etc.
2. I imagine the proposed method would be sensitive to 2 aspects: (1) the taxonomy dimensions and labels, and (2) the sorting criteria of the narrowed-down pool. However, they aren't explored or discussed in the paper.
3. There are minimal descriptions of the datasets, especially the private ones. Table 2 reports the proportion of each private dataset and the task name as called by the authors. However, I can only guess what the expected input and output look like. For an example, I don't exactly know what 'Proposal document refinement' task is. In addition, it's unclear where the data comes from, how it is annotated, and what the annotation quality is (e.g., inter-annotator agreement).
4. The paper compares against a base router, but again there isn't much description about it. L412 mentions that it is 'taxonomy based', but the taxonomy has several dimensions, and it's unclear which dimension this baseline focusses on. I'd suggest to train a base router for each dimension as baselines.

# Comments
1. L057: missing citation
2. L194: foundation -> large language
3. L246: modelss -> models
4. L306-307 says that 'evaluation is performed on open-source benchmarks' but Table 2 reports that the evaluation set contains private datasets. Please clarify.
5. Figure 2 can be reported more succinctly in one plot where the x- and y-axis are the accuracy and cost respectively.

# Comment after author response
I have updated my rating accordingly.

title: Select-then-Route : Taxonomy guided Routing for LLMs
review:
To balance performance and cost on natural-language tasks across multiple LLMs, the paper proposes a two-stage framework: it first identifies a task-specific subset of LLMs, then cascades through this subset using a confidence-based search to select the most suitable model. The approach is evaluated on six public, domain-diverse benchmarks.
Strengths
1.	The idea of tailoring model selection to each task to trade off accuracy against cost is appealing and could help enterprises operate within tight budgets.
2.	The paper is well-structured, with clear and concise explanations that are easy to follow.
Weaknesses
1.	The contribution largely recombines existing ideas—namely taxonomy-based routing and cascading—so its novelty is primarily incremental rather than conceptual.
2.	For the cascade stage, the key component is the evaluator that scores each model’s output. Yet the paper provides neither a detailed description of this evaluator nor an assessment of its reliability, which undermines confidence in the experimental results.
3.	The experimental section is weak: the methodology is not fully introduced, and the origin of Figure 2 remains unclear.
4.	Several typos persist:
– Line 57: “proves accuracy is well established ()”
– Line 196: “a closed-source model … ot an”
– Section 3.2: With only one subsection, the label “3.2.1” should be removed.

title: EPAS: Efficient Training with Progressive Activation Sharing
review:
EPAS proposes a method of faster training and flexible inference of language models using progressive activation sharing with a switchable decoder layer. This method focuses on minimizing the computation of redundant activations in deeper layers of a language model through an elegant and intuitive use of a switchable decoder. The paper is easy to understand and is well motivated, and shows that the proposed method leads to lower model FLOPs and higher training and inference throughput for models of the Llama family. Moreover, they propose an important application of their method to pretrained models, by continuous finetuning with flexible inference paradigms without loss of accuracy. I believe this method has significant applications in throughput-constrained environments.

Some questions and limitations of this work in its current state:
1. Fig. 4 states that models trained with EPAS exhibit faster convergence, however the loss curves are quite close-- is this claim significant, or is it possible the figure is misleading? Can you quantify the time taken to converge with and without EPAS for these models?
2. While the proposed method shows good improvement over the baseline, it is not apparently clear to me how what improvement the proposed method provides over some of the methods discussed in lines 075-100 of the Introduction (eg. flash attention, distillation, etc). I believe such a comparison could be used to further strengthen the validity of the proposed methods
3. I believe the continual pretraining to be an important practical application of the algorithm, and would like some clarifications on this process- could the process be used for the continued training of instruction tuned or models that undergo RL? Would performance scale with data size? 
4. Some minor typos are present in the tables, and should be corrected in the final version

title: EPAS: Efficient Training with Progressive Activation Sharing
review:
This work investigates progressive activation sharing during pre-training rather than post-training. By enabling activation sharing already during (continued) pre-training, the training through put can be improved while maintaining accuracy. Similar to other activation sharing techniques, inference speed is improved as well.

This work is easy to follow and to understand and provides both results on GPUs and NPUs showing the applicability to industry.
However, I am wondering why training has been conducted on NPUs but not inference which would be the more interesting scenario.
Furthermore, I think the experimental setup for training is limited and it would have been better to focus on smaller model sizes but then provide a full training run with EPAS.
All in all, given the experimental setup, it is hard to derive clear conclusions from this work for industry applications.

Some small remarks:
- Line 214: Citation is broken
- Table 3: Parentheses are missing
- e.g line 320, 346: missing space before parentheses or extra space after parenthesis

title: EPAS: Efficient Training with Progressive Activation Sharing
review:
The paper describes a strategy of re-using activations across layers, and doing so in a progressive fashion.

The paper is, unfortunately, not written in a way that I can understand what is done. I had to google to be able to guess what is actually done. The concept of cross-layer activation sharing is an interesting one, but the paper makes no effort to properly introduce it to the reader. Requiring the reader to read up the references on the key concept that this paper improves upon is not acceptable IMHO.

This paper also has serious grammar issues, like numerous missing articles and mangled sentences. On the other hand, certain formulations read like AI-generated. Example: "However, a significant gap remains, as holistic approaches to efficiency that applies across all aforementioned stages is inherently susceptible to accuracy efficiency trade-offs" sounds like AI slop, yet is ungrammatical and even hard to understand. The paper has numerous examples like this.

Because it was impossible for me to know what exactly is done, I stopped this review at Section 3.

It is clear that this paper is not ready for publication.

title: Toward Reliable Clinical Coding with Language Models:  Verification and Lightweight Adaptation
review:
This manuscript presents an LLM-based pipeline to adapt off-the-shelf LLMs towards accurate clinical coding. Several lightweight techniques (that do not involve retraining the LLM) such as prompt engineering and model fine-tuning are attempted, aimed towards resolving hierarchically near-miss (but medically-relevant) errors. Additionally, a reference double-annotated benchmark dataset is provided to evaluate the method. Of the examined LLMs, Sonnet with CoT generally achieved the best performance, as measured by various F1 metrics.

While the potential to quickly boost clinical coding performance is extensively evaluated, some issues might be considered:

1. In Section 3.3, it appears that the proposed structured verification pipeline searches siblings, cousins (in tabular list), 1-hop and 2-hop neighbours (in index list) at each expansion step. It might be briefly stated as to what percentage of the full ICM-10-CM list is typically searched at each stage.

2. In Section 3.3.2/5.3, it is claimed that broader expansions can raise accuracy but increase candidate count and inference cost. However, Table 4 suggests that the broadest expansion type (all combined) actually decreases accuracy (to a minimum among all expansion types). This might be briefly clarified, possibly together with the above point.

3. In Section 5.3, it is stated that oracle selection shows an upper bound of 67.3 F1. From Section 4.2, F1 refers to the standard F1 metric. If so, should the upper bound not be 100.0 (or 1.0) F1 - indicating perfect precision and recall - if gold labels are available at each level? This might be clarified.

4. In Section 5.4, insights relating to semantic similarity are presented. It might be stated as to at which ICD code level errors typically occur, for error cases - does the LLM typically fail by going off-track early or late?

5. In the Appendix, LLM hyperparameters (including temperature, if relevant) should be stated for all LLMs used. Moreover, was any optimization attempted for such parameters?

6. In Appendix B.2, a CoT step is mentioned. More details on the CoT implementation might be presented.

title: Toward Reliable Clinical Coding with Language Models:  Verification and Lightweight Adaptation
review:
The paper addresses the problem of reliable clinical coding with large language models (LLMs), focusing on errors where predictions are close in the ICD-10 hierarchy but still incorrect. The authors propose lightweight improvements through prompt engineering, small-scale fine-tuning, and a new clinical code verification step. They also release a double expert-annotated outpatient dataset to address limitations of existing resources. Experiments cover a range of LLMs and show that verification improves accuracy across models.

Strengths

1. Clearly defined problem with real-world impact in healthcare documentation and billing. I think there needs to be more work using LLMs for ICD coding.
2. Solid error analysis showing the prevalence of near-miss hierarchical mistakes and why exact match metrics are insufficient.
3. The method is also interesting methodologically, e.g., the verification step makes sense and the code expansion makes sense given the large number of codes.
4. Comprehensive experiments covering multiple model families and sizes.

Weaknesses

1. The new dataset is small (207 examples, 67 for training), it is unclear how this is enough data for fine-tuning, given the ICD label set size.
2. More importantly, I do not think the reason for not using MIMIC is well supported. It is clear that MIMIC is not perfect. However, it has been used as a testbed for ICD coding for nearly a decade. Hence, understanding performance on it would give a better picture of how LLMs fit within the larger space. Moreover, contrasting it to the small study with the newly collected data would result in more interesting insights, e.g., comparing how errors made on MIMIC may not be realistic for medical coding. Overall, I don’t think using MIMIC is 100% needed, but it does reduce my enthusiasm for this paper and its broader implications, particularly because of the limited data size.

title: Toward Reliable Clinical Coding with Language Models:  Verification and Lightweight Adaptation
review:
This study identifies the limitations of large language models (LLMs) in automated ICD-10 coding from clinical notes, particularly highlighting that traditional exact match evaluations fail to capture a substantial number of hierarchical “near-miss” errors.
The proposed approach combines prompt engineering, lightweight fine-tuning, and a novel code verification step leveraging the ICD-10 hierarchy to significantly improve coding accuracy.

The core idea of the paper is natural and reasonable; however, the overall readability is poor, making it difficult to follow the concrete workflow.
Although Figure 1 attempts to illustrate the process, it lacks sufficient detail.
I recommend focusing more explicitly on the key component — verification — and describing it based on a concrete example to enhance clarity.

title: Scaling Multimodal Reasoning for Pharmaceutical Content Understanding Using Vision-Language Models on Industrial GenAI Platforms
review:
This paper introduces a "large-scale GenAI Platform architect", or perhaps an multimodal architecture that combines different models for different purposes (Qwen, Claude 3, Llama 3) that seem to index video data. The authors list 4 disjoint contributions. (1) video "reasoning" improves with the availability and uses of metadata, (2) selecting the right attention mechanism matters for performance (3) video summarization works but key frame detection doesn't, (4) splitting up and compressing videos is not an efficient solution.

It is a bit unclear to me what the key problem is that this project has addressed. It seems that the authors built a big system to somehow analyze or index video data, and this paper presents a coarsely ordered set of insights gained while doing so. None of the aforementioned key findings are carefully evaluated, or presented. For example, Fig 3. ("multimodality matters") show me some bar charts (without error bars) comparing a "without_subscription" and "with_subscription" condition. The word "subscription" isn't explained anywhere in the paper, so I'm not sure what I'm looking at. The two charts on the left show line graphs, suggesting an ordering and continuity in the x axis which I don't follow (it's categorical - many different models are listed, which can be barely read when zooming in because the graph is grainy).

The authors seem to make an argument on speed/accuracy tradeoffs with respect to attention (table 2). This is likely sensible in principle, but also not a novel insight. Even at the model level, there are well-known charts showing, for example, cost-accuracy tradeoffs.

I think, constructively, this paper wants to do too many things, without being able to present convincing evidence or insights in any of these -- there is only so much space.
I would also reconsider the writing style. "poised to revolutionize", many bolded+italic sentences, introductory, general language under "Business and Technical Impact" that briefly reintroduces a healthcare context... It does not seem that this paper would, in its current state, be an EMNLP publication.

Perhaps the authors can pick their strongest finding and construct an argument around it, with a careful quantitative evaluation against the most meaningful, SOTA baselines? This way, the paper can provide generalizable and useful insights.

title: Scaling Multimodal Reasoning for Pharmaceutical Content Understanding Using Vision-Language Models on Industrial GenAI Platforms
review:
This paper presents a comprehensive study of GPT-4V’s multimodal reasoning across diverse tasks, including VQA, chart understanding, science QA, and text-rich image analysis. The authors propose a four-stage reasoning framework—perception, grounding, reasoning, and reflection—and evaluate GPT-4V on both existing benchmarks and a newly curated dataset, MMReason. Results underscore the importance of scale and iterative prompting for optimal performance.

While the contribution is not particularly novel, the comprehensive empirical results offer valuable insights and may have meaningful implications for the field. The paper is well-presented, with a clear and logical flow. However, the motivation behind the study could be further strengthened, and the paper lacks sufficient detail on how hallucinations are addressed or mitigated.

title: Scaling Multimodal Reasoning for Pharmaceutical Content Understanding Using Vision-Language Models on Industrial GenAI Platforms
review: It is claimed that by utilising the power of GenAI, particularly video and audio language models, an advanced, large-scale production system is proposed that is capable of autonomously analyse content, generate faithful captions and sign semantically rich tags. However, the system itself has not yet been presented in detail, and it is not clear what experiments have been conducted. The so-called key technical results: Multimodality, Attention Mechanism, Temporal Reasoning, and the trade-off of Long Video Split and Cut are either known or unsubstantiated in the paper, or both. The experiments of which the authors speak are not presented in detail and are therefore not comprehensible.

title: LEAF: Learning and Evaluation Augmented by Fact-Checking to Improve Factualness in Large Language Models
review:
This paper introduces LEAF, a framework for improving the factual reliability of large language models in medical question answering. It combines a Retrieval-Augmented Factuality Evaluator, a Fact-Check-then-RAG generation strategy, and self-training mechanisms using fact-checking scores as pseudo-labels. Experiments on five medical QA datasets demonstrate improvements over existing approaches.

---

**Strengths**: 

The paper addresses an important issue—factual reliability of LLMs, especially in high-stakes domains like healthcare. Uses open-source tools (Qwen2-72B, LLaMA 3), avoiding closed-source dependencies—a strong point for industry applications.

---

**Major Concern**: 
The final decision is based on the proportion of supported statements, implicitly assuming that a response is factually correct if the majority of its sentences are supported. This can misrepresent factuality, especially (1) when critical errors appear in a minority of unsupported sentences, and (2) when correct statements are labeled as unsupported simply because the retrieval source lacks coverage.

Additionally, the evaluation lacks nuance in two important ways. First, each claim is labeled in a binary manner (supported or not) without accounting for borderline or uncertain cases. Second, claims are assessed in isolation at the sentence level, ignoring inter-sentence dependencies. This is inadequate for handling multi-step reasoning, co-reference, and the contextual complexity common in medical explanations.

---

**Suitability to the Industry Track**: 

The paper lacks the industrial perspective and deployment focus expected for the EMNLP Industry Track. It is primarily a research-oriented evaluation of a method to improve LLM factuality, with no discussion of real-world deployment or production use. Moreover, it does not clearly identify and deal with the practical challenges of medical QA in industry, e.g., curating reliable knowledge sources or mitigating retriever sensitivity, which may be more critical than factuality evaluation alone.

---

**Minor Concern**:

The proposed approach increases model calls and token generation by about 3×, but no analysis of the accuracy–cost trade-off is provided, which is critical for real-world applications. Additionally, it is unclear whether experiments were conducted with a single run or multiple iterations, leaving open questions about potential improvements or instability from repeated self-training cycles.

title: LEAF: Learning and Evaluation Augmented by Fact-Checking to Improve Factualness in Large Language Models
review:
This paper aims to improve factual accuracy in medical domain. For this purpose they introduce a novel method called LEAF, which brings 3 strategies Retrieval-Augmented Factuality Evaluaton,  Fact-Check-then-RAG, Learning from Fact Check via Self-Training.


The paper is well-structured, well-written and novel parts are explained clearly. I recommend the paper for the conference.


Still I have a question for the authors, on which platform did you work I assume GPU? Please include experimental setup subsection under experiments section. Include GPU type, training/experimenting hyperparameters i.e. leraning rate and batch size , how much time it took and possibly the cost of the whole process.

title: LEAF: Learning and Evaluation Augmented by Fact-Checking to Improve Factualness in Large Language Models
review:
The paper describes LEAF as a frame that comprises three key contributions: (1) the Retrieval-Augmented Factuality Evaluator (RAFE)
 (2) Fact-Check-then-RAG, (3) Learning from Fact Check via Self Training.
The paper is well written and addresses the important question of how hallucinations should be addressed by LLMs, particularly for the medical domain, which the paper focuses on.

The paper falls short in its experiment section and evaluation, for instance the paper only uses multiple choice questions in medical domain. Considering that this is an industry track paper, it is lacking details on how this model would have performed on long form Q&A which are the actually the real use case of medical Q&A form in most cases. See hosseini2024benchmarklongformmedicalquestion ( https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09834)

The paper is lacking details on the Self Suprvised Module.

There should have been additional experiments with other hallucination safeguard methods (e.g. iterative prompting, self-correction, etc.)  as well.

title: <SYNTACT>: Structuring Your Natural Language SOPs into Tailored Ambiguity-Resolved Code Templates
review:
# Paper Summary
The authors introduced \<SYNTACT> which maps unstructured Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) into a structured but also executable plan.\<SYNTACT> is made of 3 modules: A Clarifier, a Planner and an Implementor. The clarifier is shedding light on missing information or ambiguous part of the input. The planner is converting the unstructured SOP into a structured plan. The implementor is generating executable Python code.

# Strengths
The paper is easy to follow and clear overall. The paper proposes an interesting architecture to transform SOP (free text) into a structured representation which can later be used, executed and also indexed and retrieved. The paper is clear enough to reproduce the different modules. The experiments with the ablations of the different modules (Mc, Ms, Mi) are really appreciated. An evaluation on noise resilience was also conducted.

# Weaknesses
Each module is actually heavy for production as increasing the runtime significantly (10X more compared to Sonnet 3.7 for instance). 
The lengths distribution of the SOPs is also missing. This would add more information also on the final results. Indeed, some modules might be more useful for longer SOPs. The same comment applies for the random sentence removal operation. The amount of information removed here is difficult to quantify. 
Another critical weakness of the paper lies on the number of competitive baselines. I was disappointed not seeing much more baselines for the the comparison and/or more sophisticated approaches when dealing with 'from unstructured to structured' task. (Like ReAct for instance)

# Questions/Comments
1. What is the length distributions of your SOPs? 
2. Since having the Implementor as an intermediate step seems to be crucial, would a constrained ReAct approach coerced to generate a Python script be performing on par with \<SYNTACT> (or similarly)?

title: <SYNTACT>: Structuring Your Natural Language SOPs into Tailored Ambiguity-Resolved Code Templates
review:
- Paper Summary: This paper presents <SYNTACT>, a three-stage multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework designed to transform unstructured, ambiguous Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into structured plans and executable code templates. Unstructured SOPs, common in domains like finance, retail, and logistics, often contain vague references, missing details, and inconsistent logic, hindering automation.

- Strengths:
  - The three-stage Clarifier–Planner–Implementor pipeline is well-motivated and clearly addresses common SOP automation challenges (ambiguity, missing details, inconsistent formats).
  - The authors use different LLMs for different subtasks (e.g., Sonnet 3.7 for complex clarifications, Haiku for simpler deterministic steps) to balance accuracy and cost.

- Weaknesses:
  - Performance drops for SOPs exceeding ~100 lines due to context compression and ambiguity propagation; the proposed solution (hierarchical decomposition) is left for future work.
  - While the evaluation includes multiple domains, the number of real-world SOPs (only four) is small, which may limit the generalizability of results.
  - The current system cannot process multimodal SOPs that include diagrams, tables, or videos, despite their prevalence in industrial settings.

title: <SYNTACT>: Structuring Your Natural Language SOPs into Tailored Ambiguity-Resolved Code Templates
review:
**Review for "SYNTACT: Structuring Your Natural Language Tasks via Declarative Task Decomposition**

**Summary**: This paper presents a novel three-stage LLM framework designed to convert unstructured and ambiguous Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into structured plans and executable code templates. SOPs are used by many employees across organizations to complete routing procedures, however, ambiguous language and wording such as "the system", or "if needed" can lead unclear next steps, and inconsistencies. The proposed system comprises a Clarifier module for disambiguation, a Planner for structured pseudocode generation, and an Implementor for deterministic code synthesis. The approach is evaluated on both real-world and synthetic SOPs, although the sample size is pretty small (4 real-world SOPs and 20 synthetic SOPS), demonstrating the merits and potential of the approach.

**Author Anonymity**
- **Assessment:** No breaches detected.
- **Details:** The paper does not include author names, affiliations, acknowledgments, or explicit self-citations that reveal identity.  
  No non-anonymized links to repositories or preprints are present.  

** Limitations section**
Limitations are called out comprehensively along with some proposed ideas. These are the following:
- Performance goes down with the length of the SOP. However, no charts are added to Appendix to support this data point. The authors propose creating sub-SOPs and following a hierarchical sub-task generation approach.
- Lack of ability to handle multi-modal SOPs. There can be images, figures and weblinks present in SOPs which are not understood today.
- There are many LLM calls in this process. The authors wish to explore distillation, caching etc. to address these. A discussion on time taken, token cost etc. would have made this stronger for an Industry paper.
---
**Strengths:**
**Novelty & Impact**
- Proposes a multi-step declarative framework for task decomposition, enabling explicit specification of subtasks and their relations in NL workflows.
- Addresses a clear gap in current LLM and workflow orchestration research: the lack of interpretable and reusable declarative task plans for complex workflows.
- Well-aligned with **practical applications** in enterprise automation, and structured domain-specific execution.
- **However**, the contributions and benefits are not clearly stated and compared vis-a-vis multi-agents and other related work.

**Reproducibility**
- Adequate detail on syntax design, compilation process, and execution engine.
- Dataset descriptions and benchmark setup are included.

**Clarity & Structure**
- The paper follows a logical structure and is easy to follow: motivation; related work; method; experimentation; discussion; limitations.
- Effective use of figures and tables. However, Figure 1 lacks an example and the text is left obscure. This would have benefitted from an example and show how it flows through the workflow. 
- Generally clear and concise writing style.

----
**Weaknesses:**

** Novelty and Impact **
- Needs stronger positioning against related work in **agent planning languages** (e.g., PDDL) and workflow automation DSLs.
- Evaluation is mainly on execution performance and correctness; could be strengthened with **real-world deployment scenarios**.

**Reproducibility**
- No public code, sample specifications, or tooling artifacts are provided — making replication difficult.
- Some evaluation details (e.g., parameter settings, hardware specs, detailed error analysis) are missing.

** 4. Clarity & Structure **
- PDDL format is mentioned many times in the paper, without showing an example for it.
- The methodology section is dense. The paper will be strengthened by simplifying the nested expressions.
- Motivation could include more **real-world pain points** to strengthen relevance.
- Declarative syntax section could use **step-by-step annotated examples** for clarity.
- Would benefit from **full example specifications** in SYNTACT with corresponding compiled execution plans. No reference provided to the movie critic example shared in the Appendix.
- Metrics are introduced only in the Appendix, not mentioned in the paper. This makes the evaluation weaker.
---

** Suggestions to the authors **
- Enhance clarity by providing some examples of PDDL.
- The paper can be strengthened by sharing some real-world use cases and deployment case studies. 
- Simplify the methodology descriptions and expressions. 
The main limitations are **lack of shared reproducibility artifacts** and **few real-world case studies**. Addressing these would enhance both adoption and impact.

title: Agent-in-the-Loop: A Data Flywheel for Continuous Improvement in LLM-based Customer Support
review:
This paper introduces a data flywheel approach of online annotation and iterative model training for a RAG system used in chat-based contact centers. Given the long delays and loss of context of offline data annotation, having the agent provide feedback and search relevance decisions while live on the interaction allows faster model training cycles and less annotation cost.

The authors introduce their method and show a screenshot of the agent annotation interface used in their evaluation study. They describe the different tasks the agent labels in the tool and how the feedback data is used to improve the RAG system through iterative training on the ranking model, retrieval model, and generation model. The authors then conduct several experiments comparing their labeling approach to traditional offline labeling, and use retrospective SME review to evaluate quality of online agent labels.  The authors also track the amount of time spent doing annotations prior to response and evaluate the quality of result compared to annotations after response.  They have not released their code or models, but have detailed much of the experimental parameters in the appendix that it should be possible to recreate a similar system from the paper and appendix.

In full disclosure, I was on the PC for this paper in the ACL industry track where there were several concerns raised by reviewers.  The authors have addressed all of the concerns that I can see in this version and the paper is much improved (good job authors! always good to see examples where peer review does work to produce better papers).  The authors also conducted additional experiments which helped to address many of the concerns with gaps in the previous paper and adds value to this version.

Some formatting issues remain, but are minor.
1) lines 68-76 appear to be just a reformatted copy of lines 51-67.  Remove these?
2) citation missing in line 624 in Appendix D
3) there are spaces in the numbers in line 339 that make them harder to read

title: Agent-in-the-Loop: A Data Flywheel for Continuous Improvement in LLM-based Customer Support
review:
LLMs can go out of date in terms of what  they know about very quickly since they are trained on static data. While RAG augmentations help to some extent, they are not a complete solution. For LLM-based customer support systems, this can be a big problem. 

The current paper proposes a "flywheel" approach, an iterative and interactive method for incorporating some human feedback using an annotation interface and a method for continually injecting new information into the training pipeline. 

A human "support agent" looks at two responses to a customer query, potentially from different LLMs. LLM generated relevance and verification is also provided. A different human agent looks at this information along with the actual interaction the support agent had with the customer and annotates the relevant components  accordingly.  These annotations are collected and fed into the training pipeline which it is hoped will lead to continuous model improvements.

As a baseline to compare against they use a system that processes production logs and simulation data with annotations, validated by human review. Updating models with this pipeline took three months, they say.

The pipeline system was evaluated in a live setting, collecting annotations from more than 5k customer support cases. Using a mixture of human and LLM based judging, annotation agreement levels were found to be higher in the pipeline system, as were precision and recall for relevant pieces of information. Likewise, pipeline model responses were preferred by human judges over the offline ones the majority of the time.

Pro: interesting work; clearly described; tested in a realistic scenario; limitations spelled out.

Con: it is not clear how valuable the LLM judging and input components are compared to the human annotation and preference judgements. What would be the chances of a full automation of this pipeline?

title: Agent-in-the-Loop: A Data Flywheel for Continuous Improvement in LLM-based Customer Support
review:
The paper proposes and productionizes a data flywheel for agent-in-the-loop preference optimization of a RAG-oriented 8x7B Mixtral LLM for a customer support application. The authors attain improvements for many metrics and outperform an offline baseline, demonstrating the efficacy of online optimization.

Pros:
- The methodology is practically novel, simple, and effective, with sufficient experimental results.
- The applicability to industry is broad, covering any business performing preference optimization of online LLMs.

Cons:
- It would be nice to validate the results on more LLMs and preference optimization strategies beyond Mixtral and ORPO. Further analyses are also somewhat lacking, e.g., how does model size affect results?

title: Building Resource-Constrained Language Agents: A Korean Case Study on Chemical Toxicity Information
review:
This paper presents an innovative approach to developing language agents in resource-constrained environments, specifically focusing on Korean chemical toxicity information. The authors introduce Tox-chat, a domain-specific language agent that leverages a hierarchical information retrieval architecture and an efficient tool-using dialogue generation methodology. The work demonstrates significant improvements in database consistency and reliability, making it a valuable contribution to the field of language agents for specialized domains.

## Pros
1. The hierarchical document-section structure effectively reduces context length requirements, addressing the limitations of traditional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods. This approach is particularly useful for specialized databases like Tox-info.
2. The paper provides a detailed description of the Tox-chat architecture and the process of generating training data. The use of scenarios to simulate user interactions is particularly noteworthy, as it ensures diverse and meaningful conversations.

## Cons
1. There is a slight decline in preference scores when applying the Tox-chat architecture to commercial LLMs. This is partly attributed to the DB-only constraint, which limits the agent's ability to generate content outside the database. While this ensures reliability, it may affect fluency and coverage.
2. After sampling multi-turn dialogues, it would be better to perform quality filtering.

title: Building Resource-Constrained Language Agents: A Korean Case Study on Chemical Toxicity Information
review:
This paper presents Tox-chat, a Korean chemical toxicity information agent, including context-efficient architecture and a scenario-based dialogue generation methodology.

The paper simulates human information-seeking behavior and proposes tox-chat architecture has six tools, including BM25 search, keyword search, read general, QA specific,  carcinogen filter search and toxic dose search, for the context-efficient architecture.

This paper collects scenario-based dialogue generation through personal, situation, intention and question informations.

The experiments demonstrate the better performance of proposed Tox-chat agent in metrics and user case study.

But this work still needs some human effort in the initial phase and how to evaluate the robustness and generalization of this agent.

title: Building Resource-Constrained Language Agents: A Korean Case Study on Chemical Toxicity Information
review:
Quality:
This is an interesting paper addressing the important topic of LLMs based on relatively narrow topics in less common languages (Korean). It is well-organized and clearly written. This topic is always of interest.

Originality:
Although the importance of applying LLM techniques to problems with smaller amounts of data is important, it wasn't clear that the techniques that were tested were particularly novel.

Does this paper introduce the "DB-only" constraint? If not, there should be a citation. If it does, ideally the constraint should be evaluated.

Significance: 
This paper should be useful for other researchers investigating similar problems.

Pros:
An interesting and clearly written paper on a generally useful topic. Although the focus of this paper is fairly narrow, there is nothing specific about Korean or the toxicity data that restricts the techniques to those applications. 

Cons: 
The paper claims to have made innovations in the areas of hierarchical architectures and dialog generation, but how these were evaluated is not clear. In addition, the hierarchical search technique was not clearly explained. It was hard to understand how it worked, making it potentially difficult to replicate the experiment.  

The paper should describe the Tox-Info data in more detail, especially since it's in Korean, and it would be hard for many readers to get more information about it. 

The ablation studies, which are essential to demonstrating the effectiveness of the innovations, are only included in an appendix. In addition, the results in Table 4 (in the Appendix) for "our system" are different from the main results in Table 1 (Tox-chat [GPT-4o-mini]). I think they should be the same, since this represents the non-ablated basis of comparison. If they shouldn't be the same, the paper should explain the difference. 

The paper looked at three different data variations (dialogues, summary pairs, and QA pairs) but these do not seem to be broken out into separate results in Table 1. Is there a difference among the three types of data?

None of the baselines in Table 1 used fine-tuning or tools. Does that make a fair comparison to the Tox-Chat systems?

It would be good to see a multi-turn dialog. Figures 1 and 2 only shows one turn.

I was confused by Figure 4 -- where does it compare ToxChat vs. GPT-4o?

Typos: "genearte"

title: No Label? No Problem. MedASR: Unsupervised Continual Learning for Adaptive Medical Speech Recognition
review:
This paper introduces MedASR, which is an effective approach for continual unsupervised learning for ASR systems under the medical domain. The proposed pipeline effectively addresses the challenges of acquiring high-quality annotation in the medical domain. Overall, the work presented could be informative to industry practitioners working under a similar environment.

Strengths:
- The paper presents a real-world use case for speech technology and is generally clear and easy to follow.
- The proposed workflow is comprehensive and several components that improve the system performance, e.g. use of confidence score, adaptation of the loss function as well as the adaptive training.
- The benchmark result and ablation study demonstrate the effectiveness of the workflow as well as the key components, which justifies the choice of each proposed component in this pipeline

Weaknesses:
- Overall, the techniques used in the paper are not novel, the main contribution limits to putting together existing methods as an integrated pipeline.
- The selection of confidence threshold in section 2.2 is a bit unclear to me. Why it's necessary to have at least 95% of the audio data selected? Also it'd be helpful to provide the distribution of the confidence score.

title: No Label? No Problem. MedASR: Unsupervised Continual Learning for Adaptive Medical Speech Recognition
review:
The main idea of the paper is to use improve the performance of an ASR system on an out-of-domain medical use-case. The paper proposes to use an existing ASR model (such as Whisper) to pseudo label the unsupervised medical domain data along with measuring the confidence estimates. The pseduo-labelled data is then used with EWC method to prevent catastrophic forgetting while performing the finetuning of the ASR model. 


The main weakness of the papers are as follows:

(1) While pseudo-labelling is useful as suggested in the paper, there is no comparison with iterative pseudo labelling which works even better. [1][2]

(2) In general, to prevent catastrophic forgetting, data replay (i.e, using a portion of the training data of the pre-trained ASR model) is useful, which for Whisper model some of the training datasets are publicly available. But it is not clear why catastrophic forgetting is a key step here? The model can be for medical use-case only.

(3) There are no ablations provided on assessing the usefulness of each design decision made in the paper. I.e, what happens if we fine-tune all of the parameters on all the data. What is the effect of EWC? Why not use Low-rank adaptation which also reduces catastrophic forgetting? 

(4) How good are the confidence measures on an out-of-domain medical domain? What percentage of the data is high confidence, low-confidence and discarded? The overall confidence scores (average of all token confidences) may be inflated as within a sentence there are only few medical named entities. 

(5) The biggest weakness for the paper is that there are now new ideas or novel extensions proposed in the paper. Whatever extensions are provided are not properly ablated to assess their impact. 


References:

[1] Xu, Qiantong, et al. "Iterative pseudo-labeling for speech recognition." arXiv preprint arXiv:2005.09267 (2020).
[2] Meng, Qingliang, et al. "ILT-Iterative LoRA Training through Focus-Feedback-Fix for Multilingual Speech Recognition." arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.08477 (2025).

title: No Label? No Problem. MedASR: Unsupervised Continual Learning for Adaptive Medical Speech Recognition
review:
This paper describes a data processing pipeline for continuously adapting a whisper-based medical transcription system with data collected on-the-fly from a live system.  The pipeline involves transcribing the data, computing a confidence score, filtering, adding background noise and then fine-tuning using a EWC loss weighted by the confidence score.  The system is evaluated by filtering and fine-tuning on a corpus of 1.3 million medical audios and testing on a  hand-transcribed test set of 6000 audio samples.   The process results in WER reduction from 3.13 to 2.64 and a medical key term error rate reduction from 41% to 35%.

Strengths

The paper addresses a real problem in the deployment of large scale transcription services where key vocabulary is changing over time and where the speaker population is highly diverse.  The authors have assembled a sensible collection of techniques and appear to be getting useful results.

Weaknesses

It is not possible to reproduce these results because the data is proprietary.  The authors could also have tried applying the technique also a publicly available dataset to demonstrate robustness and to allow for some benchmarking.  

The authors claim that this system allows for continual learning, but in fact, it is a large-scale adaptation exercise.  The data presented does not provide evidence that continuous fine tuning over months and years does not result in drift.

title: On-device System of Compositional Multi-tasking in Large Language Models
review:
The submission focuses too much on describing the system framework, while both, comparison to the most relevant related work (Bohdal et al.) as well as experimental description & execution falls short.

Bohdal introduces a benchmark comprising four practically relevant compositional tasks. Therefore, a more direct comparison to Bohdal would have been possible. Yet the authors chose only one of these tasks (summarization + translation) — on a different data set. It’s curios that Table 1 does not list the method described in Bohdal while however clearly drawing inspiration from Bohdal, listing many of  the comparative approaches Bohdal et al lists.

The implementation details are too scant, missing data statistics and more detailed explanations. Thus, the lower accuracy of the joint expert LoRA usage compared to the projection merge approach is insufficiently discussed. It likely stems from the fact that it suffers from not having seen any TEDTalks English-to-Spanish translation data, which likely boosts translation quality of the two-step and projection merge approaches.

title: On-device System of Compositional Multi-tasking in Large Language Models
review:
The paper presents a system for improved efficiently in jointly summarizing and translating text with experiments on English into Spanish chats. The authors go in very fine detail on all engineering techniques used to achieve this and present results which outperform zero-shot and two-step approaches while maintaining output quality.

The authors do note that `inference times of over 20 seconds may be too long for some use cases` which indeed would be true for a mobile user, making the reader wonder if slightly decreased output quality for further improvements on efficiency would be a worthy tradeoff? 


Some major issues with the paper:
 * 15 out of the 40 references are citing arXiv and not the actual publication venues for those papers. This is a very bad style of work and should never be acceptable aside from some rare cases when a couple of papers truly only were submitted to arXiv and nowhere else.

 * The references section in general should be fully redone. It seems like the authors are not using the ACL Anthology bibliography file. Most papers lack proper publication venue descriptions and details, such as:
   *  In NeurIPS
   *  In ACL
   *  In TMLR
   *  In ICLR
   *  In COLM
   *  In ICML
   *  In EAMT
 * Some citations do not have any venue or details at all:
   * Ondrej Bohdal, Mete Ozay, Jijoong Moon, Kyeng-Hun Lee, Hyeonmok Ko, and Umberto Michieli. 2025. Efficient compositional multi-tasking for on-device large language models.

Some minor issues:
 * The abbreviation `MLP` is never introduced (line 325).

title: On-device System of Compositional Multi-tasking in Large Language Models
review:
The authors present a method for combining the LoRA adaptation weights of two tasks via interpolation and applying an additional, global, low rank projection matrix on top of the interpolated LoRA weights.

The authors evaluate their method on the composite task of summarizing an English conversation and then translating it into Spanish.
They compare the performance of their approach against several alternative approaches, such as zero shot instructions without LoRA, selecting one of the LoRA weights, different atlernative LoRA merging techniques, and performing the compositional task by pipelining the two individual tasks, using task specific LoRA weights.

The rank of their additional projection task is especially low (rank of 4), introducing only 0.1M additional parameters to a model of size 1B plus 22.5M LoRA parameters.

Their approach offers performance that even slightly outperforms the pipelined approach and clearly outperforms all other approaches.

The paper then describe the work performed, to integrate the approach into an on-device application that performs the compositional task and helps to evaluate performance and compute time.

Using this implementation the authors then examine the resource requirements during inference, both on a CPU sever and on an Android device, on a subset of the test set, comparing zero shot prompting, two-step LoRA and their approach.

As predicted by theory, the author's approach should has clearly lower computational requirements than the two step approach, and slightly lower requirements than the zero-shot prompting (due to the prompt being additional input).
In theory, the joint-expert LoRA should have a slightly lower compute requirement that the authors' approach (while needing extra storage for storing the full, additional set of LoRA weights, instead of only the small adapter of the authors' approach). But the authors did not measure it.

The on-device measurements indicate, that even for the authors' approach the response time of the model (>20s on average) might be too long for practical use.

The advantage of the approach proposed by the authors is, that in the presence of multiple compositional tasks, the storage need for adaptation weights is greatly reduced compared to using a joint-expert LoRA weight set (the only other competitive method), as is the training effort for training the adaptation weights. This advantage should be made more clear, and it should also be made clear, that the computational needs for joint-LoRA and the authors' approach is otherwise the same.

title: Open-Domain Safety Policy Construction
review:
**Contributions**:
- Introduces DPR, a first-of-its-kind end-to-end open-domain policy construction framework driven by LLMs, minimizing human intervention.
- Validates DPR across both text-based and multi-modal content moderation tasks, demonstrating robustness and generalizability.
- Proposes a keyphrase-based clustering mechanism to improve policy structure and readability.

**Areas of improvement**:
- The paper primarily uses F1 score of downstream moderation tasks as a proxy for policy quality, which may not capture policy interpretability, consistency, or fairness. More nuanced evaluation metrics, such as those used in Deliberative Alignment (Guan et al., 2024, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.16339), could enrich the analysis.
- While quantitative gains are reported, there is little discussion of the linguistic or ethical quality of the generated rules (e.g., are they overly vague or overly specific?). This limits interpretability of the policy improvements.
- The paper does not sufficiently isolate the contribution of individual system components (e.g., query generation vs. clustering) or hyperparameters (e.g., number of iterations), which affects reproducibility and interpretability.
- The DPR system heavily relies on external web search, which may introduce instability, lack of reproducibility, and potential misalignment with platform-specific values. No mitigation strategies (e.g., filtered sources) are discussed.

title: Open-Domain Safety Policy Construction
review:
**Summary**

This paper presents Deep Policy Research (DPR), an automated framework that uses LLMs and web search to construct domain-specific safety policies. Starting from high-level domain specifications, DPR iteratively generates search queries, extracts policy rules from web content, and organizes them into structured policies. The authors evaluate DPR on OpenAI content moderation and in-house advertisement moderation tasks, showing consistent improvements over baselines.


**Strengths**

1. Simple yet Effective Approach: The three-step iterative process (query generation → information extraction → indexing) is straightforward and generalizable across domains.

2. Consistent Performance Gains: DPR shows improvements across all tested domains and models, with particularly strong gains in subjective categories (Violence, Harassment, Self-Harm).

**Concerns**
- The paper relies primarily on F1 scores, it might be worth considering other factors beyond F1 scores, such as policy interpretability, coverage, and consistency, to get a fuller picture of the policy's quality.
- It would be interesting to explore how the quality of search results impacts the final policy, as search results can change over time, making exact reproduction a bit challenging.
- The “additional round of self-critique” (lines 180-182) is mentioned but isn’t systematically evaluated, so it could be helpful to explore that in more detail.
- The advantage of keyphrase-based clustering over direct rule clustering (lines 194-196) could be further validated with empirical data.
- It might be beneficial to include statistical significance testing for the results in Table 2, to strengthen the evidence behind the claims.
- Line 174: Incomplete sentence "A list of webpages are then."
- Line 343: Unclear notation "S.P." (should be "S.S."?)

title: Open-Domain Safety Policy Construction
review:
This paper introduces Deep Policy Research (DPR), an agentic framework that automatically constructs domain-specific safety policies by leveraging LLMs and web search. Given a high-level domain specification, DPR iteratively proposes subtopics, performs open-domain search, and distills retrieved information into structured policy rules. The authors evaluate DPR on the OpenAI content moderation dataset and an in-house multi-modal advertisement moderation benchmark.

The paper presents a novel framing of safety policy generation as an open-domain research problem, shifting from manual rule-writing to automated LLM-driven synthesis. However, a notable drawback is that the evaluation is limited in scope and depth. Testing on only two relatively narrow moderation tasks leaves generalizability to more complex safety areas uncertain, particularly for domains like biorisk, finance, or real-time interactive use cases -- which I believe are major areas that the AI safety field cares about. The evaluation focuses solely on F1 scores with a single LLM reader, lacking human audit of rule quality, robustness testing against adversarial prompts, or analysis of longitudinal maintenance needs.

title: RePo: A Recursive Algorithm for Automated Prompt Optimization
review:
# The Review
This paper proposes a recursive algorithm called RePo, which aims to improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in classification tasks through automated prompt optimization. Its core idea is to adopt a "divide-and-conquer" recursive strategy, generate targeted rules for misclassified samples (false positives and false negatives) in the training data, and merge them with basic rules to form the final prompt. The work is of high quality with a clear methodology and certain innovativeness, holding significance in the field of iterative self-optimizing prompt engineering.

## Strengths:
- **Innovative recursive optimization framework**: Through a recursive strategy focusing on misclassified samples, it systematically addresses the insufficient utilization of erroneous samples in existing methods, achieving "precision error correction". Compared with traditional single-prompt optimization, recursive partition tuning can better handle data heterogeneity and improve adaptability in complex scenarios.  
- **Flexible baseline compatibility**: It supports integrating existing optimizers such as OPRO and ProTeGi as baselines, and experiments have shown that the stronger the baseline performance, the more significant the improvement effect of RePo, demonstrating the framework's scalability and practicality.  

## Weaknesses:
- **Limited application scenarios**: Currently, it only supports classification tasks and relies on classification-specific error definitions such as false positives and false negatives. It cannot be directly applied to generative tasks (e.g., text summarization, dialogue generation), which limits the algorithm's generality.  It is expected that future work will achieve this. 
- **Insufficient validation experiment design**: Currently, only two models have been used in experiments, making it impossible to obtain solid results. It is hoped that more models can be added to verify the experimental outcomes.  
- **Lack of related work section**: The authors did not mention mainstream related works in recent years, and this section should be added.

title: RePo: A Recursive Algorithm for Automated Prompt Optimization
review:
This work proposes RePo, a recursive pipeline to that use smaller sub-examples to continuously arrive at better prompts. RePo demonstrates performance improvement against baseline methods such as ProTeGi and OPRO.

Additional points that can enhance the paper are:
* Stronger Baseline: OPRO and ProTeGi are well known methods, but they are also relatively old (published in 2023). I suggest more recent methods to serve as stronger baseline, even from last year.
* Cost Analysis: RePo relies on based optimizer to generate the starting candidates. That makes it more expensive than the already expensive optimizers, making it less practical in industry setting.

title: RePo: A Recursive Algorithm for Automated Prompt Optimization
review:
### Summary of "RePo: A Recursive Algorithm for Automated Prompt Optimization"
**Core Problem**: Optimizing prompts for Large Language Models (LLMs) is critical for task performance but remains manual and suboptimal. Existing methods (gradient-based, trajectory-based, evolutionary) lack granular feedback, ignore misclassified samples, and fail to address data heterogeneity.

**Proposed Solution**: **RePo** (Recursive Prompt Optimization) — a novel divide-and-conquer algorithm that:  
1. **Recursively partitions data** based on classification errors (false positives/negatives).  
2. **Generates tailored prompts** for each partition via a baseline optimizer (e.g., ProTeGi, OPRO).  
3. **Merges specialized prompts** into a single concise prompt using LLM-based set operations (union/intersection).  

**Key Innovations**:  
- Targets misclassified samples directly for actionable feedback.  
- Handles data heterogeneity via partition-specific tuning.  
- Flexible integration with existing optimizers (e.g., ProTeGi + trajectories).  
- Extends to multi-class tasks via one-vs-rest binarization.  

**Results**:  
- Achieves **+1.3–1.7% accuracy** and **+1.5–2.9% F1-score** over baselines across 9 datasets.  
- Outperforms ProTeGi, OPRO, and simple rules on internal/external binary/multi-class tasks.  
- Ablations validate recursion depth, batch size, and baseline optimizer choices.  

**Limitations**:  
- Currently **supports only classification tasks** (due to FP/FN dependency).  
- Union/intersection rules rely on LLMs, causing performance drops in some cases (Table 8).  

**Reproducibility**:  
- Detailed prompts (Appendix A), datasets (Table 2), hyperparameters, and LLM settings provided.  
- Internal datasets anonymized; external datasets named (e.g., SST-2, Ethos).  

**Anonymity**: No breaches detected (no self-citations, affiliations, or non-anonymized links).  

---

### Strengths

1. **Novelty and Practical Impact**:  
   - RePo introduces a recursive, divide-and-conquer strategy to address misclassified examples systematically, which is a significant improvement over ad-hoc iterative methods.  
   - The integration of textual gradients and historical trajectories enhances actionable feedback, making the approach computationally efficient and scalable for industrial use cases.  
   - The algorithm’s ability to handle data heterogeneity (e.g., tailored prompts for distinct data subgroups) aligns well with real-world deployment challenges.  

2. **Technical Contributions**:  
   - Clear mathematical formulation of the prompt optimization objective (Equation 1) and recursive algorithmic steps (Algorithm 1).  
   - Empirical validation across diverse datasets (e.g., Ethos, SST-2, AG_News) demonstrates robustness and generalizability.  
   - The multi-class extension (via one-vs-rest binary classification) and ablation studies (e.g., batch size, recursion depth) strengthen the paper’s technical rigor.  

3. **Clarity and Structure**:  
   - The paper is well-organized, with intuitive figures (e.g., Figure 2) and tables (e.g., Table 1) to illustrate the methodology and results.  
   - The industrial use case (Figure 1) and practical motivations (e.g., handling evolving customer needs) are clearly articulated.  

---

### Weaknesses and improvements

#### **1. Limitations**  
**Current State**:  
The paper briefly mentions limitations in the conclusion (e.g., RePo’s focus on classification tasks and reliance on LLMs for rule merging). However, a dedicated "Limitations" section is missing, which is increasingly expected in modern conference submissions.  

**Suggestions for Improvement**:  
- **Generalizability**: RePo is evaluated only on classification tasks (binary/multi-class). A limitations section should explicitly state that the method does not support generative tasks (e.g., summarization, dialogue generation), where prompt optimization is equally critical.  
- **Scalability**: The recursive approach may face computational bottlenecks with large datasets or high-dimensional data. The paper does not discuss how RePo scales with increasing data size or complexity.  
- **LLM Dependency**: The merge step (Equation 2) relies entirely on LLMs for union/intersection operations. This introduces potential errors or biases from the LLM itself (e.g., hallucinations, alignment issues). A limitations section should address this dependency and its risks.  
- **Rule Overlap**: The union/intersection of rules via LLMs may lead to redundancy or conflicting rules (e.g., overlapping conditions in merged prompts). The paper lacks analysis of such edge cases.  

---

#### **2. Reproducibility Issues**  
**Current State**:  
While the paper provides sufficient methodological detail for replication, critical implementation details are missing.  

**Suggestions for Improvement**:  
- **Hyperparameter Transparency**:  
  - The paper mentions hyperparameters like batch size (B~128), recursion depth (NIte=20), and K=5, but lacks exact values or ranges for parameters like LLM sampling temperature, top-k/top-p thresholds, or stopping criteria for recursion.  
  - For reproducibility, authors should provide a table of all hyperparameters, their ranges, and the rationale for their selection (e.g., why B=128 is optimal).  
- **Code Availability**:  
  - The absence of a public repository or detailed pseudocode for the merge step (Algorithm 1, line 198–204) hinders reproducibility. Even if code sharing is not mandatory, the paper should provide a clear, step-by-step explanation of how the LLM executes union/intersection operations (e.g., specific meta-prompts in Appendix A.2.1–A.2.3).  
- **Dataset Preprocessing**:  
  - The paper references internal datasets (ID 1–4) but does not specify preprocessing steps (e.g., tokenization, balancing, or noise filtering). For external datasets like Ethos or SST-2, the paper should clarify how they were split into train/validation/test sets.  

---

#### **3. Comparative Analysis**  
**Current State**:  
The paper compares RePo with ProTeGi and OPRO, but the analysis lacks context for broader relevance and trade-offs.  

**Suggestions for Improvement**:  
- **Broader Baselines**:  
  - Compare RePo with **Chain-of-Thought Prompting** (CoT) or **Self-Consistency Decoding**, which are widely used for complex reasoning tasks. This would highlight whether RePo’s recursive strategy is suitable for tasks beyond classification.  
  - Include ablation studies on **computational efficiency** (e.g., runtime, number of LLM calls) to quantify the trade-off between accuracy gains (1.3–1.7%) and resource costs.  
- **Qualitative Analysis**:  
  - The paper provides qualitative rule examples (Table 6) but does not analyze **why** RePo’s rules are superior. For instance, how do the merged rules address misclassified examples compared to baselines? A case study on a few failure cases (e.g., ambiguous samples in the Ethos dataset) would strengthen the analysis.  
- **Task-Specific Trade-offs**:  
  - Discuss scenarios where simpler methods (e.g., one-shot rule generation) might outperform RePo. For example, in low-data regimes or when computational resources are constrained, RePo’s recursive approach may be overkill.  

---

#### **4. Technical Depth and Clarity**  
**Current State**:  
The recursive merging of rulesets is described at a high level, but the technical details are insufficient for full understanding.  

**Suggestions for Improvement**:  
- **Algorithmic Details**:  
  - Algorithm 1 (Recursive Prompt Optimization) is presented as pseudocode, but the merge step (line 198–204) is ambiguously described. The paper should:  
    - Provide pseudocode for the LLM-based union/intersection operations (e.g., how the LLM parses input rules and generates merged rules).  
    - Clarify how the LLM ensures **consistency** between rules during merging (e.g., resolving conflicting conditions).  
- **Mathematical Formulation**:  
  - The objective function (Equation 1) is well-defined, but the paper lacks a mathematical explanation of how the recursive partitioning improves accuracy. For example, does the recursive approach reduce the search space exponentially, or is there a theoretical guarantee for convergence?  
- **Error Propagation**:  
  - The paper does not discuss how errors in earlier iterations (e.g., misclassified examples in FP/FN) propagate through subsequent recursive steps. A formal analysis of error bounds or sensitivity to initial conditions would strengthen the technical contribution.  

---

#### **5. Broader Impact and Ethical Considerations**  
**Current State**:  
The paper focuses on industrial applications but neglects ethical and societal implications.  

**Suggestions for Improvement**:  
- **Bias and Fairness**:  
  - LLM-generated rules may inherit biases from the training data (e.g., racial, gender, or cultural stereotypes in the Ethos dataset). The paper should discuss how RePo mitigates or amplifies such biases, particularly when merging rules via LLMs.  
- **Scalability in Low-Resource Settings**:  
  - RePo’s reliance on powerful LLMs (e.g., Claude 2, Mistral-7B) may limit its adoption in resource-constrained environments. The paper should address whether the method can be adapted to smaller models or alternative architectures (e.g., open-source LLMs like LLaMA).  
- **Human-in-the-Loop**:  
  - The paper assumes that the final merged prompt is automatically deployed. However, in high-stakes applications (e.g., hate speech detection), human oversight is critical. The paper should discuss how RePo integrates with human reviewers or explainability tools.  

---

#### **6. Writing and Presentation**  
**Current State**:  
The paper is well-structured, but certain sections could benefit from tighter writing and clearer explanations.  

**Suggestions for Improvement**:  
- **Motivation and Use Cases**:  
  - While the paper mentions industrial applications (e.g., chatbots, auto-evaluation), it lacks concrete examples of how RePo improves real-world systems. For instance, how does RePo reduce manual effort in prompt engineering for customer support chatbots?  
- **Visualizations**:  
  - Figures 2 and 4 are helpful, but the paper could include a **flowchart** of the recursive process (e.g., how FP/FN subsets are partitioned in each iteration) to aid reader comprehension.  
- **Appendix Integration**:  
  - The meta-prompts in Appendix A.2 are detailed but disconnected from the main text. Integrating key examples (e.g., a sample union/intersection operation) into the main body would improve readability.  

---

title: From Playbooks to Probabilistic Diagnosis: A Cautious, Phased Approach to LLM Driven Workflows in Reliability Engineering
review: This paper is about reliability engineering, and it studies a system called Pathfinder that is aimed at site reliability engineers (SREs).   Most of the paper is about Pathfinder, really addressed to people interested in SRE.  It's about the workflow, the "cautious, phased approach", the evaluation and usability and similar matters.    I don't see why it was submitted to EMNLP.   So I read it again for contributions related to natural language, even loosely speaking.   In fact, it seems that Section 5.2 does say that synthesizing a natural language summary is a "key challenge" of the system.  And the work does use some work from a 2024 paper on "answer relevancy" and also "faithfulness".  So my guess is that these aspects of the work are most interesting for EMNLP, not much the details of Pathfinder that have to do with SRE.   I would have been more interested in a paper just about the language aspects of the work.

title: From Playbooks to Probabilistic Diagnosis: A Cautious, Phased Approach to LLM Driven Workflows in Reliability Engineering
review:
Strengths

In Pathfinder authors claim to provide some unique features such as 

	1. Automates the generation of incident reports. Authors mention that by delivering immediate, verifiable value as reports on non-mutating tasks is crucial for building trust and organizational confidence.

	2. Authors provide a method to explain underlying causes for anomaly detection using Bayesian networks to model the probablistic dependencies between low-level infrastructure metrics and high level service health. This enables their system to provide probablistic diagnoses for incidents and alerts

	3. Provide an approach how to build robust guardrails to put a check on agents' autonomy. Guardrails basically comprise of strict operational boundaries and permission models. In addition role-based access control is implemented to manage user acces to different features. 


Weakness

1. The evaluation of Pathfinder is limited to evaluation of summary generated from a diverse set of sources such as structured alerts, probabilistic diagnoses from our Bayesian models, and time-series anomaly data. It does not consider evaluating root cause analysis or robust guardrails. 

2. The adoption and usability scores have not been properly linked with the strengths of the tool. Ideally there should have been some way to measure the effectiveness of reporting, root cause analysis and guardrails to correlate it with the adoption and usability.

3. Overall, the novelty of the contribution is missing since authors did not clearly differentiate how their tool is different from other tools in the market. May be the hypotheses need to be clearly defined and evaluated for.

Additional Concerns

1. When authors mentions about previous SREs workflows in background they mention about themselves or they observed this phenomena across several industries or companies. I am sure there has been tons of contributions in this space to automate IT incident resolutions from companies like IBM, Microsoft, Datadog etc. May be authors could provide a recent citations to make it a valid claim.

2. In Section 3.1 authors mentioned that generation of incident reports previously required manually pulling and analyzing data from disparate ticketing and monitoring systems. IBM's Cloud Pak for Watson AIOps, Microsoft's Azure SRE Agent,  certainly automates this. There are several other companies which do so. So the claim is a bit confusing. May be authors can clarify the difference in approach or deliverables.

title: From Playbooks to Probabilistic Diagnosis: A Cautious, Phased Approach to LLM Driven Workflows in Reliability Engineering
review:
The authors present details of an end-to-end implementation of SRE work leveraging advances in AI/ML, Gen AI and Agentic AI.
The work is timely and practically relevant.

My main concern is that the paper does not propose anything technically novel. It is basically an application of known techniques in a specific enterprise environment.  These types of solutions currently exist in a scattered form in the ServiceNows and ELK stacks of enterprises. And, it is not that the technical capability is not there, it is just how the enterprise teams operate in silos and the multitude of applications / platforms involved having their own siloed observabilitiy environments that makes the problem complex. So the fundamental problem still remains.

Having said this, the authors do a good job bringing a subset of these capabilities together in a form that can be applied today at enterprises. There are some interesting observations in terms of how context formatting strategies can be applied to improve retrieval accuracy. Change management is of course very important for the rollout of such systems, so the adoption and usability observations in Section 6 are also quite relevant.

title: PolyNorm: Few-Shot LLM-Based Text Normalization for Text-to-Speech
review:
This paper proposes a new LLM-based approach to text normalization (TN) for Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems. The aim is to provide a sustainable and cost-effective solution that minimizes human intervention and enables a reliable, language-independent process for curating and evaluating data across different languages. This system addresses the limitations of traditional rule-based TN, which are often expensive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale or adapt to new languages. By employing a few-shot prompting strategy with In-Context Learning (ICL) examples, PolyNorm guides LLMs to normalize text across various categories and languages, eliminating the need for extensive fine-tuning or manual rule engineering. The approach is designed to be multilingual and context-aware, handling ambiguities and domain-specific constructs, and has been evaluated across eight languages. Ultimately, PolyNorm seeks to accelerate TTS development by reducing manual effort, lowering the barrier for TN in low-resource languages, and improving consistency and generalization across multiple languages.

The novelty and utility of this work are particularly high, representing a contribution to the Text-to-Speech (TTS) research community. The introduction and public release of the "PolyNorm-Benchmark," a new multilingual dataset covering 27 normalization categories across eight diverse languages, is a significant achievement that will support and standardize future research in this area. The extensive evaluation across these languages demonstrates the proposed system's robustness and scalability, offering a practical path forward for developing high-quality TN systems, especially for low-resource languages, thereby lowering development barriers and accelerating progress in the field.

The soundness of the experiments is difficult to evaluate because several key details are missing. First, this paper provides no specific information about your production rule-based normalization baseline system, which makes it impossible to judge whether it is a strong baseline. Second, the error analysis is largely qualitative. A quantitative analysis of the remaining PolyNorm system errors by category would provide a more detailed understanding of its current limitations. Finally, the methodology lacks a clear explanation of the selection strategy for the 80-100 In-Context Learning (ICL) examples, which is crucial for reproducibility and for understanding the extent to which performance depends on expert curation.

title: PolyNorm: Few-Shot LLM-Based Text Normalization for Text-to-Speech
review:
Polynorm is a prompt based system for text normalisation in text-to-speech that aims to reduce the time and effort of creating manually crafted rule-based systems while also offering broader linguistic applicability. They also  provide a language agnostic pipeline for automatic data curation and evaluation. 

Polynorm is tested on a diverse multi-lingual setting where 8 languages are tested. The data curation and evaluation pipeline shows promise for creating TTS systems for low-resource languages. The performance reported for the 8 languages is compared with a rule-based system and the WER and BLEU scores are reportedly  improved across all of the 8 languages. 



Strengths:

The primary strength of this study is its extensive multilingual focus, which is a significant departure from previous research predominantly concentrated on English. The paper’s claim of scalability to low-resource languages is a notable contribution, as it addresses a key challenge in developing TTS systems for less common languages. 

The paper also provides a text normalisation benchmark which consists of data curated by the use of LLMs and proofed by TTS experts. It covers 27 categories of errors and examples of these. It provides a reusable resource for future research and standardised evaluation.

The paper reports improvements on WER (CER for no space languages) and BLEU scores across all of the languages in the benchmark when compared to a traditional rule-based baseline. 


Weaknesses:

The paper has significant issues regarding its methodology and evaluation. Particularly, the “Error analysis and Hillclimbing” section gives details about how the system is refined incrementally. One major issue with this is that the process is not explained in detail in the paper. How many iterations had to be done? What were the error rates before and after and more importantly what are the criteria for selecting the few zero-shot examples. This lack of transparency raises concerns about the reproducibility and soundness of the methodology. A more formal and thorough approach, such as documenting each stage of the hillclimbing process and its impact on performance, would significantly strengthen the paper's claims.


Related to the methodological vagueness, the system’s dependency on the curated, zero-shot examples makes it prone to error propagation and might also have error biases. The system’s reliance on a limited set of examples to refine the system means it may not generalise well to novel or rare errors. A more extensive discussion on how these risks are mitigated is necessary. 

It would be nice to compare results with the related studies cited in the paper. It would be interesting to see a comparison of the results with Zhang et al 2024 for English, in particular, as the two studies are very similar. 

There are a few more minor issues/questions that arise as well:

1. Cross lingual consistency is emphasised in the paper. It would be nice to include a more detailed discussion into why this is important or required and in general what the authors mean by it. 

2. Figure. 1. In Figure 1, the English example's translation appears to differ from the others. While the text implies they mean the same thing, clarifying this discrepancy would prevent reader confusion. 

3. Ln 106: “to address these challenges… “ Do you mean the translation challenges in the previous paragraph? Might want to combine the paragraphs here.
