4. Ln 236: mentions “previously intractable normalization challenges” Providing specific examples here, such as the tokenization of URLs, would provide stronger evidence and clarity for the reader.

title: PolyNorm: Few-Shot LLM-Based Text Normalization for Text-to-Speech
review:
This paper presents an application of LLM prompting to the task of text normalization.  As the authors describe, text normalization has traditionally been performed by either complex, hand-crafted, language-specific rules or by task-specific machine learning models for sequence transduction, but recently there have been attempts to adapt LLMs to the task.  This paper builds upon prior research by
- Creating a multilingual dataset for TN using a combination of machine translation applied to a pre-existing English dataset and manual post-editing of examples
- Augmenting the LLM approach to TN using a master instruction prompt, a subset of data examples per language designated for few-shot in-context learning (ICL), and manual tweaking of the ICL set based on observed performance

Overall, the paper is well-structured, the problem well-motivated, and the selection of methodology appropriate.  The authors demonstrate significant performance improvements for their LLM prompting approach vs. a rule-based baseline.  

The most significant gap that could be addressed in this paper is the description of the “hill climbing iteration” approach in Section 3.2.  More detailed discussion of the data and process used for ICL (3.1), hill climbing (3.2) and system evaluation (4) would provide some additional confidence that the results in Table 2 are not clouded by potential information leakage from the test set during training.

title: SFAL: Semantic-Functional Alignment Scores for Distributional Evaluation of Auto-Interpretability in Sparse Autoencoders
review: The paper proposes an automated way of evaluating automated annotations of sparse autoencoder (SAE) features. SAEs compress activations of LLMs into sparse vectors, whose elements, when activated, in turn, hopefully correspond to interpretable input features. In published models, the sparse vectors are themselves often highly multidimensional, which makes manual inspection of the inputs and corresponding activated sparse features impractical. Methods were therefore proposed to automatically construct textual descriptions of SAE features based on input sets. The paper proposes a method to evaluate these "auto-interpretations". Two SAEs are targeted in the study, but it is not described in detail how their auto-interpretations are generated. The core idea is that features that have semantically similar textual descriptions (as measured using a suitable sentence-embedding model) should also be correlated in their activation patterns. This core postulate is not well motivated (e.g., a feature such as "a transitive predicate" and "a direct object" are likely to have a very high correlation but a low description-level similarity). It is shown, however, that the quality scores derived in this way correlate moderately well with human judgments, which means that at least for some features this connection holds, so the method has some utility, as long as SAE feature are sufficiently redundant/overlapping. The results are predictably noisy, but the paper acknowledges this and argues that this is compensated for by low computational complexity of the proposed method.

title: SFAL: Semantic-Functional Alignment Scores for Distributional Evaluation of Auto-Interpretability in Sparse Autoencoders
review:
This paper introduces SFAL (Semantic-Functional Alignment Scores), a novel and efficient method for evaluating the quality of auto-interpretations for features learned by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). To address the financial impracticality of evaluating every feature generated against the LLM, this new method maintains a tractable computation complexity of O(N^2). 

For the SAE features, the authors defined "semantic neighborhood" based on the similarity of their textural auto-interpretation to others using embeddings, and "functional neighborhood" based on how frequently it co-activates with other features using co-occurrence statistics and the phi coefficient. The alignment between these two neighborhoods is computed using Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG), resulting in the SFAL score. The higher the score is, the more consistent the textual description is with the actual behavior within the model. 

Pros:
* The work directly addresses a major bottlneck in the practical application of interpretability techniques: the intractable cost required for evaluation. The proposed method is novel, cheap and efficient, serving as a practical alternative to the LLM-based scoring. 
* The idea behind the method is intuitive but novel and sound. It frames the interpretability as a consistency computation problem which is well-understood and easily computed (with cosine similarity).
* The authors involved human experts to verify the effectiveness of their proposed method, demonstrating high inter-rater agreement. 
* The paper is well-written and clearly structured. 

Cons:
* As the author acknowledged in the limitation section, the reliance on co-occurrence as a proxy is not perfect. Features can co-occur for various reasons, and not all the co-occurrences imply functional relationship. However, this is a reasonable assumption since the purpose of the paper focuses on presenting a cost-efficient approach as an alternative.
* The user study is small-scaled, with 4 expert users. A larger pool would further strengthen the claims in this paper.

title: SFAL: Semantic-Functional Alignment Scores for Distributional Evaluation of Auto-Interpretability in Sparse Autoencoders
review:
This paper proposes SFAL for assessing the auto-interpretability of features learned by SAEs. SFAL quantifies the alignment between a feature’s semantic neighbourhood and its functional neighbourhood. Experiments demonstrate that SFAL correlates well with human judgments while being computationally efficient.

---

**Strengths:**
- Introduces a principled semantic functional alignment approach
- Reduces computational and financial costs, enabling evaluation of millions of features; only ~2 GPU hours needed for large-scale runs.
- Includes human evaluation study with expert raters 
---

**Weaknesses:**
-  Functional neighbourhoods rely solely on co-activation statistics, which may not fully capture causal or mechanistic relationships
- SFAL slightly underperforms fuzzy scoring for Llama-3.1-8B in correlation with human ratings
- Fixed top-K neighbourhoods may not adapt optimally across features with different activation sparsity patterns

title: Fin-ExBERT: User Intent based Text Extraction in Financial Context using Graph-Augmented BERT and trainable Plugin
review:
The paper presents the Fin-ExBERT framework for extracting user intent–relevant sentences from annotated financial service calls. The proposed approach builds on a domain-adapted BERT model enhanced with LoRA adapters using limited labeled data.


**Strengths**:
1. The problem is interesting and may have real-life applications.

2. The idea of using combination of BERT representation and GNN-based representation (based on dependency tree) is good.


**Weaknesses**:
1. The main aim of the paper as state in the abstract is to extract user-intent relevant sentences from financial service calls. The methodology in Section 3.1 starts with input as premise-hypothesis pair. There absolutely no description which explains how the original task of extracting user-intent relevant sentences is related to premise-hypothesis pairs (and the NLI task).

2. The paper is not well-written. The problem definition is not clear. If the aim is to identify sentences corresponding to user-intents then why is it not modelled as a sentence classification task instead of span extraction task.

3. The construction of the new proposed dataset CreditCall12H is not properly described. It is not clear how many annotators were used, what was their background, what was the inter-annotator agreement, etc.


**Other comments**

1. The sentence-transformers or other text embedding based models are known to learn better representations than the [CLS] embeddings of the BERT model. Why these models were not explored in place of vanilla BERT?

title: Fin-ExBERT: User Intent based Text Extraction in Financial Context using Graph-Augmented BERT and trainable Plugin
review:
This article proposes a relatively light-weighted model, the Fin-ExBERT, for extracting user intent–relevant sentences from financial service dialogues. It uses a two-stage training strategy with progressive unfreezing and a dynamic thresholding method for robust sentence selection.

Pros:
1. The method is relatively easy to implement.
2. It shows decent results.
3. The paper also provides a financial conversation dataset, the CreditCall12H, which consists of 1,200 anonymized long-form customer service transcripts.

Cons:
1. The methods are not particularly innovative.
2. There is no comparison of results with recent LLMs, although there may be practical reasons.

title: Fin-ExBERT: User Intent based Text Extraction in Financial Context using Graph-Augmented BERT and trainable Plugin
review:
Strengths: 

1) The paper proposes a methodology to combine graph and textual transformers to find relevant snippets from financial dialogues
2) Experimental results based on domain-specific LLM-based judges show that the proposed framework has the best score
3) Ablation study shows that dependency graph-based augmentation helps.


Weaknesses:
1) The method is evaluated only based on domain-specific LLM-based judges. A properly human-labeled extractive summarization dataset is required to assess the quality of the algorithm and report results on metrics such as ROUGE and BERTScore.

title: Assessing LLMs' Factuality on Proprietary Data: A Benchmark Generation Methodology
review:
### Strengths
- Addresses a relevant and underexplored problem of LLM factuality in business-specific proprietary contexts.
- Clear and reproducible methodology for generating subtly misleading facts from structured triples.
- Realistic evaluation scenario by embedding misinformation in longer contexts.
- Public release of a benchmark instantiation enhances reproducibility.
- Empirical findings reveal significant performance gaps between true- and false-fact detection.

### Weaknesses:
- There could be a bias from using the same LLM for paragraph generation and evaluation.
- LLM-as-a-judge reliance may propagate model-specific biases into ground-truth labeling.

### Questions for Authors
1. Can the methodology be adapted to semi-structured or unstructured proprietary datasets?
2. What is the effect of varying the ratio of truthful to misleading facts in context paragraphs?
3. How does the choice of paragraph generation model impact benchmark difficulty?
4. Would combining multiple judging mechanisms improve reliability?
5. Could the benchmark also serve as a training resource for factuality improvement?

title: Assessing LLMs' Factuality on Proprietary Data: A Benchmark Generation Methodology
review:
This paper proposes a methodology to construct dynamic benchmark datasets using proprietary data to assess the factuality of LLMs. This is a relevant problem for the application of language models in business setups.

The stochastic nature of LLMs is the core problem here. The authors aim to assess how good an LLM response is given a prompt that requires a reliable response in a business use case. The idea is good, and the state of the art is relevant to the problem; however, there are a few core topics that were not covered, and a weak validation of the hypothesis.

It's known that small and large language models are mainly trained using world knowledge from open-access encyclopedias and books. For specific use cases, fine-tuning of these models is a requirement in business applications, which takes the shape of task fine-tuning or continued learning with additional relevant data. One of the assumptions in the paper is that, given enough context, the LMs will apply a higher weight to given data since it's "correct" and a lower weight to their training data. This is key, and it's mentioned but not validated at all. I'd like to see how the reasoning given by the models can help determine the truth value of a triple.

The motivation and framing of the problem based on proprietary data is not accomplished, in my view, as the data used is open access. This is a simplification of the problem, and yet the evaluations show that most LMs tested fail. Another assumption taken is that of a closed-world assumption, where the KG used is taken as complete, and anything that's not in the KG is assumed to be false. This affects the corruption technique to generate "false" triples and phrases. It's also unclear if additional semantic knowledge about the relations is used to determine the validity of triples, as they can be symmetric or asymmetric. The corruption mechanism is the same used for KG completion models in the Link Prediction task.

Minor comments:
1. The reference "Team, 2024" should be "IBM, 2024"
2. The RDF abbreviation is not defined, and not everyone may be familiar with it.
3. Section 3.2 is a bit unclear and may benefit from having a few examples.
4. Table 1 should also include the source fact (true triple) to understand the corruption applied.
5. The paper refers to "facts", "triples", "triplets", and "assertions" interchangeably. Please choose one and stick to it.

title: Assessing LLMs' Factuality on Proprietary Data: A Benchmark Generation Methodology
review:
The paper proposes a methodology for evaluating the factuality of LLMs on any given structured database (typically triple stores). The idea is to focus on the LLM's ability to detect erroneous claims.
1) select a set of triples
2) randomly swap the subjects of triples with the same relation, to get erroneous triples
3) for each erroneous triple, use an LLM to generate a paragraph that contains the erroneous information
4) provide the paragraphs to the LLM to be assessed, and ask it to extract the erroneous information from the paragraph
5) Compute the ration of erroneous triples from step 2 that were successfully detected
The benchmark is then applied to evaluate several LLMs on triples form the WebNLG dataset.

The paper is well written, proposes an interesting and relevant idea for assessing knowledge in LLMs. Moreover, the experiments seem reproducible. However, I think that the work suffers from several limitations and provide little added-value in its current state: the implementation seems pretty straightforward, and no effort is made to evaluate the methodology itself. Moreover, I think that most of the author's conclusions (Section 5.2) do not hold.

A) Potential weaknesses of the methodology:
- A model could get a low score because of a low ability to extract triples from natural language, or because it uses unconventional aliases for entities. The methodology might be improved by controlling for these biases
- The LLM's ability to identify falsehood might not entail that the LLM will never generate falsehood

It could be interesting to see whether the author's metric correlates with human judgement or with other knowledge assessment metrics. See for example: Qingxiu Dong, Jingjing Xu, Lingpeng Kong, Zhifang Sui, and Lei Li. 2023. Statistical knowledge assessment for large language models, NeurIPS 2023.

 
B) Section 5.2:
- The authors state that the tasks of identifying correct and incorrect triples are theoretically equivalent, which is only true for functional triples. It is not possible to logically deduce that (China, shares a border with, Luxembourg) is wrong from (China, shares a border with, Mongolia).
- The authors interpret Table 2 as a confirmation of the fact that models are better at correct facts identification than false assertion identification. However, the tasks corresponding to both columns are very different: the task corresponding to false-assertion identification is probably simply harder do to the fact that the erroneous information has to be extracted from a paragraph
- How the first column of Table 2 is obtained is unclear unless we read the appendix; this should be clarified when describing the experiment design


C) Less important remark:
- The erroneous triples are not necessarily "subtly" false. Such a method could generate facts such as "Donald Trump is the father of Karl Marx", which is grossly false.

title: Distilling Cross-Modal Knowledge into Domain-Specific Retrievers for Enhanced Industrial Document Understanding
review:
**Summary**

This paper aims to address the problem of RAG systems underperforming in industrial domains due to a lack of domain knowledge and understanding of document structural elements.  A distillation approach is proposed to distill knowledge from LLMs and VLMs into a smaller domain-specific retriever. Experiments are conducted using datasets from two domains (shipbuilding and electrical equipment), showing that the domain-specific retriever outperforms alternative approaches at a lower inference cost. Ablations are conducted to study the importance of different components of the framework, with additional analyses provided for errors and query types. 

**Strengths**

1. The problem that this work addresses is important and is well-motivated in the introduction. 
2. The paper is written well and easy to follow overall.
3. Ablation studies provide empirical evidence to justify different components of the proposed approach.
4. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the domain-specific retriever at outperforming alternative methods while also being much more efficient. 

**Weaknesses**

1. Only two domains are studied in the experiments (shipbuilding and electrical equipment), which raises questions about how well the approach will generalize to other domains.
2. Additionally, the size of the datasets used for each domain is relatively small – for example, only 10 PDFs were used for training and 9 PDFs for testing in the shipbuilding domain. 
3. The error analysis is very brief and is lacking quantitative details of the analysis that was conducted (e.g., how many errors were analyzed, what was the distribution of error categories). 

**Questions/Suggestions**

1. The caption of Figure 1 should include some description of the notation that is used in the figure for better readability. 
2. Was any analysis conducted to validate the proposed method for constructing the hard negative set (as described in Section 3.1)? 
3. What is the intuition behind the student model outperforming the teacher model (lines 350-352)? Shouldn’t the student model only be able to approach the performance of the teacher model in practice?

title: Distilling Cross-Modal Knowledge into Domain-Specific Retrievers for Enhanced Industrial Document Understanding
review:
Strengths
1. High industrial relevance The paper addresses a real and pressing challenge—enhancing RAG in industrial domains where domain understanding and document structural elements (DSEs) like tables, figures, and formulas are critical. This makes the work highly applicable for industry adoption.
2. Strong performance and efficiency The proposed framework outperforms larger baselines while requiring significantly less computational complexity, which is especially valuable for real-world deployment where resources are constrained.
3. Thorough empirical evaluation The experiments are extensive and cover multiple real-world industrial datasets (shipbuilding and electrical equipment), offering convincing evidence of the method’s utility.
4. Clear presentation The paper is well-structured, easy to follow, and presents results in a way that facilitates understanding.

Weaknesses
1. Insufficient positioning against related work While the related work section reviews relevant literature, it does not clearly articulate how the proposed framework differs from or improves upon existing Domain-Specific RAG or Multimodal RAG approaches. A clearer discussion of the conceptual and technical distinctions would strengthen the contribution.
2. Gap addressing not explicit The paper would benefit from a more explicit explanation of which limitations of prior RAG variants are addressed by combining LLM and VLM knowledge distillation, and why this particular approach is uniquely suited to industrial domains with rich DSEs.

Overall Assessment

The paper proposes a practical, efficient, and high-performing solution to a problem of clear industrial significance. The method is well-implemented and convincingly evaluated, demonstrating both domain-specific understanding and the ability to handle visual-structural elements effectively. However, the lack of explicit differentiation from prior Domain-Specific and Multimodal RAG frameworks makes it harder to judge the novelty of the contribution. Strengthening the related work positioning would significantly improve the paper’s impact.
Recommendation: Marginally above acceptance threshold.

title: Distilling Cross-Modal Knowledge into Domain-Specific Retrievers for Enhanced Industrial Document Understanding
review:
Contributions
----------------
- This paper introduces (1) an effective method to distill data and ranking “groundtruth” from strong teacher VLM + LLM models to curate a dataset and (2) a training objective leveraging the curated dataset to train a lightweight retriever model for a domain specific RAG for documents containing structural elements.  This framework is designed to transfer textual and visual understanding from large teacher LLM (description of DSE) and VLM (ranking) into a student model for domain specific RAG. The framework involves 2 steps 

1.  Multimodal synthetic dataset: 
 - Distilling from teacher LLM (query): Parsing documents at page level into cropped DSEs and (using Qwen2.5-VL-7B) to generate captions that contain visual and structural semantics and anchor the generated caption in , sampling with hard negatives (semantically similar but contextually irrelevant wrt to positive document) and using VLM to generate descriptions that distinguish positive from hard negatives.
 - Distillation from teacher VLM (Synthetic Ranking Loss): Prompt VLM teacher with an input containing a set of (query, positive, hard negatives) for output relevant scores for each image. 
2. Retriever Training: Use the (query, positive, hard negative) tuple generated above as an input and train the student on a combined loss represented by the sum of the contrastive and distillation losses. The author stated that this combined loss enabled the model to capture both semantic and Document Structural Element (DSE). 

- The retrieval benchmarking results show that the fine-tuned student retriever model performs competitively with the teacher model (ColQwen-2.5-3B) across benchmarking metrics but the student model is ~5x smaller (in terms of no. params) compared to the teacher model and much model computationally efficient (9x faster, > 2000x fewer flops). 
- RAG benchmarking is performed using 100 human curated queries against strong baseline multiple RAG models. The results show strong performance against SoTA multimodal RAGs but still doesn’t beat the teacher model (ColQWen-2.5-3B with LLM). 
- Ablation results show that each component in the framework contributes positively toward the retrieval performance of the student retriever. 

Clarity: 
----------------
- The paper follows a standard publication format
- Figures and table captions are very terse in general, requiring the readers to jump back and forth between the main text and the data in the table to fully understand the results. 

Originality: 
----------------
- To the best of reviewer's knowledge, the main originality of this paper are 
1. The preprocessing - using the visual elements using VLM and insertion of the DSE description into the text part of the document, and including hard negatives into the prompt to the LLM to generate text description.
2. The distillation of ranking from VLM teacher. 
3. The use of fine-grain ranking loss from VLM teacher

Reproducibility: 
------------------
The distillation details and the prompts used and brief details of the experiments are provided in the Appendix. However, the code and the dataset are not shared.

Significance: 
---------------
This paper focuses on a novel method to train a compact, inference efficient retriever model by inferencing and distilling data from larger VLM + LLM teacher models. The performance of the fine-tuned student model is competitive with using the teacher VLM + LLM. For downstream applications, it’s worth asking whether it is more cost effective to fine-tune and deploy many domain retrievers or to use one strong VLM + LLM teacher model.  

Questions for the authors: 
------------------------------
In the error analysis section, the author observed an error type where the student model matches the incorrect condition reversing the entities (e.g. B fixed, A varying → A fixed, B varying). Could the author please suggest concrete further queries required to improve on this?

title: Advancing E-commerce Merchants Telemarketing with Synthetic Data-Driven LLMs
review:
This paper introduces a series of strategies, including multi-task extraction, role-playing between sales and merchants, prefix completion based on common Q&A pairs and post-processing, for data synthesis framework in e-commerce telemarketing field. 

This paper evaluates this work from comprehensive perspectives, offline and online evaluation, A/B test, and also propose and use different metrics.

This paper is easy to follow and also has enough contributions.

title: Advancing E-commerce Merchants Telemarketing with Synthetic Data-Driven LLMs
review:
This paper outlines and evaluates a strategy to synthesize data for fine-tuning a AI agent for telemarketing. It proposes generating three datasets --- one that is focused on the specifics of telemarketing, one that leverages these specifics to generate a conversational dataset, and one that incorporates session information --- that are then used to train a TeleBot. Using offline and on-line evaluation, the paper shows that these three datasets yields the best overall result on average, while focusing on specific ones may be better according to certain metrics. 

Strengths: This paper is relatively clear and is going in a great direction. The evaluation is comprehensive and the ablation studies are effective at providing necessary depths to the results. The use of an actual on-line evaluation is nice and would be something that should be given more attention. 

Weaknesses: Ultimately, readers of this paper will struggle with reproducibility and the results are moderate at best.  Given the differences shown by the ablation studies with LLM as a judge, it is critical that human evaluation is done on those as well. It leaves the reader with an open question as to whether the various datasets are beneficial or not in practice. All and all, I feel like there is still work to do around a stable foundation for the right synthetic data to generate.

title: Advancing E-commerce Merchants Telemarketing with Synthetic Data-Driven LLMs
review:
Pros:

1.	How to create high-quality supervised data for learning an effective conversational merchant-telemarketing agent is an useful topic to study in practice.

2.	The experiments are extensive.

3.	This paper is well-organized, and the writing is easy to follow. The visualization is nicely presented.


Cons:

1.	The statistical significance of human evaluation is not reported.

2.	Section 4.4 lacks necessary details about the post-processing pipeline.

title: On Assigning Product and Software Codes to Customer Service Requests with Large Language Models
review:
In this paper, the authors investigate the effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) in automatic assignment of product names and software version labels to customer Service Requests (SRs) under the environment of BLIND, a company operating in the networking domain. Since SR can be categorized into Metadata and Case Notes, LLMs need to use them for predicting their corresponding software version and product names for automatically dealing with SRs. For this purpose, the authors propose a pipeline-based system that refers predefined taxonomy filtered by a classifier to predict product names and software version labels by LLMs. Experimental results on the extracted BLIND data show the effectiveness of the MCQ prompt and GPT-4o compared with other LLMs.

Strengths:
- The proposed pipeline-based system is specifically constructed for the BLIND environment.
- The dataset used for the experiments is newly constructed based on the extraction from the actual BLIND data.
- To restrict the number of candidate labels, the pipeline has a specific classifier (filter) to remove unrelated labels from the candidate labels.
- The experimental results support the importance of the proposed pipeline system.

Weaknesses:
- Other knowledge-intensive approaches, like retrieval augmented generation, are not considered in the experiments.
- In terms of effectiveness, small language models (SMLs) should have been covered, considering this submission is for industry fields.

Comment:
There is no explanation what is the meaning of the MCQ prompts. The authors at least need to explain that MCQ means multiple-choice question for broad readers.

title: On Assigning Product and Software Codes to Customer Service Requests with Large Language Models
review:
# Summary

This manuscript introduces a prompting-based system for information extraction from customer service requests (SRs) at a networking company referred to as "BLIND." The core innovation lies in reframing the NER task as a multiple-choice problem, using the company's internal product and software ontology to provide a list of potential answers. To address the high cost of LLM API calls, the authors also developed a filtering classifier that identifies and isolates relevant documents within each SR, thereby reducing token volume. The experimental results demonstrate strong accuracy across both proprietary and open-source LLMs.

# Questions, Comments, and Suggestions

-   A crucial aspect of using proprietary LLMs for this task is data privacy. Given that service requests often contain sensitive customer information, it is unclear how the data is anonymized or handled before being sent to these models. A discussion on the anonymization process and compliance with data regulations would be a valuable addition to the manuscript.
-   The system appears to be heavily dependent on the completeness and accuracy of the pre-existing product and software ontology. It would be beneficial to include an analysis of how inaccuracies, omissions, or the introduction of new products not yet in the ontology could impact the system's performance and lead to specific failure modes.

title: On Assigning Product and Software Codes to Customer Service Requests with Large Language Models
review:
### Overview
- In this work, the authors investigated the use of SOTA LLMs for assigning product names and software version labels for customer service requests (SR) data, previously requiring human intervention. The work focusses on building classifiers which act as intermediate data generators for the final LLM call which makes the overall decision on product names and software versions.

### Significance
- This work is solving a specific problem and it is hard to see the generality in the approach. Neither is any attempt made by the authors to explain how this can be generalized to other problems. So, I think in the current state it is not suitable for publication at an esteemed venue such as EMNLP. It may be suitable for a patent or a workshop focusing on solving this specific problem.

### Additional Comments (Cons)
- Have the authors tries a RAG based approach where from the SR case notes and metadata they could extract only the relevant chunks and provide those to the LLM? It would be a good baseline to prove the usefulness of the approach defined here.

- There doesn't seem to be any attempt to even fine-tune the Q Prompt a little to make it understand the complicated nature of Product Name and Software version definitions. Mentioning "Product names are a mix of alphanumeric characters and look like: ABC-PN1805-X, D3500-WAS6K, CM3-IU" may not be enough. Instead the authors should try to be a little more descriptive on defining what a product name is made up of and how those parts are assembled to form the overall name, in case it is possible i.e., there is a pattern.



### Minor Formatting Comments
- MCQ is introduced in line 241 for the first time and as an abbreviation. It should be in full form.

title: A Proactive Reliability Metric for Detecting Failures in Language Model Training
review:
This paper focuses on a critical and costly problem in both industry and academia: predicting failures during large-scale neural network training. The authors propose a multi-signal fusion reliability metric, called R-Metric, designed to proactively and proactively predict training instabilities, thereby avoiding wasted resources. This method integrates signals from three levels: hardware, training, and model (λ, σ², ΔL). The experimental design utilizes controlled fault injection, validating the metric's effectiveness across 720 simulation runs and achieving impressive results (F1-Score 0.986, average 5.6 minutes of lead time). While the paper is clearly structured and robustly argued, it still has some weaknesses and areas for discussion regarding the methodological details and generalizability of the experimental design.

Strengths:

1. The paper addresses the pain points of "post-facto" fault handling in large-scale model training, and once addressed, these issues have strong practical value. 2. Fusion of three distinct signals—hardware failure rate (λ), gradient variance (σ²), and validation loss drift (ΔL)—into a unified reliability metric makes sense, is more comprehensive, and is logically sound.
3. The experiments cover a variety of modern model architectures (Llama-3, Mistral, MoE) and different types of faults, making the evaluation relatively comprehensive.

Weaknesses:

1. The gap between simulation experiments and real-world complexity: The core verification of the paper is based on controlled, predefined fault injections, and I'm concerned about the comprehensiveness of the coverage. For example, `GRADIENT_EXPLOSION` and `LR_SPIKE` are both transient and well-characterized faults. However, real-world training failures often stem from more complex, subtle, and gradually accumulating problems, such as (1) sporadic, subtle bit flips in a GPU's memory, which cause occasional errors in gradient calculations, which accumulate over time and ultimately lead to model crashes; (2) a minor bottleneck in data preprocessing or the I/O pipeline, which causes periodic delays in some worker nodes, disrupting the rhythm of synchronous training and affecting gradient consistency; (3) a rare bug in a distributed communication library (such as NCCL) or optimizer implementation that is only triggered under specific conditions. I suggest that the authors try to obtain and replay more historical failure logs in real production environments to verify the performance of R-Metric in these real-world scenarios.
2. The paper mentions that the weights are determined by grid search on the validation set. This raises a key question: Do these weights (and the threshold of 0.57) have good generalization properties? When the model architecture, scale (from 8 to 1024 cards), task, or dataset changes, is it necessary to re-run the expensive grid search? What are the specific definitions and parameters of the normalization method in Equation 4?
3. The writing needs to be improved. For example, the label at the top of each figure is inconsistent with the caption; Table 4; Table 2 presentation

title: A Proactive Reliability Metric for Detecting Failures in Language Model Training
review:
This paper provides a metric to reliably detect training failures early in LLMs. The authors point out that existing monitoring relies on overly simplistic metrics while more sophisticated systems like DeepSpeed are designed to fix failures rather than prevent them. The proposed metric design is three-fold - a Hardware Failure rate, a Variance metric measuring gradient norms to detect instability, and a Validation Loss Drift metric to detect a sudden deviation from the expected loss trajectory indicating that model quality is degrading. These three metrics are tested with a controlled fault injection protocol. 
The approach shows strong performance on common instability types, although the lead time could be larger. The comparison against Isolation Forest is a bit weak since this is not really a system designed for anomaly detection and such systems were not mentioned earlier in the paper.  It isn't truly necessary in my opinion anyway as these results are fine as standalone information. Perhaps better to use the space to calculate actual savings in real-world scenarios.
In other words, it seems clear that this tool could save considerable time and money for users. The authors should propose a plan for steps to improve the lead time.

title: A Proactive Reliability Metric for Detecting Failures in Language Model Training
review:
This paper introduces a dynamic metric for detecting LLM training instability. In the controlled experiments, the proposed metric successfully outperformed any individual signals and industrial baseline method. The experiments were carefully designed. However, as authors themselves pointed out, the experiments were limited due to academic constraints. Even though the authors had carefully selected three different types of models for testing their metric, all training runs were performed on 8 accelerators. So the ideal weights for combining different signals into a single metric, could have varied at different distributed training setup. It would be expensive to require each user to perform similar grid search for selecting weights, under their application scenario. It is also unclear whether the lead time measured on 8 accelerator, would be informative for a different training setup. Finally, the instabilities were artificially injected but the paper did not discuss how they were injected. Thus it is difficult to judge the soundness of the test. In Figure 2, it is confusing that the R metric raised even before fault injection, leading to doubt about the trustworthiness of the metric. 

Nitpick, the appendix also has some formatting issue.

title: From 2:4 to 8:16 sparsity patterns in LLMs for Outliers and Weights with Variance Correction
review:
The paper explores the use of 8:16 semi-structured sparsity as a method for compressing large language models (LLMs) to make them more efficient without significantly harming their performance. The authors argue that while techniques like quantization have been successful, structured sparsity methods have been less so due to their inflexibility and the negative impact of removing important "outlier" weights.

I found the presentation limiting: the authors jump into details very quickly w/o explaining the problems with existing approaches and their limitations. Same for the presentation of experimental results: it is hard to tease out the main findings from the plethors of results/tables. 

I suggest reorganizing the description of both the approach (2-4 main points), as well as main experimental results that make the work noteworthy. The details can then follow, as long as the related experiments.

Baselines should be clearly marked, and included in the tables, e.g. Table 4.

There are occasional typos, one right in the abstract ("perfromance").

title: From 2:4 to 8:16 sparsity patterns in LLMs for Outliers and Weights with Variance Correction
review:
- Strength:

This paper introduces a new sparsification scheme: the 8:16 semi-structured sparsity pattern, combined with simple techniques such as Variance Correction and SmoothQuant-inspired weight rebalancing to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) during compression. The experiments show that the model with the 8:16 sparsification pattern achieves comparable performance to the original model in terms of perplexity and zero-shot tasks, while the use of Structured Salient Weight Storage effectively boosts performance. These methods provide a new approach to compressing LLMs and hold potential industrial application value.

- Question&Weakness

1. The paper mainly focuses on the 8:16 sparsity pattern and does not explore or conduct ablation studies on other similar N:M patterns (e.g., 4:8, 6:12). If such experiments or comparisons have been conducted, could the results be provided to support the rationale for choosing 8:16? If not, besides flexibility, what are the specific theoretical or empirical reasons for selecting the 8:16 sparsity pattern?

2. From Tables 2 and 3, it is observed that the paper primarily reports zero-shot task accuracy. However, sparsification often also impacts inference time and computational overhead. Has the impact of 8:16 sparsification on inference time and resource consumption been considered? Specifically, in practical applications, inference latency and computational efficiency are important metrics for evaluating the effectiveness of sparsification methods. The lack of such evaluations may limit the industrial applicability of the proposed approach.

title: From 2:4 to 8:16 sparsity patterns in LLMs for Outliers and Weights with Variance Correction
review:
This paper investigates 8:16 semi-structured sparsity patterns as an alternative to the commonly used 2:4 pattern for LLM compression. The authors propose combining 8:16 sparsity with structured storage of salient weights, variance correction, and SmoothQuant-inspired weight equalization. 

Strengths:
1. The paper addresses a practical problem of LLM deployment efficiency, with direct implications for resource-constrained environments. 
2. The authors test multiple model families (LLaMA2, LLaMA3, Mistral) across various benchmarks, providing robust empirical evidence.
3. The finding that structured sparsity for outliers outperforms unstructured approaches has important implications for hardware-efficient implementations.

Weaknesses:
1. Lack of comparison with recent quantization methods and with other N:M patterns beyond 2:4 and 8:16
2. It would be better if more detailed analysis such as FLOPs analysis are conducted.
3. The limitations of N:M sparsity are well articulated, but the paper doesn't adequately address how 8:16 specifically overcomes these limitations beyond flexibility.

title: VENUS: A VLLM-driven Video Content Discovery System for Real Application Scenarios
review:
This paper presents VENUS, a new VLLM-driven Video Content Moderation (VCM) system.  It also presents a new VCM benchmark (VCM-bench).  The approach is also evaluated on 3 real-world scenarios.  The work clearly fits the scope of an industry research paper given an introduction of a new method, a new dataset, and offline and online evaluations that show the method works well.  My main concern is that there is so much packed into this 6 page paper it is hard to evaluate each of the contributions thoroughly (for this reviewer).  I would have recommended submitting the dataset as a separate paper and then focus on the approach and evaluations for the industry submission.

One other concern is that it was not clear if the dataset and code would be released.

title: VENUS: A VLLM-driven Video Content Discovery System for Real Application Scenarios
review:
This paper poses visual content moderation as a VQA task, and trains a VLM to solve it. To that end, they use an automatic annotator to collect a large amount of training data to fine-tune a VLM. The answer and its confidence score are calculated from the VLM logits. The resulting VLM VENUS is evaluated on the proposed benchmark VCM-Bench and shown to achieve SOTA results.

Strengths
- VCM-Bench is an important contribution that would enable systematic research into video content moderation systems.
- The proposed automatic annotator is a scalable way of collecting training data, and critical to the model performance.
- The proposed model VENUS achieves SOTA results on VCM-Bench, as well as some VQA benchmarks.
- VENUS has been deployed in real-world scenarios with success.
- Detailed ablation studies have been conducted with interesting insight.

Weaknesses
- (minor) Equations 1 and 2 would be easier to understand by breaking them into smaller steps using intermediate variables.
- (minor) The description of the inference support module should appear in the architecture subsection.

title: VENUS: A VLLM-driven Video Content Discovery System for Real Application Scenarios
review:
This paper presents VENUS, a VLLM-driven video content moderation system designed for real-world industrial deployment. Its primary contribution lies in the Automatic Policy-guided Sequential Annotator (APSA), which generates high-quality, reasoning-rich, policy-specific data to address the scarcity of annotated samples for rare or evolving moderation policies.

Pros:
1. This paper proposes a strong practical motivation and problem relevance.
2. Novel data engine (APSA) with sequential evaluation ensures high-quality annotations.
3. Demonstrated performance gains in both domain-specific and general benchmarks.
4. Real-world deployment results and measurable business impact.
5. Lower training cost compared to high-performing baselines (e.g., LLaVA-OV).

Cons:
1. The experiment depends on the specific LLM. Cross-architecture generalization is not fully explored.
2. The processing time of the proposed model is not well-compared with baselines.
3. Although the performance is significantly improved in a few real scenarios, the authors do not discuss whether the computational cost is acceptable in real scenarios.

title: BookFactory: A Modular Pipeline for Generating Information-Rich Ultra-Long Books
review:
This paper tries to solve the challenges of ultra-long book generation with a modular pipeline BookFactor. and proposes an evaluation metric BookScore. 

Strengths:
- The well-designed modular pipeline including draft-then-refine outline generation, iterative decomposed content generation, trivia enrichment, and semantic-guided image grounding, makes sense.
- The experiments show empirical gains.

Weaknesses:
- Unfair evaluation: The proposed evaluation metric is designed for this proposed method.  The size of test set is small. Use limited baselines.

title: BookFactory: A Modular Pipeline for Generating Information-Rich Ultra-Long Books
review:
### Paper Topic And Main Contributions
- **Problem addressed:**
The authors propose a pipeline able to generate long-form structured books. They adopt a modular approach able to incrementally build an outline, refine it using keywords and generate paragraphs that contain trivia retrieved using RAG. Finally, they also integrate image generation to complement the generated text.
- **Main contribution(s):**  
	- Modular long-form generation pipeline
	- RAG for trivia and image integration (grounding)
	- Evaluation corpora
	- *BookScore* composite score to assess quality
- **Relation to prior work:**  
	- Integrates with prior work on long-form generation with the added benefit of grounding generation of facts and images.
- **Key results/claims:**  
	- Incrementally generating chapters leads to higher overall ROUGE and results on LLM-as-a-judge evaluations than previous SOTA.
	- Refining an outline for generation leads to better structure.
	- Grounding image and trivia generation helps to build better quality content.

### Reasons to Accept
1. Tackles long-form generation with grounding
1. Inclusion of trivia retrieval and image generation seems promising (Figure 2)
1. Specific evaluations highlight the benefit of the approach for trivia retrieval and context grounded image generation
1. Writing is overall clear, some details are provided in the appendices

### Reasons to Reject
1. Authors only evaluate against only two long-form generation pipelines; additional methods could help gain perspective (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.07170).
2. Introduction talks about proficiency on multiple genres and domain. Yet, no evaluation and too few details about the 18 evaluation books are given to support this claim.
3. Building on remark 2., evaluation on other (shorter) long-form evaluation datasets could give more strength to these claims (LongWriter-6k).
4. *BookScore* metric is able to take into account trivia retrieval and image generation. Yet, the pipeline proposed is the only one considering such content, thus favoring it if we consider all the scores contributing to the metric.
5. Evaluation relies solely on metrics and LLM-as-a-judge. Yet, human evaluation of excerpts could help gain insight into the real benefit of trivia inclusion and quality of generated content (e.g A/B testing against baselines).
6. \[minor\] Baselines could be more fairly evaluated against CATE and SGIG  using Qwen3-32B/Qwen2.5-VL-32B in place of GPT-4V and DALLE-3

### Questions For The Authors
1. Line 150: How are $K_O$ words extracted from the draft outline?
2. Does the 100K word limit arise from the model constraints (Qwen3)?
3. Dataset is discussed lines 260-263, 290-294, 372-375 but details about it are lacking.
4. In the unified RAG pipeline, what are the sources retrieved in the vector DB, how are they integrated in prompts ?
5. Line 302: Please provide more details and references for factual accuracy and interest level scoring

### Typos Grammar Style And Presentation Improvements:
1. Line 151 *Thoese* -> *These*
2. Line 186  *insufficient* -> *sufficient*

title: BookFactory: A Modular Pipeline for Generating Information-Rich Ultra-Long Books
review:
This paper proposes a "Bookstore" pipeline for generating long form books with enhancements by adding trivia and images. The paper also proposes a new metric called "book store"in order to assess the generations. 
The proposed pipeline include the following steps: 
1. Generating an outline
2. Generating content in an iterative fashion with keyword based retrieval to ground the generations
3. trivia enrichment
4. image addition

Strengths:
1. The propose adding images and trivia to increase the interestingness of the generated books. This inductive bias seemed interesting. 
2. The paper gives nice ablations describing the importance of various components and enrichments. 

Weakness: 
1. No human evals were done. Specifically for more open ended task of creative text generation, human evals are able to give a perspective which "LLMs as a judge" are still not able to have. 
2. One major outcome of the paper is BookScore metric. But it is barely defined in Section 4.3 . I think it should be moved from appendix to the main text. 
3. Although the authors propose tis pipeline of generating storeies, the novelty is limited. Each step is limited in novelty. If the main contribution was efficiently or scale, it's not mentioned in the paper. 
4. The baselines in the evaluation are limited. Why not compare with Seed-Strong StoryLLava (which the authors themselves mention in the related works section) as being able to generate multi-modal output.

title: From Understanding to Engagement: Personalized Pharma Video Clips via Vision-Language Models
review:
The paper proposes a use case in generating video highlights from long videos, by using multiple available MLLM tools. Claimed benefits are lower cost and high customization.

Based on the report, I am unable to see significant contributions and scientific relevance to the conference. Some concerns below:

1. The project aims to improve the efficiency of video highlights generation based on generative models. Authors claim to evaluate the proposed system on Video-MME, however I did not see specific results on Accuracy on the benchmark.
2. While the focus problem is interesting, I fail to see technical novelty in the presented work, which is focused on a step-by-step application of existing tools/models like Gemini 2.5, Whisper V2/V3, Claude 3.5 Sonnet. If I am missing a major aspect of the work, happy to learn more.
3. Writing is unclear and often not to the point. For instance, in Main Results, there is a rather long discussion on FFMPEG related issues. The role of this paragraph in the section is not clear.
4. Unknown aspects - there are certain claims about parts of the work which are missing important details. Examples below.
Line 337: what is the “method” being referred to? Please describe in detail - the problem being discussed is quite interesting.
Line 246: what is the “cut and merge” algorithm?
5. Related work: I found it hard to connect the discussion in related work with the present work. The discussions about technical methods like diffusion based video generation does not seem relevant. Paragraphs mentioning closed-source models seem incomplete.
6. Minor: is “property” dataset intended to be “proprietary” instead? If not, please elaborate.

title: From Understanding to Engagement: Personalized Pharma Video Clips via Vision-Language Models
review:
The paper proposes a framework to extract salient short clips from a lengthy video in the pharmaceutical domain. The idea behind is to extract the video and the transcripts, extract the important clips from this information and eventually generating a voice-over when required.

Video summarization is a relevant task with many potential applications, thus the paper has eventually some potential. But at the current state there are really many issues to be addressed.

The introduction does not seem to properly explain and define the task. It talks about Frames-to-Video, Video-to-Video (chosen), Prompt-to-Video, and pharmaceutical domain, but without explaining at all the end task and how the domain plays a role here. Only from the hard-to-follow methodology it becomes more clear that this is a clip extraction method, but again the target and requirements of the desired clips are not clearly specified.

By looking at the framework explanation, there is no information about what is really new about it compared to prior work, and why it should be significant. There is also no evaluation whatsoever, neither in automatic terms to check whether it can really extract the most salient clips (for instance in terms of precision and recall with an annotated evaluation dataset), nor through human evaluation against other baselines. Section 5 explains a lot of engineering details and empirical findings in building the framework, but without a clear objective and baselines to compare with, they seem a bit out of context. And in no way the specific domain seems to play any role in the overall framework design. Furthermore, for a framework to be used in real-world applications, I would expect also an analysis of non-functional requirements such as complexity, cost, latency and other relevant metrics.

In conclusion, this submission seems more a project report than the description of something really novel. From the information given, it is hard to identify which are the really novel elements, how much the framework as a whole would be useful, especially compared to other off-the-shelf methods, and the specific pharmaceutical domain seems almost lost. I would strongly suggest a deep revision, starting with the comparison with other state-of-the-art clip extraction methods to identify potential strengths and weaknesses.

title: From Understanding to Engagement: Personalized Pharma Video Clips via Vision-Language Models
review:
### Paper Summary

This paper proposes a Video-to-Video Clips Generation framework based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Audio-Language Models (ALMs), which aims to solve the problems of low efficiency and high cost in processing long video content in the pharmaceutical industry. The method combines Whisper for speech transcription, uses LLM and VLM for paragraph selection and personalized generation, and optimizes the smooth connection of audio and video through the cut & merge algorithm. The paper conducted experiments on the Video-MME benchmark and its own pharmaceutical video dataset, claiming to have achieved a 3-4 times increase in processing speed and a 4 times reduction in cost, while also having high customizability and privacy protection capabilities.

### Strengths

1. The paper focuses on long video summaries and high-fidelity clip generation, and has strong applicability.
2. The proposed solution is not just an algorithm improvement, but a complete pipeline combining Whisper (ALM), Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash (VLM), and prompt engineering.
3. The author provides a detailed processing time comparison, showing that the proposed method has significantly improved the speed of long video processing and reduced the cost by about 4 times.
4. The paper emphasizes the cost and speed advantages of the "single modality (ALM) + LLM" solution, and introduces VLM for image content understanding in the absence of speech. This idea has reference value for industrial applications.

### Weaknesses

1. The current experimental results mainly focus on the comparison of processing speed and cost, while the evaluation of the "quality" of the generated video clips only focuses on the number and length of clips. The lack of automated indicators (such as Clip Coherence Score, Summary Informativeness) or interpretable results based on user surveys makes it less persuasive.
2. The core "cut & merge algorithm" and personalized generation strategy are only presented in descriptive language, lacking pseudocode or complexity analysis, and cannot ensure that the method can be reproduced.
3. The paper proposes that personalization can be achieved through "role definition" and "prompt injection", but does not show quantitative indicators of its improved effect. For example, does the user's choice of different roles significantly affect the topic coverage of the clips?
4. There is a lack of end-to-end comparison with widely used commercial SaaS tools (such as OpusClip and Synthesia), especially in long video processing and compliance support, which is key for Industry Track papers.

title: Memory-Efficient Backpropagation for Fine-Tuning LLMs on Resource-Constrained Mobile Devices
review:
This paper introduces Memory-Efficient Backpropagation (MeBP), a novel method for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on resource-constrained mobile devices like smartphones. The key challenge is that standard training methods, which use backpropagation, consume too much memory for mobile hardware. The proposed MeBP solution offers a way to perform this fine-tuning with a memory footprint of less than 1GB, making it practical for on-device applications.

The baseline chosen is the (zeroth-order) ZO optimization method. 

The MeBP method is built upon gradient checkpointing, a technique that reduces memory usage by re-computing parts of the model during the training process instead of storing them in memory. 

To further optimize for mobile devices, MeBP incorporates several key features:
. Lazy Weight Loading and Decompression: the main model weights are kept in a compressed state (using 4-bit quantization) and are only decompressed and loaded into memory when they are needed for a computation.
. Memory-Mapped Activations: intermediate values, known as activations are written to and read from storage using memory-mapping, which significantly lowers the RAM usage.
. LoRA Fine-Tuning.

I found the paper well written and the experimental results convincing. 

Not being intimately familiar with the area, I am not sure to what extent the baseline chosen is indeed representative.

One meta-point is that it's unclear why such optimizations need to be carried out on-device instead of on the server and then sending the resulting LM to the device. The authors should explain.

title: Memory-Efficient Backpropagation for Fine-Tuning LLMs on Resource-Constrained Mobile Devices
review:
### Summary

The paper introduces a method for memory-efficient backpropagation that enables LoRA training of language models on mobile devices. The approach is evaluated on Qwen models (0.5B, 1B, 3B) and Gemma3 models (1B and 4B), demonstrating successful training within a 1GB memory constraint. The proposed method converges significantly faster than baseline Zero-Order (ZO) optimization techniques and their recent variants, while also achieving superior results. The memory footprint remains under 2× in the worst-case scenarios. This is accomplished through base model weight compression and by splitting the backpropagation computation into separate graphs, where checkpoints and weights are lazily decompressed and loaded on demand.

### Strengths

- The paper addresses a practical and relevant problem with real-world use cases.
- It demonstrates clear improvements in language modeling tasks over ZO methods, both in terms of convergence speed and model quality.
- The paper is well-written and accessible; even readers without deep expertise in the field can follow the methodology and results.

### Weaknesses

- The evaluation is limited to a single language modeling dataset, which may represent a keyboard completion task. It would strengthen the paper to include additional tasks representative of mobile training scenarios to assess generalizability.
- While the method outperforms the baseline MeZO, it would be valuable to compare results against standard fine-tuning approaches without memory constraints, even as a high bar.
 
### Originality

- Based on a preliminary search (noting that I am not an expert in this specific subfield), I could not find prior examples of first-order optimization techniques applied to training on iPhone or similar mobile platforms. This suggests a novel contribution.

### Reproducibility

- Although the overall algorithm is clearly described, the absence of shared code makes reproduction challenging. This is particularly important given the likely presence of numerous implementation details that affect efficiency and stability.

title: Memory-Efficient Backpropagation for Fine-Tuning LLMs on Resource-Constrained Mobile Devices
review:
The authors present a memory-efficient method for finetuning small LLMs on mobile devices like iPhone 15 Pro Max. Their method makes use of existing techniques like quantization, gradient-checkpointing and LoRA to achieve low-memory finetuning on mobile devices. While none of these techniques are new, together they form a practical solution that outperforms existing zeroth-order methods like MeZO for finetuning on mobile devices. The evaluation is based on the WikiText data and the authors did a careful comparison of the runtime, memory requirements, and convergence speed of their method compared to MeZO. Overall this is a good paper with practical innovation.

Suggestions:
- It would be more convincing to have experiments on more datasets beyond just WikiText.

title: eSapiens's DEREK Module: Deep Extraction \& Reasoning Engine for Knowledge with LLMs
review:
This is an advertisement posing as a paper. It lacks key citations and explanations, and does not contain sufficient detail to be of value to the community.

1. Limitations Section

A limitations section is included, but mostly discusses generic limitations of RAG systems. Deeper thought into specific limitations of this implementation (and potential fixes) would make the section more insightful.

2. Author Anonymity

The paper is clearly written by employees of eSapiens. While using company names is not necessarily a violation of author anonymity, given the positioning and limited content of the paper it is highly suspect.

3. Novelty & Impact

RAG systems are well-established in the field, and this paper purports to enhance the state of the art. While it is likely there is novelty and impact in the implemented system, there isn't enough detail to thoroughly support that conclusion, likely because the authors are trying to protect intellectual property and/or maintain a competitive advantage. Unfortunately, you can't do both, and in this setting that severely detracts from the value of the submission.

The experiments compare against a baseline of a previous implementation and an out-of-the-box FAISS system, neither of which are sufficient to show true improvement in SOTA. It is understandable that some specifics about the VC example must be omitted, but there is no information about the experimental setup; did they perform a controlled test? what data was collected? how long was the testing period? did they control for differences in complexity of deals that went in the old vs. new system? Or was it all anecdotal from the client?

4. Reproducibility

There are not nearly enough details included to allow for reproducibility. If the goal of the paper were for others to be able to use the innovation and impact supposedly present in the system (rather than advertise a product), it would for example include:
- specific examples of re-prompting a user query into CO-STAR format
- implementation details about how the LangGraph verifier actually works, ideally with examples
- any detail at all about how TRACe is implemented
As written, none of this information is present so a reader would have to guess on significant parts and functionality of the system.

5. Clarity & Structure

The paper is laid out well in a standard structure, but as noted above is missing important reproducibility details. In addition, however, citations to TRACe, CO-STAR, and what a langgraph verifier, or even a two-sentence explanation of each of them are missing.

title: eSapiens's DEREK Module: Deep Extraction \& Reasoning Engine for Knowledge with LLMs
review:
The author proposes developing a software package or module to perform question answering on existing documents. The approach uses RAG and LLMs by first ingesting the data into a vector database, retrieving the required documents, and then generating an answer. However, this pipeline—using existing frameworks such as LangChain—is not novel. This is currently a common practice for hosting such systems.

Besides the lack of novelty, the author has used the LegalBench dataset, which is already well-known to the community and does not provide new insights. This falls short of the industry track’s expectation to present knowledge or findings not already known to the academic community.

The paper also requires proofreading (e.g., missing figure reference in line 197).

Finally, the manuscript is not well-positioned and does not compare its approach with other existing methods, making it difficult to see how it advances the field.

title: eSapiens's DEREK Module: Deep Extraction \& Reasoning Engine for Knowledge with LLMs
review:
The authors present a RAG-based system that controls the construction of prompts based on retrieved task-relevant documents, which somehow constrain prompt engineering so that users can find more relevant information.

Pros:
P1: The system described seems to be very straightforward and relevant to the targeted task. It would be great to use it in one's own work. 
P2: The system description is easy to read and provides detailed information on some evaluations in the appendix.
P3: The system combines a variety of methods and technologies, seemingly offering the desired added value for the intended users. It is reasonable to expect this paper to attract the attention of the relevant industry community, who will want to learn about the system's potential.

Cons: 
C1: The paper is written in a very repetitive manner. In many places, the authors reiterate basic information about the approach and its evaluation, which seems unnecessary. Some passages read like verbatim repetitions, and this occurs several times in this rather short paper. This wastes valuable space that could have been used to discuss the topic in more detail.
C2: The interesting aspect of the paper concerning the retrieved documents, specifically how they constrain prompt engineering by necessitating reflection or proper citation, is not addressed sufficiently. Instead of providing an explanation to help the reader understand the approach taken, the paper merely mentions what has been done. One therefore gains the impression that something interesting is being done here; however, the description remains too superficial, so that one does not get any deeper deeper understanding of the underlying algorithm.
