This seems unexpected for vision models considering the complexity of the problem space as compared to text-only models, and could provide guidance to future work seeking to get the most out of limited parameter space in vision-language training.

Cons:
- The work basically uses an existing model (PatentFormer) to restructure the patent data for a VLM without any significant changes to the VLM's training or evaluation framework. To call PatentVision a novel model is not entirely accurate, considering that PatentFormer is already well-defined and hasn't been changed when applied in this study. It would likely be trivial for a future study to make substantial improvements on a PatentVision model using data augmentation or more complex reasoning at inference time, or to implement a solution that more effectively leverages the structured nature of the patent images. The authors should reconsider whether the work's main contribution is an entirely new model for patent image processing, or a robust evaluation of how readily VLMs in general adapt to challenges in the problem space of patent image reasoning, which seems to be the current interest of the results.
- The results focus mainly on the effect of LoRA rank on model performance rather than exploring the novelty of the model training method. While interesting, studying the utility of LoRA rank as a hyperparameter doesn't seem directly relevant to the specific task of reasoning over patent images. Additionally, the extensive analysis of LoRA rank generally seems to point to an expected tendency toward using rank values toward the middle of the distribution, rather than low or high values, when training a model on a new task. If the authors choose to focus on LoRA, it would be more productive to run further ablation tests to test the interaction of rank with vision-specific considerations such as image resolution as in Fig. 7. One can imagine many other considerations related to the patent images specifically that are worth studying, including the level of detail provided in the images, complexity of the drawings, and presence/absence of text. Ideally, the paper would focus more consistently on the value of the structured data provided by PatentFormer, particularly through ablation of the different types of information added by PatentFormer. Furthermore, the paper is missing the obvious test of training PatentVision on non-preprocessed data, i.e. determining the relative value of the PatentFormer preprocessing versus the typical use case of providing only the raw data to the model.
- The results are difficult to parse due to the inconsistent presentation of data, e.g. sometimes in bar charts, sometimes in radial plots. The authors really should present most of the results as simple tables to standardize the data organization and allow for a more coherent narrative across sub-results. The radial plots in particular become very difficult to parse with more than a few axes to consider, and the many sub-colors and axes in Figure 3 make the plots appear virtually identical.
- Some of the metrics seem redundant, e.g. the Rouge L (sum) results largely mirror the Rouge L results. More explanation for why each metric is necessary would help address possible redundancy among metrics.

title: PatentVision: A multimodal method for drafting patent applications
review:
Weaknesses:

Some details are unclear:

1. The dataset section mentions patent experts, but the annotation process, evaluation methods, and expert feedback are not described. 

2. The matching between patent images and the corresponding claims is often ambiguous — does this introduce noise into the dataset?

3. The comparison between PatentVision and PatentFormer is primarily based on metrics. Including some qualitative generation examples to highlight the differences between PatentVision and PatentFormer would help clarify the advantages brought by using LVLMs.

Strengths:

1. The paper proposes a multimodal patent specification generation framework that combines images, patent claims, and optional figure descriptions. It leverages fine-tuned vision-language models for generation.

2. The authors annotated the dataset with fine-grained information such as images and claims. If released, these annotations would greatly benefit the research community, and we hope the dataset will be made public.

3. The paper compares the proposed multimodal approach with text-only methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating multiple modalities.

4. The authors provide thorough discussions on the role of image descriptions, resolution, and other contributing factors.

title: PatentVision: A multimodal method for drafting patent applications
review:
I thank the authors for working on this topic, it is a useful application to use LVLMs to draft patents specifications and make the process smoother. he authors fine-tune models with LoRA on a newly constructed dataset of 230K claim+diagram-to-specification samples in the CPC code G06F. I first look at the strengths of the paper, followed by key weaknesses and suggestions. 

Strengths:
- The paper extends text only previous methods (patent former) that look at section generation of patents to complete specification generation.
- Dataset contribution: Creation of a large-scale 230K multimodal dataset for CPC code G06F with careful preprocessing.
- Shows (some) improvement over patent former on n-gram based metrics like ROUGE


Weaknesses:
- Figure 3 is very hard to understand and follow. What am I looking at? The results seem to show marginal gains over patentformers scores on the metrics.
- Figure 4: Shows that finetuning helps as compared to plain pre-training, while interesting, it is to be expected.
- Figure 5: There is limited consistency in the number of epochs and performance gain. 
- The first question I see is how do Commercial LLMs do out of the box? Given all LLM providers sell services to other companies, where they ensure data privacy.
- Additionally, many of the previous research has shown insufficiency of all n-gram based metrics in evaluating nuanced domain specific summaries. For example https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.13249. How about LLM as a judge or other fine-grained rubric based evaluation metrics? 
- Human studies are missing: I understand that human studies are not always doable, but I would assume this would fall into real life deployment considerations to ensure experts would use this tool and support it.


Suggestions:
- Writing: Many statements do not add value to the the key contributions of this paper. For example, likes 13-16 in abstract could be made concise and effective in portraying both, the goals and the actual results.
- Inference costs: The paper claims to have high inference costs for evaluation and randomly samples 1000 instances for evaluation. It would be good to know how much is the said inference costs as compared to training costs.
- **Strongly recommend** re-making the figures and presenting some data as tables.

**Update**: I thank the authors for the reply, I will keep the scores as is.

title: Language Model Adaptation for the French Defense Domain
review:
The paper addresses domain adaptation of large language models for the French defense domain. The authors describe a pipeline involving two main steps, CPT and IFT applied to Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, using curated domain-specific texts and generated instructions. They also construct an evaluation benchmark combining synthetic tasks and general-purpose datasets to assess performance in the mentioned domain and also being able to generalize on out of domain.
Pros : 
* Comprehensive evaluation results. The authors cover synthetic benchmarks, small expert-curated sets, and general-purpose datasets (MMLU, IFEval), at least in concept.

Cons: 
* The paper describes concepts/recipes that are quite standard and well documented already. Synthetic data augmentation using LLMs and grammar based variations are also quite standard practices.
* Limited technical insights : The paper is well written with clarity, but it reads more like an internal project than a research paper. No deep analysis of why certain adaptation strategies work or fail or how results compare to alternative methods (parameter-efficient tuning, multi-domain mixtures)

title: Language Model Adaptation for the French Defense Domain
review:
Paper establishes the problem of language adaptation in French defense domain and lack of publicly available benchmarks. It provides comprehensive details of results and evaluation, however, it lacks novelty of their solution beyond what's already publicly available.
Contributions - 
    1. CPT, IFT isn't novel and so results of better adaptation are generic and expected.
    2. Dataset curation and benchmark.

Authors don't provide any defense domain specific challenges, for instance, sensitivity of data, ethical concerns, domain vocabulary, etc. and related solutions adapted for the same. Such details would have given more context on novelty of the paper beyond generic CPT, IFT methods.
Paper can further benefit from examples of instructions generation and task results.

Minor points -
- Authors give some details on processing dense information like glossaries, acronyms into tabular structures (line # 133-136). Some more details on how these tables were further processed would have been helpful. Same thing applies for images, diagrams also but authors pointed it as a limitation.
- Table 6 reference is not found or at least I couldn't find it. Appendix C seems to be empty. It's difficult to follow appendix sections arrangement in the flow of main sections. Paper can be restrutured a little bit for easier follow ups.

title: Language Model Adaptation for the French Defense Domain
review:
Novelty & Impact

The work addresses language model adaptation but presents only minor variations on existing fine-tuning and domain adaptation approaches. The methodological differences from prior work are incremental, and the reported performance gains are relatively small. As a result, the novelty is limited, and the potential impact on the research community appears modest.

Author Anonymity

The submission generally maintains author anonymity, with no explicit self-revealing content. However, some dataset selections and phrasing could implicitly point to the authors’ previous work, slightly weakening strict anonymity.

Reproducibility

Reproducibility is hindered by incomplete details on training setups, hyperparameters, and dataset preprocessing. While high-level descriptions are provided, there is no accompanying code or configuration files, and the evaluation process is not described in enough depth to ensure a faithful replication of results.

Clarity

The paper’s organization is acceptable, but certain technical sections lack sufficient explanation, especially regarding how the proposed adaptation method diverges from standard fine-tuning. Figures and tables are present but not always easy to interpret in the context of the narrative. The related work section does not clearly differentiate the proposed method from existing literature.

title: Language Model Adaptation for the French Defense Domain
review:
This paper describes the procedure to conduct the adaptation of large language model for the French defense domain. Specifically, the authors collect corpus from the French Defense Domain, synthesize instruction dataset and benchmarks, and compare language models under different domain adaptation settings. Experimental results show that the model adapted for French defense domain exhibits strong performance on domain-specific benchmarks with the nearly intact general ability.

- **Pros**: The domain adaptation setting, where language model have strong domain-specific performance and general ability after adaptation, maybe benefit future work.

- **Cons**: 

  (1). It is unknown that the reliability and similarity between LLM-as-a-judge and human evaluation. I recommend the authors to conduct human evaluation experiments to show the superiority of the language model adapted for this domain than other models.

  (2). There are some spelling errors and missing contents:

      (a). Line 044: (Ruiz and Sell, 2024) --> Ruiz and Sell (2024) (The same problem in the Line 048)
      (b). Line 372: Tun3 --> Run 3
      (c). Table 4: missing the "Closed-run2" row
      (d). Line 403: The and --> The xxx and (missing something)

title: Enhancing Food-Domain Question Answering with a Multimodal Knowledge Graph: Hybrid QA Generation and Diversity Analysis
review:
This paper proposes a novel pipeline to enhance food-domain question answering (QA) by integrating recipe retrieval and multi-granularity instruction tuning. The authors introduce a framework that retrieves relevant recipes as context, combines them with food knowledge, and fine-tunes an LLM using coarse- and fine-grained instructions. A new dataset, RecipeRag, is also presented to support food-related QA grounded in retrieved textual data. Experiments on multiple QA models demonstrate consistent improvements across metrics.

1. It is an interesting work that combines large-scale multimodal knowledge graph like nutritional and visual data crucial for in- 067 gredient recognition and dish presentation to enhance the diversity of foodie qa. 

2. The presentation is good, with organized logical flow.

3. The extensive results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed structured knowledge graph on LLMs.

title: Enhancing Food-Domain Question Answering with a Multimodal Knowledge Graph: Hybrid QA Generation and Diversity Analysis
review: The proposed application is interesting and compelling. The strategies applied sound solid, but the evaluation is only automatic, and based on shallow metrics that compare the surface of productions. A more reliable, insightful, qualitative analysis is needed for everyone to assess how well this approach work: you need expert human evaluators and inter-judge agreement!

title: Enhancing Food-Domain Question Answering with a Multimodal Knowledge Graph: Hybrid QA Generation and Diversity Analysis
review:
**Summary**

This paper proposes a framework for question-answering in the food domain by augmenting LLMs with a multimodal knowledge graph (MMKG). An large-scale MMKG for the food domain is introduced, along with 40k QA pairs that were constructed from the MMKG using templates and LLM augmentation. Fine-tuning experiments are conducted using LLaMA-3.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5. Multiple evaluations and analyses are conducted using the MMKG and generated QA dataset, including a clustering-based diversity assessment and hallucination detection. 

**Strengths**

1. The constructed MMKG and QA dataset are valuable resources for the understudied food domain.
2. Experimental results show that augmenting QA models with the MMKG generally improves performance.
3. Analyses on diversity, hallucination, and retrieval vs. generation strategy provides evidence to support different aspects of the proposed framework. 

**Weaknesses**

1. Overall the paper is poorly organized and difficult to follow. The abstract is overly dense in describing experimental results without providing motivation for the work. The organization of the introduction is also odd – having multiple subsections seems unnecessary and the entire section would benefit from being re-organized to simply start with the motivation, a description of a problem, and a more brief/concise description of the contributions. 
2.  The related work section is lacking citations to substantiate parts of the discussion. For example, what “recent NLP benchmarks” are being referred to in line 186? What “prior MMKGs” are being referred to in line 196? What are the “existing methods” which you refer to in line 184? Is there no other related work on question-answering in the domain of food? 
3. The paper is lacking in details necessary to fully understand the work that was done. For example, the authors refer to “joint fine-tuning” of LLaMA-3.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5 without ever actually defining what they mean by this. Other examples of statements which are unclear include lines 311-313 (what does “ground truth images generate QA pairs” mean?) and lines 323-325 (what does “model refinement” mean?)
4. While the breadth of results and analyses are appreciated, Section 5 is lacking in discussion of the results and seems to instead simply describe them without providing much if any commentary.
5. The image hallucination detection approach seems flawed in that it assumes any missing details in LLaVA’s description of an image are attributed to those details being missing in the image. Couldn’t this failure alternatively be attributed to LLaVA’s own deficiency in fully describing the image? As no human evaluation was conducted, it’s hard to judge the validity of this approach.

title: Think-Search-Patch: A Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning Framework for Repository-Level Code Repair
review:
This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented reasoning framework, Think-Search-Patch, for code repair. Specifically, the model first decomposes the coding task, then searches for relevant code snippets, and finally generates standardized patches. The system is constructed via a two-stage training pipeline, comprising supervised fine-tuning in the first stage and direct preference optimization in the second. Experiments conducted on the SWE-bench Lite benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
Building an autonomous agent for programming tasks is highly valuable, particularly for realistic scenarios such as repository-level code repair. This work shows strong potential for real-world application.
The proposed Think-Search-Patch framework is well motivated, enabling the model to break down complex tasks and retrieve relevant information from the repository. This design enhances the controllability and interpretability of the reasoning process.
Experimental results on SWE-bench show that the proposed method outperforms strong baselines, including GPT-4 and Claude 3 Opus.
There are also some weaknesses.
1. While the Think-Search-Patch framework is reasonable, its novelty is somewhat limited. The idea of reasoning before retrieval, and retrieval-augmented decision-making, has been widely explored in prior work. However, given the industry track context, this may not be a critical concern.
2. The experiments are only conducted using Qwen2.5-coder-7B-Instruct. Evaluating additional models would help assess the generalizability of the proposed approach.
3. Including comparisons with more advanced models, such as OpenAI O1 or DeepSeek R1, or at least providing evaluation results against them, would help clarify the current method’s limitations.

title: Think-Search-Patch: A Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning Framework for Repository-Level Code Repair
review:
The paper proposes **Think-Search-Patch (TSP)**, a retrieval-augmented reasoning framework for repository-level code repair, and introduces a novel dataset and training strategy tailored to this task. It addresses a significant gap in current LLM capabilities: the poor performance of models on multi-file repair tasks with cross-file dependencies, as seen in benchmarks like SWE-bench.

**Strengths**:
-  The assumption for low accuracy is clearly stated as the long file context length pulled by RAG. It would have been helpful to validate this with some experiments eg. does shorter context lead to better pass rate.
- Novel approach to improving retrieval by moving beyond file level retrieval (typical in RAG methods) and instead using AST-based indexing at the class/function level, which demonstrably reduces irrelevant context and improves repair precision. 
- In terms of training, the two stage pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) using LLM judged preferences is explained clearly, well structured and tailored to the TSP architecture. The design aligns well with first improving the retrieval-augmented reasoning systems and then using preference learning in the second stage.

**Weaknesses**:
- In the related work section, the description towards the end clarifies that there are two main approaches used to solve this problem, 1) agent based approaches and 2) Pipeline based approach. However, the section abruptly ends there. It is left to the reader to identify which approach TSP falls under and why.
- Most of the discussion focuses on comparing with RAG based solutions, not presenting a position with respect to the recent agent-based paradigms like the SWE-Agent. The authors omit benchmarking results with agent-based architecture as well, given that SWE Agent has high repair rates. This is a missed opportunity to compare the perf vs token consumption tradeoff between the two architectures, which is a significant concern in industry settings.
- Dataset description section is not clear and presents changes to the set without providing any examples or empirical backing. For eg. Line 161 starts with mentioning the extension of "rigorous filtering logic of the SWE-Fixer dataset", but the exact details of the filtering logic being referred to are not clarified to the reader. The assertion in Line 163, "samples with ambiguous problem statement or non-textual content are eliminated to ensure precision" is hard to ground in any examples, and it is not clear whether it will have an impact on the performance. Some examples would help understand these choices and their impact better.
- In the results section, Qwen is shown to have a 0 pass rate with the TSP approach, no analysis of the reasons is presented. It will be helpful to have a discussion on the perf differences for each of the sub-tasks.
- The paper is missing an in-depth discussion about the token usage compared to RAG. They did mention the context window is reduced by 78%, more alation studies in this regard or explanation of this would make the paper stronger.
- Regd. the LLM judge, the paper did not present an evaluation of agreement rate with human evaluators. As such, it is hard to understand what the percentage variations in the judge accuracy mean for the Final Results.
- The authors say the dataset will be shared. It is crucial to share at least some examples, for the reader to grasp the extent of changes made to the original SWE-bench dataset. The changes to the dataset make it hard to compare the results reported with other approaches on this dataset in the past. This also raises reproducibility concerns.
- Awkward phrasing instances in the paper: 
a) "our framework involves the following steps: Think stage guides...” → better phrased as “Our framework involves the following steps. In the Think stage, the model...”

b) “retrieved-associated code snippets” → likely intended as “retrieved relevant code snippets”

c) “...model’s ability to locate recalled relevant code...” → awkward phrasing; possibly “to accurately locate relevant recalled code”

title: Think-Search-Patch: A Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning Framework for Repository-Level Code Repair
review:
This paper proposes a framework named Think-Search-Patch(TSP) for the repository-level code repair task. Specifically, the large language model first conducts thinking stage and decomposes the problem, searches relevant code snippets, and generates code patch. A datasets with 60K samples are built to train the reasoning process of Think-Search-Patch framework. Experimental results show that models trained on TSP datasets outperforms other retrieval-augmented methods on the SWE-bench. 

- **Pros**

  (1) The framework proposed show a promising results for the retrieval-augmented methods, especially on improving the quality of search query.

  (2) Think-Search-Patch datasets will benefit the future works after public.

- **Cons**

  (1) The general procedure of Think-Search-Patch is not novel on the retrieval-augmented generation task.

  (2) It will be better to apply your method on more large language models, e.g., larger parameter amount or other series model, to improve the soundness.

title: DREAM: An End-to-End Framework for Document Digitization, Metadata Extraction, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
review:
The paper presents an end to end framework for enabling RAG in SME environments that they called DREAM. The framework contains two components: 1) Document Digitization, and 2) Retrieval Phase. In the document digitization, the authors utilised "conventional" OCR solutions first to extract the textual and structural contents, and then pass the result along with the original input image to a VLM. The authors claim that this solution will reduce hallucinations in VLM. Similarly, for the Retrieval Phase, the authors first used Metadata filtering (which required some manual work to construct the metadata), followed by semantic or lexical retrieval. The results are then inputted to LLM. 

The idea mentioned in the paper are not novel. The authors have combined existing tools available to achieve their tasks' objectives. They have not done ablation study to understand the impact of each tool on the final results. The example results that the authors have reported in the paper, seems to indicate that the impact of the "conventional" tools are not significant. It is not clear whether the correct results outputted is coincident (i.e. when you are running the Dream framework 5 or 10 times, the average accuracy might not be 100%), or it is because the "conventional" routes really helped improve the accuracy of the overall system. Furthermore, there was not any discussions on the "failure" case or the limitations of the system (apart from the creation of the metadata is expensive).

title: DREAM: An End-to-End Framework for Document Digitization, Metadata Extraction, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
review:
Strengths:
- The paper aims to solve multiple practical problems in information retrieval for small and medium sized enterprises: scalability/latency, and accuracy, which includes retrieving both correct and complete information.
- The presented framework (DREAM) combines both OCR techniques and Visual Language Models to address these issues.
- The DREAM framework leverages multiple filtering methods and existing techniques to efficiently prune the search space and retrieve information. 
- Qualitative evaluation has shown that the system is user-friendly.

Weaknesses:
- There are some claims in the earlier sections that are not supported by related scientific research, or only by older research. For example:
    - p. 3: "Although both lexical and semantic retrieval methods are effective, neither of them have deemed to be performant in industry-grade applications, mainly due to larger document repositories within SMEs which have complex search spaces" => and then a references from 2012, which was years before the first pre-trained transformers were released.
    - p. 3: "RAG solutions are leveraged off-the-shelves predominantly, without major changes, into industry-grade applications with their vast and complex knowledge bases. However, these solutions, have proven to be having underwhelming performance [...]" => no examples or references at all
- While mentioning that "standard OCR techniques [...] disrupt  essential business information encoded in structured tables, hierarchical formatting [...]" etc., it is mentioned on p. 3 that conventional OCR is used to "first extract its [text] textual and structural contents", which is completely contradictory.
- Similarly, it is written that VLMs suffer from hallucinations, although VLMs are used in DREAM after step 1 (OCR). Nevertheless, there is no quantitative evaluations showing (improvements in) the number of hallucinations, or OCR disruptions in DREAM. 
- It is not quantified how DREAM improves latency compared to VLM/LLM information retrieval (which was one of the main problems), only accuracy.
- No new methods are proposed in the paper; only a combination of methods.

title: DREAM: An End-to-End Framework for Document Digitization, Metadata Extraction, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
review:
The paper describes a system for document OCR and RAG-style question answering with hybrid retrieval with the motivation that such a system can  help SMEs—especially in the Global South—that still rely heavily on analogue documentation to benefit from AI. The proposed system focuses on two improvements over standard RAG.

1. Faithful digitization of structurally complex documents (tables, hierarchical formatting, spatial layouts) using a combination of traditional OCR and VLMs pipeline to produce structured Markdown output.
2. Hybrid retrieval with metadata-based pre-filtering followed by lexical and semantic embedding-based search.

Experiments on with different size corpora are shown to illustrate the stability of the approach.

The motivation to improve digitalisation of documents is valid and reflects real business needs. Unfortunately the paper lacks impactful, novel insights into the solution and lacks clarity in the presented experiments.

- The presented methods (combine traditional OCR and VLMs, hybrid retrieval with lexical + embeddings and filtering rules) are well known and do not add any novel contribution to the methods and algorithms in this space
- Almost all the accuracy seems to come from the meta-data filtering which seems to be manually engineered and is not described in sufficient detail
- The dataset and experiments are not described in detail - while industry papers can gloss over some proprietary details they need to provide enough details to make the contribution of the paper clear
- Challenges of real-world document search as specific terminology, heterogenous data formats etc are not discussed
- several components are referred to as agents but there is no agentiveness in the proposed approach - it is a straight forward pipeline


Minor:
- p. 1 75 The claim IR methods are not scalable to large corpora is hard to follow as large scale IR systems clearly exist, also for Enterprise Search. The citation (He et al 2012) seems very old and not supporting this claim  
- p.1 50 "failed gracefully" - do the authors mean "not failed gracefully"?
- accuracy is not the right metric for IR
- p.3 209 OCR is not heuristic based, modern OCR systems use ML
- Casing in references: eg "nlp" -> "{NLP}"

title: Towards a Declarative Language for Customer Service Chatbots
review:
The paper presents a declarative declarative agent programming framework called ADL that enables creating customer service chatbots by describing its functionality in natural language. ADL splits the prompt typically used for such tasks into explicit fields -- for example, list of arguments, fallback (what to do when the the scenario is different from what the agent is programmed to handle), and if-then-else syntax such as if user says X then the bot should say Y, etc.  Further, the paper compares ADL using code examples of how to accomplish similar tasks in two of the common multi-agent frameworks (Swarm, and Crew) to attempt to demonstrate that ADL is simpler than those frameworks that require a combination of python code and prompt in natural language.

The paper seems to be very out-dated and seemed to ignore the plethora of low-code / no-code agent/multi-agent frameworks that are widely available today. In fact, ADL is more complicated than the no-code paradigms where one simply describes the behavior of the agent in natural language. Also, ADL is pretty limiting in at least two ways: (i) the if-then-else resembles more like chatbots of the past, for example, DialogFlow., and (ii) it is limited to customer service chatbots and these are two easy to build using no-code frameworks today.

Also, the evaluation presented in the paper is educational not useful -- the results comparing different multi-agent orchestration strategies are both well known and obvious.

The paper lacks novelty, innovation, and usefulness in the opinion of this reviewer.

title: Towards a Declarative Language for Customer Service Chatbots
review:
Strenghts

1. Authors propose to write agents conversation using a declarative language (ADL) that provides meaningful abstract representations. 
2. Authors also provide MICA a multiagent system to execute programs written using ADL.


Weakness

1. Authors have not provided a substantial justification or evaluation for the approach. That is how beneficial is ADL to human users compared to other languages in writing agents' conversations.

2. Some of the hypotheses are ill-defined. For example, in case of maintainability authors mention that adding more lines code is difficult to maintain. It needs a detailed user study based evaluation. Also, in case of debugging authors claim that program written using ADL are easier to debug again without a valid justification or evaluation.



Few additional questions

1. In the case of "interactive syntax", the example of an autogen script shown by authors, I wonder if the agent awaits for a response, why it is not being considered as interactive? The autogen example shows it sends a message and awaits for a response. Once it obtains a response, it infer the intent and then respond accordingly. This seems more clear and straightforward than the ADL representation provided by the authors.

2. In the case of "natural language condition", the abstraction provided as "if the user asks anything related to baggage", I wonder how agents will respond to an intent that is not part of the agents vocabulary. Ideally all intents have to be expressed correct?

3. In the case of "natural language policy", LLM agents can be provided a complex rule to understand. So how different is ADL incorporation from policy than LLM agents.

4. Does more lines of code is a clear indication of an issue with code maintenance? More lines of code can also mean well structured, readable, and expressive code. I think may be clear hypothesis is missing.

title: Towards a Declarative Language for Customer Service Chatbots
review:
Which programming languages (that ADL is interpreted into) does ADL support?

At the example in section 3.1 (top of page 3), while I see that ADL is simpler to use, I don't fully understand how in the AutoGen it is not clear where the input comes from.

How can someone define details such as which LLM to call, endpoints, APIs, etc?

How are policies such as "if there is no input for 30 seconds" actually implemented? How prone to errors is this approach?

How does ADL compare to other frameworks in per token cost and latency? Also a single-agent baseline would be good as a reference.

In the case study (section 5), doesn't ADL also need an intent classifier under the hood, requiring the same kind of maintenance as Python code? It's not clear to me how ADL bypasses that - I'm assuming that at some stage ADL needs to be translated to executable code. Also, for complex scenarios it can be equally hard to maintain if-else statements, even if the code is simpler.

The above comment also applies to debugging. Whouldn't someone need to dive deeper and see the actual model calls etc to identify a bug (for bugs that are not obvious or easily identified by external LLMs)?

Overall it is a nice idea that can help non-experts build and maintain LLM-based multi-agent systems. I am not thoroughly convinced, however, for its benefits - other than simplicity.

There are some typos in the paper.

Figure 1 would be more easily readable with bolder colors.

The authors mention MICA (e.g. abstract & top of 2nd page) which reveals their identity.

title: Enhancing Archival Research for Journalism with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
review:
The proposed RAG system offers a promising solution to enhance archival research, with a strong focus on practical utility and factual accuracy. The focus on citation accuracy and mitigating hallucinations is useful for journalistic applications. The initial positive user feedback underscores the potential impact of this technology in supporting sustainable journalism.

Strengths:
- Applying RAG to news archival search is a compelling approach that improves retrieving pertinent information, generating responses with contextual framing, citations, and key quotes.
- The design explicitly addresses the issue of hallucinations by integrating academic-style indexing and prompting LLMs to cite articles by index.
- Beyond automated metrics, the inclusion of a human judgment evaluation, assessing citation relevance and response accuracy, adds qualitative insights into the system's effectiveness from a user perspective. The initial user study with reporters provides real-world feedback.

Weaknesses:
- The paper acknowledges that the evaluation uses a small test set with ~50 queries for manual curation. While a start, this size might not fully capture the diversity and complexity of real-world journalistic queries, especially given the rapidly evolving media landscape. A larger and more varied benchmark would strengthen the evaluation's generalizability.
- While error analysis is mentioned, a more granular breakdown of the types of errors, particularly for Factoid Queries where the system struggled to return responses despite citing correct articles, would be beneficial. Understanding why the retriever failed to find the relevant chunk in these cases could lead to more targeted improvements.
- The paper states that the system supports multi-turn conversations but does not evaluate its performance on follow-up questions. It is a significant limitation, as journalistic research often involves iterative querying. Future work should prioritize this evaluation to ensure the system's utility in dynamic research scenarios.
- While not explicitly a weakness, the paper could benefit from a brief discussion on the scalability of maintaining an index of 120,000+ articles, as well as the computational resources required for running SOTA LLMs and dense retrievers in a production environment.

title: Enhancing Archival Research for Journalism with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
review:
### Paper Summary

This paper proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, which aims to improve the efficiency of journalists in archival search and information integration. The system builds an index based on 120,000 news articles, combines dense retrievers with LLM, and introduces query decomposition and temporal inference modules in query processing to achieve decomposition, semantic retrieval, result fusion, and response generation of complex problems. The paper uses indicators such as BERTScore, Citation Relevance, and Response Accuracy, as well as user tests by journalists, to show that the system can shorten research time by about 50% and achieve a response accuracy rate of 77%.

### Strengths

1. The system adopts a multi-stage processing flow: query decomposition, temporal inference, two-stage retrieval (BM25+dense retriever), and LLM generates responses with citations. The logic is clear and has engineering feasibility.
2. In the offline evaluation, NDCG@k and MAP@k are used to evaluate the retrieval effect, and the response quality is analyzed based on BERTScore and manual annotation. The performance differences of different query types (Factoid vs Event Coverage) are analyzed.
3. The system has been deployed in practice and analyzed based on 65 sessions and 131 real queries. At the same time, interviews with journalists were conducted to prove that the solution can improve information coverage and retrieval convenience in actual scenarios.

### Weaknesses

1. The current offline evaluation is only based on Factoid Queries (28) and Event Coverage Queries (31), and the manual annotation is concentrated in a limited range, resulting in insufficient statistical significance and difficulty in generalizing to a wider range of news tasks.
2. The paper mainly uses BERTScore, but its sensitivity to factual consistency and information coverage is limited, and the manual evaluation is only for GPT-4, not covering other models.
3. Although the paper mentions error cases (such as Factoid query not hitting the chunk), there is a lack of systematic analysis: Do long-tail queries, cross-topic retrieval, and multilingual news affect performance?
4. Although the paper analyzes the performance of different backbones of LLM, it is not compared with existing news retrieval tools (such as LexisNexis, Bloomberg Terminal) or commercial RAG solutions, making it difficult to prove industry leadership.

title: Enhancing Archival Research for Journalism with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
review:
**Summary**

The paper presents and explores a RAG system for aiding newsrooms in conducting source research and presents with a benchmark dataset. A system is introduced and challenged using both automatic and manual evaluation. To conduct the evaluation a small dataset is created, consisting of 28 factoid questions and 31 event-driven questions. Evaluated is reported for retrieval models (OpenAI embeddings + Azure specific) and LLMs (GPT-4, Phi 4 and Llama 3.1 8B). Both automatic and human evaluation suggest there are plenty of improvements to be made on both retrieval and LLM generated responses. Despite this, a small user study indicated that reports found the output of the system useful and helped them find more resources than traditional web searches.

**Review**

The paper is well written and presents plenty of potentially interesting insights. However, in its current form it could be strengthened by adding details related to its central contributions: data creation and overview of existing LLM performance in the domain. For data creation,  It would a be of great interest to know whether the dataset will be public and adding design decision around its creation, e.g. how was the data sourced, who/how many annotated data, and whether any quality control was conducted. For model evaluation (retrieval + llm), adding implementation details like prompts, as well as details related to the conducted human evaluation would add significant value, e.g. detailed prompts, post processing and what users where instructed with for evaluating response accuracy, and what the user study entailed. Without such information the reader is unable extract conclusive insights from the results, nor translate the findings into replications or repurposing in other use cases. Lastly, I'd like to challenge the authors on the application. It is becoming increasingly well documented that when humans get access to information via an LLM it affects their critical ability and will generally be prone to accepting system outputs without scrutiny. Looking at the first example in Table 1, it contains the phrase "[...] what are some important moments?" it is clear that some responsibility is transferred to the LLM which might be problematic for a domain like journalism?

title: PreMind: Multi-Agent Video Understanding for Advanced Indexing of Presentation-style Videos
review:
Summary:
PreMind is a multi-agent, multimodal framework that first uses a vision-language model to slice presentation videos into slide-based segments. It then extracts the visual content of the slides, transcribes the speech, and fuses the two to generate a highly reliable index. Compared to traditional methods, it can capture details such as abbreviations that appear only on the slides, enabling precise question-and-answer-style search. Its effectiveness has been verified through systematic evaluation and analysis of both public LPM datasets and internal enterprise datasets.

Pros:
1. The integration of a visual language model (VLM) and PySceneDetect significantly outperforms traditional purely visual approaches.
2. Through a multi-agent pipeline combining visual understanding, speech recognition, knowledge memory, ASR error correction, and dynamic reflection, it generates a rich and accurate multimodal index, supporting retrieval of details that appear only on a slide.
3. On public LPM and internal enterprise datasets, search-enhanced question-answering accuracy improved by up to 40+ percentage points, demonstrating its significant value for downstream tasks such as question answering and summarization.

Cons:
1. The core components of the framework all rely on proprietary models such as GPT-4 and Whisper, which are costly. Switching to open-source models may result in significant performance degradation.
2. It is designed specifically for lecture videos with a "slideshow + lecture" style and has not been verified for general applicability to freestyle videos without slides or other types of courses.
3. The quality of visual understanding and the accuracy of question-answering require extensive manual annotation or GPT-4 judgment, which is subject to subjective bias. Furthermore, the evaluation dataset is still relatively small, limiting the reproducibility of the results.

title: PreMind: Multi-Agent Video Understanding for Advanced Indexing of Presentation-style Videos
review:
Summary:
- This paper introduces PreMind, a system to understand and index presentation-style videos using both audio and visual content. 
- It uses LLMs and VLMs to segment the video, fix transcription errors, extract knowledge, and answer questions about the content. 
- The design uses multiple agents that work together, and the system is tested on both public and company videos.

Pros:
- The multi-agent design is clear and works well.
- It uses slide visuals to help fix speech-to-text errors, which is smart.
- The critic agent improves results by checking and refining the output.
- Evaluation is strong, including both internal tests and QA results.
- Useful for education and enterprise video content.
- The idea of combining vision and audio for better indexing is well done.

Cons:
- It depends on closed-source models like GPT-4 and GPT-4V.
- Only works well for slides-based videos, not general videos.
- Human evaluation is used for vision understanding, which could be subjective.
- No details on speed or how it performs with large-scale deployment.

Overall Evaluation:
- This paper is original, useful, and well-written. 
- It shows a smart way to mix vision and audio with LLMs for better video understanding. 
- The design is practical and tested in real-world settings.

title: PreMind: Multi-Agent Video Understanding for Advanced Indexing of Presentation-style Videos
review:
## Strengths
### Novelty of the Framework
* Creative combination of video segmentation, multimodal extraction, and self-refining multi-agent collaboration.  
* Knowledge memory and critic-based reflection go well beyond traditional OCR + ASR lecture indexing.

### Comprehensive Evaluation
* Both intrinsic (human pairwise judgment of vision descriptions) and extrinsic (retrieval-augmented QA) evaluations are provided.  
* Ablation studies separately probe knowledge enhancement, ASR correction, and the critic mechanism.

## Weaknesses
* **Single-frame vision understanding.**  
  The vision agent samples one frame per segment and asks a VLM to “describe the slide.” This can miss animations, overlays, laser pointers, or instructor annotations. The paper itself blames animations for lower LPM scores, underscoring the risk. The frame-selection rule (mid-point? text density? face/slide detector?) is not specified, yet it drives all downstream indexing.

* **Name-only embeddings & Sentence-Transformer mismatch.**  
  Only the concept _name_ is embedded using a Sentence-Transformer trained on full sentences. One-word labels or acronyms (“ERP”, “BI”) therefore may yield noisy vectors. Moreover, averaging “similar” names may cause distinct meanings (enterprise resource planning vs. event-related potential) to collapse. Embedding full definitions or keeping separate vectors per sense would reduce such semantic drift.

* **Different PySceneDetect detectors, not just thresholds.**  
  The proposed pipeline uses *AdaptiveDetector* (“minimize missing slides”) while the baseline uses *ContentDetector* (threshold = 12). AdaptiveDetector is more sensitive to gradual changes, so the large F-score jump may stem from the detector swap rather than the VLM refinement. A fair baseline should search detector + threshold grids and then add the VLM layer; results for both detectors under both pipelines are needed.

* **Tiny segmentation test set.**  
  The headline segmentation gain is measured on just 13 videos (~116 min): six LPM clips (only the first 10 minutes) and seven short enterprise videos. Such a small sample may miss real-world variance (pauses, demos, low contrast, handwriting, pans) and can bias results.

* **Circularity & model-alignment bias.**  
  GPT-4 Turbo creates the QA questions, supplies the ground-truth answers, and then judges correctness, while the answerer is GPT-3.5. The judge may prefer GPT-4-like phrasing, systematically disadvantaging the system under test. Human spot-checks or alternative LLM judges are needed.

* **ASR ablation design.**  
  No standard WER or human transcript-quality metric is reported. Instead, the authors build a QA test set from the module’s own predicted fixes, so the evaluation is circular and almost certain to show an improvement, raising concerns about data-leakage and biased gains.

## Suggestions to Authors
1. **Multi-frame or saliency-guided vision understanding.** Describe (and justify) the frame-selection heuristic or adopt multi-frame sampling to capture animations and overlays.
2. **Fair segmentation baseline.** Report a detector+threshold grid search for PySceneDetect and show gains after adding the VLM refinement.
3. **Larger, unbiased segmentation test.** Evaluate on the full LPM corpus (or a stratified subset) and release the exact video list for replication; provide confidence intervals.
4. **Decouple question generation and judging.** Use human-written questions or an independent LLM judge; include human spot-checks for answer correctness.
6. **Standard ASR metrics.** Report WER/SER before and after correction and test on a neutral QA set not derived from the module’s own edits.

title: Enhancing Financial Knowledge Graphs Through Ontology-Driven Data Filtering Techniques
review:
Review (Quality, Clarity, Originality and Significance):

1. Overall - 

The overall idea is simple and straightforward, and should work. However, similar techniques may have been used in other domains. For example, this is a general blog on this topic:  https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/knowledge-graph-rag).

The paper is well organized and the presentation is reasonable. Some place consistency of the terminology is needed, for example, Raw Node, First parent, Second parent can be referred to as Child, Parent, Grand parent. 

Section 5.4 (Path Search): It can be better explained, especially what the metric means and its usage.

Typos:

a. Are there Appendices like A2, A3 etc which should have been there in the paper. A6 is mentioned somewhere in the paper (Page 5, Line 240), but is not present in the Appendix.

b. Page 12, Table 10: "What" instead of "hat".

As mentioned above, the main issue the paper faces is its novelty. The idea is reasonable and in-principle should work. To make the paper more interesting, concentration should be on "where the system is doing better" and "where it is worse" and WHY. It is interesting to note that the simple RAG system has its own wins on occasions (Table 8: Assessment and Causal Factor; table 11: Predict and Policy). These insights can help readers, especially the ones who are not from the domain of finance, in understanding what is going on. So moving from "What is happening" and including  "Where and Why it is happening"  will be insightful for many. Also, complementary results do show that combining the two systems may be beneficial on occasions, and could be another possible area of research. This may be beyond the scope of the current paper, though.

Are the citations done correctly? When there are 2 authors, "et al" is not used, The way in-text referencing is done seems incorrect. For example, Vamsi et al (Kommineni et al, 2024) on Page 2. This has happened at many places. In the Bibliography, the case should be preserved for abbreviations. For example, LLM instead of llm on line 466. Again, this needs to be corrected at many places.

title: Enhancing Financial Knowledge Graphs Through Ontology-Driven Data Filtering Techniques
review:
This paper focuses on knowledge graph (KG) construction for financial data. It proposes an ontology mapping method to reduce complexity and variability of the extracted KG. In addition, it proposes a graph search method on the extracted KG to support the typical applications such as GraphRAG. The experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The strengths include:
1. Practical AI technique in finance.
2. This paper shows the importance of ontology management in LLM-KG integrated applications such as GraphRAG.

The weaknesses include:
1. Unclear task definition and contribution. It is unclear whether the main focus of this paper is ontology construction or graph search. In addition, the Abstract and Introduction lacks necessary conclusion of the main contribution or technical improvements. The word "theme/thematic" seems to be an important term in this paper, but it never appear in Abstract and Introduction.
2. Lack of technical details. The main focus of this paper is the ontology mapping. However, section 3.1 lacks the details of how to achieve the ontology mapping, maybe it relates to the Appendix C Ontology Builder?
3. Style problems. For example, the figures are in low-resolution; The introduction section is written in one paragraph, which is difficult to read.

title: Enhancing Financial Knowledge Graphs Through Ontology-Driven Data Filtering Techniques
review:
### Strengths
1. Addresses a practical and relevant problem in financial knowledge graph construction: reducing variability in entity and relation types to improve retrieval.
2. Well-structured pipeline integrating LLM-based extraction, taxonomy/ontology mapping, and thematic retrieval.
3. Multiple experimental evaluations (statement extraction, triple extraction, ontology mapping, retrieval performance).

### Weaknesses
1. Limited novelty: The core idea—mapping entities/relations to parent types in a taxonomy to improve retrieval—is standard in RDF and knowledge graph literature. Similar type-aware retrieval techniques have been used in many domains; this is not acknowledged. AN example among many:
   - Fernández et al. Semantically enhanced information retrieval: An ontology-based approach.
2. Conceptual clarity:
   - "Ontology" is used where "taxonomy" would be more accurate. An ontology can be much more complex than a taxonomy
   - "Host ontology" and "theme" are introduced without clear, formal definitions.
   - Unusual notation and recursive definition artifacts reduce readability. For instance, definition 1 use the symbol $O$ two times: is it a recursive def? This would make little sense from my understanding. If not, then use different symbols.
3. Methodological gaps:
   - Annotation process lacks detail on annotator expertise, count, and agreement. Were there multiple annotators? Are they experts? etc.
   - No statistical significance testing of reported gains.
   - No ablation studies to isolate contributions of individual pipeline components.
4. Citation quality:
   - Inconsistent or mismatched references in the related work section, which is a red flag.
   - Missing acknowledgment of directly related RDF/type-aware retrieval work (see first point of the weaknesses).
5. Clarity issues in writing:
   - Ambiguous phrasing like "1000 financial messages daily" (Do you mean you used 1000 messages to build the graph? The "daily" in the sentence is not clear at all)
   - filler sentences (eg lines 222-226)

### Questions for Authors
1. How does your method differ from standard RDF/SPARQL query expansion or type-aware indexing using class hierarchies? Can you provide a literature comparison?
2. What precisely is the "host ontology," and how does it evolve? Is it an ontology in the OWL sense or a hierarchical taxonomy?
3. Who performed the annotations, and what was their domain expertise? How was inter-annotator agreement measured?
4. Are the retrieval improvements statistically significant? Could you provide confidence intervals or significance tests?
5. Could the "theme" layer be expressed directly as SKOS concepts or OWL classes to leverage existing KG tooling?

title: ACME: Robust and Explainable Detection of LLM-Generated Texts
review:
This paper introduces ACME, an industrial AI-generated text detector combining a hierarchical multi-task classification architecture with two novel interpretability components: Deep Scan (sentence-level attribution) and Natural Language Explanations (NLE). The system is evaluated across multiple domains, adversarially modified texts, and paraphrased AI bypass attempts. Results show strong performance on both in-domain and challenging adversarial benchmarks.

**Strengths** 
1. ACME achieves state-of-the-art results in diverse scenarios, including multiple domains and adversarially perturbed texts (Tables 1–2).
2. The work explicitly addresses the problem of users paraphrasing AI text to evade detection. The inclusion of a dedicated “AI Paraphrased” class and the use of NLE-inspired augmentations yield high performance.

**Weaknesses** 
1. The proposed class hierarchy (human, AI, mixed; with pure AI and AI paraphrased under AI) does not capture realistic cases such as human-written and AI-proofread or AI-generated and human-polished. These hybrid authorship modes are increasingly common and may require explicit representation for accurate classification.
2. The sentence-level prediction framework may be too coarse for detecting minimal edits. Many human or AI interventions occur at the word or phrase level within otherwise untouched sentences. Without token-level attribution, the system might miss such fine-grained authorship mixing.
3. The paper a user-oriented case study evaluating whether NLEs actually improve human decision-making.
4. (minor) The performance comparisons rely on strong open-source and some commercial detectors, but omit direct evaluation against the most competitive proprietary systems, which would strengthen the empirical claim of “state-of-the-art.”

title: ACME: Robust and Explainable Detection of LLM-Generated Texts
review:
This paper proposes ACME, a practical solution for differentiating human and AI text, featuring better robustness and explainability. The ACME adopt a hierachical classification taxonomy and provides natural language explantion. 

Pros

1. The training data is large in scale and wide in coverage.
2. Careful data cleaning ensures the reliability of this work.
3. ACME provides _Deep Scan_ to attribute the impact of sentences on the prediction of the document, which is a good feature in practice.
4. The experiments illustrate the strong performance of ACME.

Cons

1. Authors should clarify the key issues to be addressed in the introduction section to illustrate the necessity of proposing their methods. In the current version, it is more like an introductory and examination report for several issues in machine-generated text detection.
2. It seems that several existing works also take the ternary classification into consideration [1,2]. It’s recommended for authors to include them in the related work and consider revising the statement in lines 161-164.
3. I wonder know the extent to which pure AI and AI-paraphrased content can be distinguished. The current paper provides a simple performance description. It would be better to detail this, and a comment about its impact on the effectiveness of hierarchical classification should be provided.
4. It would be better to elaborate on the essential experimental settings (such as the selection of the backbone).
5. The GitHub repository provided by the authors is empty.

> [1] Towards Detecting AI-Generated Text within Human-AI Collaborative Hybrid Texts. IJCAI’24
>
> [2] Automatic Authorship Analysis in Human-AI Collaborative Writing. COLING’24

Other questions:
- Does the aggregation method mentioned in Section 3.3 have a significant impact on the performance?

title: ACME: Robust and Explainable Detection of LLM-Generated Texts
review:
The authors outline a proprietary method for hierarchical AI-generated text detection that features three top-level-classes (Human, Mixed, AI) and two AI-label sub-classes (pure, paraphrased). The method is trained on a large proprietary closed-source dataset using multi-task loss for predictions on document- and sentence-level, as well as "Deep Scan", a proprietary method that attributes the document-level prediction to sentence-level probabilities by selecting the most relevant sentences using proprietary heuristics. They provide a short evaluation on small subsets of both publicly available large-scale datasets and proprietary internal datasets. Additionally, the authors outline briefly how dataset corrections and user-feedback form their own platform is integrated into their system.

### Summary of Strengths

The paper is well written & compact.

- (S1) Hierarchical Ternary-to-Binary (3+2) Classification
- (S2) Combination of Document & Sentence Level Predictions
- (S3) Weighting of Sentence-Level Probabilities with Attribution to Document-Level Predictions

### Summary of Weaknesses

#### Major Weaknesses 

- (W1) In §3.2 in line 161ff. the authors claim that their approach is distinct from other AI-generated text detection approaches in that it frames the task as a ternary classification problem. However, this is a well established paradigm going back to at least 2022 with the publication of "CoAuthor: Designing a Human-AI Collaborative Writing Dataset for Exploring Language Model Capabilities" (Lee, Lian & Yang, CHI 2022).
- (W2) The authors make multiple erroneous claims about the availability of benchmarks and available data. Additionally, their own data is proprietary and the repository they claim to use to share their own benchmarking data in is empty. Furthermore, their evaluation data is **much, much** too small to allow for a meaningful evaluation, despite a vast abundance of available data.
    - In numbers:
        - Table 1: 1000 yelp reviews, 500 scientific abstract, 200 Essays
        - Table 2: 600 RAID Adversarial Data, 1000 M4-PeerReviews, 300 FDGTP-Writing
        - Table 3: 4000 documents for formatting ablation
        - 40.000 documents for "internal evaluation" (?)
        - §6.3: 500 AI-paraphrased documents
    - (W2a) Yet, they cite the RAID benchmark multiple times, which contains **millions of documents** but omit it in their claim that "there is a lack of standardization regarding which datasets are used to evaluate models both in the research literature" (ln. 457f). Instead, they use 600 documents from RAID but do not participate in the public benchmark the authors of RAID offer via GitHub pull requests, and are consequently neither listed on the RAID leaderboard nor is there an open or closed pull request that pertains to this submission.
- (W3) The EMNLP industry track call outlines evaluation criteria that are not met by this submission: "experimental methods and results should be clear, well executed, and repeatable (though the data may be proprietary)"
    - All details about the architecture are note to be proprietary as well as most details about the data used. The authors describe their architecture as "data driven" (ln. 140f.) and having multiple, hierarchical classifier heads (ln. 165), but everything else is withheld; see ln. 208f: "Architecture and hyperparameters are proprietary."
    - This includes under-specified descriptions of pre-processing (ln. 213f.), document-level aggregation methods and the "remapping function R3 -> R3" (ln. 218ff., 223ff.), the "Deep Scan" method that is used to rank sentence level predictions (ln. 228ff.), the "Natural Language Explanation" features (ln. 259ff.), etc.
- (W4) The evaluation misses public benchmarks, like RAID.
- (W5) The evaluation misses a comparison with other data-driven, trainable classifiers.

#### Minor Weaknesses

- (M1) The formatting examples omits even the most ubiquitous of all AI-generated text artifacts: the em-dash. A more detailed analysis of typical AI formatting that also covers HTML, emojis & unusual Unicode characters (lower quotes, en-/em-dashes, etc.), and references to related work in this regard are missing.
- (M2) Figure clearly shows 5 stages with 4 steps but only has three numbered arrows and the text only mentions three steps. Which is it now, 3 or 4? How do we get from Feature Extraction to Clustering?
- (M3) Figure 5 should not be a line plot, as the x-axis has no meaning other than the document index. Maybe try a boxplot across the three types.
- (M4) Binoculars outputs scores $>= 0$, with lower scores indicating AI, making $sigmoid$ a bad choice to transform the scores into probabilities. Maybe try $1-tanh(binoculars(t))$

### Comments/Suggestions/Typos

- Figure 6 is too small.

title: Analysis of Automated Document Relevance Annotation for Information Retrieval in Oil and Gas Industry
review:
The work should be of interest in addressing the challenges posed by the lack of high-quality evidence collections in information retrieval (IR) for specialized domains. However, the truth is that the conclusions were no less expected for being conclusive.

Demonstrating that a carefully designed supervised classifier outperforms all LLM-based configurations, even following a simple cost-effectiveness criterion, is generally assumed by the community in the current state of knowledge. 

In my opinion, and despite the shortcomings of the experimental framework, the main interest of this work is the experimental confirmation that the use of LLMs does not currently represent an indisputable advantage in terms of performance.

If we stick to the results described, there is, therefore, as expected, room for research work in the field of LLMs.

The work presents numerous shortcomings, expressly acknowledged by the authors themselves, regarding the definition of the experimental environment. The immediate consequence is that the conclusions section can only be considered a crude assessment at best. In this context, its practical relevance is questionable even at the level of the specific application domain considered.

title: Analysis of Automated Document Relevance Annotation for Information Retrieval in Oil and Gas Industry
review:
This paper is a well-constructed study addressing the challenge of creating evaluation test collection within the specialized domain of oil and gas exploration. The findings  demonstrate that a supervised relevance classifier built upon a general-purpose embedding model and trained on a modest amount of expert-labeled data is more effective than LLM-as-judge, and is significantly less expensive.  LLMs are too biased towards their training data to understand relevance to human retrieval tasks.  

While this study is well-designed and documented, it would help a non-specialist to know more about the corpus: what are drilling reports like?  Could metadata and provenance be leveraged as well to provide relevance feedback?  What are the queries like?  Please provide some details in the final paper.

title: Analysis of Automated Document Relevance Annotation for Information Retrieval in Oil and Gas Industry
review:
## Strengths:

* Detailed empirical comparison between supervised classifiers and zero-shot Large Language Models (LLMs), benchmarking both against human expert judgments.
* Impact of the automatic annotation methods on downstream IR systems including reliability scores.
* Highlighting the cost-effectiveness of classifier based annotation methods as compared to high API costs.


## Weaknesses:

* No results are shown for parameter efficient finetuning of language models like BERT and RoBERTa.
* The assessment did not include the complete range of LLM performance based on few-shot prompting or chain-of-thought reasoning.
* The primary annotator’s perspective was only considered for training the supervised classifier. 
* The dataset's train/test/val splits for specialized classifiers are unspecified.
* In Table 2, why were PetroBERT results not considered in terms of extracted features or finetuning ?

title: Real-World VLM-Powered Pipeline for Automated Web UI Testing
review:
This paper introduces an iterative pipeline for automated Web UI testing powered by a fine-tuned Visual Language Model (VLM) called WebTestAgent. The method utilizes a VLM that uses natural language instructions to interact with web pages, aiming to replace traditional, script-based testing methods. The approach improves the success rate compared to baseline models and public benchmarks, which often lack the specificity needed for real-world industrial deployment.

This paper presents an interesting approach to automated Web UI testing using a fine-tuned VLM. The proposed iterative pipeline and the domain-specific dataset are contributions that effectively tackle a real-world problem. However, some technical details need to be further clarified. For example, in subsection 3.1.1, the paper mentions that it used a rule-based extractor to obtain key textual information from the web page's accessibility tree. However, the paper does not provide information about this extractor. How are these rules? Subsection 3.1.2 also needs more details about the set of actions performed by the agent.

The paper provides an application example in Appendix C, but I expected a more meaningful and detailed example. The provided example seems simple. It would be better explored to emphasize the contribution of the paper.

Finally, the paper does not include its conclusions. I noticed that a conclusion section is missing.

title: Real-World VLM-Powered Pipeline for Automated Web UI Testing
review:
The paper presents a pipeline for automated Web UI testing. Its core component is the WebTestAgent, a VLM-powered agent developed by the authors. While the outline of the proposed framework is comprehensive, the description of the experimental setting is lacking in detail.

Summary of Weaknesses:

1. While the authors indicate the development of an 'iterative training pipeline' as their primary contribution, the Experiments section focuses primarily on WebTestAgent, with no experiments provided to justify the proposed iterative approach.

2. The description of the dataset is vague. The authors state that the training set contains 1,850 data points, but it is not clear how many websites are considered. It is also not clear whether the same collection of websites was used to construct both the training and test sets.

3. No fine-tuned baseline is considered. While the authors discuss previous approaches in detail in the Related Work section, they unfortunately do not compare their approach against at least one of them.

4. There is no Conclusion section in the paper to summarize the findings.

title: Real-World VLM-Powered Pipeline for Automated Web UI Testing
review:
Strengths

1. Authors provide their own dataset mimicking real-world Web UI testing scenarios. This is available via anonymous github.
2. Authors provide an iterative pipeline that has a WebTestAgent based on a finetuned VLM.

Weakeness
1. One of the major concern I see in the paper is the dataset constructed has missing details. For example, authors did not provide details of the choice of applications i.e., how many different kinds of applications are considered to construct the dataset. Thanks to authors for sharing the dataset. However when I saw ``train_text.jsonl`` it is in Chinese. When I translated it into English, it seems they all belong to the same application. Thus, this may not really suggest how the approach can generalize across different kinds of Web Application.

2. The contribution is slightly misplaced here. For example, authors mentioned they provide a pipeline for implementing WebTestAgent. However, it is basically training and testing few close source and open source models. Considering the dataset details is missing as pointed above, and nothing significant in terms of model has been provided, it is difficult to interepret the signficiance of the novelty of the paper.


Few additional concerns

1. Figure 3, the input portion is in Chinese. Can it be translated to English? This is difficult for non-Englisher readers to interepret.

2. What is role of Claude-3.7-Sonnet in the construction of the dataset? I understand it is being used a teacher VLM but what exactly it being used to create is not specified.

3. I am a bit confused on open source availability of Hunyuan-7B-MoE for finetuning. If this model is close source, how come authors could train on this. 

4. Why there is a significant gap in terms of scores for scripts comparing Hunyuan-7B-MoE vs other finetuned models.

title: TelAgentBench: A Multi-faceted Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Agents in Telecommunications
review:
### General Comments:
This is a benchmark paper for korean telecommunication industry, covering five tasks to test LLM's ability, including action, plan, reason, instruction following, and RAG. Each task is well adapted to the korean telecom industry. It seems an intereting paper and contributes to the related industry

### Strengths:
- The industry is interesting and the industry need is justified, since we do have similar clients from the telecom industry
- The experiment and testing are complete, covering both thinking and no-thinking models, and in the appendix, a large number of user cases in Korean (with English translation) are provided

### Weakness:
- W1: Since it is a benchmark paper, I will expect more statistical description about the benchmark dataset, in the form of bar charts or pie charts, and a deeper analysis, e.g., the distribution of the difficulty/complexity level of the tasks / sub-tasks. 
- W2: From our telecom clients, another frequent task is actually intent classification and routing. The author can also add this task.

title: TelAgentBench: A Multi-faceted Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Agents in Telecommunications
review:
The paper proposes a benchmark for telecommunication tasks involving the following dimensions: execution of actions, planning, reasoning, instruction following and retrieval augmented generation. The paper clearly motivates their benchmark and carefully prepared the benchmark for telecommunication use cases in Korean. 

Strengths:
The paper explains the benchmarks on distinct dimensions for telecommunication use cases. Authors group models into Thinking models and not thinking models and present the consolidated results in Table 2. I really think this benchmark will be beneficial to the research and industry communities.

Weaknesses:
Authors mention throughout the document two groups, Thinking and Non-thinking models, however there is not explanation (at least not in the main paper) of which models belong to one group or the other. This makes difficult to follow the discussion of the results. Also many tables that are discussed in the results are missing in the paper. The paper must be self-contained thus relevant information must be included in the main paper, not in the annexes.

title: TelAgentBench: A Multi-faceted Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Agents in Telecommunications
review:
It is always exciting to see evaluation datasets for various domains that can be potentially used by industrial NLP practitioners. This paper presents a small (~2000 example) synthetic dataset in Korean language from telecom domain. The examples cover a variety of task categories such as request for action or information, tasks that require planning, tasks that require instruction following, etc. 

The paper is confusing at several places. For example, it says "To support plan generation, we constructed a database with 7,801 entries across seven tools, including travel destinations, flights, restau-rants, and telecommunications roaming plans". I fail to understand what does this have to with Telecom domain?

The evaluation presented in the paper appears to be flawed. Could the results observed have to do with LLM support for Korean language support as opposed to the ability of LLMs on the different telecom tasks such as action/planning/instruction following, etc.?

Similarly, could the RAG evaluation be influenced by the specific embeddings chosen and not much to do with the LLMs or the task?

It would be great if the authors could include a better study to address these concerns. It would also be great if the authors could consider releasing the benchmark in other languages such as English.

title: Disambiguation-Centric Finetuning Makes Enterprise Tool-Calling LLMs More Realistic and Less Risky
review:
This is a well-written industry-track paper that addresses a practical challenge in deploying LLMs in enterprise environments particularly for tool disambiguation. The proposed DIAFORGE pipeline is thoughtfully designed, and the experimental results are strong, demonstrating significant improvements over capable open-sourced and proprietary models. The public release of the dataset and benchmark is a valuable contribution to the community.

Strengths:
- The paper tackles the real-world problem of LLMs failing to distinguish between similar, near-duplicate APIs in an enterprise setting. 
- The proposed DIAFORGE workflow is methodologically sound.
- The results presented are convincing.
- The commitment to publicly releasing the dataset is a major strength.

Area for Improvement:
- The analysis could be deepened. A more detailed qualitative or quantitative analysis would provide valuable insights.
- The fine-tuning is performed exclusively on the specialized DIAFORGE dataset. This single-task focus raises a significant risk of catastrophic forgetting. It would be beneficial to acknowledge this limitation and, ideally, include an evaluation of the fine-tuned models on a standard, general-purpose benchmark to quantify any potential loss in out-of-distribution performance.
- The paper positions fine-tuning as the primary solution. It would be interesting to explore the headroom for improvement using advanced prompting techniques alone.

title: Disambiguation-Centric Finetuning Makes Enterprise Tool-Calling LLMs More Realistic and Less Risky
review:
## Summary

This paper addresses the challenge of tool selection in enterprise LLM applications where near-duplicate tools exist and user requests often contain underspecified arguments. The authors propose a framework consisting of persona-driven multi-turn dialogue generation, supervised finetuning with reasoning, and dialogue-level evaluation. The key contributions include a data synthesis pipeline that generates confusing near-duplicate tools and handles underspecified arguments through slot-value generation, and a dynamic evaluation setup that supports disambiguation-centric multi-turn exchanges. Experiments show that open-source models (12B-49B parameters) finetuned using their synthetic data outperform even commercial models on their test set.

## Strengths
- The end-to-end solution spans from data synthesis to model training and evaluation, providing a complete pipeline for improving tool selection in ambiguous scenarios.
- The framework's emphasis on multi-turn disambiguation exchanges aligns well with how underspecified requests are resolved in practice through iterative user-agent conversations.

## Weaknesses
