- The paper does not clearly establish why the near-duplicate tools problem is critical or provide evidence of its severity in real-world enterprise use cases.
- No production impact or deployment results are presented to demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed approach.
- The evaluation may favor the proposed approach since models trained on the authors' synthetic data are tested primarily on the authors' test set, raising questions about whether the improvements would generalize to other tool-calling benchmarks or real-world scenarios.

## Comments and Suggested Revisions
- The authors may want to provide concrete statistics or case studies demonstrating how frequently near-duplicate tools cause failures in enterprise settings and the associated costs or user friction.
- Consider testing all models (both finetuned and baselines) on established independent tool-calling benchmarks to demonstrate that improvements are not specific to the authors' test distribution. Additionally, the authors may want to discuss whether the superior performance of finetuned models over commercial models holds when tested on out-of-distribution tool sets or different types of unseen ambiguous queries.
- Adding ablation study showing which components of UTC-GEN are critical to the performance gain of the proposed approach.

title: Disambiguation-Centric Finetuning Makes Enterprise Tool-Calling LLMs More Realistic and Less Risky
review:
## Summary
This paper introduces **DIAFORGE**, a three-stage pipeline for enterprise-grade LLM tool-calling that focuses on two challenges:  
1. Multiple nearly identical tools compete for the same user intent.  
2. Necessary parameters are not fully specified. 

The approach integrates synthetic dialogue generation, supervised fine-tuning with reasoning traces, and a dynamic evaluation benchmark (**DIABENCH**) that simulates real-world deployment. Experiments show substantial improvements over strong baselines, including GPT-4o (+27 pp) and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (+49 pp), while reducing false-positive tool calls and tool-call abstention.

## Strengths
1. The UTC-GEN framework is a major strength of this work. The UTC-GEN design, with distractor tools, under-specified requests, and a validator cascade, ensures realistic and high-quality training data.
2. Goes beyond static correctness by testing on-policy robustness, capturing cascading errors and real-world failure modes.
3. Covers accuracy, failure rates (FTR, TAR), and dialogue-level quality (CONVREL, TTR, NGD), offering a comprehensive assessment.
4. Release of 5,000 validated enterprise APIs and dialogues supports reproducibility and has strong industry relevance.

## Weaknesses
1. The paper provides limited discussion on the representativeness of the synthetic data. While 5,000 dialogues are sufficient for fine-tuning, it remains unclear whether such generated dialogues truly reflect the complexity and variability of real-world enterprise applications.  
2. Missing analysis of which components (validator cascade, distractor sampling, reasoning traces) drive the performance gains.
3. Paper does not adequately discuss potential risks, such as synthetic dialogue bias, fragility of semantic nearest-neighbor retrieval, and limited applicability to noisier or less-structured APIs.

title: Tagging-Augmented Generation: Assisting Language Models in Finding Intricate Knowledge In Long Contexts
review:

- The proposed method is clearly stated against the related work, and the experimental evaluation shows it outperforms the baseline on two benchmarks.

title: Tagging-Augmented Generation: Assisting Language Models in Finding Intricate Knowledge In Long Contexts
review:
This paper proposes a lightweight prompt augmentation technique (TAG) for long-context LLM tasks that injects semantic tags into the context and/or prompt to guide LLM attention. The proposed approach shows modest gains on two benchmarks. It also slightly mitigates performance degradation over longer contexts. The method is model-agnostic and computationally inexpensive.


Strengths: 
1. Addresses a well known long-context limitation of LLMs.
2. Proposed enhancement is simple, model-agnostic and computationally inexpensive.
3. Method and results seem easy to reproduce.
4. Experimental results are somewhat comprehensive with two benchmarks. Benchmarks and code are open-sourced. 

Weaknesses: 
1. The idea is incremental and closely related to existing tagging methods. Technical novelty seems low for an industry track paper.
2. Performance gains are modest and sometimes inconsistent across settings. In some cases short-context performance decreases, and extremum drop rates remain high.
3. Evaluation is a bit narrow. Not many models are evaluated. Only QA datasets are considered, that too synthetic. It is unclear how the results will generalize to realistic datasets common in the industry.
4. The paper could benefit from deeper analysis of why TAG works and when it does not work. Breaking down performance by tag type, tagging accuracy, tag distribution, would provide even more useful insights. For example, in real-world industry use cases, automated tagging will have errors. In such scenarios it is unclear how sensitive the model is to noisy, incorrect tags.
5. Since inserting tags changes token distribution, some performance differences could be attributed to better positioning of relevant information rather than semantic guidance.

title: Tagging-Augmented Generation: Assisting Language Models in Finding Intricate Knowledge In Long Contexts
review:
Quality
Strengths: 
	The paper is well-structured, with clear methodology, rigorous experiments, and comprehensive results. The use of two benchmarks (NoLiMa+ and NovelQA+，with varying context lengths 250–32K tokens) and multiple tagging strategies (LLM-based, traditional NER) demonstrates thorough validation.
	Moreover, the paper provides detailed prompts, labeling pipelines, and dataset augmentation steps, ensuring reproducibility.
Weaknesses:
	Only Anthropic Claude models are tested, generalization to other LLMs is unverified.
	TAG adds latency during document tagging, though less than RAG.

Clarity
Well-structured with intuitive figures (e.g., Figure 1) and definitions (TAG, TD+TC). Technical details (prompts) are in appendices.

Originality
This work introduces a novel framework that is the first to leverage inline semantic tags—using an XML-style syntax—for long-context guidance, offering a distinct alternative to retrieval-based approaches (e.g., RAG) or positional encoding modifications. In addition, the framework demonstrates strong agentic flexibility by supporting multiple tagging strategies, including LLM-driven, traditional NLP, and hybrid methods, setting it apart from rigid fine-tuning paradigms such as Tag-LLM.

Significance
Accuracy significantly improves with a 32K-token context, addressing the critical LLM limitation of attention decay.

Overall evaluation
Pros
	Lightweight & Infrastructure-Free: No need for retrieval systems or model retraining.
	Consistent Performance Gains: Demonstrated improvements across varying context lengths and reasoning tasks.
	Flexible Tagging Methods: Supports LLM-based, traditional NER, and hybrid approaches.
	Interpretability: XML-style tags provide transparent guidance for model attention.
	Resource Sharing: Public release of code, benchmarks, and tagging pipelines.

Cons
	Preprocessing Overhead: Tagging requires initial computational effort, though less than RAG indexing.
	Domain Dependency: Performance relies on well-designed semantic categories, which may be challenging for niche domains or low-resource languages.
	Hallucination Risk: LLM-based tagging could introduce incorrect tags (mitigated by hybrid approaches).
	Limited Task Validation: Evaluated primarily on QA, broader validation is needed.

title: MobileCity: An Efficient Framework for Large-Scale Urban Behavior Simulation
review:
This paper introduces MobileCity, an urban simulator that uses tile-based representations and LLMs to simulate human behaviors at scale. The city simulator focuses on efficiency and scalability while still gaining the benefits of LLMs as human-simulators. Humans are modeled with personality traits as well as long-term preferences, and take actions to satisfy a set of "basic needs" including "fullness", "happiness", "health", and "energy". 

**Strengths**:
* MobileCity offers a way to scale urban simulation of humans without incurring the high costs of running LLMs for every possible human action or decision by offloading many decisions to probabilistic sampling according to pre-computed preferences and actions.
* MobileCity is ranked as more human-like with an LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) than baselines.
* MobileCity bases the human profiles and preferences off of real survey data, creating synthetic profiles that represent true underlying human distributions.

**Weaknesses**:
* Elements of the MobileCity work are left unclear or seem to be mistakes. For example, Section 3.2 says: "In general, bus routes have the lowest time cost but the highest monetary cost." and later says: "Higher income agents are more likely to choose PMV due to its time efficiency, whereas lower-income agents may opt for walking or bus to reduce costs." These are directly contradictory statements, thought it could simply be a typo.
* Route calculation is not very clear. How are the embedding parameters derived for each transportation modes and routes? It seems to be a similarity between how often it is chosen vs. how often it is available for each survey respondent, but surely this is a poor approximation for route similarity or transportation-mode similarity?
* In a similar vein, action embeddings are not clear. Agents have a pre-defined action space, and actions are chosen by measuring the similarity of a human-action embedding to a human-agent embedding. The appendix explains that actions are language sequences, and the paper begins to make more sense, but this information should be in the main paper.
* Figure 3 and Table 3 both display the agent category as though that is somehow useful to the reader, but this information is buried in the appendix. I would recommend (1) informing readers that the information is in the appendix and (2) briefly explaining the most important categories for understanding the plots and tables.

Overall the work is interesting and it seems to be an important step in the urban modeling landscape, but there are central pieces of the paper that are not explained clearly, are in the appendix but should be in the main paper, or require the reader to make guesses about the framework.

title: MobileCity: An Efficient Framework for Large-Scale Urban Behavior Simulation
review:
This paper proposed a lightweight simulation system to mimic human urban mobility behaviors. Compared to previous previous work, the system further introduce a transportation mode where simulation agent can select when take the action. The agent profile is constructed via collecting a survey data. Experiment comparing to prior work show the proposed system could generate more human-like behaviors based on LLM-as-judge method. It also shows that simulated activities are close to real survey data. 

Pros:
1. The proposed design of transportation system with a tile-based city map seems a novel idea.  This helps to capture closer to human mobility activities. 

2. The agent actions are generated based on both static profile and dynamic needs seems to a good idea. The designed agent also conduct social interaction via exchanging past experience, which is a simple but representative idea to mimic how human actually socialize. 

3. The paper is clearly written and organized well. The examples shown in the appendix really help understand the simulation process.  

Cons:
1. There is a lack of comparison of other metrics, e.g., efficiency, micro and macro simulated activities, to prior work. The only metric compared across methods is how the generated actions are human-like using LLM-as-the-judge. It is not sufficient to prove the superiority of the proposed method. 

2. It is lack of ablation study to prove the effectiveness of the newly proposed module added to the agent. For example, what if we don't consider the transportation mode selection. 

3. The paper claimed "we explore the broader implications of MobileCity for urban planning and social studies", while it remained unclear how the results present in the experiment connects with such exploration. A discussion is needed here. 

4. The reproducibility is limited.  There is no software or code shared, and prompt design for the agent was not provided or showcased in the paper. 

5. The experiment show a simulated urban environment (10s of buildings and venues with transportation networks) which is rather small-scale. It would be nice to discuss what was goal of "large-scale" contribution claimed in the paper.

title: MobileCity: An Efficient Framework for Large-Scale Urban Behavior Simulation
review:
- The paper attempts to enhance urban behavior modeling by incorporating human parameters and personality traits into agent decision-making, comparing its approach to existing frameworks like SmallCity and HumanoidAgent. However, the core concepts largely reiterate prior work without introducing a substantially novel modeling technique or breakthrough innovation. The paper's main novelty—using similarity-based probabilistic action selection without LLMs in large-scale experiments—is insufficiently justified or demonstrated as impactful for industry adoption.

-The paper generally follows a logical flow but suffers from verbosity and some unclear explanations, particularly around the methodology of similarity computation and the experimental setup. The motivation for selecting certain modeling components over others is weakly articulated. Sections such as agent interaction mechanisms and environmental dynamics would benefit from more technical detail. Tables and examples, while informative, do not compensate for the overall lack of clarity in key technical processes.

-The paper fails to provide adequate detail to enable replication. Although the proprietary dataset is described, there is no indication of dataset availability or specifics on preprocessing steps, model parameters, or computational environment. The absence of shared code or pseudocode further limits reproducibility. For an industry track paper, practical implementation guidance is essential but largely missing.

However, 
positive:
1-Addresses a relevant problem in urban behavior simulation with some integration of agent personality traits.
2-Comparative analysis with existing methods is included.
3-Identification of future research directions shows awareness of current limitations.

Negative: 
1-Limited novelty; largely incremental advancement over existing works.
2-Insufficient methodological detail to reproduce experiments or validate claims.
3-Weak motivation and unclear explanation of key modeling components.
4-Lack of practical applicability demonstration or industrial case study.
5-No public release of code or dataset, hindering reproducibility.

title: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Reasoning towards Multi-Step Multi-Source Search in Large Language Models
review:
This paper presents R-Search: It is a unified single LLM framework for multi-step, multi-source search that addresses significant limitations in current approaches. It uses four structured components (`<think>` for reasoning, `<search>` for a natural-language DAG of sub-queries, `<result>` for retrieved passages, and `<answer>` for synthesis). Along with them it trains ReFT with a GRPO-based reward checking answer correctness and DAG validity.

The work cleverly combines reasoning, search planning, and answer synthesis in one coherent inference process. This avoids the computational overhead of multi-agent systems while maintaining strategic depth. Other popular approaches (such as Search-R1) embed individual search calls inline within a chain-of-thought, without any enforced plan structure or execution ordering. R-Search instead generated a fully specified plan first (represented as a DAG in natural language with explicit edge relations) before any execution. This separation of planning, execution, and synthesis is baked into the model’s output format and enforced by the environment parser.  
GRPO along with a multi-component reward function ( which includes format compliance, DAG validity, answer accuracy) helps get to a better system.

The paper does n automated dataset construction pipeline for training. The authors experimentally show non-triviaal improvements on both search-specific benchmarks (78.13% vs 76.20% accuracy on FinSearchBench-24) and standard Q&A tasks (41.87% performance). They also get efficiency gains (70% token reduction, 50% latency reduction). The ablation studies also validate the importance of both multi source search and ReFT.

title: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Reasoning towards Multi-Step Multi-Source Search in Large Language Models
review:
# Main contributions:

This paper focuses on search-augmentation method that proposed to dealing with the LLM factual limitation when responding to time sensitive queries.

Authors propose a multi-components reasoning structure for single-LLM ,called ReFT, that involves reasoning, search planning, retrieval and final answering steps.

Different with the multi-agent search frameworks, which employ planing, execution and synthesis steps with independent LLMs, ReFT unifies the multi-components in one coherent inference process.

This paper also proposes a specialized reinforcement fine-tuning method with GRPO to jointly optimize the four reasoning components .

# Strengths

1.  Readers can easily catch the main idea, and follow the training and inference processes.
2.  The experiment results exhibit the proposed method is useful for rag task.

# Weaknesses

1.  Authors claim that tool-calling search methods limit access to genuine, real-time information, which is caused by the search engine ability but not the search algorithm.
2.  ReFT still needs to execute the tool calling request after the <\search> tag, which likes a special type of tool calling method with parallel searching.  Earlier works, such as ReWOO, GOT,  have proposed similar methods. More comparisons are needed.
3.  The difference between the proposed reinforcement fine-tuning method and GRPO is not clear, besides on the reward function.

title: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Reasoning towards Multi-Step Multi-Source Search in Large Language Models
review:
This paper introduces the R-search framework that combines multi-step search, planning, execution, and finally QA in one pipeline. Basically, they want to address two issues: 1) multi-agent search is costly but effective, on the other and 2) single-llm search is efficient but less effective. The method structures output into four components: reasoning, search plans as natural-language directed acyclic graphs, retrieved results, and final answers. To train models for this structured output, the authors propose a specialized Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (ReFT) method based on GRPO with a multi-component reward function optimizing answer correctness, DAG structural validity, and format compliance. With their approach, they can do multi-source searching across different repositories and have high accuracy compared to current SOTA methods/models. I think the key is the DAG, which enables the search plans, which are then executed.

Strengths:
- The paper overall studies a key problem that needs to be explored, creating a unified framework for search and planning and balancing between multi-agent and single-agent systems.
- The paper has the standard set of optimization tricks that is also used in other methods (see eq (3)).
- The paper conducts extensive experiments.

Weakness:
- My main concern with the paper seems to be that the results are too good to be true. See questions.
- The exact novelty of the method is not clear to me.

Overall, I like the idea, and if my questions are answered, I will raise my score.

Questions:
- Why in the baseline LLama3 8.1b aacuracy is better than gpt4o? This requires some explanations.
- The R-Search DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B reached an accuracy of 78.13, compared to SearchAgent gpt4o, which is 46.33%. Why? I understand that non-search baselines should be poor, but the jump against search baselines is too much. Can you explain this?
- You have a complex framework and good work that you conducted the ablation study. However, the message from Table 3 is mixed. In FinSearchBench-24, you have better accuracy just with FinSearchBench-24. However, in SearchExpertBench-25, you have better accuracy with multi-source search. So there is a sort of conflict. Can you explain this?
- Suggestion: Reinforcement finetuning is not new, and there are a lot of recent works on this. More discussions on the related work is required on this.

title: Can LLMs Narrate Tabular Data? An Evaluation Framework for Natural Language Representations of Text-to-SQL System Outputs
review:
This paper addresses an underexplored stage in Text-to-SQL pipelines: converting SQL execution results (tabular data) into Natural Language Representations (NLRs). While most research focuses on SQL query generation, the authors highlight that errors or information loss in narrating tabular results can degrade user experience in conversational agents.

**The paper introduces:((
1. NLR-BIRD – the first dataset dedicated to evaluating NLRs, covering 11 domains with 1,468 annotated samples.
2. Combo-Eval – a hybrid evaluation method combining automatic text similarity metrics (e.g., ROUGE-1 recall) and LLM-as-a-judge to improve correlation with human judgment while reducing LLM calls by 25–61%.
3. A thorough benchmark of 15 LLM “judges” and several NLR-generation models, under scenarios with and without ground truth NLRs.

** Quality ** 
Strengths
 - Solid problem motivation: highlights a real gap in NLR evaluation for Text-to-SQL systems.
 - Well-designed dataset (NLR-BIRD) with diverse domains and clear annotation guidelines.
 - Rigorous experiments comparing multiple evaluation methods, models, and settings.
 - Combo-Eval’s efficiency gains are practical for large-scale deployment.

Areas for Improvement:
 - Provide a more detailed statistical significance analysis of improvements over baselines.
- Include more real-world conversational agent case studies to show downstream impact of improved evaluation.

** Clarity **
Strengths
 - Clear separation of scenarios (with and without ground truth).
 - Good use of diagrams (e.g., Combo-Eval flow, error breakdowns).
 - Comprehensive appendices detailing prompts, thresholds, and datasets.

Areas for Improvement
 - Use more plain-language summaries after mathematical sections to reinforce intuition.
- Move certain low-impact numeric threshold details fully to the appendix.

** Novelty **
Strengths
 - First to introduce a benchmark dataset specifically for narrating SQL execution results.
 - Novel hybrid evaluation method (Combo-Eval) that targets both accuracy and cost-efficiency.
 - Frames the evaluation problem in the broader context of real-world conversational DB interfaces.

Areas for Improvement
 - Discuss how Combo-Eval could generalize to other structured-to-NL tasks (e.g., chart-to-text, spreadsheet narration).
 - Compare against more advanced metric+LLM fusion strategies, not just simple thresholding.

title: Can LLMs Narrate Tabular Data? An Evaluation Framework for Natural Language Representations of Text-to-SQL System Outputs
review:
The paper introduces a new evaluation method for LLM-generated natural language representations of text-to-SQL system outputs, promising to significantly minimize LLM calls and reduce computational demand. The compare 'Metrics-as-a-Judge' involving several popular automated metrics, and LLM-as-a-Judge using  GPT-4o against their proposed Combo-Eval approach, which combines the two approaches based on a set threshold. Authors report strong results and the method could be a useful addition in evaluation workflows. However, the main text barely fits within the 6 pages and the reader is directed to the appendix 17 times for many important details, which is 10 pages long.

Some of the main issues with the paper:
 * The authors keep sending the reader to the appendix for several key information pieces - seems like this could have been easily formatted as a long paper our journal publication with more of the content at one place.

 * 12 out of the 38 references are citing arXiv and not the actual publication venues for those papers. This is a very bad style of work and should never be acceptable aside from some rare cases when a couple of papers truly only were submitted to arXiv and nowhere else.

 * The references section in general should be improved - there are websites cited without a proper author or access date. Or perhaps those could be footnotes? 
    * xAI. Grok.
    * Greg Michnikov Vijay Venugopal. 2024. Chat with your business data - conversational analytics comes to gemini in looker.
    * OpenAI. 2025. Openai o3-mini system card.
    * Cohere. a. Cohere’s command r+ model (details and application).
    * Cohere. b. The command r model (details and application).
    * Riza Farheen. 2025. Building an agentic workflow: Orchestrating a multi-step software engineering interview. 
 * As well as incomplete citations
    * Jyotika Singh. 2023. Natural Language Processing in the Real World: Text Processing, Analytics, and Classification. Chapman and Hall/CRC.

Some minor issues:

title: Can LLMs Narrate Tabular Data? An Evaluation Framework for Natural Language Representations of Text-to-SQL System Outputs
review:
Summary

This paper introduces Combo-Eval, a novel hybrid evaluation framework for assessing natural language representations (NLRs) of tabular outputs generated by Text-to-SQL systems. It also releases NLR-BIRD, the first dedicated dataset for benchmarking NLR generation. The study benchmarks multiple LLMs on NLR generation, compares evaluation strategies (metrics-based, LLM-as-a-judge, and the proposed Combo-Eval), and shows that Combo-Eval improves fidelity with human judgment while significantly reducing computational costs.

Strengths

Novel contribution: Addresses a clear gap in industry-relevant evaluation of NLRs, an underexplored but practically important aspect of Text-to-SQL systems
.

Practical focus: Industry track–relevant emphasis on evaluation efficiency and cost (Combo-Eval reduces LLM calls by up to 61% with GT and 24% with UQDB)
.

Dataset release: NLR-BIRD provides 1468 annotated samples across 11 domains, enabling reproducibility and future benchmarking
.

Robust methodology: Evaluation in both with-ground-truth (GT) and without-ground-truth (UQDB) scenarios mirrors real-world deployment constraints
.

Comprehensive analysis: Error categorization (missing elements, hallucinations, formatting inconsistencies) provides diagnostic insights valuable for industry adoption
.

Clarity of findings: Results consistently highlight that larger result-sets degrade both NLR generation and evaluation reliability, motivating research into summarization strategies
.

Weaknesses / Limitations

Narrow domain coverage: While NLR-BIRD spans 11 domains, it may not fully capture the breadth of industrial tabular data needs
.

Focus on evaluation, not generation: The paper explicitly states that improving NLR generation is outside its scope, which limits its immediate impact for practitioners seeking end-to-end improvements
.

Scalability for large result-sets: While Combo-Eval optimizes evaluation, the generation side still struggles with large tables. The proposed framework highlights the problem but doesn’t provide actionable solutions for summarization in production
.

Dependence on LLM-as-a-judge: Although Combo-Eval reduces calls, it still inherits biases and failure modes of judge models, particularly with large result-sets
.

Evaluation bias toward GT: The method works better with GT references than with UQDB, which could limit applicability in settings where annotated references are unavailable
.

Clarity & Structure

The paper is well-written, logically structured, and clear. The motivation is well framed, related work is thorough, and experimental setup is transparent. Figures (e.g., error type distributions, threshold analysis) are informative. A constructive point is that Section 5 could be streamlined—currently results, error analyses, and method comparisons are interleaved, making the narrative dense.

Originality & Impact

The evaluation framing is novel: prior work has largely focused on Text-to-SQL generation, not the equally important narration of tabular results.

The impact for industry is high, as Text-to-SQL conversational agents are widely deployed, and the lack of robust evaluation has been a bottleneck.

Releasing both a dataset and a method strengthens the paper’s long-term utility.

Reproducibility

The dataset (NLR-BIRD) and methodology details (including prompts, thresholds, and inference settings) are provided
.

This ensures reproducibility, even though model code is not required per industry track norms.

One gap is the exclusion of very large result-sets (rc+cc ≥ 500). Practitioners may face precisely these cases in deployment, so reproducibility across full spectrum of data remains limited.

Pros and Cons (Condensed)

Pros

Novel evaluation framework (Combo-Eval).

Dataset release (NLR-BIRD).

Strong alignment with human judgment.

Efficiency gains (25–61% reduction in LLM calls).

Clear industrial applicability.

Comprehensive error analysis.

Cons

Limited domain and result-size coverage.

Focuses only on evaluation, not improving generation.

Combo-Eval still partly reliant on judge LLM biases.

GT scenario outperforms UQDB, limiting no-reference settings.

Results section could be more streamlined for readability.

Recommendation

Good paper, accept (Industry Track).
This paper makes a significant and novel contribution to an underexplored but crucial area: evaluating natural language representations of tabular results. The release of a new dataset and the practical efficiency of Combo-Eval make it particularly relevant for industry. While limited in scope on the generation side, its focus on evaluation aligns strongly with track priorities, and the work will be valuable to both researchers and practitioners.

title: AutoDSPy: Automating Modular Prompt Design with Reinforcement Learning for Small and Large Language Models
review:
This paper proposes AutoDSPy—the first reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework for automating DSPy pipelines. The idea is reasonably novel, but there are shortcomings—insufficient comparative experiments and inadequate explanations for observed experimental phenomena—and the manuscript needs further revision.

Strength: Applying RL to automatically synthesize modular prompt pipelines is a novel direction that fills the gap of DSPy’s reliance on manual configuration.

Weaknesses:
   1. The paper repeatedly mentions the training overhead introduced by RL but lacks concrete quantitative metrics such as training time, GPU hours, peak memory usage, and energy consumption. I cannot assess the method’s feasibility in resource-constrained environments or for large-scale deployment. 

 2.  Why is a binary reward (exact match) used during training? Have the authors tried finer-grained or continuous rewards (e.g., step-level rewards, LLM semantic scoring)? If tried, what were the results; if not, why not adopt them?

  3. Experiments are limited to GSM8K and HotPotQA. Do the authors have plans or preliminary results demonstrating AutoDSPy’s applicability to code generation, multimodal tasks, or non-English corpora? If not, can they clarify the limitations of extending the method?

4.  Experiments show that GRPO’s performance decreases with larger k on GSM8K but improves on HotPotQA. The manuscript offers speculative explanations (gradient noise, diversity) but lacks theoretical grounding or direct empirical evidence to support these claims.
5. What is the exact implementation of the LLM-based evaluation used as a fallback? How is the evaluator’s confidence and consistency ensured, and could evaluator errors introduce reward noise?

6. "Teleprompter" is inconsistently spelled/cased between the main text and the algorithm (e.g., §3.2 uses "Teleprompter" while Algorithm 1 uses "teleprompter").

title: AutoDSPy: Automating Modular Prompt Design with Reinforcement Learning for Small and Large Language Models
review:
Review
Summary

This paper introduces AutoDSPy, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based extension to DSPy that automates the design of modular LLM pipelines. Instead of relying on manual selection of modules, input–output signatures, and optimization strategies, AutoDSPy employs an RL-tuned policy network to dynamically construct task-adaptive pipelines. The authors demonstrate that AutoDSPy improves accuracy (up to +4.3% over DSPy baselines) and reduces inference time across reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, HotPotQA)
.

The work positions itself as a practical contribution for industry, offering automation, scalability, and efficiency in building high-performing LLM solutions.

Strengths (Pros)

Novelty & Contribution: The first fully automated DSPy extension, replacing manual pipeline construction with RL-based synthesis. This is a meaningful innovation with potential to reduce human expertise barriers in industrial adoption.

Practical Impact: Addresses real bottlenecks in industry—time-consuming prompt engineering, lack of scalability, and expertise dependence.

Strong Empirical Evidence: Comprehensive experiments across multiple policy models (GPT-2, LLaMA, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi-4, DeepSeek) and RL algorithms (REINFORCE, PPO, GRPO). Demonstrates consistent improvements over DSPy baselines
.

Clarity in Results: Clear reporting of trade-offs (accuracy vs. inference time). For instance, GRPO maximizes accuracy while Reinforce minimizes latency.

Industrial Relevance: The decision to exclude teleprompters due to latency overhead highlights thoughtful design for real-world deployment
.

Reproducibility: Includes datasets (GSM8K, HotPotQA), model variants, hyperparameters, ablation studies, and implementation details (Appendix A)
.

Weaknesses (Cons)

Scope of Evaluation: The framework is only validated on GSM8K and HotPotQA. Broader benchmarks (e.g., multilingual tasks, domain-specific datasets like legal or biomedical QA) would strengthen claims of generalizability
.

Computational Overhead: RL training introduces significant costs, potentially limiting adoption in low-resource industrial settings
.

Limited Module Pool: AutoDSPy currently relies on a small set of DSPy modules and teleprompters. This restricts the diversity of compositional strategies
.

External Validity: While performance gains are clear, it remains uncertain how AutoDSPy behaves in real-world noisy environments or tasks beyond curated benchmarks.

Clarity Issues: While generally well-structured, some technical explanations (e.g., policy network learning dynamics, reward shaping) could benefit from more intuitive illustrations for practitioners unfamiliar with RL.

Detailed Evaluation
Quality

The technical quality is high. The paper leverages established RL algorithms (REINFORCE, PPO, GRPO), adapts them to modular prompt design, and empirically validates their strengths. The ablation studies are thorough (episodes, dataset sizes, teleprompters, GRPO hyperparameter sensitivity), which demonstrates careful experimentation
.

Clarity

The paper is generally well-written and logically structured. Figures (e.g., pipeline workflow, ablation results) provide helpful visualizations. However, some sections are dense and may be less accessible to an industry practitioner audience. More examples of real-world use cases would improve accessibility.

Originality

The work is original in its full automation of DSPy pipeline synthesis using RL. While prior work (e.g., EvoPrompt, RLPrompt, PromptWizard) addressed prompt optimization, AutoDSPy is the first to extend modular pipeline design with RL-based adaptability
. This represents a meaningful step forward.

Significance

The significance is high for industry. Automating modular prompt pipelines can reduce development costs, broaden access to LLM capabilities, and improve consistency across applications. Although generalizability remains to be fully proven, the presented framework could set a precedent for scalable LLM deployment in industry.

Suggestions for Improvement

Expand Benchmarks: Include multilingual datasets, code synthesis tasks, or domain-specific challenges to demonstrate robustness.

Real-World Case Studies: Show how AutoDSPy performs in industrial applications (e.g., customer support, workflow automation).

Efficiency Enhancements: Explore lightweight RL or curriculum learning to reduce training overhead, as hinted in the conclusion
.

Interpretability: Add diagnostic tools or visualizations showing why certain pipelines are preferred by the policy network.

Limitations Discussion: While limitations are acknowledged, providing mitigation strategies (e.g., module expansion roadmap, hybrid manual-automatic modes) would strengthen the paper.

Recommendation

Marginally above acceptance threshold

AutoDSPy is a timely and practical contribution that balances novelty, industrial relevance, and empirical rigor. Its limitations (scope, computational cost) do not overshadow the clear value it provides in automating LLM pipeline construction. With some refinements—particularly broader benchmarks and interpretability—the work could have strong impact both in research and industry.

title: AutoDSPy: Automating Modular Prompt Design with Reinforcement Learning for Small and Large Language Models
review:
This paper proposes using an LLM-based policy-gradient RL method to automate LLM reasoning pipelines within the DSPy framework. The approach shows improvements over DSPy’s internal optimization methods. While combining LLM agents and RL is a popular research area, it is challenging to find truly novel ideas. The key question is whether this method offers better power efficiency compared to DSPy’s teleprompter-based optimization, given that increased compute generally improves reasoning pipelines.

Major concerns:

- Training data size: Fine-tuning a 127M-parameter policy network with only 200–300 episodes seems limited, raising overfitting and robustness concerns. Including learning curves or comparisons with naive policies would help.

- Evaluation methodology: Clarify whether accuracy is based on exact string matches or semantic equivalence. Providing exact match rates would strengthen the paper and improve its clarity.

- No Reward shaping: Assigning the same reward for exact and approximate matches may omit valuable feedback signals.

- Statistical significance: No confidence intervals or tests are reported, making it hard to assess if observed differences are significant.

- Ethical considerations: The high computational cost also raises environmental concerns. Further discussion on this trade-off would be appreciated.

Minor remarks:

- Figure references lines 090 to 100: Use different labels (e.g., (i), (ii), (iii)) instead of (a), (b), (c) to avoid confusion.

- Clarification line 298, specify: “The policy network is an LLM fine-tuned to generate pipelines as...”

Conclusion:

The paper presents potential improvements in query time and quality from DSPy. However, the limited training data and fragile evaluation methodology render difficult to assess its scientific relevance. The technical contribution seems however solid enough for an industrial track.

title: Advanced Retrieval Strategies for Large Language Model Applications
review:
The paper presents a evaluation of retrieval strategies by testing embedding models, score approaches and reranking approaches across a set of 4 common retrieval benchmarks.
Pros
1. Wide model usage in experiment to test wide variety of retrieval task. 
2. Clear ablations for chunk sizes and prompts along with clearly reproducible setup. 
3. Very practical insights on how to best optimize models for usage and well documented.

Weakness
1. Does not discuss how these datasets being over fit to via MTEB and other leaderboard can impact the true signal of model quality. 
2. Results are purely quantitative. No clear examples of why systems actualy beat eachother. Look at the results and find our whats happening. 
3. Lack of novelty

Comments
1. While RAG is mentioned in a lot of places it seems this is mostly focused on retrieval. Perhaps focus on that and update the title/wording to reflect the focus. 
2. Consider adding embedding merging. yes RRF can work but approaches for concating embeddings also work very well. 
3. Careful about claiming meaningful gains without statistical rigor. 0.4% is very unlikley to be "meaninful"
4. Typos like "datastet" 
5. When possible results with NDCG@K are preferable.

title: Advanced Retrieval Strategies for Large Language Model Applications
review:
This paper conducts an in-depth evaluation of advanced retrieval techniques designed to enhance document relevance for LLMs. These techniques include using LLMs as re-rankers, context-aware embeddings, adaptive context windows, comparative analysis of embedding models, model fine-tuning, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) for result aggregation.

Strengths:

The paper is well-written and easy to understand.
The experiments are thorough.
Results on multiple datasets demonstrate that prioritizing retrieval augmentation can ultimately improve the response quality of LLMs.

Weaknesses:

The methods are mostly combinations of existing RAG techniques, and the level of innovation is insufficient.

title: Advanced Retrieval Strategies for Large Language Model Applications
review:
*Summary*:

This work tries to reveal the effective retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches through comprehensive comparisons in text retrieval tasks, mostly focusing on the usefulness of reranking strategies. For this purpose, the authors compared cross-encoder reranking, LLM reranking, and meta-prompting on FiQA-2018, HotpotQA, and SciDocs from the BeIR benchmark with various embedding models (retrievers), stella 1.5B, text-embedding-3-large, gemini-large-03-07, gte-Qwen2-1.5B-instruct, and BM25. The experimental result shows that LLM reranking for dense retrievers outperforms other reranking methods in many cases, whereas sparse retrievers with cross-encoder reranking or LLM reranking commonly outperform other reranking methods in terms of recall.

*Strength*:

- The aspect, reranking of retrieved results, focused on by this work is novel and important considering the existence of many related downstream tasks.
- The experiments used both dense and sparse retrievers for the comparison. This setting meets the demand of industrial researchers who need to consider the running costs of retrievers.
- The observed results clarify the effectiveness of LLM-based reranking. This is a useful takeaway for industrial researchers.
- Reranking costs are also reported in the Appendix.

*Weaknesses*:

- This work does not cover the effect of retrievers on downstream tasks like QA tasks. Thus, the importance of performance differences on the reported result is uncertain in practical situations.
- Even though the authors report the cost of using LLM reranking, the discussion lacks the viewpoint of cost performance, which is one of the most important things in the industry.
- This work only considers the importance of coverage (recall). However, in downstream tasks, due to the hallucination issues, precision is also important. Thus, this work misses one important aspect of using RAG in LLMs.

title: Advanced Retrieval Strategies for Large Language Model Applications
review:
This paper identifies that often large gaps exist between Recall@10 and Recall@50 for retrievers, indicating that correct/relevant documents are not ranked high enough for the LLM to use effectively. Thus, it investigates how LLMs can be used a re-rankers. It evaluates a wide spectrum of retrieval and re-ranking methods on three public benchmarks (FiQA, HotpotQA, SciDocs) and a proprietary support chatbot dataset. Overall, this work provides practical guidance on designing retrieval pipelines and highlights the tradeoff between cost and benefits for adopting LLM-based re-ranking in industry setting.

Strengths ==
1. Identifies several key takeaways. This includes: a) LLM-based re-ranking often outperforms cross-encoders and matches/outperforms specialized retrieval models. b) RRF consistently yields performance gains while hybrid search with BM25 degrades performance. c) Fine-tuning smaller embeddings with synthetic data can enhance recall in some cases. d) Embedding selection -> RRF -> LLM-reranking is an effective retrieval pipeline. 
2. The empirical evaluation is quite comprehensive. Several retrieval and re-ranking methods are evaluated. Datasets are also diverse. Ablation experiments are plenty: chunk size, fine-tuning, prompting strategies.
3. Core idea of re-ranking top candidates with LLMs in zero-shot setting is fairly simple but generally effective.  
4. Also evaluated commonly used BM25 and cross-encoders and showed their limited utility in modern retrieval pipelines.

Weaknesses ==
1. Although the empirical results are comprehensive, novelty of methodology is low. No fundamentally new methods are introduced.
2. Re-ranking only explores basic prompting methods. Fine-tuned LLMs and retrieval-specific adapters over LLMs could also provide additional insights into different design choices.
3. Could have considered other retrieval metrics like nDCG. End-to-end accuracy would have also provided insights into how robust retrieval should be for downstream reasoning. This is particularly important since LLMs can now handle large and noisy contexts more effectively.

title: LLM-Based Dialogue Labeling for Multiturn Adaptive RAG
review:
This paper tackles the challenge of deploying multi-turn RAG in the wild, specifically in determining when to leverage it and issues around context. It proposes using an LLM to generate data to address each in two ways. For deciding when to perform retrieval, the paper compares an intent-guided approach with that of and explanation one. For the query reformulation, it compares a natural language approach to that of keywords. It finds that the explanation guided and the keyword approach are more effective then the others. 

Strengths: This paper addresses a timely topic that is an area of active industrial attention. It is well written and provides good evaluation within the methods and conditions it covers. I am confident that the approaches are reproducible, given that they leverage a public LLM, while the results may differ given differing RAG setups. 

Weaknesses: The primary weakness of this paper is the lack of comparison to the data and RAG setup itself. This means that the approaches that excelled here may not excel for others if they are using a different chunking strategy or have markedly different conversational characteristics. However, I feel like the framework provides readers a place to start and guidance as to how to optimize other RAG architectures.

title: LLM-Based Dialogue Labeling for Multiturn Adaptive RAG
review:
### Summary

The paper describes how LLMs can be used for annotation tasks, specifically for adaptive retrieval and query reformulation for multi-turn RAG systems. The authors make use of the huge amounts of real customer-agent conversations from their e-commerce platform and annotate them using LLMs, significantly reducing dependency on manual annotations.

Two approaches are proposed for adaptive retrieval:

- Intent-guided labeling which prompts the LLM to identify the intent of the utterance, and use it as the basis for deciding whether retrieval is needed or not.
- Explanation-guided labeling which prompts the LLM to explain why it should make a retrieval or not and then make the decision.

Similarly, for query reformulation, two approaches are proposed:

- Natural Language Query reformulation which prompts the LLM to generate a natural language query that is grammatically correct and resolves any ambiguities based on the previous context and the utterance.
- Keyword reformulation which prompts the LLM to generate the keywords necessary to perform the user’s query.

### Review

- The paper is very well-written and easy to understand. It has clearly presented the motivation, the methods and the results and how it is applicable to the industry as well as the impact this method has had in their production system.
- The method is novel and takes advantage of the huge amount of real conversation data available to the authors to enrich for downstream tasks for multi-turn RAG.
- The quality of the synthetic annotations generated using the has been evaluated rigorously for both tasks. The LLM-annotations have been evaluated against human annotations as well as with models

title: LLM-Based Dialogue Labeling for Multiturn Adaptive RAG
review:
## Paper Summary

The authors state that a multi-turn RAG-based chatbot for real-world customer service profits of components like adaptive retrieval and query reformulation. These components typically require substantial annotated data, which are often scarce. Therefore, the authors propose and evaluate methods to be able to automatically generate labels out of real customer-agent dialogue data.

The authors introduce two different labeling strategies (using LLMs) for the adaptive retrieval process: (1) intent-guided and (2) explanation-based strategy. Furthermore, two query reformulations strategies: (1) natural language query reformulation and (2) keyword-based reformulation are proposed. 

The conducted experiments reveal that the explanation-based strategy yields the best results for the adaptive retrieval process, while the keyword-based reformulation improves document retrieval quality. 

## Summary of Strengths

The authors propose two novel adaptive retrieval labeling strategies and two reformulation labeling strategies for building adaptive retrieval and query reformulation models to support multi-turn RAG systems.

The need of adaptive retrieval and query reformulation is comprehensible. The rationale behind adaptive retrieval is clear, demonstrating its capacity to reduce latency and context length. The authors also explain how the query reformulation component employs conversation history to generate more precise queries for the retrieval module, ensuring responses are relevant to the context.

Clear description how adaptive retrieval and query reformulation are integrated into a RAG system to support multi-turn conversations.

An interesting finding is that, although natural language question (NLQ) reformulations are commonly used in conversational question answering (CQA), the authors show they are not always necessary. Instead, keyword-based reformulations can be sufficient to retrieve high-quality documents within their framework.

The usage of human annotations for evaluating both adaptive retrieval and reformulation strategies is well-executed and adds credibility to the results. Additionally, the clear and detailed description of the evaluation procedures is highly appreciated and strengthens the paper.

The findings offer valuable insights for practitioners of multi-turn RAG systems in real-world customer service applications. The practical approach, utilizing existing dialogue data—without the need for extensive manual annotation—is especially noteworthy, as it enables the development of effective and responsive chatbots with greater efficiency.

## Summary of Weakness

The "conversation history" and the "latest query" are sent to the "adaptive retrieval" component, which determines whether an answer is generated directly or if an additional retrieval process is triggered to provide more context. Therefore, in Figure 1, the arrow from the top-left box to "Answer Generation" should originate after the "Adaptive Retrieval" box, possibly with an additional "no" label for clarity.

In Section 4.1, it is unclear that both input types, “full dialogue” and “context + query”, are used across both labeling strategies, “Intent-guided” and “Explanation-guided.” 

In Section 5.1, the authors mention that they only used a training- and a test-set and implemented an early stopping procedure. However, the test set should not influence the training process in any way. Therefore, a separate validation set should be used for early stopping.

In Section 6.1. the authors validate the accuracy of different prompting strategies for generating adaptive retrieval labels, which seems to relate to "we first assess different annotation strategies by manually examining 500 sampled test set" of Section 5.1. right? Did you compare the 500 test samples against the human annotations? Clarifying the role of these samples and providing a more detailed description of the procedure would strengthen this part.

Space missing in line 503 after the punctuation mark.

title: SCorPion: A Strategic, Controllable and Personified Conversational Companion
review:
Problem: Fixed prompts underperform in open‑domain conversation where different situations call for different “skills.”

Method: Build a knowledge graph from several datasets via GraphRAG; replace GraphRAG’s community summaries with community summarized strategies (CSS: Condition, Skill, Demonstration). At inference, score and top‑k select CSS; optionally reweight scores by controllable factors per category (empathy, morality, etc.) before prompting the generator LLM.

Data: DailyDialog, ESConv, EmpatheticDialogues, MIC (morality), GYAFC (formality), Shakespeare (style). CSS categories are tagged via GPT‑4o plus manual checks.

Experiments: Compare against Direct, Self‑Refine, CoT, and BOT. Report BLEU‑2/ROUGE‑L across datasets; Cskills multi‑turn results; safety on S‑Eval; ablations and sensitivity curves; examples of controllability.

Results: Consistent gains over listed baselines on n‑gram metrics; improved multi‑turn engagement on Cskills; controllable style trends; some evidence of safety alignment and emotional intelligence shifts.

Paper type: System/engineering report (methodology with deployment angle).

Strengths:
Clear, industry‑oriented pipeline: offline strategy extraction and tagging; online lightweight ranking with explicit cost/latency controls (k, ε, smaller Mg).
Practical controllability: simple reweighting delivers tunable empathy/morality/formality with illustrative cases.
Sensitivity and ablations: show impact of CSS structure and system hyperparameters; discuss perf‑cost trade‑offs.
Breadth: applies one framework across open‑domain, ESC, morality, and style transfer; leverages well‑known datasets.

Weaknesses and Limitations:
Evaluation choices: BLEU/ROUGE are poor proxies for dialogue quality and empathy; safety comparison relies on one benchmark and figure without controlled settings; statistical significance and CIs are missing.
Baseline coverage: Missing comparisons with strong recent domain‑specific systems for ESC and empathetic dialogue (e.g., newer ESC‑oriented LLMs and alignment methods), and with controllable alignment approaches like SteerLM; BOT is adapted but retrieval and hyperparameters may not be fully matched.
Reproducibility gaps: Incomplete disclosure of hardware, decoding parameters, exact seeds, annotator counts/IAAs, CSS inventory size, and the database/graph persistence setup.
Safety risks: Aggressive/irreverent styles can be harmful in support contexts; moderation/guardrails policy is not operationalized.
External model dependence: Uses GPT‑3.5/4o for tagging/scoring in places; cost and repeatability implications are not quantified.
Some edits/maturity: table/figure references could be tightened; a few grammar issues.

Novelty and related work:
GraphRAG for QFS: Edge et al. introduce community summaries over a knowledge graph to answer global corpus questions; this paper repurposes that pipeline to store and retrieve conversational strategies rather than factual summaries.
Buffer of Thoughts (BoT): retrieves distilled thought templates for reasoning tasks; authors compare against BOT and claim better performance when swapping the retriever for GraphRAG in conversational settings.
CSIM “think before you speak”: inner‑monologue prompts to cultivate communication skills (topic transition, empathy, etc.); SCorPion instead queries a strategy index for skill application.
Ask‑an‑Expert: dialogue models consult an LLM expert for strategic reasoning in mental health support, close to the paper’s motivation of situation‑specific guidance; provides a relevant baseline concept not directly compared here.
Multi‑expert Prompting: simulating multiple experts and aggregating outputs; offers a complementary prompt‑level alternative to SCorPion’s retrieval approach.
SteerLM: attribute‑conditioned SFT enabling inference‑time control (e.g., helpfulness, humor), a supervised alternative to RLHF; comparable to SCorPion’s controllable factors but via finetuning rather than retrieval.
ESC datasets/benchmarks: ESConv (strategy‑annotated) and EmpatheticDialogues underpin the ESC evaluation and are appropriate references.
Style transfer resources: GYAFC (formality) and Shakespeare style pairs are standard style‑adaptation testbeds used here.
Safety evaluation: S‑Eval provides an automated safety testing framework; cross‑model comparison requires careful control of versions and settings.
Negotiation strategy graphs (DialoGraph): earlier use of graph structures to model conversational strategies, conceptually adjacent to this work’s strategy graphing.

Overall, the contribution is incremental‑to‑moderately novel: it adapts GraphRAG to store/retrieve strategy triplets (CSS) and adds simple reweighting for controllability. The engineering integration is practical and useful for industry scenarios; methodological novelty is modest.

What’s missing/ambiguous:
Exact dataset versions/URLs and licenses; acquisition dates; precise train/val/test splits for datasets without official splits; number of CSS and category distribution; tagging workflow (how many GPT‑4o calls, cost, manual verification criteria).
Decoding settings (temperature, top‑p, max tokens), random seeds, and run counts.
Compute details: GPU types/counts, memory, quantization, throughput, latency distributions; cost estimates for indexing and per‑turn inference; persistence of the graph/index and datastore stack.
Human evaluation: annotator counts, demographics/compensation, IAA statistics, and blinding.
Statistical testing methodology.

Industry relevance and deployment considerations:
Positive: Explicit control knobs and a clear dial between quality and cost (k, ε, Mg size) are deployment‑friendly. The approach is model‑agnostic and works without finetuning.
Gaps: No detailed SLO/SLA targets, on‑call/monitoring plan, or rollback strategy when CSS produces unsafe styles; no A/B test or post‑deployment metrics (retention, satisfaction, harm reports).
Suggestions: Add a production section with latency p50/p95, throughput per GPU, cost breakdown (indexing vs per‑turn), and a moderation policy (pre‑filters, refusal behavior, escalation paths).

Questions for authors:
How many CSS items are in the final index, and how are categories distributed? Please report the overlap between CSS sources and tasks.
What decoding parameters and seeds did you use across all experiments? How many runs per setting; any variance/CIs?
For BOT, did you replicate its retriever settings (embedding model, top‑k, threshold) identically to SCorPion where applicable?
How is the CSS scoring function implemented (prompt and rubric)? Is the 0–100 score well‑calibrated across categories/models?
Can you provide latency p50/p95 and cost per interaction for the production configuration (M=70B, Mg=8B, k=10, ε=80)?
What moderation safeguards prevent unsafe outputs when aggressive styles are prioritized, especially in ESC?
How many human raters participated; what were the IAA metrics; were raters blinded to model identity?
Did you evaluate with semantic metrics (BERTScore/BLEURT) or preference wins to complement BLEU/ROUGE?
How often must the graph/CSS index be refreshed in practice, and what is the operational workflow?

Typos and minor comments:
Several minor grammatical issues (articles/capitalization); consider a proofread pass.
Please label all axes/units (e.g., RT).
Table/figure cross‑references: ensure all are numbered consistently and referenced in text.
Double‑list references (e.g., Bachorowski and Braaten 1994a/1994b appear duplicated) — clean bibliography.

title: SCorPion: A Strategic, Controllable and Personified Conversational Companion
review:
The paper focuses on the limitation of fixed-prompting methods in developing open-domain conversational agents, which often fails to provide personified, strategic, and stylistically appropriate responses. To this end, it introduces a framework for building a conversational companion that uses GraphRAG to create a dynamic repository of conversational knowledge. It works by first extracting and structuring conversational strategies, principles, and styles from various text corpora into a KG. The KG is then used to generate CSS. At inference time, it retrieves and ranks the most relevant strategies for a given user query.

Strengths
- It uses GraphRAG to build a queryable repository of conversational strategies, which moves beyond simple RAG or fixed prompt templates (CoT/BOT) by creating an interconnected understanding of conversational dynamics. It is a significant step towards more sophisticated dialogue management.
- The mechanism for stylistic control via explicit factors (C_cate) is a major strength, which provides a direct and interpretable way to tune the agent's behavior without needing to retrain or finetune the model.
- The paper is well-grounded in practical deployment considerations. The authors explicitly discuss the performance-cost trade-off and detail their deployed version, which uses a powerful 70B model for response generation and a more efficient 8B model for the GraphRAG backend. Such architectural choice demonstrates a clear understanding of the resource constraints and latency requirements of real-world conversational systems.
- An extensive appendix with prompts and evaluation details significantly enhances the paper's reproducibility.

Weaknesses and questions
- Online querying process involves asking M^g to score each CSS candidate (up to k=100 in the experiments) for every user turn. It seems computationally intensive and could introduce significant latency, which is critical for real-time conversation. What is the average end-to-end latency added by the SCorPion strategy retrieval and ranking process? How does this latency scale as the repository of CSSs grows from the current sub-hundred to potentially thousands of strategies required for a truly comprehensive open-domain agent?
- The system's performance is dependent on the quality of the CSS generated in the offline phase. It, in turn, depends on the source corpora and the summarization capabilities of GraphRAG. The paper mentions manual checking to ensure quality. Could the authors elaborate on the extent of manual effort required to curate the source data and validate the generated CSS? How does the system defend against learning and amplifying undesirable or low-quality conversational strategies from noisy or biased source texts?
- The system relies on strategies extracted from a set of predefined datasets covering specific domains (daily chat, empathy, morality, etc.). How well does SCorPion generalize to conversational topics or situations that are not well-represented in the initial source corpora? Does the performance degrade gracefully, or does it tend to fall back to a generic response style when no relevant CSS is retrieved?

title: SCorPion: A Strategic, Controllable and Personified Conversational Companion
review:
In this work, the authors introduce Scorpion, a framework that produces stylized, anthropomorphic, and controllable responses. The framework operates on top of various styles extracted from a text corpus and incorporates GraphRAG and top-k ranking mechanism.

Strengths & Weaknesses:
1.  The proposed approach for condition and personalized response generation is interesting and offers some benefits for designing such systems. 
2. More information is needed regarding how the Tagging of CSS is done. Examples would be valuable for readers to understand the work. The motivation behind this framework needs strengthening.
3. Why only automated metrics? Why not use LLM as a Judge or human evaluation to get some metrics with regard to how accurate the stylistic responses are?


Comments:
1. Add citations for C0

title: Auto-Weighted Group Relative Preference Optimization for Multi-Objective Text Generation Tasks
review:
To optimize both quality and diversity for ad text generation, this work proposed to perform dynamic weighting of different rewards in the GRPO framework. However there are several weaknesses in this version:
1. The equation (1) that describes GRPO objective is wrong.
2. The Table 3 for illustrating averaged learned weights during training only shows the result of the simplification task (machine translation) with two rewards, other than the core task (ad text generation) with more rewards. Also, it only represents the averaged value other than the dynamics during training. Therefore the effectiveness of the proposed dynamic weighting method is not verified. 
3. The baseline in experiment is incomprehensive. Although there are several rewards to be optimized, we can built expert data satisfying all rewards to perform SFT training. However the author only considers GRPO as the baseline. 
4. The test set only contains 500 samples. The reliability of the conclusions from the experiment is questionable. 
5. The results of Table 5 and Table 6 are inconsistency with their captions, such as "keyword validator" in Table 5's caption and "the rate of five-sentence outputs" in Table 6's caption. 
6. It could be better to report the averaged results and std of multiple runs because RL training is usually unstable and the proposed method largely relies on the learning status during training.

title: Auto-Weighted Group Relative Preference Optimization for Multi-Objective Text Generation Tasks
review:
This paper propose Auto-Weighted Group Relative Preference Optimization (AW-GRPO), a variant of GRPO for multi-objective text generation. The method add an adaptive weighting strategy to balance rewards during training, and try to fix the issue of reward hacking.

Strengths

-The contribution is incremental but still meaningful. While the core framework stay the same, the adaptive weighting improve stability and balance across objectives.
