title: Nyay-Darpan: Enhancing Decision Making Through Summarization and Case Retrieval for Consumer Law in India
review:
The paper presents Nyay-Darpan, a dual-task system targeting Indian consumer law. It includes (i) a structured summarizer that extracts six key legal elements from consumer case documents using part-wise and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting with various LLMs, and (ii) a similar case retrieval component that uses hybrid lexical-semantic matching filtered by sector classification. The authors also introduce CCFMS, a small annotated dataset of 152 consumer cases with gold summaries and relevant case matches, as well as a prompt-based evaluation framework covering 8 metrics, validated through both human and LLM-based assessments.
This paper tackles an underexplored but important domain. However, several core issues  including terminological ambiguity, weak grounding in prior work, unclear evaluation setup, and misuse of citations — limit its strength as a technical contribution. If the authors address these concerns, the work could mature into a solid contribution. In its current form, I lean toward a borderline reject.



- Line 19, 83: The repeated use of the term accuracy in the context of summarization is vague. Summarization quality should be better framed in terms of faithfulness, completeness, or coherence.
- The claim that consumer law is distinct from civil law is factually problematic. Civil law encompasses multiple subfields including consumer protection, contract law, and torts. While it is reasonable to focus on consumer law, positioning it as separate from civil law as a motivating claim is misleading and weakens the domain framing.
- [minor] The motivation for studying consumer law is not adequately developed. The introduction speaks in general terms about legal complexity without explaining the unique importance or challenges of consumer law in India.
- [Line 61-68:] It speaks on decision assist tools as broad category of works and only talk on retrieval works in later as UCREAT and a misplaced reference to Kipf and welling et al 2017. Neither it talks about other works related to other tasks.
* Line 76: “Similar case prediction” is a confusing term. The correct description should be similar case retrieval, aligning with common usage
* Line 91–92: Referring to it as a “judgment predictor” further amplifies confusion. The system does not predict outcomes or judgments, it retrieves precedent cases.
- Line 122-123: how does multieurlex relates to india and support reasoning tasks as it is just a topic classification task? Even in case of iL-TUR, one can argue on how does it link to reasoning? May be using the phrase reasoning is misleading here
- I would have appreciated authors to describe more one existing works in summarization techniques and retrieval techniques used for legal documents, rather than the very recent ones like u-creat in passing [1,2,3,4]
- Section 3.1: No details on how expert created them? background of expert, instructions or criterion to provide summary or even what is deemed “Relevant” for similar case is not even described
- [Minor] line 173-174: the phrase enabling full accuracy can be removed, if the intent is just to say “gold-label”
- [minor2] Why is there a link (or arrow) from 5 most similar cases into material summary? Are these provided as input to material summary?
- Table 3 caption: precision and accuracy are two different terms and authors have used it together. Please clarify that 
- Line 292-294: By overview, do authors refer to overview generated by LLMs? Or the whole case itself or the golden overview?
- Line 320-323: Please do not use accuracy as a conflated term, it can be termed  as “faithfulness” in description, but again described as accuracy in name. 
- Why overview, do authors mean overall ? I would suggest removing that word. It is not clear why this metrics is provided as reference-free or with reference. For faithfulness evaluation, I expect the evaluator to have access to input case, such details are missing in metric description, 
- Line 324-328: Metric 2 (oversimplification) and Metric 3 (overview retrieval) appear overlapping. Clearer differentiation is needed.
- Line 329-332: Metric 3’s name (“retrieval”) is confusing - consider renaming to “content coverage” or “comprehensiveness.”
- It’s unclear why some metrics (e.g., evidence/relief accuracy) are binary while others are Likert-scale. Any explanation on that?
- Line 341-351: is it really “accuracy” that is being computed ? 
-  but those points are not described.
- Lines 320-351:  The distinction between reference-free and reference-based evaluation is unclear. Some metrics can be evaluated just based on summary (issue formatting), some need both summary and input. Hence, I assumed all of them can be reference-free except sector relevance, but from Appendix A.4–A.5, it seems all metrics are evaluated against gold summaries, contradicting the claim of reference-free assessment in the main text. 
- Are these evaluation on table 2 and table 3 on all 152 cases ? (It is provided in A4, but would have expected this in main text)
- Line 380 - “predicted” is not right word, retrieved may be better
- Line 383- is it accuracy or precision? the label should be consistent and technically correct.
- Line 400–403: While the text claims that hybrid retrieval performs best, Table 3 does say the opposite. 
- Lines 427–430: The authors acknowledge limitations in defining “relevant” similar cases but offer no description on how legal experts selected them in dataset creation process. 
- Figure 3 provides an example for product review analysis. The contrast between simple restructuring and CoT prompting is somewhat superficial. Both techniques rely on explicit user described prompt segmentation; the main difference lies in narrative instructions in prompt, not functional methodology.
- Including a detailed qualitative case study (I admit that quantitative human evaluation is provided and I appreciate authors for that) or expert feedback of model outputs would greatly improve the reader's understanding of error patterns and system limitations in practice.


Inappropriate claims with citations:
- [Line 38–40]: The claim about hallucinations and jurisdictional reasoning is supported by Polsley et al. (2016), a summarization paper that does not substantiate this point. Citation does not align with the claim.
- [Line 68]: Kipf and Welling (2017), a graph convolutional networks paper, has no direct relevance to legal retrieval—its inclusion is unjustified.
- [Line 122]: MultiEURLEX has no stated application or alignment with the Indian legal context, yet it’s referenced as supporting it. The authors should revise or remove this claim.

References
- [1] Elaraby, Mohamed, and Diane Litman. "ArgLegalSumm: Improving Abstractive Summarization of Legal Documents with Argument Mining." Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Computational Linguistics. 2022.
- [2] Santosh, T. Y. S. S., Weiss, C., & Grabmair, M. (2024, November). LexSumm and LexT5: Benchmarking and Modeling Legal Summarization Tasks in English. In Proceedings of the Natural Legal Language Processing Workshop 2024 (pp. 381-403).
- [3]  Deroy, Aniket, Kripabandhu Ghosh, and Saptarshi Ghosh. "How Ready are Pre-trained Abstractive Models and LLMs for Legal Case Judgement Summarization?." (2023).
- [4] Santosh, T. Y. S. S., Nolasco, I. M. O., & Grabmair, M. (2025, April). LeCoPCR: Legal Concept-guided Prior Case Retrieval for European Court of Human Rights cases. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL 2025 (pp. 1654-1661).

title: Nyay-Darpan: Enhancing Decision Making Through Summarization and Case Retrieval for Consumer Law in India
review:
# Summary of Contributions

This paper describes a tool to aid in summarizing and retrieving consumer law cases. The approach provides a standardized format (Overview, Sector, Issues, Evidence from both parties, and Relief) to simplify the research process for both consumers and legal professionals. This tool should improve the consistency, speed, and quality of decisions across consumer forums.

The paper provides a robust evaluation with eight metrics on various domain-specific aspects of the summary. One strength is that the assessment includes prompt-based methods, which are compared with human evaluations. However, the evaluation's scale and scope are limited to a few hundred cases.   There is no interannator agreement and limited error analysis.  

The key contributions are as follows:
1. A summarization component that produces an overview with sector classification. The system also extracts the legal issues, evidence/facts, and remedies (outcomes), which are key components in comparing cases.  
2. A domain-adapted retrieval system that leverages the summarization and extraction component to achieve 75% precision for similar cases.
3. A curated consumer law dataset with 152 cases and gold summaries.
4. A domain-adapted evaluation framework that used prompt-based scoring that aligns with human judgements.

## Strengths

- The domain-specific approach focuses on key elements for consumer law decisions. Issues, evidence, and remedies provide a solid legal framework to understand the case.
- The approach provides a comprehensive system design that incorporates summarization, extraction/classification, and retrieval components. The approach filters the cases by sector and then does similarity searches.
- The author took a multi-faceted evaluation approach, which includes reference-based metrics on the gold summaries, reference-free metrics using prompt-based methods, and human-based metrics using a Likert scale on accuracy and relevance.
- The prompt-based metrics evaluation method was compared to the human-based metrics, with a Spearman correlation of 0.43 to 0.85.


## Weaknesses

- The size of the datasets (152 and 570 cases) used is relatively small compared to the corpus size (over 500K cases). There is no discussion on hold-out sets for any prompt development or tuning that the authors may have done.
- While the annotators were legal professionals or law grad students, there was no interannotator agreement created.
- There was limited discussion on error analysis or weakness with the prompts. The best evidence extraction accuracy was 0.67 in the human evaluations. It would have been helpful to understand the issues there.  


# Feedback & Question

The evidence extraction accuracy was 0.67 in the human eval. Does that mean 0.67 of the summaries had no issues or 0.67 of the evidence statements are accurate (assuming each case has multiple statements of evidence)?  How do you prevent hallucinations in legal contexts where accuracy is critical?

Was there a hold-out set for any prompt development or tuning?

*Line 075*: Is consumer law simular to adminstrative law in the US where the litigants don't necessarily have lawyers?  If so, how often do consumers lack representation? That migth be important to point out to help support the impact of a decision tool like this.

*Line 070*: Replace 5.45 lakh with 545,000 or 545K.

title: Nyay-Darpan: Enhancing Decision Making Through Summarization and Case Retrieval for Consumer Law in India
review:
## Pros:
- Addressing a challenging problem of summarizing consumer case
- Providing an useful dataset of 152 annotated cases
## Cons:
- Paper is in parts hard to follow 
- Evaluation methodology is not sound and confusing (accuracy vs. Likert scores vs automatic metrics)
- no inter annotator agreement

The research provides a valuable data set of 152 consumer cases that could be useful to other researchers and I suggest to make this data set the core contribution of an improved version of this paper. In order to make the paper publishable though, the authors want to work on the following issues:
- add inter annotator scores (Kappa) to make sure the annotations are reliable
- compute correlation scores (use significance tests) between human annotators and automatic metrics
- show the scores for all base models  (not only llama 3.1 8b)
- use an IR metric for the similar case prediction (mean average precision, Normalized discounted cumulative gain etc.)

## Detailed comments:
- the introduction mentioned accuracy values of 70 and 75 percent but those values are not mentioned in the paper. Instead other metrics such as ROUGE or Likert scores are mentioned. There are also several individual scores mentioned that are not very well motivated.
- 064:  CoT is introduced the first time but not defined as Chain of Thought but it is defined at least twice throughout the later part of the paper
- Figure 1: Labels are too small
- 0261: name the baseline methods (I assume it's Llama 3.1. 8b), but why aren't the other models not used as baselines (Mistral, DeepSeek and Qwen)?
- Evaluation section needs to be more connected. Sentence are not very well connected
- Results show some interesting results, but they are not further explained or discussed. E.g., DeepSeek receives a very big score for sector relevance, but why? more error analysis required
- 400: the hybrid retrieval method is which method?

title: Benchmarking LLM Faithfulness in RAG with Evolving Leaderboards
review:
In this paper, the authors presented their public leaderboard for benchmarking LLM hallucination rates, along with a novel JudgeX prompting framework that leverages human-annotated hallucination examples to improve hallucination detection performance.

Pros:
* The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow.
* The authors provided detailed implementations via an anonymous git repo, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed JudgeX framework.

Cons:
* The structure of the paper can be a little confusing to navigate as it's not following the traditional paper structure. The section title `JudgeX` appeared twice, as Section 5 title and Section 6.3 title.
* The proposed JudgeX approach relies heavily on human-annotated hallucination examples on the same passage; up to 10 examples are shown during ICL prompting. One might argue that this approach can be challenging to adapt to new domains, as human annotations are expensive; yet, the authors claim that this approach can `adapt naturally to new domains`. I guess the big asterisk here is `given annotations`.
* In section 6.3, the authors mention that the ensemble approach did not outperform o3-mini-high alone. It would be great if the authors could further elaborate why this is the case.
* Writing issues:
  * Line 108: `difficult to identify hallucinations` -> `difficult-to-identify hallucinations`.
  * In figure 2, the legend shows `JudgeY` instead of `JudgeX`.

Despite the aforementioned drawbacks, I believe this is still an outstanding paper.

title: Benchmarking LLM Faithfulness in RAG with Evolving Leaderboards
review:
This paper is well written. The proposed benchmark and JudgeX are presented clearly.

My main question is how similar between the prompt summaries and the target summary? If they are very similar, then it explains that JudgeX can directly use the few shot prompt to determine the quality of the given summary. Is there a way to measure and visualize how similar the summaries are? Maybe some embedding methods, and show the distribution of their cosine similarities?

title: Benchmarking LLM Faithfulness in RAG with Evolving Leaderboards
review:
** Quality **
Strengths:
 - Strong empirical evaluation across four challenging datasets (FaithBench, AggreFact, RAGTruth, TofuEval).
 - Comparison against both state-of-the-art fine-tuned models and zero-shot LLM judges.
 - Comprehensive error analysis (confusion matrices, judge bias, performance scaling with examples).
 - Extension to multiple RAG tasks adds robustness.

Areas for improvement:
 - Include cost and latency benchmarks for JudgeX vs. other methods, since industry adoption depends heavily on inference efficiency.
 - Analyze domain transfer: How does JudgeX perform when trained on news summarization but evaluated on, say, legal or medical RAG tasks?
 - Address annotation scarcity via few-shot synthetic generation pipelines.

** Clarity **
Strengths:
 - Well-structured, following a logical progression from problem motivation → background → method → experiments → analysis.
 - Figures (e.g., distributions in Fig. 1, sensitivity/specificity curves in Fig. 2) support the narrative.
 - Technical terms like “balanced accuracy,” “claim-wise classification,” and “Benign/Unwanted” hallucinations are explained.

Areas for improvement:
 - Provide a clearer visual diagram of the JudgeX pipeline showing input context, annotated examples, and judge reasoning steps.
 - Reduce repetition in dataset descriptions across sections.

** Novelty ** 
Strengths:
 - The in-context learning approach for LLM-as-a-judge using annotated peer outputs is novel and distinct from prior zero-shot LLM judging.
 - Integrating leaderboard infrastructure with a dynamic, annotation-informed evaluation framework is an innovative way to track RAG faithfulness.
 - Application beyond summarization into QA and data-to-text is valuable for broader adoption.

Weaknesses:
 - While JudgeX is innovative, it builds on the already well-established LLM-as-a-judge paradigm — the novelty lies in the conditioning mechanism rather than a completely new evaluation approach.
 - Dependence on human-labelled examples from the same context limits the “plug-and-play” novelty that zero-shot methods offer.

Areas for improvement:
 - Explore meta-learning or adapter-tuning for the judge model so that once trained on several domains, it generalizes without requiring fresh annotations each time.
 - Compare with alternative context-conditioning methods (e.g., retrieval of similar cases without task-specific annotation).

** Significance **
Strengths:
 - Faithfulness evaluation is critical for industry adoption of RAG systems, especially in high-stakes domains like legal, healthcare, and finance.
-  The leaderboard and open evaluation framework can serve as a community benchmark, shaping future hallucination detection research.
-  Quantified improvements (up to +15 F1 on FaithBench over baselines) indicate meaningful impact.

Areas for improvement:
- Include a case study showing how JudgeX rankings changed model selection for an actual enterprise RAG deployment.
- Demonstrate live integration in a RAG pipeline to measure real-world effectiveness beyond static benchmarks.

title: End-to-End Aspect-Guided Review Summarization at Scale
review:
The paper presents aspect based summarization of reviews that is used in a production grade system. The paper highlights that by extracting and consolidating meaningful aspects from all the reviews, the LLM can write concise and meaningful summaries.
- The paper is well written and well-organized in sections. Although the Limitations section is missing.
- The aspect extraction and usage section is well explained.
- The evaluation procedure involves both offline (manual) evaluation as well as online A/B testing which validates the proposed methodology.

*Critical feedback*
- The introduction section should mention the past work done in the space of LLM summarization. There are some articles that discuss the generation of guided summaries by performing topic modelling. Aspect generation is just an extension of topic modeling.
- There is no discussion or comparison of the proposed methodology to the LLM generated summarizes without aspect extraction. Why does aspect-based summarization better than just generating LLM summarizes on all reviews?
- Even though the title and abstract mention that the system was used at scale, there is no explanation how the methodology is scalable. The proposed method involves various LLM calls, and there is no discussion around the latency of the system.

title: End-to-End Aspect-Guided Review Summarization at Scale
review:
This paper presents an aspect-guided review summarization method using LLMs. For each item, the method first extracts aspect–sentiment pairs from individual reviews, then consolidates various forms of aspects, retrieves reviews corresponding to each consolidated aspect, and finally generates the summary.

Weaknesses
- It is difficult to identify the novelty of this work compared to existing studies on aspect-guided summarization using LLMs. Moreover, there have been numerous previous work that perform aspect extraction and consolidation [1, 2]. This paper does not provide sufficient discussion or comparison with these previous work, making it challenging to assess the superiority of the proposed approach.
  * [1] Gunel et al., STRUM: Extractive Aspect-Based Contrastive Summarization, WWW 2023
  * [2] Gunel et al., STRUM-LLM: Attributed and Structured Contrastive Summarization, arXiv:2403.19710

- The proposed method does not clearly explain how reviews corresponding to each consolidated aspect are sampled. Without such details, it is difficult to judge whether the sampled reviews are truly representative.

- In the offline evaluation, this paper states that all generated results were evaluated, but does not provide sufficient details on the experimental setup, e.g., how many annotators participated, whether inter-annotator variation was measured, or whether it is even feasible to read and evaluate summaries for multiple reviews across 341 items. Furthermore, the proposed evaluation uses a 6-choice question format, whereas previous summarization studies [3] typically employ multiple evaluation criteria. This paper should clarify in what way this offline evaluation is superior to prior approaches. Notably, in the introduction, the authors claim that the proposed structured approach mitigates ``hallucination and factual inconsistency issues,'' but no evaluation is provided to support this claim.
  * [3] Shmuel Amar et al., OpenAsp: A Benchmark for Multi-document Open Aspect-based Summarization, EMNLP 2023

- This paper does not provide any samples from the constructed dataset, making it impossible to assess data quality. Beyond merely describing the data format, it would be helpful to present statistics such as the number of reviews per item, average review length, and comparisons to other existing datasets. Such information would also help evaluate the quality and relevance of the dataset the authors intend to release.

title: End-to-End Aspect-Guided Review Summarization at Scale
review:
This paper presents a pipeline/workflow to generate aspect-based summaries of products based on reviews of the product. The pipeline consists of 4 stages - aspect extraction from reviews, then consolidation of these aspects to get rid of the long tail of terms that could result from the first stage, then selection of reviews that contain the important aspects for each product for prompt construction, after which the summary is generated. The underlying LLM can always be changed. 

Offline evaluation was done by humans - the evaluation criteria make sense. Online evaluation was done via an AB test. I would have liked to see some more ablations and analysis on what factors could possibly improve results. 

One detail that I wasn't clear about is how the sentiment is handled during the aspect consolidation stage - are only the aspects consolidated and then the sentiment is tacked on later or do you somehow handle sentiment in consolidation as well? 

Questions:
- line 156: would be good to understand what is the 95th percentile number to give us a gauge on the histogram

title: Recon, Answer, Verify: Agents in Search of Truth
review:
## Summary/Contribution:

This paper makes two main contributions:

1- A new datasetbenchmark  in the political domain  called: Politi-Fact-Only (PFO): a 5-class benchmark dataset of ~3k political claims from politifact.com, where all post-claim analysis and annotator justifications were removed manually from evidence article to prevent information leakage.

2- A new agentic method for fact verification with LLMs called RAV (Recon, Answer Verify): iteratively generates and answers sub-questions to verify different aspects of the claim before finally generating the label. In summary, it creates three agents: 
- QG_agent: generates a structured follow-up question, either a verification question that checks a fact or a question that seeks information about a single entity or relation.
- AG_agent: answers the question using the available context
- LG_agent: predicts the final veracity label, combining the accumulated QA history with the original claim.
QG and AG agents interact multiple times to disambiguate different parts of the claim, and then LG finally outputs the label with the justification.

The evaluations show significant uplift on PFO benchemark and on other more common benchmarks. It also shows that RAV is more robust when deprived of annotator cues.


## Strengths:

- The new PFO benchmark takes into account two important aspects of fact verification:
- -  information leakage (and bias) from annotator judgements or statements: it removes them manually 
- - evidence completeness: unlike other approaches where content published only before the claim was used, this approach uses all available evidence
This should lead to more accurate and realisitic fact verification with less bias.


- The appendix is comprehensive, showing important details for replication like prompts and more in depth analysis.

## Points to Improve:

- The manual removal of cues and analysis from the dataset is appreciated but hard to scale to other datasets, a bigger impact would be to try and automate this pipeline to remove analysis and cues using LLMs and compare that to a subset of manually stripped evidence.

- I am surprised to see that the baseline models did not includ any of the leading models like Claude or GPT. Especially for the zero-shot approach.

- Using GPT-3.5 might be necessary due to some of the older baselines, but with GPT-5 released recently, it's hard to justify using 2+ generations old model.

title: Recon, Answer, Verify: Agents in Search of Truth
review:
# Paper Summary

The authors contribute to fact-checking research by proposing a benchmark dataset, PFO, in the political domain (a subset of an existing dataset). A filtering step is applied to this subset to make it more challenging and better simulate real-world scenarios where post-claims are unavailable at inference time.
The authors also introduce RAV (Recon-Answer-Verify), a method that breaks down fact verification by generating intermediate, targeted questions that each interrogate a single fact. A QG_{agent} generates structured follow-up questions to check a single triple, an AG_{agent} answers these questions using provided evidence, and finally, an LG_{agent} predicts the final label for the claim. The intermediate answers are then used to derive the final verdict. Reported performances show significant gains on the PFO and HoVer datasets.

# Strengths

- The proposed filtered dataset is valuable for the fact-checking community. Future research can use this version for comparison and to quantify the performance drop when models are exposed to post-claims.
- The dataset statistics and analysis are welcome. A proper overview is provided.
- The automated use of multi-agent systems to check facts helps alleviate manual work.
- An ablation study is provided in the Appendix.
- The performance on the filtered dataset (PFO) demonstrates the superiority of RAV compared to other approaches.

# Weaknesses
- In Table 4, the number of "True" labels is consistently lower than "False."
- The performance of RAV is not always the best on all datasets, though it remains competitive and on par with other approaches.
- The use of three distinct agents, rather than a single one, is questionable. The three agents do not seem to cooperate deeply but instead interact as independent agents with specific roles rather than sharing a common goal.
- The models used are not recent. For instance, ProgramFC uses text-davinci-003. It would be interesting to include more recent models to see the performance gap and how they perform at fact-checking.

# Comments/Questions
- What strategies could be adopted in industry for fact-checking, given that missing evidence accounts for 41.9% of the errors?

# Minor Typos
- Line 025: 'two 2' → 'two'
- Line 035: 'including work' → 'including works' or 'including previous work'
- Line 289: 'Compared to ProgramFC we observe' → 'Compared to ProgramFC, we observe'

# Overall
The paper introduces an interesting benchmark for the community but would benefit from an evaluation that includes more recent LLMs.

title: Recon, Answer, Verify: Agents in Search of Truth
review:
## Summary
This paper introduces Politi-Fact-Only (PFO), a leakage-reduced benchmark of 2,982 political fact-checks (five labels) produced by removing post-claim annotator commentary from Politifact articles, and proposes RAV (Recon–Answer–Verify), an agentic three-stage pipeline (question-generation, answer-generation, label-generation) that iteratively decomposes claims into simple verification/inquiry questions. RAV shows large gains on the filtered PFO dataset and competitive improvements on other benchmarks (the paper reports a ~57.5% relative increase on PFO and modest gains on HOVER), and the pipeline is designed to improve interpretability and enable fine-grained error analysis.
## Strengths
* This work addresses a real evaluation problem (annotator leakage / post-claim cues) that inflates model performance in many fact-checking datasets. PFO is a well-motivated, manually filtered dataset that reduces post-publication leakage and quantifies the drop in model performance when cues are removed.
* Comprehensive empirical work: evaluation across multiple datasets (PFO, unfiltered PFO, HOVER, FEVEROUS, RAWFC, LIAR-RAW), multiple LLM backbones, ablations (question strategies, k iterations), and a human analysis of failure modes.
* Practical insight: the paper quantifies reasoning complexity (average number of subquestions per claim category) and shows diminishing returns beyond ~10 iterations — useful engineering guidance.

## Weaknesses & suggestions
* Reliance on gold evidence in experiments. Most evaluations use gold/author-written evidence rather than an end-to-end retrieval+verification stack; this limits claims about real-world deployability. Suggest evaluating RAV with a realistic retriever (or at least a retrieved evidence ablation).


* Comparability / fairness of baselines. Some baseline numbers are reported with different model backbones (and some prior results use text-davinci-003). It’s unclear whether improvements come from RAV’s algorithmic design or from stronger LLM backbones. For example, RAV will not outperform ZS baseline with the same LLaMa-3.1-70b model.


* Cost / latency vs accuracy tradeoffs. The pipeline runs multiple LLM calls per instance; while there’s a brief runtime comparison with HiSS, a more detailed cost/latency analysis (tokens, wall time, and inference cost across backbones) would help practitioners decide when to use RAV.
* Clarify exact preprocessing rules used to remove annotator commentary (examples, heuristics, scripts) and consider releasing the code for reproducibility.


* Report token counts / average questions per claim in main text (some stats are in appendices) to improve accessibility.

title: Efficient Semi-Supervised Fine-Tuning of Small Vision–Language Models for Product Attribute Prediction
review:
In this paper, the authors investigate efficient semi-supervised fine-tuning of compact Vision-Language Models for image-based product attribute prediction in e-commerce. Starting with a small labeled dataset annotated via over-the-counter APIs, the authors use Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) with LoRA adapters and leverage unlabeled product listings through Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

Strengths:
* DPO for semi-supervised learning to leverage unlabeled data with self-consistency
* Practical approach for e-commerce
* Ablation studies

Weaknesses:
* The small API-annotated dataset could be an uncertain part of the proposed method without proper study.
* Limited study on different models and datasets (e.g., only qwen-family models are examined in the paper).
* Lack of details of experimental setup for the reproducibility.

title: Efficient Semi-Supervised Fine-Tuning of Small Vision–Language Models for Product Attribute Prediction
review:
This paper investigates semi-supervised fine-tuning strategies for compact VLMs applied to e-commerce product attribute prediction. The authors proposed using DPO with self-consistency-based pseudo-labeling to leverage unlabeled product listings and achieved significant improvements over supervised baselines.

**Strengths:**
- Applying DPO in a semi-supervised setting, with self-consistency as a correctness proxy, is well-motivated.
- Well-designed experimental framework with proper baselines and ablations.
- The experiments convincingly show that DPO consistently outperforms SL and that performance improves with more unlabeled data.

**Weaknesses:**
- The core contribution is applying existing techniques (DPO + SL) to a new domain.
- Missing comparisons with other semi-supervised learning methods beyond self-learning.
- Heavy reliance on initial labels introduces potential biases that may favor similar model architectures.

title: Efficient Semi-Supervised Fine-Tuning of Small Vision–Language Models for Product Attribute Prediction
review:
This paper deals with automatically generating product attributes from images in an e-commerce setting at scale. Specifically, the authors wanted to generated these product attributes using smaller and thereby cheaper VLM instead of using a large VLM through APIs. The authors do this in the following ways: 

First the use a large VLM in a very limited capacity to get annotate a few examples. 
They then use PEFT and the above examples to Fine-Tune a Qwen2.5-VL-3b model.
They use the above SFTed model to generate pseudo-labels and reasoning chain to generate preference pairs. 
Finally the use those preference pairs and finetune the model using DPO. 

The authors show efficacy of their proposed approach using a manually labeled held-out dataset. 

Strengths:
 1. The paper is a great example of applying the latest generative AIs technique to solve problems at scale (and cheaply).
 2. The authors go into a lot of details and justify their each decision using ablations. For example, the paper has ablations around:
      2.1Using just pre-trained vs Peft model

      2.2 ablations around consistency threshold 

      2.3 around self-learning (iterative labeling)

      2.4 and effect of number of unlabeled samples

Weaknesses:
 1. The novelty of the paper is limited. Individually the techniques applied (PEFT fine-tuning, DPO based finetuning) are very well known. 
 2. There's obviously uniqueness in the way they are applied to this specific problem, but overall it can be said to be a bit limited. 
A big component of the paper is to use smaller and cheaper models, presumably for cost savings. It would have been great to see some estimate in terms of cost saving to round it up.

title: Petro-ColBERT: A Domain Adaptation of ColBERTv2 in Oil and Gas Industry
review:
The paper presents a practical domain adaptation of ColBERTv2 for Portuguese oil & gas retrieval using LLM-generated synthetic queries and hard negative mining, showing clear performance gains. However, the experimental scope is narrow, and broader model comparisons and metric justifications are needed for stronger generalization.

Strengths:
- Effective Leverage of Available Data:
The paper makes good use of LLM-generated synthetic queries to address the scarcity of annotated datasets in Portuguese O&G. Additionally, it mines hard negatives and analyzes the effects of various mining strategies, providing further practical insights.

- Resource-Efficient and Reproducible:
 Presents a methodology that can be replicated in other domains without expensive annotation or large-scale computational resources.

- Clear Pipeline and Implementation:
 Details each step of data preparation, query generation, and training, making the approach easy to follow.


Weaknesses:
- Limited Architecture Comparison:
It would be highly valuable for other resource-constrained domains to see how the synthetic data and fine-tuning pipeline perform with alternative retrieval models or backbones. Evaluating additional architectures or dual-encoder models, using the same synthetic triples, would provide broader insight into the generality and practical applicability of the proposed approach.

- Lack of Metric Justification:
The choice of evaluation metrics is not well-justified. The paper reports multiple variants of Precision (P@1, P@3, P@5, P@10, P@20) and NDCG (NDCG@10, NDCG@20), but does not explain why so many precision cutoffs are included, nor why precision is prioritized over recall or other relevant IR metrics. Clear motivation for metric selection and its relevance to the domain use case would strengthen the evaluation.

- No Comparison to Other Adaptation Techniques:
Does not compare with other domain adaptation or semi-supervised methods, limiting insight into relative strengths and weaknesses.

- Minimal Analysis of Synthetic Data Quality:
Lacks human evaluation or ablation studies to assess the quality and diversity of synthetic queries, or their direct impact on performance.

_Edit after the authors' late response_:

My main concern remains unresolved: the current experimental design ties the contribution too tightly to ColBERTv2, which makes it hard to draw actionable, generalizable conclusions for practitioners who must choose among different retrieval implementations with very different deployment trade-offs.
Concretely, without a cross-architecture check it is unclear whether the gains come from the proposed pipeline (synthetic triples + hard negatives) or from ColBERTv2’s . For industry readers, the retriever choice determines index footprint, latency, and serving complexity; a pipeline that only shows benefits for a single late-interaction model is difficult to adopt.

Minimal additions that would address this:

* Model-agnostic validation:
Keep the synthetic triples and mining fixed and train at least one dual-encoder baseline (e.g., BERT-base or MiniLM; adapters/LoRA acceptable) and one BM25→cross-encoder re-ranker. Report P@k/NDCG@k on your test set. Even a lightweight pass would show whether the pipeline lifts multiple families or only ColBERTv2.

* Efficiency table (deployment relevance):
 For BM25, the dual-encoder, and ColBERTv2 (your best Petro-ColBERT), report index size, build time, peak GPU/CPU mem, and per-query latency. These numbers are critical for practitioners, since late-interaction (models like ColBERT typically incur higher per-query latency and larger index footprints than dual-encoders. This lets readers trade accuracy against cost and pick an implementation that fits their constraints.


If you include the above, the paper’s central claim becomes model-agnostic and industry-relevant—i.e., a domain adaptation recipe that improves retrieval quality across implementations—rather than “a pipeline that works for ColBERTv2.” Without this, the generalizability and practical utility for similar settings remain limited.

title: Petro-ColBERT: A Domain Adaptation of ColBERTv2 in Oil and Gas Industry
review: The paper demonstrates a well-executed experimental workflow, achieving measurable improvements in effectiveness over a zero-shot baseline on the O&G domain dataset. The methodology is presented with sufficient clarity to enable reproducibility, and the engineering-focused narrative suggests potential for cross-domain applicability. To further strengthen the work, the authors could explicitly address the broader implications of their approach—for instance, by discussing generalizability to other industrial domains or identifying specific conditions under which their method outperforms alternatives.

title: Petro-ColBERT: A Domain Adaptation of ColBERTv2 in Oil and Gas Industry
review:
#### Summary

This paper introduces an approach for domain-specific adaptation of BM25 and ColBERTv2 retrievers against Portuguese oil and gas textual corpus.

#### Strengths

- While the paper targets specific language (Portuguese) and domain (technical reports oil and gas domain), the motivation and main ideas of the approach is fairly straightforward. The paper could have been an useful resource for future researchers and practitioners if it weren't for various weaknesses I have found (see below.)

#### Weaknesses

- It would have been great if the paper provided some examples of queries and candidate documents, in order to understand the nature of queries in this particular domain.
- According to Table 1, there are 47 queries in the final dataset, which seems quite small considering the fact that there are over 108K documents, each of which were processed by a LLM to generate n queries. Or is this the number of "real" queries mentioned in line 298? Line 319 says there are "50K validated queries" per dataset, so I'm quite confused here.
- Speaking of the real queries, it is not clear to me how these queries validated by the domain experts were used. I'm guessing from line 304-305 that these were used to train a relevance model, but the authors need to be clear about this as the experimental results depend on relevance scores provided by this model.
- It would have been great to also report results separately for two different query types ("questions" and "search queries" according to Figure 2), as the two have fairly different characteristics.
- Many of the experimental details are not available, such as the GPUs used for training/inference and the codes used to run BM25 and ColBERT experiments. Also, it appears that the experiments were done for a single seed.
- Table 2 shows that the difference between the BM25-based retrievers and ColBERT-based ones are very small, with the BM25 outperforming ColBERT in many cases. This seems odd as it's usually other way around. 
- Lastly, I don't think I agree with the overall findings of this paper - especially the discussion on hard negative sets in Section 4.3. As there are exactly 1 relevant document per query and all hard negatives are obtained from vanilla ColBERT results, there's no "gold" or "silver" ranking information within the dataset the authors have constructed. Hence, it doesn't make any intuitive sense that increasing the number of "hard negatives" are actually helping to better rank the candidate documents. It seems that the authors are making this claim based on P@5 ~ P@20 scores for ColBERT with top-100 negatives, but I don't think the differences are strong enough to support this claim.

title: ColMate: Contrastive Late Interaction and Masked Text for Multimodal Document Retrieval
review:
COLMATE is a new model for multimodal document retrieval. Stale and incomplete information in language models makes it necessary to employ RAGs but multimodal RAG has its challenges. Existing models often repurpose retrieval techniques optimised for text-text retrieval without addressing the challenges of visually rich documents. Despite these challenges multimodal RAG makes progress with the introduction of models like ColPali. This paper introduces COLMATE, and proposes three main contributions by applying known but “ignored” techniques to the problem in addition to a novel similarity scorer. 

1. “Masked OCR based pre-training objective, a self-supervised masked contrastive learning objective and a late Interaction mechanism suited to multimodal document structures and visual characteristics.” These components are designed to improve the model's ability to understand and retrieve documents with complex layouts and visual elements. The code and the model weights will be made available by the authors.
2. State of the art performance on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. 
3. Insight into the 3 components they added to the conventional pipeline by extensive experimentation. 
 
The three novel modifications to the conventional pipeline they suggest makes it possible to “bridge the gap between existing document retrieval methods and advances in multimodal representation learning for effective document retrieval”. 

Current methods like patch tokenization of images create challenges for visual document retrieval as they are designed for natural images and not documents. These methods use tokenisation for images in patch based settings which means one word can end up being fragmented into different patches. This problem is solved by TopKsim which is a variation of late interaction for visual documents. TopKSim refines document scoring for visual contexts by averaging top-K similarity scores instead of relying on a single maximum.

Strengths:

The paper is well written. The experiments are well thought of and executed. The arguments for the solutions to the problems are well articulated and extensive experiments show the solutions in fact work. 

MOLM directly tackles the issue of suboptimal visual feature optimisation in many VLMs.

TopKSim provides a clever solution to the tokenisation mismatch between text and image patches, a fundamental issue when applying text-based late interaction to visuals.

MaskedCL offers a practical, self-supervised approach for scenarios where annotated data is unavailable, which is a common real-world problem.

Weaknesses

The in-domain (ViDoRe V1) results seem to be marginal. This might be related to the specific model architecture COLMATE was applied to.  It would be interesting to see results with other models as the authors also mentioned in future work.

Minor issues: 
Ln 54: and and —> and

title: ColMate: Contrastive Late Interaction and Masked Text for Multimodal Document Retrieval
review:
The paper introduces COLMATE, a novel model for multimodal document retrieval that addresses limitations of existing methods designed for text-only retrieval. COLMATE leverages three components: 1) an OCR-based masked language modeling strategy for better vision-language pretraining; 2) a self-supervised contrastive learning technique for robust cross-modal alignment; 3) a late interaction mechanism (TopKSim) optimizing token aggregation in visual contexts. The work is built on the ColPali model and sets a new state-of-the-art by improving retrieval accuracy by 3.61% on ViDoRe V1 and V2 benchmarks over the baseline. 

A few shortcomings:
1) As the authors stated, the system is primarily built on top of the ColPali model for computational efficiency. It would be interesting to see how such findings apply to more powerful VLMs, such as Qwen2.5-VL.
2) The performance gain over baseline ColPali is modest, especially on in-domain tasks.

title: ColMate: Contrastive Late Interaction and Masked Text for Multimodal Document Retrieval
review:
### **Summary**
This paper presents ColMate, a multimodal model for document retrieval. ColMate is trained using three new ideas: i) OCR-based masked language modeling (ii) TopKSim, a means of performing late-stage similarity between K vision tokens and text tokens and (iii) masked contrastive learning. The authors find that ColMate outperforms previous SOTA model on document retrieval on both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization.

### **Novelty & Impact**
- Multimodal RAG is an important area and the authors present 3 clear ideas about how to train an improved retrieval model. The task itself is applicable to industry because having strong, smaller open-source models is a solid alternative to proprietary models. ColMate is a small model (3B parameters) with good performance.
- The new approaches, particularly OCR masked language modeling and the masked contrastive learning, leverage task-specific visual information without needing any labels. It’s helpful in a domain where the labeled data would be very expensive. Additionally, the framework is applicable to most VLMs and the authors explained their model choice due to computational efficiency.
- One weakness is that the performance gap between ColPali and the training ideas introduced here is quite small (<1% for ViDoRe V1 and ~3-4% for ViDoRe V2). While I understand that the out-of-domain gains (V2) are more significant, they feel under-explored.

### **Reproducibility**
This work is reproducible. In addition to sharing the code and model after acceptance, the authors also describe the base model being finetuned, the training and evaluation datasets being used and the hyperparameters for training.

### **Clarity & Structure**
- The paper adheres to the general conference format and is also straightforward and easy to read. Section 3 neatly introduces the main contributions described in the abstract + introduction (OCR-based MLM, top-K similarity and masked contrastive learning). They include both equations to clearly see the approach as well as grounding related work.
- Section 4 could benefit from explaining why ColMate-Pali and ColPali are the comparison models. It seems like including additional models, even open-source ones of similar size that are not explicitly RAG trained, would be a helpful comparison.

### **Questions/Suggestions**
- Potential typo: “... for cross-modal alignment textual and visual modalities in structured
- documents.” →“... for cross-modal alignment between textual and visual modalities in structured documents.”
L54: “and and” → “and”
- It’d be nice if at least one other VLM could be compared against for a baseline.
- The visual in Figure 1(b) was not immediately clear to me. Perhaps including a small image and showing both a positive and negative pair would make this easier to read.
- The font in Table 2 on the axes is a bit small – can you increase the size?

title: Banzhida: Advancing Large Language Models for Tibetan with Curated Data and Continual Pre-Training
review:
### Strengths

- Great effort for improving LLM quality for Tibetan (a low resource language) by creating a large pre-training corpus (72 GB) with dedicated data cleaning applicable to Tibetan.
- Additionally created a benchmark to better assess the quality of trained models by automatically translating existing benchmarks into Tibetan and proofreading by native Tibetan speakers.
- Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B-base for `{Tibetan, Chinese, English}` (with expanded tokenizer) to demonstrate that the provided corpus is valuable for the community as it leads to better Tibetan quality.
- Easy to follow and well written.


### Weaknesses

- Table 2 / 3 do not include proprietary LLMs such as Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4, Claude Opus 4, etc. which is weird given that the initial translation of the benchmarks was created using Claude Sonnet 3.7 due to its "strong Tibetan generation capabilities".
- For Flores-200 what is the evaluation metric? BLEU, chrF? To make it reproducible, `sacrebleu` should be used and the signature should be included.
- I'm not too versed in the Tibetan language but it seems like there are plenty of dialects and locales that aren't considered in the presented paper and instead the focus is on Central Tibetan. Maybe it would make sense to indicate the specific locales in the dataset and/or benchmarks and expand on this aspect in the paper.

title: Banzhida: Advancing Large Language Models for Tibetan with Curated Data and Continual Pre-Training
review:
This paper builds a pre-training corpus for Tibetan from public datasets, web pages, translated and private corpora. Then Qwen2.5-7B-base model continual pre-trains on the mixed corpus with the processed Tibetan data, extends long context, and conducts instruction tuning. Empirical results on the Tibetan  benchmarks, which are translated from English, show that Banzhida models outperforms other multilingual models and Tibetan models. 
- **Pros**: The processed Tibetan corpus, models and benchmarks will be a contribution for the Tibetan NLP community if they will be public after review. 
- **Cons**: Limited technical novelty and insights for the common pipeline used for building the language-specific corpus, large language model, and benchmark. I cannot find any insights or problems that the Tibetan large language model will meet, but not for the other low-resource language Mongolian.

title: Banzhida: Advancing Large Language Models for Tibetan with Curated Data and Continual Pre-Training
review:
The paper looks at the creation of an LLM specifically targeting Tibetan, which is considered a low-resource language. The aim to provide an LLM which is centric to Tibetan is very good. The authors approach this by collecting data from various sources in English, Chinese and Tibetan. They also use pre-training datasets translated into Tibetan using the Google Translate API. Moreover, a set of private Tibetan language sources is used. The paper states that the data is solely used for research and model training purposes only, but does not state whether the resulting model(s) will be commercially available. The data is preprocessed before training.
The approach takes Quen2.5-7B-base and further pretrains the model. To ensure proper representation, the BPE tokeniser is extended. The pretraining is done through short context and long context training, providing the Base and the Base-32K models respectively. This is then followed by instruction tuning, providing the SFT model. 
To benchmark the resulting LLMs, a number of datasets are used, some of which are created by translating the English datasets using the Claude-Sonnet-3.7 model. The results show that the Base model or the SFT model obtains the best results. 

One severe weakness seems to be that the authors filter out any document containing the "Dalai Lama". This is serious since it grossly misrepresents Tibetan culture, irrespective of one's political beliefs and standings. Moreover, I have several questions below: 



q1: Why do you choose to describe Tibetan as "one of China's minority languages"? Why not choose a more inclusive description, such as "a language that is spoken in the Himalayan region", so as not to avoid politicising this work? 

q2. On line 243, you mention including content from books. Do you have explicit consent from authors/publishers to use these books? Since the model will be made public, how do you ensure that the original text cannot be generated? 

q3. In lines 262 - 264, you state that you use Google Translate to translate pre-training datasets to Tibetan automatically. However, in lines 443 - 446, you use Claude-Sonnet-3.7. Why do you choose to use different translation systems? Is cost an issue, and if so, what is the difference? 

q4. For your experiments, you focus on using English and Chinese as high-resource languages. Have you considered including medium-resourced languages such as Burmese, which is linguistically closer to Tibetan? What do you think the implications would be for including such a language?

q5. In section 4, you justify the choice of the Qwen model due to its cross-lingual transfer to low-resource languages - do you have an empirical evaluation of at least a few models and their zero-shot performance on Tibetan? Otherwise, this claim does not hold. 

q6. In Table 1, you provide the pretraining data volume for the languages used - could you give a clearer indication of the ratio of synthetic vs authentic data? (Maybe I missed this detail.)

q7. In lines 382-385, is it only the Tibetan data that is not used in the first stage? 

q8. Why do you choose to translate from English to Tibetan for both the pretraining (not sure of this) and the benchmark? Did you consider Chinese benchmarks? Did you consider the impact of cultural differences, especially for the benchmark?

q9. Why is Flores not included in Table 2?

q10. Can you provide translations for Table 7? I tried automatic translation, and it seems that 3/4 of the phrases translate to "His Holiness Dalai Lama". What scientific reasons could motivate deleting entire documents containing such phrases? Isn't this too aggressive as an approach and don't you think that the cultural representation of the language would suffer without this representation? What is the ratio of data removed because of these phrases? Moreover, if certain Tibetan aspects are considered as sensitive topics, according to the ACL Code of Ethics, this should be clearly outlined in an Ethics section.

q11. The paper states that annotators were used. How much were they paid, and how many hours on average did they work? How were they selected? Again, this information should be provided in the Ethics section. See here for better guidelines: https://aclrollingreview.org/responsibleNLPresearch/

Since tables 2 and 3 have the same header and the first three rows are the same, they could be merged with an additional column. The difference in the current captions (different tasks/different benchmarks) is rather confusing.

title: Building Data-Driven Occupation Taxonomies: A Bottom-Up Multi-Stage Approach via Semantic Clustering and Multi-Agent Collaboration
review: This submission presents CLIMB, a fully-automated system that creates occupation taxonomies from raw job postings. The proposed methodology address two key challenges in automated taxonomy creation; that of the initial concept extraction and that of hierarchy construction. To this end, the authors employ LLMs at various stages of their approach; at concept extraction and description generator, at leaf-node generator and at hierarchy construction, in a procedure that resembles adversarial training. The authors proceed in evaluating their approach against a similar LLM-based baseline on three distinct datasets they scrape from an equivalent number of online job-posting websites and report on their results. Overall, it is a nice paper that would be of interest to the conference audience.

title: Building Data-Driven Occupation Taxonomies: A Bottom-Up Multi-Stage Approach via Semantic Clustering and Multi-Agent Collaboration
review:
The paper proposes a fully automated, bottom-up pipeline for building occupation taxonomies from raw job postings. The method first detects relevant chunks with a lightweight classifier trained on LLM labels, learns a pairwise “same-occupation” similarity (LLM-labeled, XGBoost over embedding features), clusters postings (Affinity Propagation) into leaf occupations, then uses a reflection-based multi-agent LLM loop (Generator + Evaluator) to construct higher levels of the hierarchy. 
The authors present experiments on 3 data sets and compare against an expert taxonomy another LLM-based baseline method.

Strength
=======
- Clear industry use-case fit (job search, HR analytics, policy).
- Fully automated method
- code and dataset will be released


Weakness
=========
- the paper is not specific what a "good" taxonomy really should be. As the authors point out, this can depend on the domain and specific requirements, eg how fine or coarse a taxonomy should be. For example, should "data scientist" and "ML engineer" be the same or different job? I would say this depends. This aspect is not sufficiently discussed how it affects the evaluation, in particular when comparing against the ESCO standard taxonomy
- Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge for both training labels and eval without sufficient details on the prompts and the accuracy of the results. The authors should report the accuracy of the labels against human-expert labels
- more details and some examples of the dataset would be helpful to illustrate the challenges of the domain 
- while the method appears to be sound, the main contribution of the paper is a pipeline that uses LLMs to create labels and then trains cheaper models to scale (instead of using LLMs for the clustering directly) and the proposer - critique model. 

Questions:
- how much is the method specific to job postings and how well could it be applied to generate taxonomies for other domains

title: Building Data-Driven Occupation Taxonomies: A Bottom-Up Multi-Stage Approach via Semantic Clustering and Multi-Agent Collaboration
review:
## Executive Summary

This paper presents CLIMB (CLusterIng-based Multi-agent taxonomy Builder), a framework for automatically constructing occupation taxonomies from raw job postings. While the work addresses an important problem and demonstrates reasonable empirical results, the paper has significant methodological limitations, particularly in its evaluation design and theoretical contributions. The primary value lies not in novel algorithmic innovations, but rather in the careful study design and annotation methodology.

## Strengths

### 1. Strong Inter-Annotator Agreement Scores

The paper reports substantial Fleiss' kappa scores across datasets, with values reaching 0.73 for Palestine, 0.63 for Botswana, and 0.54-0.67 for the USA dataset. These scores approach the threshold of 0.8 that is generally considered reliable for annotation tasks. The hierarchical agreement analysis (Table 3) demonstrates a coherent pattern where agreement improves at higher taxonomic levels, reaching "almost perfect" agreement (κ > 0.81) for broader categories. This suggests the generated taxonomies have meaningful semantic structure that human annotators can consistently recognize.

However, these scores must be interpreted cautiously. The use of LLM annotators rather than human experts may inflate agreement scores, as LLMs may exhibit similar biases or systematic patterns in their responses that don't reflect genuine semantic understanding.

### 2. Well-Designed Annotation Study

The paper's most significant contribution is its careful annotation study design and methodology. The authors employ a three-LLM panel (Gemini 2.5 Flash, O4-Mini, and DeepSeek R1) as annotators, which represents a reasonable approach to scalable evaluation. The multi-stage annotation process includes:

- Contrastive data sampling with deliberate inclusion of hard cases
- LLM-as-HR-expert annotation for training similarity classifiers
- Systematic evaluation across multiple metrics (accuracy, comprehensiveness, efficiency)

This methodological rigor in evaluation design represents a valuable contribution to the field, particularly for researchers working on similar taxonomy construction problems.

## Critical Limitations

### 1. Insufficient Information About Annotators

Despite the reviewer's note about the importance of annotator information, the paper provides inadequate detail about the LLM annotators used. While the models are named in Appendix B.5, there is minimal discussion of:

- Model-specific biases that might affect annotation consistency
- Validation of LLM annotations against human expert judgments
- Analysis of systematic differences between annotator models
- Temperature and sampling parameters that could affect reliability

Research on inter-annotator reliability emphasizes the critical importance of annotator characteristics and training, yet this paper treats LLMs as black-box annotators without sufficient characterization.

### 2. Limited Theoretical Novelty

The paper's core algorithmic contributions are incremental rather than groundbreaking:

- **Semantic clustering**: Uses standard embedding models (Qwen3-Embedding-8B) with XGBoost classification, which is a straightforward application of existing techniques
- **Multi-agent hierarchy construction**: While described as "novel," the generator-evaluator pattern is well-established in LLM systems and the paper cites this precedent (Anthropic, 2024; Kalyanpur et al., 2024)
- **Bottom-up approach**: The contrast with top-down methods is not as stark as claimed, since the method still relies heavily on LLM priors about occupational categories

### 3. Evaluation Methodology Concerns

The evaluation design has several problematic aspects:

**Circular Validation**: The paper uses LLMs both to generate annotations for training classifiers and to evaluate the final taxonomies. This creates potential circularity where the evaluation may favor taxonomies that align with LLM biases rather than genuine semantic quality.

**Limited Baselines**: The comparison with TnT is acknowledged as using "minimal adaptation" of prompts not designed for hierarchical structures. The ESCO comparison is weakened by reducing it to a two-level taxonomy due to context window limitations.

**Missing Human Validation**: Despite claiming to replace manual curation, the paper provides no validation against human expert taxonomies or domain specialist evaluation.

## Methodological Assessment

### Study Design as Primary Contribution

The reviewer's observation that "the main contribution is the human annotation and study design" is astute. The paper's value lies primarily in:

1. **Systematic evaluation framework**: The three-dimensional evaluation (accuracy, comprehensiveness, efficiency) provides a comprehensive assessment approach
2. **Multi-dataset validation**: Testing across three diverse regional datasets (Palestine, Botswana, USA) demonstrates some generalizability
3. **Reproducible methodology**: The detailed implementation descriptions and promised code release support reproducibility

## Comparison with Related Work

The paper positions itself against existing taxonomy construction methods, but the comparison reveals that CLIMB's advantages are often marginal:

- **vs. TnT**: Better inter-annotator agreement but unfair comparison due to adapted prompts
- **vs. ESCO**: Better utilization but ESCO was artificially constrained for evaluation
- **vs. Manual curation**: Claims of "full automation" are overstated given heavy reliance on LLM priors

## Recommendations for Improvement

1. **Human Expert Validation**: Include validation by domain experts in HR, labor economics, or occupational classification
2. **Annotator Analysis**: Provide detailed analysis of LLM annotator characteristics, biases, and inter-model agreement patterns
3. **Stronger Baselines**: Compare against human-curated taxonomies or adapted versions of existing automated methods

## Conclusion

This paper makes a solid empirical contribution to occupation taxonomy construction with reasonable inter-annotator agreement scores and a well-designed evaluation study. However, the work is primarily an engineering contribution rather than a fundamental advancement in taxonomy construction theory or methodology. The study design and annotation approach represent the paper's strongest contributions, providing a template for future work in this area.

The paper would benefit from clearer positioning as a methodological study rather than claiming algorithmic novelty, and from more rigorous validation against human expert judgment. Despite these limitations, the work provides value to practitioners working on similar problems and establishes useful evaluation frameworks for the field.

title: Learning from the Future: Anticipating Residual Returns via Forward Relevance Modeling
review:
This paper presents the forward relevance modeling framework to improve the prediction of next-day residual stock returns from financial news headlines. The key insight is to label day-T headlines using distant supervision from day-T+1 via leveraging different mechanisms to train an XGBoost model. Using a proprietary corpus of 1.28M headline instances and 17 rolling quarterly splits spanning 2016–2023, the study reports consistent (but quite modest) gains in accuracy, macro-F1, and Sharpe ratios from simulated long-short portfolios. Although the paper studied an important problem, proposed a nice solution, and conducted extensive evaluation, some key weaknesses are:

1. Although they proposed a complex technique to improve the prediction of future residual stock return, the performance gain is quite small (which further degrades with the increase in Returns, +2,+3). While the authors mentioned that the gain is statistically significant, no details on the statistical significance test are provided. What type of significance test is conducted?

2. The presentation requires improvement. The paper seems too text-heavy in terms of demonstrating the methodology. Should have used a figure to better demonstrate the methodology, alongside adding a detailed case study with examples. 

3. The authors should also add further ablation tests to demonstrate the effectiveness of different components used in their proposed method. 

4. The paper also lacks discussion on how it can be adapted in a practical scenario, especially in industrial deployment and usage. 

5. Why not evaluate other sentence embeddings? For instance, embeddings that are generated from financial data (check: https://huggingface.co/FinanceMTEB). 

6. Also, I think more strong baselines should be added. Why are other baseline approaches, like sentiment classification are not used? Moreover, how about using LLMs as a baseline to predict the future stock returns?

title: Learning from the Future: Anticipating Residual Returns via Forward Relevance Modeling
review:
The paper introduces a forward-relevance framework that turns next-day headlines into distant-supervision signals for forecasting the direction of residual returns. This temporal inversion is novel, well argued, and evaluated at realistic scale—more than four million headlines across seventeen rolling quarters—while tying standard classification metrics to portfolio‐level Sharpe ratios. Statistically significant, if modest, gains over a strong embedding-plus-XGBoost baseline are reported, and the promised code release will let others verify and extend the work despite the proprietary nature of the headline corpus.

Strengths include a production-style walk-forward evaluation, clear exposition of the NARS, UFRS, and DFRS variants, and careful safeguards against information leakage: relevance scores are computed only within each training window, and predictions are generated after the market close, when the same-day return used by NARS is already known. This design keeps the reported results causally clean while retaining practical realism.

Limitations remain. Performance improvements are small and unadjusted for transaction costs, recent finance-specific language models and price-aware transformers are absent from the baseline suite, and the exclusive focus on headlines may overlook information in article bodies and filings. Addressing cost adjustments and stronger baselines would sharpen the contribution, but the core idea is sound, the implementation transparent, and the industrial relevance clear. I therefore recommend a weak accept

title: Learning from the Future: Anticipating Residual Returns via Forward Relevance Modeling
review:
The paper trains predictors of the next-day returns of financial instruments using two proposed scores (UFRS and DFRS) as features, which are predicted by an additional classifier. These scores express (roughly) the similarity between a given headline and the next day's headlines.

The experimental details are lacking. The authors claim to train an XGBoost classifier, yet the input features used remain unclear. Regarding the prediction of UFRS/DFRS, they only state, "a predictive model (e.g., XGBoost)." can be used - what model was used during the experiments? During data processing, the data was "join[ed] with residual return data, computed using a multi-factor risk model" Which model was used? Additionally, they use headline embeddings constructed in an unknown way.

This also leads me to the conclusion that the paper has little relation with NLP. The authors propose a prediction system for finance which uses NLP to compute cosine similarity between two text embeddings (and it is even unclear which embeddings were used). The paper does not seem to heavily rely on NLP techniques&methodologies.

It is not clear why the authors decided to frame this problem as classification (i.e., is the return positive?) instead of predicting the return itself. The authors test an investment strategy in which they select the 20% most and least probable instruments to generate positive or negative returns. Why don't they take the magnitude of the return into account?

Other design choices are not very clear as well.  For example, why does DFRS use tanh normalization on a score that is already normalized? The key question related to their methodology is why they assume that a news representative of same-day news should be correlated with a positive return. Why are news stories about falling stocks assumed not to be representative of same-day news?

Minor
- lacking citations e.g. "Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) " (line 029), not explained abbreviations like FIGI (line 162)
- "a feature-179 augmented model that appends a regression-180 predicted (train-only) relevance score to the181 embeddin" = I assume that the features were used also during the test time, but were predicted by the additional classifier.
- typos "For Return_+1"
