title: Learning from the Future: Anticipating Residual Returns via Forward Relevance Modeling
review:
1. Summary

This paper introduces a novel "forward relevance" framework that leverages next-day news narratives and residual return direction to score headlines for anticipatory signals. The proposed NARS/UFRS/DFRS scoring system is used as sample weights or features in an XGBoost classifier to predict next-day return direction. Experiments over 17 quarterly splits (2016-2023) show modest but statistically significant improvements in accuracy (≈0.5%), F1 (≈0.28%), and Sharpe ratio (≈6.2%) over baselines.

2. Strengths
- Innovative Scoring Framework: NARS (same-day narrative-return alignment), UFRS (undirectional future impact), and DFRS (directional relevance via $\tanh$) offer a principled approach to quantify forward-looking signals.
- Effective Integration: Injecting scores as training weights (UFRS) or input features (DFRS) demonstrates methodological flexibility, with DFRS feature augmentation yielding the best results.
- Empirical Rigor: The 17 rolling quarterly splits (2016–2023) and strict prevention of future data leakage validate the approach, while a 6.2% Sharpe ratio improvement confirms practical utility.

3. Weaknesses
- Marginal Gains: Absolute improvements (0.5% accuracy, 0.28% F1) are small, raising questions about economic significance. 
- Underutilization of Modern LLMs: Missing opportunities to integrate LLMs for deeper semantic understanding. The ablation lacks modern baselines like prompt-based LLM fine-tuning.
- Limited Temporal Scope: Restricted to T+1 predictions; signal decay beyond T+2 is severe. The framework does not explore multi-day dynamics or intraday granularity.

title: Tiny Language Models for NLP Pipelines
review:
This work applies the MiniLM v2 distillation pipeline to multilingual encoder models to address a prominent problem regarding the efficiency of models deployed in a latency-constricted environment. Using MiniLM distillation, this method maintain 98% of the teacher's performance with a 3.9x speedup, and can successfully be used in applications where the student and teacher differ in terms of positional embeddings.

The main weakness of this paper is the lack of novelty- MiniLMv2 is a very prominent distillation method used in a variety of settings, and using the algorithm as-is for multilingual settings is not a novel implementation. Furthermore, a lot of design decisions (such as the choice of teacher layer chosen for distillation) is also adopted from previous works. There is also a lack of finetuning baselines for the multilingual models to compare the gain we get from KD in this setup.

A strength of the paper is the exploration of KD in a setting with teachers/students of different positional embeddings, but it would have been more interesting to adapt the method for models with vastly different architectures (eg. decoder to encoder KD) or different tokenizers. Modern encoders (such as ModernBERT (https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13663))  also use relative pos. embeddings with little change in inference due to the use of flash attention, and adapting such architectures for multilingual workloads would have also been interesting.

title: Tiny Language Models for NLP Pipelines
review:
### Summary: 

The paper presents an application of the MiniLMv2 framework used in the knowledge distillation setting. The aim is to train smaller general-purpose language models that can be utilized in various NLP pipelines, especially when processing large amounts of data, or for real-time applications. The authors used the XLM-R-Large (multilingual) and HPLT (monolingual) models as teachers, and smaller transformer encoder-only monolingual models (m, s, xs) as students. In the MiniLMv2 framework, distillation is performed at the self-attention relations level, meaning that for a specific teacher layer, the student learns to align with relations of pairs of queries, keys, and values. When distilling HPLT, the teacher and the student use different position embeddings (relative vs absolute). The experiments were conducted in multiple settings, including high- and low-resource languages, and evaluation was performed on several NLP tasks such as parts-of-speech tagging, lemmatization, dependency parsing, named entity recognition, and question answering. The results show that the smallest model distilled from XLM-R-large achieves the highest throughput, while the XLM-R-large baseline still achieves higher results. However, smaller models follow closely in terms of performance. Moreover, the experiments show that using different position embeddings does not affect performance.

### Strengths:

1. The topic is relevant to the field, and the paper shows that employing the MiniLMv2 distillation framework can significantly improve throughput, at the cost of slightly reduced performance  
2. Multiple experiments were employed to analyze the performance and throughput in several settings (i.e., 7 languages, two different model architectures, three student sizes, and multilingual to monolingual distillation)  
3. The paper states that performing distillation on models with different position encodings does not reduce performance. This is important because it allows the technique to be applied to other combinations of teacher and student architectures.

### Weaknesses:

1. The evaluation of the QA is limited: only two languages, and only two students and one teacher model were evaluated. A suggestion would be to employ the other models in this task to assess the performance difference on downstream tasks. Additionally, performance speedup could also be provided for the QA task.  
2. Novelty is limited; the paper uses a setting very similar to the one used in MiniLMv2.

### Comments:

- There is an inconsistency regarding which teacher models were used. In lines 187-190, only XLM-R-Large and HPLT were mentioned, while in lines 204-206 and 230-234, XLM-R-Base is also mentioned.  
- In Table 1, mMiniLM-L6-H384 is a distilled model, while HPLT, XLM-R-Base, and XLM-R-Large are not distilled. Separating those may improve readability. Also, they don’t seem to be in a particular order. Suggestion: Use the Baselines section for non-distilled models, add a new section with Distilled Baselines containing mMiniLM-L6-H384, and then follow Our Students.  
- In Appendix A.1, only Spacy’s transformer pipelines were compared. Why aren’t the other models also used (e.g., en\_core\_web\_sm)? These models may perform worse, but do they run faster than their transformer-based counterparts? This comparison may emphasize whether the proposed solution is still better than those models.

### Typos:

- Line 301: latency should not be capitalized.  
- Lines 368-369:  move the closing parenthesis after the number, i.e., “(vs. 87.86) for XLM-R-Base”  
- Line 775: missing figures for “Figures ??”   
- Caption in Figure 6: Danish instead of German, based on “da\_core\_news\_tft” from the figure

title: SEARA: An Automated Approach for Obtaining Optimal Retrievers
review:
Summary: Relevant content retrieval is often the limiting factor in RAG performance, but relevance judgments over large collections are very expensive (and I would add, difficult). The authors propose an approach to splitting a corpus of real user queries and using automatic judgment to evluate answers. Two chatbot case studies with different architecture choices are then preseented, showing improvements.

Quality, novelty, clarity. The paper presents an interesting idea, and I think the technique is of value. The paper is largeley well written, and structured. The only challenge is that it is a little hard to follow how the seara process affected the outcome of the choices in the case studies.

I am also reminded of work from the SIGIR community on incomplete judgments, for example Buckley, C., & Voorhees, E. M. (2004, July). Retrieval evaluation with incomplete information. In Proceedings of the 27th annual international ACM SIGIR conference on Research and development in information retrieval (pp. 25-32).. Technology has moved on a lot in 20 years, but we are using the same metrics and general model in some ways.

title: SEARA: An Automated Approach for Obtaining Optimal Retrievers
review:
This paper presents SEARA (Subset sampling Evaluation for Automatic Retriever Assessment), a cost-efficient method to identify optimal retriever configurations for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems in specific business scenarios.

Strengths:
- Strong practical relevance: Tackles a key industry challenge in RAG deployment by enabling cost-effective retriever selection under real-world constraints.
- Well-designed and efficient method: Combines subset sampling with minimal fact extraction to balance evaluation accuracy and computational feasibility.
- Robust and realistic evaluation: Uses real user queries, applies the method to two distinct RAG applications, and adopts PR-AUC for fair comparison in imbalanced retrieval settings.
- Actionable system insights: Provides detailed analysis of segmentation, retrieval strategies, and component interactions, offering practical guidance for pipeline optimization.

Weaknesses:
Nothing major

title: SEARA: An Automated Approach for Obtaining Optimal Retrievers
review:
The paper  introduces a new method for evaluating RAG systems using automatically generated ground truth rather than manually labeled data. For the ground truth generation they use LLMs with subset sampling techniques to address the costs of LLM usage. They propose to use the recall results of all evaluated retrievers as a sampled subset to ensure that the number of positive samples predicted by each retriever remains unchanged.
 
They use PR-AUC  to compare RAG systems’ output correctness across varying confidence thresholds. PR-AUC avoids preset precision recall weights, using curves to show performance across thresholds for easy retriever comparison. 

They validate the method across  two RAG applications in rednote:
* a rednote employee self service consultation assistant based on RAG systems, and
* a generative retrieval application in travel scenarios.

For the self service consultation assistant retrieval construction, three strategy dimensions were considered: segmentation strategy, retrieval strategy, and embedding model.  
This allows the construction of 24 retrievers in total and the method successfully found optimal retriever setup. 

For the retrieval based travel assistant, generative retrieval relies on rednote community note resources, with one note corresponding to one chunk. In this case, the paper constructs different retrievers through combinations of: query rewriters, filters, and rerankers. In theory, 96 different retrievers can be constructed. But, because of evaluation time, they used a staged evaluation strategy and they tested 8 different combinations of these components to understand how each affects retrieval performance. They show that it is not possible to optimize each strategy in isolation (you must consider their combined effects): 
* The query rewriter only  improves performance when both filter and reranker are also enabled. 
* The reranker improves precision and ranking quality in most setups
* The filtering improves recall by allowing more potentially relevant results, but can lower precision, especially if reranking isn't active or query rewriting introduces noise. 

The idea of evaluating retrieval systems using sampled relevant items has been explored before. But SEARA's way of using it in the RAG context and applying PR-AUC over subset-sampled answers, is a novel and smart combination of existing ideas.

I think the evaluation is complete, and I like the idea that they isolate strategies and try out each combination (a well-structured evaluation). Applied in two rednote scenarios, the method successfully found optimal retriever setups. The results show that retriever effectiveness depends on the application.
The use of real user queries to enable fully automated evaluation of retrievers is also an advantage. 

The main limitation is that the methodology depends highly on the quality of LLMs used to generate pseudo ground truth, which may introduce hallucinations or biases. 
Also, semantic segmentation and answer generation using LLMs are computationally expensive and may not scale easily to very large datasets or real time applications.
Finally, effectiveness depends on the availability and quality of real user query datasets, which may not always be accessible or representative.

Open questions and suggestions: 
* Currently, the evaluation centers on whether the system matches a reference answer. It doesn’t capture usefulness, user satisfaction, or interaction quality, which are important in business applications (at least when such information is available).
* Consider also assessing latency and memory constraints that are important for real world systems, and may rule out optimal strategies identified.
* PR-AUC is an excellent and justifiable choice for SPEAR when the goal is to compare RAG systems output correctness across varying confidence thresholds. But did you consider using complementary metrics like BERTScore?

title: From Conversation to Cognition: Dialogue-Induced Profiling in Large Language Model Agents
review:
*Summary:*
- The authors created a framework to make two agents interact. Each agent is based on a profile based of factual and non-factual information. Each agent can add and remove memories of the other. The goal of the agents is to develop the profile of the other through dialogue. 
- Leveraging the defined framework, the authors try to answer questions regarding the capability of inferring the other's profile, while varying the compatibility of agents, and their communication style
- The evaluation compares the difference between the developed and the actual profile and LLM-as-a-judge

*Novelty & Impact:*
- to the best of my knowledge this is the first experiment that explores the capability of inferring an agent profile through dialog
- the results suggest that interview style is more effective in developing a user profile, free form dialog can be used to infer profile when combined with the adequate reward function, and personality compatibility plays a statistically significant role in some information (working/study condition, job, and possible family relations) 
- the paper introduces an interesting insight in understanding how LLMs can derive profiles. A next potential step would be to study the capability of LLMs to derive profiles of real users and how it compares

*Reproducibility:*
- every agent prompt has been added to the appendix section, making the overall framework easier to replicate
- each experiment was repeated three times increasing reproducibility
- the profiles are randomly selected from publicly available data 

*Clarity & Structure:*
- overall the paper is well written and flows
- the structure based on question that are answered in a sequence makes it easier to follow
- the less clear part to me is related to what is the purpose of comparing (in-family judge) vs (out-of-family judge)

title: From Conversation to Cognition: Dialogue-Induced Profiling in Large Language Model Agents
review:
- **Summary**
  This paper explores methods for inferring the “Profile” of LLM Agents—a set of both objective and subjective attributes. The authors examine several factors:
    - **Approach**: (1) Explicitly querying the LLM vs. (2) Implicitly inferring through casual conversation.
    - **Feedback**: Providing targeted prompts to focus on unknown attributes.
    - **Interaction Style**: Role-play scenarios vs. unconstrained conversations.
      The paper also compares evaluations by “in-family” vs. “out-of-family” judges. The key finding is that explicit questioning yields more accurate and effective profiling.
- **Strengths**
  The idea of profiling AI agents through conversational interaction is intriguing, and the integration of concepts such as MBTI theory and LLM memory frameworks is appreciated. The distinction between in-family and out-of-family judging is also an interesting angle.
- **Limitations and Concerns**
  However, I do not believe the paper currently meets the publication threshold due to significant clarity and methodological issues:
    - **Clarity Gap** – There is a noticeable mismatch between the stated goals and the implemented experiments. The intended design, experimental process, and resulting analyses are difficult to follow.
    - **Experimental Design** – The paper does not clearly convey how experiments were structured, how feedback was incorporated, and how results were derived. For instance, Figure 1 suggests a scenario where two AI agents have extensive prior conversations with different people, followed by profile inference—but this is not clearly reflected in the actual experiments.
    - **Presentation** – The experimental setup could be significantly clarified with a concise table (e.g., columns for Role-play vs. Unconstrained, Feedback Use, Direct vs. Implicit Inference). Core definitions, such as “Profile,” should be moved from the appendix to the main text to aid comprehension.
    - **Missing Core Diagram** – While the appendix contains useful material, the main paper lacks a central diagram illustrating the interplay among components, which is essential for replication.
    - **Ground Truth** – The paper does not clearly explain how the “source of truth” for profiles is determined, which undermines result interpretation.
- **Overall Assessment**
The work has potential, but the lack of clarity and insufficiently described methodology limit the interpretability and impact of the findings. A major reorganization, with explicit links between research intent, experimental implementation, and results, is necessary before this work would be ready for publication.

title: CLARITY: Clinical Assistant for Routing, Inference, and Triage
review:
This paper presents CLARITY, a hybrid clinical assistant platform designed for safe, efficient, and scalable patient triage and specialist routing. It combines Finite State Machines (FSMs) for structured dialogue control with Large Language Models (LLMs) for medical reasoning. The system is modular, microservice-based, and successfully deployed in a national-scale healthcare setting, completing over 55,000 consultations in just two months. Extensive evaluations across multiple submodules (e.g., emergency detection, specialty selector, moderator) demonstrate strong performance and real-world feasibility.

Pros:

Real-World Deployment: CLARITY goes beyond academic prototypes and delivers a large-scale, operational deployment with user feedback and pilot studies. This makes it one of the few LLM-based healthcare systems with real usage data.

Hybrid Design with FSM + LLM: The combination of FSMs for safety and structure, and LLMs for flexibility, is well-motivated and effectively executed. This design choice enables control without sacrificing conversational fluidity.

Modular Architecture with Subsystem-Level Evaluation: Each component (moderator, emergency detector, readiness estimator, etc.) is well-isolated and rigorously evaluated using appropriate metrics (e.g., F1, precision@k, MAPE), contributing to system robustness.

Transparency and Safety Awareness: The paper demonstrates a strong emphasis on medical safety, regulatory alignment, and content moderation—critical for clinical use cases.

Cons:

Support Scalable FSM Management: As the clinical scope expands, the FSM may grow in complexity. It would be valuable to describe strategies for maintaining and updating FSMs at scale, such as automated transition auditing, abstraction layers, or tooling support for medical teams.

Incorporate Feedback for Continuous Learning: Integrating an active learning pipeline that leverages user corrections, clinician feedback, or misclassification logs could enable the system to continuously improve post-deployment. This would ensure it evolves alongside real-world clinical needs and shifting usage patterns.

title: CLARITY: Clinical Assistant for Routing, Inference, and Triage
review:
This paper presents a fully automated approach to diagnosis and triage of patient queries using an AI conversational system that consists of a deterministic  'dialogue manager', as well as different modules for decision making and text generation:

- For decision making, the system includes: moderator (detection of 'prohibited' topics), emergency detection, clarification question detection, readiness estimator (i.e., enough information is provided and the system has enough information to answer).

- For text generation, the system includes: information collector (to find a similar question), medical specialty selector and answer generator.

This work is very broad but I found the paper to be lacking details or...clarity, which I detail below. Also, I have some issues with the ethics of the application, i.e., the use of a fully automated approach for health diagnosis. For example, the authors value minimizing false positives for emergency detector, for economics reason. Surely a minimization of a condition (false negative) would have far more serious consequences for the user. Also is it possible for the user to request talking to a human were they not confident about the response? Generally speaking, trust is of utmost importance to users in health applications, however no human monitoring is considered. Despite the emergency detector or moderator, I do not believe that this is enough to ensure that the user query is answered safely.  

The authors mention in the limitations sections that the system is deployed on "common and well-represented clinical cases, as these reflect the majority of real-world usage scenarios": how do they ensure that the present scenario fits in one of thos cases. Are there situations where the handling of the query is given back to the human? Could a confidence threshold be used to determine whether the response is fit for the user query?

Here are additional comments/issues/questions/suggestions:


- More details about the ground truth annotation used for the off line evaluation would be nice: how is readiness measured for example? For example you mention that moderator was evaluated on a dataset of 10,000 messages: does that mean you have 10k messages annotated for moderation? What are the absolute numbers regarding 'prohibited' topics - what were the criteria regarding prohibited? Does that include out of topic?

- Regarding readiness, predicting the duration of the anamnesis collection is mentioned. Does that mean that the task is to decide whether to ask for some additional info or to start answering?

- Also a characterization of dialogues might be relevant to the audience: number of conversation turns per dialogue. Number of dialogues with explicit questions, number of dialogues regarding new queries vs follow up, specialties, etc. Also an example dialogue with the different types of turns analyzed might be helpful: clarifying question, anamesis, response, polite conversation, etc. 

- You mention conversion rate and proportion of queries with diagnosis and referral: it would be useful to have more details (e.g., how many query have a diagnosis but are not referred to a specialist). In the end it is not clear what the objective of this application is: is it to maximize referrals in order to maximize revenue or is it to 'triage' in order to answer easy problems and refer more complex or medically serious ones to a specialist?

- I wasn't clear wrt the role of the Medical Specialty Selector: is it to detect the specialty and answer the query? In what way is it important to produce the final answer, is it the selection of relevant documents?

- It would be interesting to have more details regarding the context of the evaluation for the pilot studies: how where they presented to the users? How were they recruited? Were the users regular users of the platform? Had the interacted with the platform before?

- Lines 431-435: what do you mean by online vs offline consultations?

- Some ablation evaluation, such as comparing an LLM only approach vs an FSM+LLM approach, or doing without one of the modules, would help in understanding their value.

- The shorter consultation time does not mean it translates in more user satisfaction. In the first pilot study: A total of 18.2% of users indicated that they found the consultation to be fully useful, while 54.5% of respondents rated it as partially useful. A more thorough qualitative evaluation in the first pilot would be interesting, and also further questions relating to the trust the users would put in this tool. How did you measure accuracy in the answers (i.e., no hallucinations - as discussed in A.2.2)? This seems like a critical issue for such an automated tool, that could lead to serious consequences.


Minor details:

- Line 92, space between ")" and "("
- Order of references in list is unclear, e.g., lines 92-93

title: CLARITY: Clinical Assistant for Routing, Inference, and Triage
review:
The paper presents CLARITY, an AI-powered medical dialogue system designed to improve patient-to-specialist routing, support clinical consultations, and assess condition severity. It uses a hybrid architecture combining: Finite State Machine (FSM), Large Language Model (LLM) agents and a microservice architecture to integration into healthcare systems. Authors show that CLARITY can outperform humans in first-attempt specialist routing, maintain patient safety, and improve efficiency. 

Overall the system is well designed keeping both safely and flexibility in mind. The authors have reported positive numbers for different modules. They have also deployed this system in real world setting with over 55k dialogues, and favorable user/system metrics. This is a promising stem, and while the overall archtitechture is not novel, I still feel the paper has merit in its real world applicability and learnings.

The authors claim that - "This surpasses typical human-level performance in initial routing while requiring only one-third of the usual consultation time." -- It is not clear how did the authors make this claim. I would make this a blocker for making sure claims are backed by data points clearly.

title: Training-Free Knowledge Distillation for Small Language Models Enhances Question-Answering Quality and Accelerates Response Speed
review:
**Paper Summary**:
- This paper proposes to utilize the low-latency feature of small LMs while improving the performance through a teacher-student interactive problem-solving framework.

**Strengths**:
- The paper is clear, and the method is elaborated.
- The proposed method improves the performance of small LMs (Qwen-2.5-7B) on HotpotQA and TriviaQA datasets by a large margin, compared to direct answer, planning, and few-shot baselines. The performance of the small LMs approach that of the large LMs (Qwen-2.5-72B).
- The ablation study shows the effectiveness of each proposed component in the pipeline.

**Weaknesses**:
- Intuitively, the proposed framework (as in Figure 1) involves multiple stages, which could slow down the response speed. As shown in Table 3, the method in this paper does have a higher latency than direct answering. Even if it is better than the "Planning" baseline, the observations do not support the main claim of this paper: enhancing question-answering quality AND accelerating response speed.

title: Training-Free Knowledge Distillation for Small Language Models Enhances Question-Answering Quality and Accelerates Response Speed
review:
1. Overall - 

The idea of moving away from the usual Distillation framework to distilling memory tips and using them for QnA looks very interesting. 

The paper is well organized and the presentation is reasonable in most of the sections. However, the quality of presentation drops significantly in Section 3.3.2 (Ablation Study). Usage of English in this section is poor, and because of that the explanation is not clear. For example: Line 317 to 321 - "(1) w/o four stages: We remove the four stages ..... To do this, the knowledge memory M is also removed". Can this be written as: "We remove all the four stages and also the knowledge memory M". Similar issue of explanation is faced in the remaining experiments.

Though it doesn't break the flow of the paper, English usage needs improvement throughout the paper. For example, "Industrial setup" instead of "Industrial area", "Providing an accurate and fast" instead of "Providing an accurate and timely". "The influence of the number of training samples" instead of "The influence of training numbers" Right words to express the intended intent is needed at many places. Authors are advised to get this done through a reviewer.

The main issue the paper faces is that the results are not positive even directionally if the right results are compared. 

(a) The Exact Match performance in Table 1 for 72B Direct for Hotpot QA is 27% and for ours is 26%. In Table 3, for the same dataset, 72B Direct takes 2.75 seconds and ours takes 12.53 seconds. So neither our approach is better nor faster if 72B LLM is compared for the results on HotpotQA dataset. At the same time, it needs to be noticed that the memory tips were generated from the HotpotQA so performance should have been better here.

(b) There are other anomalies in the results that are not discussed in the paper: why for the Hotpot QA and TriviaQA datasets, for 7B parameters LLM, the performance of Direct is better than that of Planning? In Figure 2, changing the number of samples doesn't seem to have a positive impact. The explanation provided is not making sense.

The minor issues in the paper are:

(a) What kind of memory tips were generated at each stage by the teacher? Some examples of how memory tips at different stages look like are needed to understand what is happening during the different stages, and what exactly the teacher is proposing to the student.

(b) What was observed during the sorting stage in terms of how many times the orders of the sub-tasks were changed, was any manual verification done to understand if the sorting is helpful and added value, etc

Overall, though the idea looks interesting, it needs to be explained better and "whys" (why something is happening) need to be understood. Since pages in the appendix are not a limitation, explaining (by example) what is captured in the memory tips and how they were utilized at the time of testing by the student model is extremely important to understand the working of the proposed method.

title: Training-Free Knowledge Distillation for Small Language Models Enhances Question-Answering Quality and Accelerates Response Speed
review:
Advantages
- The proposed method is generalizable, particularly in its knowledge memory construction component, which can effectively boost the performance of a small language model (SLM) without fine-tuning.
- Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, and the extensive ablation study clearly shows the contribution of each component.

Questions and Concerns
- The paper does not explain the rationale for choosing the current baselines. Is comparing against these baselines sufficient to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method? Are there other strong baselines that should be included for a more convincing evaluation?
- The proposed approach appears somewhat similar to auto-prompt methods or few-shot retrieval-augmented methods (e.g., retrieving few-shot examples from a gold-label set that are similar to the current sample). It would be beneficial to discuss such related works in the Related Works section and consider including strong baselines from these categories.
- Since the primary motivation is to improve the performance of an SLM without tuning, it would be ideal to include a comparison with results obtained after fine-tuning the SLM. This would help quantify the gap between fine-tuning/distillation-based methods and the proposed approach.
- After applying the few-shot setting, the ROUGE score on TriviaQA decreases significantly. What factors might explain this performance drop?

title: PlanGPT-VL: Enhancing Urban Planning with Domain-Specific Vision-Language Models
review:
Summary: This paper presents empirical evidence for in-domain VLM fine-tuning for urban planning QA. The experiments showed that VLM fine-tuning on custom data had led to performance gains. The custom data is also proposed as a benchmark for the target domain.

Strengths:
1. The experiments are rigorous and well-designed.
2. Model performance confirms the working hypothesis.

Weaknesses:
1. The main findings are predictable and lack novelty.
2. The fine-tuned models struggled with generic QA, which is problematic but also predictable.
3. It is not clear if the fine-tuned models had indeed acquired domain-specific knowledge such as policies and regulations, or had simply learned from spurious information such as geographical names.
4. The proposed benchmark used to fine-tune the models is biased toward select geographical locations and thus is not representative of the target domain.
5. The fine-tuning process was too resource-intensive to justify the approach.

General feedback: The authors' claim is not well aligned with the actual experiments: the custom benchmark only focuses on select geographical locations, while the authors' intended focus is on generic urban planning QA. Thus, my suggestion is that the authors take a deep dive into their benchmark and tailor their solution to this specific case, so that the paper's focus is aligned with the experiments.

title: PlanGPT-VL: Enhancing Urban Planning with Domain-Specific Vision-Language Models
review:
**Summary**

This paper introduces PlanGPT-VL, the first domain-specific Vision-Language Model (VLM) tailored for urban planning maps. To address the limitations of existing general-purpose VLMs in interpreting complex planning maps and to reduce hallucinations, PlanGPT-VL employs three innovative approaches: First, PlanAnno-V framework to generate high-quality instruction-response pairs, in which Critical Point Thinking (CPT) is proposed to reduce hallucinations. The paper also proposes PlanBench-V, the first comprehensive benchmark professionally annotated by urban planning experts for evaluating VLM performance on urban planning map interpretation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that PlanGPT-VL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art general VLMs in specialized planning tasks

**Strength**

1.	This work represents a pioneering effort in the context of urban planning maps, filling a significant void in the understanding and application capabilities of general-purpose VLMs within this specialized domain.

2.	This work proposes a relatively comprehensive evaluation framework for urban planning, covering dimensions such as perception, reasoning, association, and implementation.

**Weakness**

1.	Although the paper compares the performance across different base models (2B, 7B, 13B) and varying data scales (100, 500, 1000 maps), it does not explicitly report the training time and computational resources required to achieve these results.

2.	To what extent can the “revise” mechanism proposed in the paper substitute for human expert judgment? Especially in planning scenarios without clear “correct answers” or involving complex trade-offs, the model's revise capability may have an upper limit.

3.	The paper does not provide a dedicated experiment or analysis to evaluate the accuracy of the standalone “ExtractCriticalPoints” step in Algorithm 1.

title: PlanGPT-VL: Enhancing Urban Planning with Domain-Specific Vision-Language Models
review:
Pros:
1. Clear problem framing and first dedicated VLM for planning maps; three concrete contributions (PlanAnno-V, CPT, PlanBench-V).
2. Strong domain gains: PlanGPT-VL-7B tops PlanBench-V (overall 1.566) and excels in Professional Reasoning and Implementation.
3. Transparent data pipeline (5k → 1,050 → expert annotations on 800 examples) indicates care in curation. 

Cons:
1. Domain specialization degrades general capabilities (MMMU −11.2%, GQA −10.1%); mitigation strategy remains preliminary. (I think this is fine for industry track)
2. Limited qualitative error analysis of hallucination types on real planning artifacts; CPT effectiveness is mostly numeric.

title: Constrained NLP for Education: A Stakeholder-Informed Framework for Query-Focused Summarization using RAG and SLMs
review:
The paper presents retrieval-based approaches for summarizing multi-document for non-factoid questions, it is especially targeted to teaching proposes. For document retrieval authors compared with extractive baselines, showing, unsurprisingly, that abstractive approacher either SLMs or LLMs performed better.
The evaluation of the retrieval uses classical objective metrics such as ROUGE and BLUE scores. For evaluating the answer, LLMs as a judge was used.

Strengths:
The paper proposes an interesting approach for the education domain.

Weakness:
Authors claim that the teacher is involved the pipeline, with a teacher in the loop approach, however the results felt short, since no human evaluation is presented.

Typos: please describe every acronym including NLP.

title: Constrained NLP for Education: A Stakeholder-Informed Framework for Query-Focused Summarization using RAG and SLMs
review:
The paper describes a framework for query-focused summarisation in educational domain. Several abstractive and extractive models are tested for this task, along with RAG-based methods.

# Strengths: 
A wide range of LLMs and retrieval strategies are used to test the framework the paper deals with the importand topic for education community

# Weaknesses:
- the paper could do a better job to show how the framework was informed by stakeholders (e.g., by including more details about a real-time feedback loop, l. 309) little discussion of LLM-in-the-loop and teacher-in-the-loop components: what are their respective performances? How many responses were flagged? What was feedback from teachers who participated in the experiment? I think this user evaluation could be a strong point of the paper.
- the approach is tested only on one public dataset (QuerySum)
- dataset characteristics while introduced in the beginning (factoid vs. non-factoid questions) are not explored in evaluation. What were performances on factoid/non-factoid questions?
- reproducibility is limited: prompts used to query the LLMs are not given; same for the validation check metric.
- latency is mentioned several times througout the paper but final results didn't show any numbers concerning latency
- SLMs and BART/T5 as baselines: no surprise that without finetuning these models gave low results. Did you try to finetune these models to gain in performance? Especially, LLMs such as llama-8b, Phi can be promising.
- metrics to assess summarisation could be revised. E.g, n-gram-based metrics were heavily critised for summarisation. I think more focus could be made on human evaluation, especially via teacher feedback.
# Suggestions and questions:
- please include an example of query-focused summarisation
- examples of interface would also be helpful to showcase your work from the user point of view
- 163: how is the coherence score defined? what is its range?
- 244-247: "significant inference costs": not clear why because most models are open while the chosen gpt-4o-mini is the closed model
- 327: it was not clear how LLM Evaluation is different from the Retrieval Effectiveness criterion (which is also based on llm-as-a-judge)
- 350: I would appreciate adding more information why gpt-4-mini was chosen as a final model. In Table 1, the llama-70B model has the best performance, and it's also a free model comparing to gpt-4-mini

title: Constrained NLP for Education: A Stakeholder-Informed Framework for Query-Focused Summarization using RAG and SLMs
review:
The paper proposes to use Query Focused Multi-Document Summarization (QFS) as an alternative to a full unconstrained  LLM chatbot in the context of educational QA.

The accent is put on the efficacy of the approach in terms of computational cost, and the transparency of the approach.

 

Positive aspects:

    The authors experiment on the QuerySum dataset and put significant effort to analyze the dataset and justify how it is relevant for their use-case. They mention that they rely on professionals to assess the suitability of the dataset.
    The authors provide a good analysis of the dataset, providing statistical descriptions that help apprehending the problem.
    The paper addresses relevant ethical issues along the paper, including in the introduction, which is appreciated in this context.
    The authors conducted human evaluation through educator review.
    They also provide evaluations in terms of cost and token use.

 

Shortcomings :

    In general the paper lacks methodological novelty and there is a mismatch between the statements announced in the introductory parts and the evaluations that are made. In the end, the paper evaluates a RAG setup and it is difficult to find originality in the approach. I don’t really see why this RAG setup should be qualified as an “optimized summarization” approach. In the end the message appears to be quite confusing and discards the practical innovation that could have been brought by this study.
    « stakeholder-informed QFS » it is not clear what the authors mean by this, and there is no mention of this notion in the introduction nor in related work.
    The paper is not very easy to follow and on the overall its structure is rather unconventional. Section 4 is very short and the scientific contribution is not clearly stated before the experimental part. Section 5.1 is supposed to cover query type distribution, which is already disclosed in section 3. Pre-processing in section 5.1 doesn’t correspond to an exploratory dataset validation. Section 5 presents the approach as a project report, mixing preliminary evaluations and implementation choices without clearly introducing the proposed approach beforehand.
    Regarding experimentation, I am not convinced that is really useful nowadays to provide results with extractive baselines. For such a complex task it is very likely that performances will be insufficient.
    There are several unclear passages in the experimental section.
    « Models that hallucinated or relied on pretraining were excluded » : I don’t understand that sentence. All models can eventually hallucinate, how could this be a reason to discard a model? All models rely on pre-training, what does that mean here? Why exactly was Phi-3 small disqualified?
    The paper should clearly provide the number of parameters for each of the evaluated SLMs. Even if this number is not publicly available for GPT4o-mini, this should be commented.
    There is no qualitative feedback from the educator review.

title: BengaliMoralBench: A Benchmark for Auditing Moral Reasoning in Large Language Models within Bengali Language and Culture
review:
**Summary**:

This paper introduces BengaliMoralBench, the first large-scale ethics benchmark designed to audit the moral reasoning of Large Language Models (LLMs) within the Bengali language and its socio-cultural context. Addressing the gap of existing benchmarks that are predominantly English-centric and based on Western moral frameworks, BengaliMoralBench consists of 3,000 handcrafted scenarios. These scenarios span five key domains of daily life in Bangladesh: Daily Activities, Habits, Parenting, Family Relationships, and Religious Activities. Each scenario is evaluated through a unique triadic moral framework inspired by South Asian traditions, comprising Virtue, Common Sense, and Justice ethics. The authors evaluated prominent multilingual LLMs, such as LLaMA and Gemma, and found wide performance variations, with accuracies ranging from 50% to 90%. The results reveal that current models struggle with cultural grounding, commonsense reasoning, and moral fairness, highlighting the limitations of scaling model size alone without culturally specific data and alignment. Ultimately, BengaliMoralBench provides a foundational resource for the responsible and inclusive development of AI technologies in diverse, non-Western markets.

**Strength**:
- Cultural differences are a critical yet underexplored aspect in the ethical domain.
- Data is annotated by Bengali experts, and has gone through a consistency check to ensure high quality.
- An interesting phenomenon was discovered: using the Bengali language in prompting enhances performance.
- The author provided details about how to collect data and reproduce the work.


**Weakness**:
- The benchmark only focuses on binary choice problems, which have some gap to real-world use cases. Including open-ended QA or multi-round conversations related to ethics will make it more comprehensive.
- I feel like the results part is more of a listing of numbers instead of presenting insights. I'd like to see more discussions on 1) why this benchmark is worth trying for LLMs; 2) what information these results convey.
- While Bengali social norms are a novel research topic, investigations on other small languages (e.g. Thai) have already been conducted. This makes the contribution of the paper somewhat marginal (although I totally agree it's useful).

**Question**:
- The author mentioned that Bengali social norms could be different from England or America. How different are they quantitatively (i.e. how many of the questions will have a different answer for an American) ?

title: BengaliMoralBench: A Benchmark for Auditing Moral Reasoning in Large Language Models within Bengali Language and Culture
review:
The paper "BengaliMoralBench: A Benchmark for Auditing Moral Reasoning in Large Language Models within Bengali Language and Culture" presents work on assessing the moral reasoning of LLMs within the Bengali language. The motivation behind this is that most AI systems are based on the cultures and languages of Western/Countries from the Global North. So this is definitely an important aspect of widening and broadening the way LLMs deal with elements that are not part of these cultures and/or languages. 

Nevertheless, there are a few issues with the paper at hand.

* Considering the complexity of the task, an inter-annotator agreement of \kappa = 0.61 and 0.87 respectively is impressive. There are missing details about how this was calculated and which \kappa has been used, as there are different varieties. 
* While the paper argues that a benchmark on Bengali Culture and Moral is being created, the examples are often quite generic. In Figure 7 of the Appendix both the first as well as the last example could apply to any culture/language. It might strengthen the paper to see more examples that are less generic. Similar aspects also apply to Figure 8, for example removing shoes indoors could also come from the Japanese culture. 
* I am also missing a discussion of related work which looks into previous work on evaluating morals and cultural questions in LLMs. 
* Some aspects of the paper seem to be in violation of the template -- i.e. distance between Section Header 4.2 and Section Header 4.2.1 and also the gap between the caption for Figure 4 and the remaining text. In some venues this could count as a desk reject.

Some minor issues are: 

There are a few ungrammatical sentences, such as line 025: "Results show (a) wide variation in performance ..." and line 127 "The benchmark comprises (of) 3000 carefully ..."

title: BengaliMoralBench: A Benchmark for Auditing Moral Reasoning in Large Language Models within Bengali Language and Culture
review: This paper proposes a moral reasoning benchmark for a low-resourced language Bengali. Considering that most benchmarks are in English, this is a contribution to the research area of moral reasoning. I would suggest a clear acceptance.

title: How Accurate Are LLMs at Multi-Question Answering on Conversational Transcripts?
review:
This paper presents a study of characterizing call center transcripts using LLMs to, as I understand it, check that various elements of a call center protocol are exhibited: did the call center operator identify themselves?  Was account information verified?  The study shows that LLMs can answer multiple questions in one prompt accurately and that small models can be finetuned to achieve comparable accuracy.
I wasn't clear whether the questions were always presented in the same order, i.e. is the 10 question set the same as the 5 question set, plus an additional 5 questions? I assume that the questions are ordered by importance or frequency in a transcript, so the tail of the questions is less important, but that wasn't clear to me.  How formulaic are the operator's utterances?  Are they using a script?  In general, many important details of the task and corpus are not detailed.  Is it easier to evaluate the operator's utterances than the caller's (I would guess this would be the case).  In general, while a lot of evaluation data is provided, it is difficult to understand the tasks and data for this paper to be very compelling.

title: How Accurate Are LLMs at Multi-Question Answering on Conversational Transcripts?
review:
The paper studies batch prompting for answering multiple yes/no questions over long, noisy contact‑center transcripts, adding a “Navigation” pointer to an evidential utterance index and enforcing JSON outputs. It benchmarks proprietary (GPT‑4o/mini, Gemini‑1.5‑flash) and fine‑tuned public models (Llama‑3 1B/8B, Qwen‑2.5‑7B) across group sizes N∈{10…50}. Main findings: performance drops with larger N; fine‑tuned 7–8B public models approach or occasionally exceed GPT‑4o’s Judgment accuracy at high N; fine‑tuning greatly reduces JSON decoding errors. Strengths include an industry‑motivated task, structured outputs, and practical observations about group size. The biggest weaknesses are evaluation grounded in GPT‑4o‑generated “references” (teacher‑labeled data) rather than human gold, limited reporting on cost/latency/throughput, and several missing reproducibility details.

Problem: Efficiently and accurately answer many QA items about the same long conversation in production, where repeated re‑inference over the same context is expensive.

Method/task: Batch prompting—ask N yes/no questions in a single prompt; require a structured JSON output with (a) Judgment and (b) a Navigation index pointing to a supporting utterance.

Data: 2,800 in‑house ASR transcripts from multiple contact centers; token length stats reported. Labels for training/eval are GPT‑4o outputs at N=10, justified by a 50‑call human audit showing high approximate accuracy at small N.

Experiments: Proprietary models in zero‑shot; public models in both zero‑shot and fine‑tuned variants. Evaluate Judgment accuracy, Navigation F1 and MAE, and JSON decode error rate across N∈{10,20,30,40,50}.

Results: Performance declines with N for all models. Fine‑tuned Qwen‑2.5‑7B and Llama‑3.1‑8B close most of the gap and sometimes surpass GPT‑4o in Judgment at higher N; fine‑tuning slashes JSON errors for public models.

Paper type: Benchmarking/production evaluation with an application case‑study flavor.

Strengths:
Clear, industry‑relevant problem (multi‑question QA over long, noisy ASR transcripts) with a structured output that supports auditability.
Comprehensive comparison across models and group sizes; includes a practically important JSON parseability metric.
Sensible training trick (random K≤N) to avoid overfitting to fixed group size; ablations across fine‑tuning maxima for N provide actionable guidance.
Useful descriptive statistics about transcript lengths and qualitative guidance that larger N hurts accuracy.

Weaknesses and Limitations:
Ground truth depends on GPT‑4o outputs at N=10 rather than human gold; claims such as “8B models surpass GPT‑4o at N≥30” measure consistency with GPT‑4o‑N=10, not correctness. This can inflate “gains” when teacher degrades at higher N. The paper acknowledges a small human audit (50 transcripts) at varying N but uses that only to justify using GPT‑4o labels—not to evaluate other models.
No statistical significance, confidence intervals, or multiple‑seed variability; single‑run results on stochastic systems can be fragile.
Reproducibility gaps: missing batch sizes, optimizer, schedulers, gradient clipping, tokenization/max sequence length, prompt order strategy (question ordering), seed control, training/eval wall‑clock, and exact data counts per K/N. Unclear handling of Navigation for “No” answers (returned “NA”) in F1/MAE computations.
Industry claims lack operational evidence: no latency/throughput measurements, cost per conversation vs per‑question comparisons, memory and timeout behavior at N=50, or SLA failure analyses.
Potential label leakage/bias: all systems are trained/evaluated to mimic GPT‑4o’s judgments and rationales; domain shift/hallucination risks are not assessed by humans at scale.
Dataset is internal and unreleased; replicability hinges on careful reporting (currently incomplete).

Novelty and related work:
Batch Prompting (EMNLP‑Industry 2023): Introduced batching multiple items in one prompt to reduce cost/time while aiming to maintain quality; foundational to this paper’s setup and motivates studying batch size effects. 
BatchPrompt (ICLR 2024): Proposes permutation+ensembling and early stopping to counter batch‑position effects; suggests techniques the authors could test to stabilize large‑N performance.
Lost in the Middle (TACL 2024): Shows strong position effects in long contexts; directly relevant to the observed degradation with larger N and to design of question/context ordering. 
Leave No Document Behind / Loong (EMNLP 2024): A long‑context QA benchmark emphasizing realistic context composition; supports the need for long, relevant contexts rather than synthetic padding. 
BoolQ (NAACL 2019): Natural yes/no QA dataset; contextualizes the task’s binary judgment aspect. 
CoQA and QuAC: Conversational QA datasets that differ in interactive setup but inform transcript‑style QA and evidence provision. 
Grammar‑Constrained/Aligned Decoding and Structured Outputs: Methods to guarantee JSON/structured compliance and mitigate decode errors; could complement the paper’s JSON error metric.
StructuredRAG and JSONSchemaBench (2024–2025): Benchmarks and analyses of structured generation and schema adherence; relevant to reliable JSON outputs at scale. 
Contact‑center LLM studies: Domain‑specific fine‑tuning and probing for contact‑center tasks support the application setting and could provide complementary baselines. 
Model reports used as baselines (Llama‑3, Qwen‑2.5, GPT‑4o system card): Technical references for the compared models’ capabilities and intended use.  

Overall, the work is a targeted, application‑driven benchmark; methodologically incremental relative to batch prompting and long‑context QA literature, but with an industry‑focused evaluation lens and the Navigation/JSON angle.

Missing/ambiguous:
Exact number of training instances after K‑sampling; batch size, optimizer, scheduler, gradient clipping, warmup, max sequence length/truncation strategy, padding, tokenization details; prompt formatting specifics for all models; seed control and number of runs; decoding parameters (temperature, top‑p, max tokens); timeouts/retries; early stopping; evaluation inclusion/exclusion of “NA” for Navigation.
Hardware utilization (GPU hours), training/inference wall‑clock, memory footprints.
Cost/latency and throughput vs N; stability under server rate limits; structured decoding method (free‑form vs constrained).
Data provenance details: languages, PII handling, domain mix; license/consent; ASR WER and error characteristics.

Industry relevance and deployment considerations:
Very relevant task and output format; JSON decoding error is a practical metric.
Findings about optimal N trade‑offs are actionable, but without latency/throughput/cost curves and failure budgets (timeouts, rate limits), guidance remains qualitative.
Missing operational mitigations such as: question permutation/ensembling at large N, constrained decoding (JSON‑schema), prefix/prompt caching, retry policies, or fallbacks (e.g., split into smaller batches on parse failure).

Questions for authors:
Ground truth and validity: Can you provide a human‑annotated subset across all N (e.g., 300 transcripts × 50 questions) to compare all systems, report CIs, and quantify disagreement with GPT‑4o‑N=10 labels?
Navigation metrics: How are “NA” values handled in F1/MAE? Are Navigation metrics computed only on “Yes” or on all questions? Please report class balance and both micro/macro F1.
Order effects: What is the question ordering policy within the prompt? Did you test permutation or position‑balancing and its impact on large‑N degradation?
JSON reliability: Did you try grammar/JSON‑schema‑constrained decoding or tool‑calling to reduce JSON errors? If so, how does it trade off with latency? If not, could you compare to GCD/GAD‑style constraints? (aclanthology.org, arxiv.org)
Ops metrics: Please add latency, throughput, timeout/retry rates, and cost per conversation vs per question across N, ideally on both APIs and hosted open‑weights.
Reproducibility: Provide full training/eval details (batch sizes, max lengths, seeds, decoding params, optimizer/scheduler, run‑to‑run variance).
ASR robustness: What is the WER distribution, and how do errors correlate with Judgment/Navigation failures? Any results on transcripts in other languages/accents?
Failure analysis: Where do models most often err—“borderline” policy questions, sparse evidence, or long‑range coreference? Provide qualitative examples.
Safety/privacy: How are PII and sensitive attributes handled in prompts/outputs? Any privacy filters or redaction steps post‑generation?

Typos and minor comments:
Table/figure captions: unify micro vs macro F1 notation; explicitly state micro in the metric section.
Clarify whether Navigation index refers to speaker‑turn indices after ASR segmentation or post‑processed turns.
Replace “∼0.95” with exact numbers; avoid approximate rounding in main claims.
Provide per‑N JSON error histograms and examples of structural vs semantic format errors.
Consider adding permutation+vote or smaller per‑batch N with multiple passes to probe position effects at constant token budget.

title: How Accurate Are LLMs at Multi-Question Answering on Conversational Transcripts?
review:
This paper investigates the performance of LLMs on multi-question answering tasks using long, real-world conversational transcripts from customer support call centers. This paper explores "batch processing" of the QA tasks, aiming to address the challenge of high cost and latency often accompanied by running QA tasks. They present a method to require the model to generate a structure JSON output for each question, after which the model should output a binary answer, and a "Navigate" pointer to the specific utterance that supports the answer. They demonstrated that while proprietary models like GPT-4o excel in the overall performance, fine-tuned smaller public models like Llama3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B can achieve comparable or even superior answer accuracy when more questions grouped.

Pros:
* The paper tackles a problem of significant practical importance, reducing cost and latency for QA systems in production settings. 
* The experiment set-ups are thorough, with range of models, from zero-shot to fine-tuned. 
* The finding of smaller, fine-tuned public models can outperform proprietary ones are exciting and motivating for the industry practitioners. 

Cons:
* The training data was generated from GPT-4o, albeit with some human feedback. Such use of synthetic data might be challenged in a production setting when it's productionized.
* The QA type is Yes/No which is quite limited. There are other datasets with different question types that are also conversational and multi-party such as Molweni [1] and FriendsQA [2] which should support such batch inference. FriendsQA in particular requires the model to select the span of answer in the utterance which aligns with the "Navigate" prediction. Might be worth discussing in the related work or future work on why or why not these similar datasets are not selected/evaluated.
* The "Navigate" prediction requires only 1 evidence. In real conversations, the evidence for an answer might be discrete, and sometimes entity disambiguation might be required. 

[1]: Jiaqi Li, Ming Liu, Min-Yen Kan, Zihao Zheng, Zekun Wang, Wenqiang Lei, Ting Liu, and Bing Qin. 2020. Molweni: A Challenge Multiparty Dialogues-based Machine Reading Comprehension Dataset with Discourse Structure. In Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics, pages 2642–2652, Barcelona, Spain (Online). International Committee on Computational Linguistics.

[2]: Zhengzhe Yang and Jinho D. Choi. 2019. FriendsQA: Open-Domain Question Answering on TV Show Transcripts. In Proceedings of the 20th Annual SIGdial Meeting on Discourse and Dialogue, pages 188–197, Stockholm, Sweden. Association for Computational Linguistics.

title: How Accurate Are LLMs at Multi-Question Answering on Conversational Transcripts?
review:
# Summary

This paper explores how LLMs can be used to answer "yes"/"no" questions regarding real-world call center conversation transcripts, to automatically asses the quality of customer-agent interactions. The explored method consists in analyzing how LLMs can answer multiple questions while maintaining a low amount of LLM API calls to reduce costs, by using batch prompting. Both proprietary and public models are evaluated on the Q/A task when different amounts of questions are answered per dialogue.

# Strengths

**S1:** Experiments on LLMs are not limited to zero-shot/in-context learning settings but also fine-tuned LLMs are explored for the Q/A task.

**S2:** The proposed approach and analyses are relevant for Q/A tasks in industrial applications.

# Weaknesses

**W1:** My main concern about this paper is the lack of human-annotated gold labels. While human evaluation is performed to asses the quality of GPT-4o annotations, the reported approach for the human evaluation is limited. How many annotators evaluated each conversation? Was an inter-annotator agreement score computed? Moreover, an important disagreement is observed between the human evaluations and GPT-4o annotations on the Navigation. Additional work should be done, not only in reporting how human evaluation is performed, but also to ensure that the gold labels are reliable.

**W2:** The second described contribution (l.100-l.105) is not correct. If I understood well, as explained in Section 4.1 in l.225-l.235, up to 10 questions are processed within a single prompt, and not up to 50 as it is stated on the paper contributions. Thus, actually 5 inferences are needed to process 50 prompts.

**W3:** There is a lack of information about how the sets of 10 questions are formed for the standard reference. Are the groups of 10 questions always the same for all conversations? How are the questions sampled?

**W4:** Similar to W3, there is a lack of information about how the addition of 10 questions (from N=10 to N=50) is performed on the experiments. Are groups of 10,...,50 questions always the same? Both, W3 and W4 are important to enhance reproducibility.

# Additional Comments

**AC1:** Additional information about the implementation details should be reported to improve reproducibility, especially on the models fine-tuning. They could be added maybe in the Appendix.

title: Query-Change-Augmented Intent-Aware Query Rewriting in Web Search
review:
In this paper, the authors propose the Query Change-Augmented Intent-Aware Query Rewriting (QCIR) framework to query rewriting in web search systems using large language models (LLMs). Specifically, the work aims to address the limitations of existing prompting and fine-tuning methods, which are lack of insights about user behavior. The framework includes a Semantic Clustering Unit (SCU) for clustering query changes and a Rewriting Unit (RU) for intent-aware rewriting. Besides, a Dual-Phase Adaptation (QCIR-DPA) fine-tuning method applies knowledge distillation to enable cost-effective deployment.

Strengths:
* Interesting innovation on integrating  user behavior data
* Efficient fine-tuning and distillation for deployment
* Robust A/B test for evaluation and production impact

Weaknesses:
* Only private datasets are in the experiments.
* DBSCAN is a very sensitive clustering algorithm, leading to the unknown stability to other scenarios without further experiments. 
* Lack of studies for the generalization to other languages when most experiments are Chinese-based.

title: Query-Change-Augmented Intent-Aware Query Rewriting in Web Search
review:
In this paper, authors proposed QCIR framework for query rewriting, leveraging two components, semantic clustering and rewriting. QCIR-DPA further employs a knowledge distillation approach. 
Paper can be further improved for clarity. For example, the article itself -- and also the title -- focuses a great deal into "intent" but yet I could not find a clear definition on what "primary intention" is or "secondary intention" is. Certain examples are rather unclear inherently (e.g. how tall was an eight-foot man "in ancient times"). It would be a lot easier for readers if authors can bring up a clear example, that can be used throughout different figures throughout the paper e.g. figure 1, figure 2. On a similar note, it would be great if authors can describe the Baseline/QEP more thoroughly. Performance difference between QEP vs. QEQC/QCIR-Prompting is significant for many models, and what contributes such differences? How competitive is QEP? 
Other questions include: 
For High/Medium/Low PM, what's the proportion? 
Table 2 is a bit confusing -- what is it compared to? Is this relative or absolute changes? What is the baseline

title: Query-Change-Augmented Intent-Aware Query Rewriting in Web Search
review:
This paper presents a query rewriting approach that leverages large language models (LLMs). The method clusters monthly user query change data and then employs an LLM to rewrite queries based on the resulting clusters. To enhance efficiency, this paper introduces model distillations for lightweight deployment.

Weaknesses
- The proposed method only uses the largest cluster for each query from the monthly users’ query change data (``primary'' data), thereby relying solely on the most frequently used query rewriting information.

- The query change data appears to be collected from sequences of query modifications within user sessions. However, the paper does not describe how this data is constructed. A clear and detailed explanation of the data collection process is necessary.

- The distillation process for clustering module is insufficiently explained, making it difficult for readers to understand the underlying mechanism. In Figure 2, the step in which the query change data is processed through Sentence-BERT is not described in main text. Moreover, since the embedding spaces produced by the LLM and by Sentence-BERT differ, the paper lacks a convincing justification for how these two embedding spaces can be effectively integrated.

- The paper does not provide a detailed explanation of how the method operates at inference time when a query is given. 

- The monthly users’ query change data is denoted as $S$, but since it is constructed per query, denoting it as $S_q$.

- A crucial limitation of the proposed approach is that it cannot perform query rewriting for queries that are never used within the month’s data. This point should be addressed through comparison with alternative methods.

- Regarding the ``Proportion of the Main cluster within the entire cluster'' (PM), the paper states that PM is used to adjust search behavior. However, the calculation of PM is not explicitly described. Moreover, since baseline models are unlikely to employ this strategy, this paper should also report the performance of the proposed method without applying PM to clearly demonstrate its effectiveness.

- Finally, the method is described as using zero-shot in-context learning for both clustering and rewriting. However, the provided prompt is merely a task description without any reasoning steps. Despite this, the caption refers to "Chain-of-Thought prompts," which is inconsistent and should be revised.

title: On Generating  Consistent and Attractive Promotional Introduction Text for Narrative Media Arts
review:
This paper deals with generating Promotional Introduction Text (PIT) corresponding to media (TV shows, games, anime). PIT is the little introduction text that a user reads and it meant to engage user and make them more curious about the relevant media. To do so, the authors do the following: 
1. Select a small number of media (<300) based on popularity and other heuristics. 
2. Use GPT-4o to extract their storylines from wikipedia pages corresponding to them. 
3. Anonymize them by removing named entities. 
4. Generate PITs from these strorylines using LLMs.
5. These are then evaluated by human annotator and also LLM as a judge. 

Major weaknesses: 
1. The problem statement is both niche and but at the same time can be thought of as a very basic task like summarization (with a few constraints). 
2. The approach is very basic and absolutely not novel. This seems like just a first version of a very basic application of LLM to a niche writing task. 
3. The paper is not well written, it's filled with typos (e.g Lines 17, 23, 86)
4. The basic paper is more or less just about prompting LLMs. These prompts are only in Appendix and that too in Japanese language without any translations given. Apart from not following standard ACL rules (about always having translations for text not in English), it makes reading the current worthless as one can't even understand the main points. 
5. The human annotations is done by the first author of the paper. While I appreciate that the authors are doing human annotations in addition to using LLMs-as-a-judge, I would suggesting finding a second person (not related to the paper) to do these evaluations so that they could be done without any bias.

title: On Generating  Consistent and Attractive Promotional Introduction Text for Narrative Media Arts
review:
This paper introduces a promotional introduction text task and constructs a small Japanese dataset of 263 anonymized storylines (derived from Wikipedia) to assess the generation from bullet-point summaries. The authors evaluate six open-source Japanese-capable LLMs, using GPT-4 based automatic scoring (across attractiveness, consistency, and quality), and a limited human pairwise attractiveness evaluation. The results highlight a trade-off between surface-level appeal and factual consistency, and show low agreement (~0.405) between GPT-4 scoring and human preferences.

The paper is tackles an interesting real-world problem of generation introductory narratives. The dataset construction pipeline is clearly described at a high level, and the comparative evaluation across multiple models offers useful observations for practitioners. The inclusion of qualitative error analysis and explicit measurement of automatic-human agreement adds value.

However, several limitations reduce the strength of the contribution. First of all, while the paper explores an interesting application of LLMs, the pipeline lack novelty. Furthermore, there are some punctuation errors. The dataset is very small and sourced from “popular” works, which may bias style and limit generality. Parts of the pipeline rely on closed models (GPT-4o), which reduces reproducibility (as they might get deprecated) and may introduce bias. Human evaluation is conducted by a single annotator on a small sample.

title: On Generating  Consistent and Attractive Promotional Introduction Text for Narrative Media Arts
review:
This paper constructs an evaluation dataset for the task of Promotional Introduction Text Generation for Japanase Narrative Media Arts and evaluated the performance of six LLM with manual and automatic evaluations. The major contribution is the construction of the dataset. The major conclusions are (1) there are tradeoffs between attractiveness and consistency (2) there is a gap between automatic eval and human eval.

Strengthes
- Constructed a curated dataset with anonymized entities 
- Conducted both human and automatic evaluations

Weknesses
- Incorrect evaluation metric design: There is conceptual overlap between quality and the other two dimensions. Also, attractiveness is highly subjective, yet the paper provides no clear rubric or multi-annotator calibration to make this metric reliable. Therefore, the reported trade-off between attractiveness and consistency is derived from noisy, unvalidated metrics. The gap between human and automatic scores is in fact strong evidence that the evaluation setup is misaligned with the task goal.

title: I-SEE: An Instruction-tuned, SOP-Enhanced Quality Evaluator for Product Content
review:
This paper presents ISEE, a framework for evaluating e-commerce product content, which shows promising results. The core innovations—customer-aware prioritization, SOP-enhanced instruction-tuning, and zero-shot generalization—are well-defined and address a significant challenge in e-commerce: ensuring high-quality product listings at scale. The use of LoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning is particularly interesting to the community, as it demonstrates how a compact 12B parameter model can be effectively tuned to internalize complex business logic, preserving pre-trained knowledge while adapting to specific SOPs. This approach offers a compelling, cost-effective alternative to relying on larger, more expensive models like Claude-3.7 Sonnet.

However, the paper's experimental setup has limitations that make it difficult to fully assess the pros and cons of the ISEE framework. The primary evaluation relies on a synthetic dataset, which the authors acknowledge may not fully capture the complexity of real-world defects. This makes it challenging to gauge the model's true performance and robustness in a production environment. A better experimental setup would involve a more extensive real-world evaluation dataset and clearer comparisons of how different components of the ISEE framework contribute to the final performance, rather than just comparing the full system against baselines. For example, isolating the impact of the customer-aware prioritization module would provide a more nuanced understanding of its value. Given the reliance on synthetic data and the lack of a more rigorous experimental design to understand the framework's components, a weak reject is recommended.

title: I-SEE: An Instruction-tuned, SOP-Enhanced Quality Evaluator for Product Content
review:
This paper proposes and details an approach to prioritize and better detect issues with ecommerce product metadata and text which is a major issue in ecommerce quality that affects search and recommendations. The proposal has three components: (1) prioritizing which attributes to focus on with automatic identification of attributes that are important for buyers by leveraging user behavioral data and buyer signals, (2) instruction-tuned LLM that is reliable for incorporating operating procedures and outputting well-formed results, (3) way to handle new products and product content.  
The paper includes a large synthetic dataset and comparison of several LLM baselines and the proposed system (ISEE) across all stages and for different types of errors (consistency, correctness, completeness).

Comments in order of the paper:

- Will the dataset be made available? As the authors point out, there is very little data available for researching this area and so making this available would be very helpful.

- sec3.1: How is normalization of the feature names (e.g. brand vs Brand vs brandname vs brand name) done? Minimally, there can be issues between what the NER that extracts from the user query and item title does and what the product field name is (especially if sellers can create new field names).  This is especially an issue when getting into the longer tail of features, which are less likely to be prioritized but (1) may be important for a particular category and (2) will remain long tail if they are not normalized enough to count them.

- l271: Real world catalogs are extremely noisy anywhere that allows 3rd party sellers, which is most large e-commerce sites. These often have large teams working on the catalog: those teams are exactly the people who will benefit greatly from this approach. 

-l285-311: Is there any way (and any advantage to) generating errors that are similar to seller mistakes (typos) vs ones that are of the types where sellers are trying to manipulate search and buyers (the chocolate count example is potentially like that)?

- l313-326: was any manual evaluation/checking done to confirm that majority voting worked well?  If there is room, it would be interesting to see how often 2 vs 3(=unanimous) agreed on the results.

- fig 3: include the dot for ISEE

- table 3: are all of these differences statistically significant?

- sec 6/limitations: The limitations section mentions this was done on English only.  The technique should be applicable more generally regardless of language as long as you have the NLP/LLM components to do the extraction. Chinese could be a good next language to try since there is a lot of e-commerce in Chinese and a lot of NLP/LLM available. I suggest mentioning this in the conclusion.

title: I-SEE: An Instruction-tuned, SOP-Enhanced Quality Evaluator for Product Content
review:
This paper describes a system designed to automatically detect defects in e-commerce product catalogs. The paper provides information about the architecture of the system and the results of an empirical evaluation comparing the proposed 12B-parameter model with a larger proprietary model.

Strengths
* The description of the feature selection methodology was very instructive, especially the rationale for how to select the features that will have the most impact on customer experience. This clearly demonstrates a deep engagement with the data.
* The approach taken for instruction tuning using the SOPs is pragmatic and again demonstrates a good understanding of the types of system design that lead to practical improvements for real-world problems.
* The empirical results clearly show how a lightweight model can incorporate domain-specific SOPs in an efficient way to outperform a larger, generic model that has access to the SOPs via prompting.

Weaknesses
* The use of synthetic defect data for all of the evaluations is a substantial weakness of the paper. I understand that the number of naturally occurring defects may be low, so that large-scale evaluations may require synthetic data. However, the approach should at least be validated on a small dataset of naturally occurring defects.
* Similar to my previous comment, and as I mention below, the authors do not provide any empirical evidence in the paper that the synthetically generated defects in their dataset have characteristics that are comparable to naturally occurring defects.

Here are some additional comments I have about specific passages in the paper:
